narrative_clean: a routine inline inspection on a 30‑inch, x70 grade carbon steel pipeline operating at 825 psi identified a low‑frequency echo at station 14+250. the ultrasonic tool flagged a 0.24‑inch deep, 0.7‑inch long through‑wall anomaly on the outer surface of a longitudinal girth weld. visual verification with a hot‑tap and soapy water test revealed a pinhole leak discharging approximately 0.4 mm³/s of natural gas. subsequent metallurgical examination of the removed pipe section showed an incomplete root pass and a lack of fusion between the filler and base metal, with a hairline crack propagating from the weld toe. the weld geometry was also found to be distorted by an irregular coil edge, resulting in a reduced weld throat area. the affected 15‑ft pipe segment was cut out and replaced with a new 30‑inch, x80 pipe, and a full 360‑degree radiographic and magnetic particle inspection was performed on the upstream and downstream tie‑ins. post‑repair pressure testing confirmed zero leakage at 900 psi, and the line was returned to service after a 48‑hour standby period. the incident was logged, and a corrective action plan was issued to improve coil‑edge alignment procedures during fabrication.

narrative_clean: on 4/22/23 at 09:45 a subcontractor from a local roadway improvement firm was operating a backhoe near milepost 27.6 on the southern segment of the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade b, design pressure 850 psi). the operator unintentionally struck the pipe while excavating a utility trench, creating a 3‑inch gouge at approximately the 3 o’clock position. immediate visual inspection revealed a steady release of natural gas from a ruptured longitudinal seam. the field crew placed a line stop at the nearest isolation valve at 10:12 and notified system control. at 10:28 system control logged the incident (report # 2365891) and initiated an emergency shutdown of the affected loop. a leak detection system recorded a pressure drop from 842 psi to 620 psi before isolation. damage assessment performed by the integrity team on 4/23/23 identified coating breach and metal loss, estimating repair costs at $415,000. the compromised pipe section was cut out and a new 24‑inch x 40‑foot spool piece with a triple‑seal sleeve was installed. hydrostatic testing was completed at 120 % of design pressure, and service was restored at 15:45 on 4/24/23. local fire and police units remained on scene for traffic control and site security throughout the operation.

on 3/14/24 a third‑party excavation crew was performing drainage improvements for a municipal park adjacent to county road 212 in lewis county. the crew used a mid‑size backhoe to remove topsoil when the bucket struck a 6‑inch carbon‑steel transmission pipeline operated by northern gas services. the impact sheared the pipe wall and created a 2‑inch gash near a 90‑degree elbow at 850 psi operating pressure. gas began escaping immediately, forming a vapor cloud that was detected by the crew’s handheld gas monitor at 09:17. the crew halted work, established a 150‑ft safety perimeter and notified northern gas emergency response. northern gas arrived at 09:32, isolated the line by closing upstream and downstream valves, and performed a controlled blow‑down. the leak resulted in a loss of approximately 12 800 therms before flow was stopped. no ignition occurred and there were no injuries; however, nearby residents were evacuated for 45 minutes as a precaution. damage assessment showed the pipe segment required replacement; a new 6‑inch epoxy‑lined steel pipe and a reinforced elbow were installed, and hydrostatic testing confirmed integrity at 1.5 times design pressure. service was restored at 15:20, and the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety board because repair costs exceeded $75 000.

during a routine sub‑soil preparation on a 12‑inch carbon steel transmission line owned by western energy, the crew used a vibratory plow to break up compacted soil. the plow blade struck a buried pipe at an approximate depth of 4 ft. impact caused the pipe’s longitudinal seam to fracture, resulting in an immediate loss of product. scada alarms indicated a pressure drop from 650 psig to 210 psig within seconds. the field operator shut down the affected segment by actuating the nearest isolation valve, reducing flow to zero by 10:07 a.m. emergency response teams were dispatched, and a stop‑ple plug was installed at the rupture site at 10:45 a.m. the leak was contained, and the surrounding area was surveyed for secondary damage. a temporary bypass using a 12‑inch steel sleeve was fabricated on‑site and placed in service at 12:15 p.m., restoring limited gas delivery to downstream customers. a full repair plan was developed, and a new 12‑inch api 5l pipe section was installed on 5/14/2023, with pressure restored to 630 psig after hydrostatic testing. incident was reported to the nrc within the required 24‑hour window, and a corrective action report was filed addressing excavation communication procedures.

on august 14, 2023 at 07:45 the foreman of a local irrigation contractor radioed the utility’s emergency line reporting that his crew’s backhoe had struck a 12‑inch carbon steel natural gas main near milepost 12.3 on state route 27, approximately 0.4 mi east of the county line. the line, owned by western energy, is rated for 600 psi and transports 550 mmcf/d of dry gas. the impact sheared off a 6‑inch section of the pipe, causing a rapid release of gas that ignited after 3 minutes, resulting in a flame of about 8 ft high. emergency services isolated the segment at the nearest shut‑off valve and the fire was extinguished by 08:12. approximately 180 ft of pipe was replaced with new 12‑inch schedule 40 steel, and the system was pressure tested to 1.2 times operating pressure before service restoration at 10:45. investigation revealed the contractor had not placed a one‑call before digging and the pipeline marker placed by the utility was displaced during prior road work. corrective action included revising the one‑call compliance program and adding additional surface markers at the site.

on july 7, 2024 a subcontractor operating a backhoe on a commercial development site in east cambridge inadvertently struck a 24‑inch x80 carbon steel transmission line owned by northwest pipelines. the crew had not received an updated 811 notice because the line had been re‑rated and moved in a recent right‑of‑way adjustment. at 09:15 local time the operator heard a loud pop and observed a plume of natural gas. northwest pipelines' control center received the automatic leak detection alarm at 09:18 and dispatched a field crew and emergency services. the upstream mainline isolation valve (tag 12‑b) was closed at 09:22, followed by the downstream sectional valve (tag 12‑c) at 09:28, isolating a 1.6‑mile segment. initial estimates indicated a release of approximately 2,350 mcf before the line was shut. the area was evacuated and a shelter‑in‑place order covered a half‑square‑mile radius for three hours. the injured backhoe operator was taken to the county hospital, treated for minor burns and released. after the leak was repaired, the pipe was hydrotested to 1.5 times its design pressure of 1,200 psi and returned to service on july 12, 2024.

friday 03/07/2023 at 08:42, system control received a call from the site foreman of hillcrest construction reporting that a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (line tx‑204, rated 125 psi) had been punctured by a mechanical backhoe while digging a utility trench near milepost 112+45. the operator was installing a storm‑drain culvert for a new residential subdivision in lewis county. system control opened one‑call ticket # il98321‑0723 and notified the state pipeline safety office. the leak was located at gps -97.842156, 33.217839, approximately 0.8 mi west of the town limits in section 14 township 3s, range 21w. initial pressure loss was measured at 22 psi and a steady vent of natural gas was observed. an emergency excavation crew arrived at 09:15 and established a 10‑ft safety perimeter. a temporary repair sleeve (type 96, 36‑in. long) was installed at 10:02, reducing the pressure drop to 2 psi. a standby crew from the regional repair hub mobilized at 10:30 with a pre‑fabricated 30‑inch slip‑on coupler and additional pipe sections. permanent repair work began at 12:15, involving removal of the damaged 12‑ft pipe segment, weld‑insertion of a new 30‑inch x 20‑ft pipe section, and hydrostatic testing to 150 % of operating pressure. by 15:40 the line was restored to normal service at 124 psi and system control issued a closure notice to affected customers. the incident report noted that the contractor had failed to request an 811 locate prior to breaking ground.

a call was logged by the local emergency number at 6:12 am reporting a loud bang and a smell of natural gas near the intersection of county road 12 and maple street. the caller, a construction foreman, said a crew was excavating a new storm‑drain trench when the pipe was struck. the operator’s control center received an automated pressure alarm on the 24‑in, 1500‑psi carbon steel main at 6:09 am showing a rapid drop from 1485 psi to 320 psi. dispatch alerted field crews and a mobile emergency response team (mert) was en route. by 6:30 am mert arrived, established a 100‑ft isolation zone, and confirmed a 6‑inch gouge and dented coating on the pipe. the main was isolated at the nearest block valve at 6:42 am and the line was vented to atmosphere. no fire ignition occurred; the gas dissipated quickly. the damaged section was excavated, the gouged pipe segment was cut out, and a new 24‑in, 1500‑psi seamless steel pipe with a three‑coat polyethylene protective coating was installed. repairs were completed at 3:15 pm, service to the downstream distribution grid was restored, and the site was secured. the excavation crew had not placed a one‑call request, and the incident resulted in temporary loss of gas service to approximately 150 residential customers.

the western interstate gas pipeline (operated by mountain ridge transmission), a 24‑inch carbon steel main rated at 650 psi, ruptured near elko, nevada after an excavation crew from a regional road‑building contractor inadvertently struck the line. a track‑hoe was used to remove compacted soil from a planned drainage ditch when the operator encountered a sudden loss of resistance and the blade punctured the pipe at approximately 10.2 ft depth. the breach released an estimated 1.2 mmcf of natural gas before the automatic shut‑in valve activated. the gas ignited when it encountered a nearby diesel generator, producing a brief flame but no fire spread. the incident caused a temporary loss of service to three small communities and required emergency response from the local fire department and the pipeline’s emergency operations center. investigation later revealed that the contractor had received a one‑call locate response indicating the pipeline’s presence, but the crew failed to maintain the required 30‑foot clearance and did not perform potholing before digging. additionally, the contractor’s supervisor did not verify the as‑built drawings that showed the pipe’s exact alignment, contributing to the damage. the incident was reported to the ferc and the pipeline operator filed a corrective action plan.

on 4/12/23 a subcontractor operating a back‑hoe for a road widening project struck a 24" api 5l carbon steel transmission line near the river crossing at milepost 87.5. the impact punctured the pipe wall and created a 3‑in. gash just downstream of a welded tee. immediate shutdown procedures were initiated; the line pressure, normally 720 psi, was reduced to 150 psi within minutes and the segment was isolated using the nearest block valve. emergency response crews from the operating company, the county fire department, and a hazmat team arrived on scene and established a 500‑ft exclusion zone. a small jet of natural gas escaped, igniting briefly before being extinguished by the fire crew. the leak was contained with a temporary clamp and a portable containment bag while a hot‑tap crew prepared a repair. after confirming line integrity, 45 ft of the damaged pipe and the adjoining tee were cut out and replaced with a new 24" seamless pipe and a double‑welded fitting. hydrostatic testing was performed at 800 psi, and the line was returned to service at 5:45 pm. the incident was reported to phmsa and a one‑call notification was filed the following day.

04/22/2023; at approximately 14:15 hours, field crew from a regional utility began excavating a residential driveway using a compact track excavator equipped with a 12‑inch bucket. the operator unintentionally contacted a 12‑inch carbon steel transmission line (line 210‑b) located 1.2 feet below grade, operating at 780 psi and transporting approximately 950 mcf/d of nat‑gas. the impact created a 1‑inch by 1.5‑inch puncture, resulting in an immediate gas release estimated at 4,200 mcf. the crew halted work, evacuated the area, and notified the pipeline control center. control dispatched the gas control center and emergency response team; operators began closing the nearest mainline isolation valve (valve 210‑45) and secondary shut‑off at the downstream regulator. pressure drop was confirmed within five minutes, and the leak was isolated by 14:28 hours. the leak was contained, and no fire ignition occurred. there were no injuries, and no residential evacuations beyond the immediate work zone. investigation later revealed the contractor had not placed a one‑call notification for the excavation. the damaged pipe segment was removed and replaced with a 15‑foot splice; service was restored at 18:10 hours after pressure testing. all regulatory notifications were filed on 04/23/2023.

on july 14, 2023 at approximately 0837 hours a private contractor operating a back‑hoe to widen a gravel driveway near mile point 12.45 on the western segment of the 16‑inch carbon‑steel transmission line (rated 720 psi) struck the pipe, creating a 3‑inch gash. the crew did not place a one‑call request prior to digging, although pipeline markers were present on both sides of the right‑of‑way. the leak was first reported by a nearby resident who smelled gas and called emergency services at 0842 hours. gas control was notified at 0845 and dispatched a field crew who arrived at the upstream isolation valve at 0908 hours, closing it within four minutes. the downstream valve was isolated at 0915 hours, and the line was depressurized by 0940 hours. 27 residential customers lost service; a temporary bypass was installed to restore gas to 14 of them by 1200 hours, with full service restored to all customers at 1630 hours after a 74‑foot replacement segment was welded in place and hydrostatic testing completed. the incident resulted in $78,000 in repair costs and was reported to the state pipeline safety board. the contractor acknowledged failure to follow excavation notification procedures and agreed to remedial training.

on september 3, 2021 at 08:12 am southridge utilities received a call that a 8‑inch carbon steel transmission line, rated 650 psi, had been punctured in a right‑of‑way adjacent to county road 45 west of maple ridge. the damage occurred when a subcontractor operating a backhoe for a storm‑drainage trench inadvertently struck the line while excavating to a depth of 4 ft. the crew had not placed a one‑call request or marked the underground utilities prior to digging. southridge field operations dispatched a gas control technician at 08:18 who arrived on site at 08:24 and confirmed a 3‑inch breach with escaping natural gas. an isolation valve located 0.7 mi downstream was closed and a temporary split‑tee was installed on the north side of the break to halt flow. a maintenance crew arrived at 08:38, removed the damaged segment, and installed a new 8‑inch schedule 40 pipe with reinforced couplings. after hydrostatic testing to 800 psi and confirming zero leak, the line was returned to service at 10:05 am. the contractor was later issued a citation for failing to obtain proper excavation permits and for not contacting the local one‑call center.

on august 14, 2022, a crew from frontier earthworks llc was clearing a pasture near prineville, oregon to install a new irrigation ditch for a cattle operation. the crew was supervised by foreman david "dave" murray and included equipment operator larry harris, who was operating a john deere 750e excavator. the work site was situated on the southeast quarter of section 12, township 25 north, range 13 east, in crook county. at approximately 0730, harris began back‑filling a trench that had been dug earlier in the day. unaware that a 12‑inch, carbon‑steel, high‑pressure natural gas pipeline (line designation: west‑zone iab90234) was buried at a depth of 30 inches and operating at 825 psig, he inadvertently struck the pipe with the excavator bucket. the impact ruptured the pipe, releasing an estimated 5.3 mcf of gas before the automatic shut‑off valve activated. the gas ignited when it encountered a nearby diesel generator, creating a brief fireball that singed nearby vegetation. no injuries were reported, but service to the town of prineville was interrupted for several hours. an investigation later determined that frontier earthworks had failed to submit a one‑call notification to the oregon one‑call center prior to commencing excavation, a requirement that would have prompted line locate marking and could have prevented the strike.

on september 12, 2022 at approximately 0830 hrs, spectra pipelines was alerted to a third‑party dig that had impacted the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (schedule 40, nominal pressure 720 psi) at milepoint 12.47 in the vicinity of oakridge dr and highway 89, sunnyvale county. the contractor, hillcrest earthworks, was operating a back‑hoe to install a storm‑drain culvert and failed to request a one‑call locate. the excavator struck the pipe approximately 18 in. below grade, causing a rapid depressurization and a visible vapor cloud. spectracom's emergency response team arrived on scene at 0845 hrs, isolated the line by closing the upstream and downstream block valves, and erected a containment boom. no injuries were reported and there was no ignition. the damaged section, 24 in. of pipe with a 15‑inch gouge, was cut out and replaced with a new 30‑inch seamless steel segment, re‑tested to 800 psi, and re‑commissioned at 0915 hrs. service to the 2,300 customers fed by the line was restored by 1230 hrs. total property damage was estimated at $68,300, and the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission and the department of transportation.

on 4/12/22 at approximately 9:45 am, a local utility crew was installing a new drainage culvert in the vicinity of milepost 47.3 on county road 112, near the town of lincoln, ne. while operating a hydraulic excavator, the operator unintentionally struck a 24‑inch x‑80 pipeline containing 650 psi of natural gas. the impact caused a 4‑inch puncture, resulting in an immediate gas release. emergency services were notified at 10:02 am and the area was evacuated within ten minutes. the pipeline operator initiated a remote shutdown, isolating the affected segment by closing the nearest upstream and downstream valves. a qualified crew arrived at 10:30 am, vented the line to atmosphere, and installed a temporary 30‑foot steel slip‑on sleeve to stop the leak. after confirming line integrity, a hot‑tap was performed to restore service. the permanent repair was completed on 4/13/22 by replacing a 78‑foot section of x70 steel pipe and pressure testing to 1.2 times the design pressure. the incident report noted the contractor had not obtained a pre‑excavation locate request prior to digging.

on august 3, 2024 at 07:14 mdt a subcontractor from northern build services was excavating a utility trench for a new water main along county road 112, approximately 1.2 miles east of the town of cedar ridge. the crew had placed a one‑call ticket (ticket #20240803‑018) on 07:09 mdt, and the pipeline operator, western gas transmission, responded with a locate request. field personnel from western marked the western gas 24‑inch, api 5l steel pipeline (rated 950 psi, operating at 720 psi) with orange spray paint and placed three yellow pin flags at 50‑ft intervals. despite the markings, the excavator operator proceeded to use a backhoe to widen the trench, claiming the flags were “out of the way.” at 07:22 mdt the backhoe bucket struck the pipe at station 37+450, creating a 3‑inch gouge and immediate gas release. first responders arrived at 07:30 mdt, and western gas control verified a pressure drop to 380 psi. the segment was isolated by closing the upstream mainline valve at valve station 37+300 and the downstream valve at 37+600. emergency shut‑down was initiated, and a temporary cap was installed on the damaged section. no injuries were reported, the gas did not ignite, and service was restored at 16:05 mdt after a 9‑hour repair involving replacement of a 45‑foot pipe segment and pressure testing to 1050 psi. the incident is under investigation for non‑compliance with excavation safety protocols.

on june 14, 2025 at 08:17 a.m. the western gas transmission co. 24‑inch schedule 80 carbon steel transmission line (design pressure 960 psig, operating pressure 720 psig) experienced a rapid pressure drop following an excavation incident near milepost 112.3 on the oak ridge‑hickory corridor, davis county. the excavation crew, contracted by a third‑party utility, was performing a storm‑drain upgrade and had not obtained a one‑call verification prior to breaking ground. a surface marker placed by the operator was displaced during a preceding road resurfacing project, resulting in the crew locating the pipe 4.5 ft east of its actual alignment. when the backhoe operator removed soil, a 3‑inch gouge was cut into the pipe wall, exposing the internal coating. gas control detected a pressure loss of 210 psig within minutes and initiated an automatic shutdown. 15 residential customers within a half‑mile radius were isolated. the line was isolated at 08:35, excavated and removed at 09:20, and a 12‑foot replacement section was installed by 17:00. the incident was reported to the phmsa (nrc 2025‑017) and the state oil and gas commission. corrective actions included revising marker verification procedures and mandatory one‑call compliance for all future excavations.

at 08:30 a.m. on september 12, 2022, a regional construction crew from southern earthworks was excavating a right‑of‑way along county road 47 near mile marker 23.5 to install a new drainage culvert. the crew had identified the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (class 150, operating at 550 psig) using surface markings and a handheld locate device. however, a 4‑inch abandoned service pipe, not shown on the as‑built drawings, lay parallel to the main at a depth of 2.5 feet. when the excavator's bucket struck the abandoned pipe, the impact caused the bucket to slip sideways, puncturing the active transmission line about 18 inches below ground. a high‑velocity release of natural gas was observed, and the nearby gas odor alarm activated. the operator immediately stopped work and evacuated the area. emergency response coordinated with the pipeline operator, who initiated a remote shutdown from the control center, isolated the affected segment using the upstream mainline valve and a downstream sectionalizer, and vented the released gas. repair crews arrived by 09:45 a.m., removed the damaged pipe section, installed a new splice, and performed hydrostatic testing before returning the line to service at 02:10 p.m. the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety board and a root‑cause investigation was launched.

on 6/12/2023 at approximately 0830 hours a subcontractor crew for a municipal storm‑drain project began trenching near milepost 27.4 on the northern leg of the midwest interstate gas transmission system. the operator had received a one‑call notification (ticket #2023061207) and had placed orange flags and a 2‑in. steel “do not dig” tape on the surface. however, the crew failed to pause when the flags were observed and continued to excavate with a vibratory plow. at 0915 hours the plow struck a 20‑in. x 0.5‑in. x70‑lb. x70‑psi carbon‑steel pipeline that had been installed in 1998 and was operating at 750 psi. a 6‑ft. section of the pipe was displaced, causing a rapid release of gas that ignited from a nearby diesel engine, producing a brief flame jet that was extinguished by the crew’s fire‑suppression blanket. there were no injuries and the incident was contained within the work zone. the pipeline was isolated at 0940 hours and a repair crew arrived at 1015 hours to replace the damaged segment. a report was filed with the phmsa (incident #23‑06312‑01) and a duplicate state regulator notice (dr 2023‑0456) was submitted at 1130 hours. the operator later issued a corrective action plan requiring additional training for contractors on one‑call procedures and on‑site supervision.

revised 3-22-2024 by western pipelines, inc. a crew from oak ridge excavation, llc was performing trenching for a new storm‑drain system along county road 12 near milepost 45. the crew began work at 0730 without submitting an 811 one‑call notice after their initial permit expired on 3‑15‑2024. at approximately 0945 the operator of the west‑zone control center observed a sudden pressure loss on the 12‑inch api 5l carbon steel main carrying dry natural gas at 950 psi (operating pressure 970 psi). the pressure drop was confirmed at 0952 and the incident was classified as reportable at 1005. the crew reported the strike to the site supervisor at 1010; the supervisor called 811 at 1015 and the western pipelines emergency response team was dispatched at 1030. first responders arrived on scene at 1045, isolated the downstream block valve, and initiated a controlled shut‑in. the damaged section exhibited a 3‑inch gouge and a 1.5‑inch puncture, resulting in an estimated release of 12,000 scf of gas before isolation. the incident was investigated, and oak ridge excavation, llc was cited for failure to submit a one‑call notice and for improper locate verification. the line was repaired and returned to service at 1730 on the same day.

on april 14, 2023 at approximately 9:45 a.m., a subcontractor from midwest utility services was operating a 12‑ft hydraulic backhoe to install a storm‑drain culvert on county road 23, township 5 north, range 12 west, davis county, illinois. the crew had not placed a one‑call request before beginning excavation. while digging a trench 2.5 ft deep, the backhoe bucket struck a 12‑inch × 0.250‑in. wall x‑65 grade natural gas transmission pipe owned by northern pipelines, located at milepost 12.78. the pipe, installed in 1995, has a maximum allowable operating pressure of 1500 psig and was pressurized to 920 psig at the time of the incident. the impact created a 3‑inch gash in the pipe, releasing natural gas at an estimated rate of 180 scfh. gas was odorized and detected by a nearby resident, who called 911. emergency response arrived within seven minutes, isolated the affected segment, and evacuated the immediate area. no fire, injury, or ignition occurred. northern pipelines mobilized a repair crew that excavated the damage, removed a 15‑ft section of the compromised pipe, and installed a new 12‑inch × 0.280‑in. x‑65 line with double‑welded fittings. after pressure testing, the line was restored to service at 9:30 p.m. the incident resulted in approximately 2 mmcf of gas loss and repair costs exceeding $68,000, prompting a formal incident report to the department of transportation.

on september 14, 2025 at 08:17 central daylight time the city of oakridge public works reported a line strike to the regional gas control center. a crew from oakridge utilities was installing a new storm‑water culvert along county road 112 when their back‑hoe punctured a 12‑inch, 85‑psig carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) owned by western energy at milepost 7.34. the impact caused a high‑velocity release of natural gas that ignited a small jet flame, prompting immediate evacuation of the surrounding area. western energy dispatched an emergency response team at 08:24 and a rapid response crew arrived on scene at 08:39. the line segment was isolated by closing block valve be12 at 08:45, and a controlled blowdown of the affected section began at 08:52. a 15‑foot section of pipe was removed and the surrounding gouge was excavated between 09:15 and 10:05. replacement of the damaged pipe with a new 12‑inch x80‑psig x70 steel pipe, including new girth welds and a pressure test, was completed by 15:30. service to the downstream customers was restored at 16:12 after final integrity verification. the contractor was cited for failing to obtain a one‑call excavation permit prior to digging.

on september 4, 2024, at approximately 07:42 local time, a backhoe operating on a residential subdivision in el paso county, texas struck a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission pipeline owned by norteam pipeline, llc. the pipeline, which transports natural gas at 820 psig, was located at a depth of 2.5 ft. the excavator's bucket punctured the pipe, causing an immediate release of gas that ignited when it contacted a nearby power line. emergency services were notified at 07:55 and arrived on scene within ten minutes. fire crews extinguished the flame by 08:23, while norteam personnel isolated the affected segment at 08:05 and began depressurization. the incident resulted in the temporary loss of service to roughly 1,850 residential customers, who were supplied with backup gas from a neighboring line. no injuries were reported, and there were no fatalities. the damaged pipe was removed and a pre‑tested 30‑inch replacement segment was installed; service was fully restored at 14:10 the same day. the event was reported to the national response center (nrc report no. 2478139) and the texas commission on environmental quality within the required 24‑hour window. the investigation later determined that the contractor failed to verify the pipeline’s location despite the presence of clear surface markers and a recent one‑call ticket.

on march 3, 2025 at 0830 the crew from southern midwest construction called the state one‑call center to log a planned dig for a new storm‑drain near milepost 42.5 of the westfield 12‑inch carbon steel transmission line owned by northern energy. the one‑call ticket #wi210304‑1125 was issued at 0902 and assigned to utility locate services (uls) with a required locate completion by 1130. uls technician randy cohen arrived at the site at 1115 and placed paint marks on the right‑of‑way, but due to a scheduling error the electronic locate was not performed. at 1127 the foreman, jim henderson, received a text from the project manager telling him to begin trenching immediately to meet a contractor deadline. jim ordered the back‑hoe operator, derek williams, to start digging at 1130 despite the pending locate. at 1134 derek’s back‑hoe blade struck the western side of the carbon steel pipe, which was operating at 750 psi with a 1200‑psi design limit. a loud “whoosh” was heard and the line released a 6‑inch burst of natural gas, igniting a small flame that was quickly extinguished by the crew’s fire‑suppression blanket. emergency services were notified at 1136, the line was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream valves at 1139, and the damaged 12‑inch section was later removed and replaced with a new 12‑inch x‑65 grade pipe.

construction crew using a hydraulic excavator to install a drainage culvert unintentionally contacted a 24‑inch api 5l x65 steel transmission pipeline at milepost 12.7. the excavator bucket struck the pipe while digging 3 ft deep, creating a 4‑inch gash on the lower 12 o'clock position. immediate pressure drop from 720 psi to 350 psi was observed, and approximately 1,200 bbl of crude oil began to leak, forming a thin sheen on the adjacent grass field. the crew halted work and called the operator control center at 08:42. emergency shut‑in was performed by the district control room at 08:49, isolating the segment with a remote valve. cleanup crews arrived at 09:15 and contained the spill with absorbent booms. preliminary damage estimate exceeds $85,000, including pipe repair, lost product, and environmental remediation. the contractor failed to request a locate from the state one‑call service prior to excavation.

on april 14, 2023 at 0732 hrs the pipeline operations center received a call from a contractor site supervisor reporting a possible breach in the 12‑inch carbon steel transmission line (rated 720 psig) located near milepost 27.4 on the north side of county road 212, franklin county, ky. the contractor was operating a mini‑excavator for a utility trench when the machine struck the pipe, creating a 3‑inch gouge and exposing the wall to soil. field crews arrived at 0805 hrs, isolated the affected segment, and confirmed a release of approximately 350 mcf of dry natural gas. a one‑call notification had not been placed for this location, and the pipeline marker placed 80 ft from the site was partially obscured by vegetation. the excavator operator was wearing safety glasses and a hard hat; he sustained a minor laceration to his forearm while attempting to stop the machine. the gas was vented and the line was depressurized by 0830 hrs, after which a temporary sleeve was installed and the pipe was pressure tested to 800 psig. permanent repairs and reinstatement were completed at 1630 hrs, and service to the 412 affected customers was restored by 1705 hrs. the incident was reported to the national response center (nrc # 9876543) and phmsa aid at 0900 hrs.

on october 3, 2024 at approximately 6:15 am a subcontractor operating a back‑hoe for a road widening project struck a 24‑inch carbon‑steel transmission line rated 850 psi on the south side of highway 57. the crew had not placed a one‑call request prior to digging and were unaware that the line was marked as a “high‑risk” segment in the state locates database. the impact created a 2‑foot gash in the pipe, causing a rapid release of natural gas that ignited when a nearby diesel generator was started, producing a brief flame front that was extinguished by the automatic shut‑down system. emergency services were notified at 6:22 am and the pipeline control center initiated an immediate shut‑in at 6:25 am. response crews arrived on scene at 6:38 am, installed a temporary clamp, and later installed a bypass skidded section while the damaged pipe segment was cut out. the line was pressure‑tested at 800 psi and returned to service at 4:12 pm. the investigation concluded that failure to request a locate and to verify existing utility maps were the primary causes of the incident.

on july 14, 2023 at approximately 07:45 a.m., a subcontractor operating a back‑hoe for a county road widening project struck a 24‑inch x 0.75‑inches schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line owned by western pipelines, inc. the impact occurred 0.6 miles southwest of the town of riverside, clark county, arizona, near milepost 212.5. the pipe, rated for a maximum operating pressure of 850 psig and transporting 720‑mmcf/d of dry natural gas, showed a 6‑inch longitudinal gouge with exposed threads. immediate isolation was initiated by the control center at 08:10 a.m., reducing the line pressure to 120 psig. the incident was reported to the oklahoma corporation commission at 08:30 a.m. and to phmsa via the national response center at 09:00 a.m. (nrc number 1023456). emergency crews established a safe zone, and the gas was diverted through a bypass loop installed at the nearest valve station. the damaged segment was removed and a new 24‑inch x 0.75‑inches api 5l pipe was spliced in using a field‑welded sleeve. pressure testing was completed at 03:15 p.m., confirming leak‑free operation, and service was restored to customers at 04:00 p.m. a post‑incident investigation attributed the gouge to failure to locate the pipeline with an underground utility detector prior to excavation.

on may 3, 2024 a regional natural gas transmission operator discovered a release from a 24‑inch, 600‑psi high‑density polyethylene (hdpe) main after a subcontractor’s backhoe struck the line while installing a storm‑drain culvert. the pipeline, originally installed with a 30‑inch cover, had experienced soil erosion over several years, leaving only about 9 inches of earth above the pipe at the impact site. the crew had not requested a one‑call locate (811) prior to excavation. when the backhoe bucket contacted the pipe, a 4‑inch gouge was created, causing a steady vent of gas that was detected by the operator’s gas‑monitoring system. emergency shut‑off valves at the nearest regulator station were closed within minutes, isolating the affected segment. the area was evacuated, and a qualified response team arrived to install a temporary clamp and vent the line safely. the damaged section was excavated, removed, and replaced with a new 24‑inch steel pipe, re‑coated, and re‑buried to a restored 30‑inch cover depth. service was restored to customers after 7 hours of outage. a post‑incident review led to an internal safety bulletin reminding field crews to verify locate requests and to assess potential cover loss due to erosion before digging.

on april 14, 2024 at approximately 10:45 a.m., a backhoe operated by a subcontractor for a local utility expansion project struck a buried 10‑inch schedule 40 carbon steel natural gas pipeline (api 5l, .375 in. wall thickness) owned by midwest gas transmission. the pipe, located at the 23.6 mile marker of the eastward main (tag wgn‑1023), was buried 3 ft deep in a sandy loam under a residential driveway in clark county, indiana. the line was under normal operating pressure of 820 psig and transporting 750 mmscfd of dry gas. the impact created a 3‑inch gouge and a small venting hole, resulting in a gas release of approximately 45,000 cf into the atmosphere. there were no ignition sources, and the leak was contained by an automatic shut‑down valve that activated within 30 seconds of pressure loss. emergency responders evacuated two adjacent houses and closed the nearby county road for 2.5 hours. repair crews excavated the site, removed the damaged pipe segment, and installed a 12‑inch repair sleeve with a full‑thickness splice. the repaired section was hydro‑tested to 1,200 psig for 8 hours and returned to service at 4:10 p.m. the incident was reported to the state one‑call center after the fact; no prior locate request had been filed. the total repair cost was estimated at $284,750, including labor, materials, and emergency response expenses.

a crew from southland utilities was performing driveway grading at the intersection of county road 57 and maple street in elk ridge, ga. the crew deployed a john deere 750k backhoe to remove excess soil and expose a buried 12‑inch x80‑psi carbon steel transmission line for a planned valve installation. after several passes with the bucket, the operator heard a sharp metallic snap and the backhoe bucket struck the pipe, creating a 4″×2″ gash. natural gas began venting immediately, forming a white plume that drifted toward a nearby residential subdivision. at 08:42 am cst the site foreman called 911 and the incident was reported to the gas control center. utilities operations isolated the line by closing the upstream 24‑inch mainline block valve and a downstream 12‑inch sectional valve, shutting off flow to roughly 2.3 mi of service. the evacuation order covered 28 homes, temporarily displacing about 85 residents. carbondale fire department, county sheriff’s office, and the state hazmat team responded; fire crews used water spray to suppress the gas jet while the leak was capped with a split‑clamp repair kit. the pipeline was depressurized, the damaged section was cut out, and a new 12‑inch pipe segment was welded in place. service was restored at 06:15 pm cst, with no injuries or fire damage reported.

on august 14, 2025 at 09:45 a.m. central daylight time a subcontractor for midwest earthworks was excavating a drainage ditch along county road 12s near latitude 41.342187 longitude -90.587423. the crew was using a mid‑size excavator with a hydraulic thumb when the operator felt a sudden resistance followed by a sharp “pop” sound. a 12‑inch carbon steel natural gas transmission pipe owned by central pipelines, operating at approximately 1,050 psig, had been struck and the outer coating was gouged, exposing the pipe wall. gas escaped through a 1½‑inch rupture and formed a visible plume that drifted toward nearby fields. the crew immediately halted work, contacted central pipelines dispatch, and called 911. central pipelines responded with an emergency repair crew who isolated the line by closing upstream and downstream valve stations at 10:02 a.m. the pipe was depressurized to atmospheric pressure by 10:20 a.m., and the leak was capped by 11:15 a.m. the incident resulted in a temporary loss of service to 94 residential customers, which was restored after a 15‑foot replacement section was installed. the release was estimated at 2,400,000 scf. central pipelines notified the state pipeline safety commission at 11:30 a.m. and filed an incident report with the national response center. investigation revealed that the contractor had not requested a locate through the 811 system and that as‑built drawings for a recent valve installation near the site had not been updated, leading to an inaccurate depth assessment. corrective actions included mandatory 811 calls for all future excavations, updated as‑built documentation for the valve, and a revised excavation tolerance zone of 24 inches for pipelines in the area.

on july 9, 2022 at 0834 hours, united pipeline services received an emergency call reporting a gas leak on a 12‑inch, 30‑gn steel transmission line at milepoint 14.6 near county road 112, west of roswell, nm. the line, rated to 850 psi, had been marked with orange paint and yellow flags earlier that morning. at 0847 hours a third‑party excavator crew from a local utility contractor arrived on site performing a storm‑drain installation. the crew held an active locate ticket #762310 but failed to verify the exact depth of the pipe before engaging a mechanical back‑hoe. the back‑hoe’s bucket struck the pipe at an approximate depth of 42 inches, creating a 6‑inch puncture. gas was observed venting at the surface, and a low‑odor alarm activated. united pipeline dispatch sent a field crew at 0855 hours; the mainline isolation valves v‑12.3 and v‑12.7 were manually closed by 0912 hours, reducing line pressure to 15 psi. emergency services secured the area, evacuating nearby residences. the damaged section was cut out and replaced with a pre‑tested 12‑inch segment; welding was completed by 1630 hours and pressure testing confirmed integrity. service was restored to customers at 1845 hours. total repair cost was estimated at $420,000. no injuries or ignition occurred.

on 3/14/2024 a western utilities crew was performing utility locating and excavation work on a commercial site adjacent to highway 101 near the river bend in oakland county. the crew used a backhoe to remove fill material when the bucket struck a buried 24‑inch x70‑grade api 5l steel transmission pipeline operating at 720 psi (gross). the impact created a 3‑inch by 5‑inch gouge in the pipe wall, resulting in immediate gas release. the operator stopped work, called 811 at 09:42 and reported a hit to a natural gas pipeline. western utilities incident command was notified at 09:50, and the uscgs sector command responded within fifteen minutes, assuming incident command. atmospheric monitoring detected methane concentrations of 15 % in the surrounding area, prompting evacuation of the nearby construction crew and temporary shelter for nearby residents. valves upstream and downstream were closed by the control center at 09:58, and a controlled blow‑down reduced line pressure to 120 psi by 10:15. emergency response contractors deployed a foam blanket and a temporary steel clamp to stabilize the damaged section. the pipe was excavated, the gouge was removed, and a replacement 24‑inch pipe segment was installed. pressure testing to 1000 psi for eight hours was completed by 12:30, and the line was returned to service at 13:15. no injuries were reported.

on monday, august 14, 2023 at 6:12 p.m. a local subcontractor operating a mini‑excavator on a residential redevelopment site in clark county, nebraska struck a 24‑inch, 0.5‑in. wall thickness, x70 carbon steel transmission line owned by midwest pipelines. the pipe was buried 28 in. below grade and was operating at a design pressure of 825 psi with a nominal operating pressure of 720 psi. the excavator bucket nicked the pipe, creating a 2‑inch breach that immediately resulted in a pressure drop from 720 psi to 150 psi. gas control observed the loss of pressure on the supervisory control and data acquisition system at 6:14 p.m. and automatically initiated an emergency shut‑down sequence. the line was isolated by closing valve b‑12 and valve c‑5 at 6:17 p.m., and a secondary isolation valve downstream was closed at 6:20 p.m. emergency response crews arrived on scene at 6:35 p.m., establishing a 150‑ft safety perimeter. the affected service area served approximately 420 residential customers, with 18 customers experiencing temporary loss of service. a 24‑ft section of the damaged pipe was removed and replaced with a new pre‑tested 24‑inch x70 pipe. the line was re‑pressurized and restored to normal operating pressure at 9:45 a.m. the incident was reported to the nebraska department of environmental quality at 7:05 p.m. and to phmsa at 8:10 p.m. the contractor’s one‑call notice had been filed two days prior, but the pipeline markers were placed on the adjacent county road rather than directly above the excavation trench.

on september 12, 2023 at 08:14 cd t, western pipeline operations received a 911 call reporting a strong odor of natural gas near milepost 212.4 on the 24‑inch, 800‑psi x‑70 grade steel main that serves the north ridge subdivision. the call center dispatched a field crew and notified the local fire department. at 08:37 the incident commander arrived on scene and observed an open trench where a subcontractor’s back‑hoe had been excavating a new storm‑drain line. the back‑hoe’s bucket had punctured the pipeline, creating a 3‑inch gash in the seam. the contractor did not have a valid one‑call excavation notice or a state excavation ticket. western’s emergency operations center ordered an immediate line stop; the mainline isolation valve at milepost 210.9 was closed at 08:44, and a downstream shut‑in at milepost 215.0 was completed by 09:02. a controlled blow‑down reduced line pressure to 0 psi before a repair crew installed a 24‑inch sleeve and pressure‑tested the section to 900 psi. the incident resulted in the temporary loss of service to 78 residential customers; temporary propane tanks were provided until service restoration at 14:30. no injuries or fire occurred, and the incident was reported to the nrc and state utilities commission.

on september 21, 2025 at 0830 hrs, a regional utility contractor was digging a drainage trench with a mini‑excavator along county road 542 near the intersection with state route 14, roan county, tx. the operator inadvertently struck a 24‑inch, 30‑year‑old carbon steel natural gas transmission line owned by western pipelines, operating at 825 psi and transporting 850 mmcf/d of dry gas. the impact punctured the pipe wall, resulting in an immediate release of gas that ignited briefly before being extinguished by the automatic shut‑off valve. the excavator operator sustained a laceration to the forearm and was treated on‑site; no other personnel were injured. western pipelines received the emergency call at 0837 hrs; a pipeline technician arrived at 0845 hrs and confirmed the rupture. the line was isolated, purged, and the damaged section was removed and replaced with a new 24‑inch seamless pipe. all valves were reseated and pressure testing was completed by 1730 hrs. the incident was reported to the state one‑call center, and the contractor was cited for failure to obtain a valid excavation permit and for not adhering to the posted pipeline markers. there were no fire‑related damages and service was fully restored by the following day.

on 3/5/24, at approximately 08:30 am, a subcontractor from a regional utility was excavating a new access road near milepost 27.4 on the transmountain 24‑inch carbon‑steel transmission line (rated 720 psi, api 5l). the crew was using a back‑hoe to remove topsoil when the bucket struck the pipeline at a depth of 3 ft, creating a 2‑inch gouge on the 2‑o’clock position of the pipe wall. the impact immediately caused a 0.9‑inch crack in the pipe, resulting in a low‑volume gas leak that was detected by the line’s acoustic emission monitor. the crew halted work, notified the site supervisor, and called the emergency response number posted on the pipeline marker. at 08:45 am the pipeline operator’s incident command was activated; the nearest block valve at the northside regulator station and the downstream mainline valve were closed by 09:10 am, isolating the affected segment. a hazmat team arrived at 09:20 am, established a 150‑ft safety perimeter, and evacuated two nearby residences as a precaution. the damaged pipe section was excavated, removed, and a 24‑inch slip‑on sleeve was installed. after hydrostatic testing to 900 psi, the line was returned to service at 13:45 pm. an investigation later determined that the pipeline had not been correctly located and marked, and the contractor’s excavation plan was revised accordingly.

on july 14, 2025 at 07:45 a cng operator received a call from a construction supervisor reporting a sudden loss of pressure on the 24‑inch, 720‑psi carbon steel main (segment p‑352) near milepost 12.3 in the oak ridge subdivision. the supervisor, from hillcrest contractors, indicated that a backhoe had been digging a new storm‑drain trench approximately 30 ft east of the marked right‑of‑way. the one‑call system had not been notified for this excavation and the pipeline marker, a red and white 18‑inch stake, was positioned 45 ft from the work zone. upon arrival, field crews observed a 4‑inch gouge in the pipe wall and a small gas leak venting at low pressure. the line was isolated at 08:12 and a controlled vent was conducted until pressure dropped to zero. emergency services established a 50‑ft exclusion zone while a vacuum truck removed the released gas. the damaged pipe segment was cut out and a new 24‑inch spool with a double‑welded joint was installed; hydrostatic testing confirmed integrity at 800 psi. service to the 312 residential customers was restored at 15:30. investigation later determined the contractor failed to request an excavation permit and did not adhere to the required 30‑ft clearance from the pipeline marker.

on june 3, 2022 at approximately 08:45 a.m. the county road crew began excavating a new storm‑drain culvert adjacent to the eastbound lane of state highway 12. the crew’s excavator struck a 24‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas transmission line owned by western pipelines, which was operating at 900 psi and transporting dry natural gas at a flow rate of 2.5 mmcf/d. the impact created a 3‑inch gash in the pipe, resulting in an immediate vent of gas that ignited briefly when a nearby diesel generator back‑fed a spark; the flame was extinguished by the on‑site fire‑department crew within seconds. there were no injuries or fatalities. western pipelines personnel arrived on scene at 09:20, isolated the downstream valve, and depressurized the segment by 09:55. one residential customer lost service for approximately two hours while temporary gas service was supplied. damage estimates were later calculated at $215,000 for pipe replacement, excavation restoration, and environmental cleanup. the incident was reported to the national response center at 10:30 and entered as a reportable event under 49 cfr 190.3. the investigation determined that the contractor had not obtained a one‑call notification prior to digging.

on july 14, 2023, a subcontractor crew from xyz construction was installing a new stormwater culvert along county road 12 near the town of springfield, al. the crew used a small excavator to remove soil from the right side of the road. the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line, owned by midwest pipelines, was buried 3 ft deep and marked with orange 49 cfr 192 signs on both sides of the right‑of‑way. the contractor failed to request an excavation permit from the state one‑call center and did not verify the exact location of the pipe. while the excavator bucket engaged the soil, the bucket struck the pipe at approximately 850 psig, creating a 6‑inch gash through the wall. gas escaped as a high‑velocity jet, igniting when it contacted a nearby power line, resulting in a small flame that was quickly extinguished by the responding fire department. the crew halted work, the line was isolated, and 0.7 miles of product was depressurized. a 4‑foot section of pipe was cut out and a new spool piece was welded in place. service was restored at 10:45 p.m. after pressure testing. investigation revealed the lack of one‑call notification and failure to observe the pipeline markers as primary causes.

on wednesday march 14th at approximately 9:42 am central time, the westfield pipeline operations center received an emergency call from a local utility crew reporting a sudden loss of pressure on line wk‑57. the crew was operating an excavator near milepost 112.3 on the i‑90 right‑of‑way when the bucket struck a 24‑inch x 0.375‑inch api 5l x70 steel pipe that was transporting 800 psi of crude oil. the impact created a 10‑inch gouge, rupturing the pipe and releasing an estimated 3,200 barrels of light crude into the surrounding ditch. immediate shutdown was initiated; the upstream block valve at station 57‑b closed at 9:45 am, reducing line pressure to 150 psi within minutes. emergency response teams, including hazmat and spill containment units, arrived on scene by 10:10 am and deployed booms and absorbent pads. the leak was fully contained by 2:30 pm, and a temporary bypass using a 30‑inch type‑b sleeve was installed later that evening. a post‑incident investigation revealed the contractor had not obtained a one‑call notification and the excavation plan was not reviewed by pipeline personnel. corrective actions include a revised excavation awareness program and additional surface marking at high‑risk segments.

on 5/22/2026 at approximately 07:15 a crew from a regional fiber‑optic installer began trenching along county road 112 near the intersection with state highway 45 in eastland county, illinois. the crew had a one‑call locate ticket and the 24‑inch dcp midstream carbon steel transmission main, rated 800 psi and operating at 630 psi, was marked with orange flags. despite the markings, the excavator operator advanced the backhoe blade 2 feet beyond the flagged boundary and struck the pipe at a depth of 4 ft. an immediate pressure drop was recorded by the supervisory control and data acquisition system, triggering a low‑pressure alarm at 07:18. the fiber crew called dcp emergency at 07:20; a dcp response unit and a local fire department unit arrived on scene at 07:42. the main was shut in using the nearest mainline gate valve at 07:55, and the damaged section was isolated. a hot‑tapping crew arrived at 09:30, removed the compromised 1.2‑ft segment and installed a 2‑ft replacement spool. the line was flushed, pressure restored to 620 psi, and service resumed at 15:20. incident was logged with the nrc, and a corrective action report cited failure to maintain the required clearance from marked utilities.

on september 3, 2024 at 08:14 cdt a crew from a local utility contractor was installing a new water main along county road 12 near the town of miller. the crew had not placed a 811 request prior to digging and used a back‑hoe to expose the soil. at approximately 08:45 cdt the excavator struck a 24‑in carbon steel transmission pipe operated by western pipeline services, llc. the pipe, which transports natural gas at a design pressure of 850 psig, was punctured near a 30‑ft girth weld, causing an immediate release of gas. the on‑site foreman called 911 at 08:47 cdt and notified western pipeline at 08:50 cdt. first‑responder hazmat units arrived within ten minutes, establishing a 600‑ft evacuation radius around the leak. the gas plume was detected at 09:03 cdt and a temporary shut‑in valve was activated at 09:15 cdt, stopping the flow. western pipeline deployed a repair crew that installed a pre‑tested 24‑in slip‑on sleeve and re‑pressurized the line at 14:20 cdt. the incident resulted in a material loss of approximately 1,200 mcf and minor property damage to the contractor’s equipment. a follow‑up investigation determined the excavator failed to maintain the required 30‑inch clearance from the pipeline right‑of‑way, directly causing the rupture.

on august 14, 2022, at approximately 09:20 a.m., a residential contractor operating a mini‑excavator on a property near milepost 12.47 of the oak ridge transmission line in lanark county, illinois, struck a 12‑inch x 0.250‑in‑wall x‑70 steel pipeline owned by mid‑state gas. the contractor was installing a new septic system and had not placed a one‑call request or obtained a locate. the excavator’s bucket engaged the pipe at a depth of about 2.8 ft, creating a 6‑inch longitudinal gouge that breached the coating and ruptured the pipe. the line, installed in 1998, was operating at a pressure of 820 psig carrying natural gas. gas escaped for roughly three minutes before the automatic shut‑down valve activated; no ignition occurred and there were no injuries. the operator evacuated the area and notified the company’s emergency response center at 09:23 a.m. service to the downstream towns of springfield and clinton was interrupted for 18 hours while the damaged section was cut out and a 14‑foot replacement spool of coated x‑70 pipe was installed and hydro‑tested. the incident was reported to phmsa, and the contractor was cited for failing to request a utility locate prior to excavation.

on june 5, 2024 a subcontractor from smith & sons excavation crew was clearing vegetation along county road 112 near the town of springfield, wy. the crew used a backhoe to remove a small berm when the bucket struck a 12‑inch x70‑lb carbon steel transmission line owned by western energy services. the pipe, operating at 850 psi transporting natgas, was marked with orange flags and a 30‑foot clearance zone as indicated on the 1:24,000 map provided to the contractor. however, the crew had not placed the required 24‑inch protective standoff and began digging outside the marked area. the impact caused a 6‑inch gash in the pipe wall, resulting in an immediate release of gas at an estimated flow rate of 120 mmscfd. downstream pressure dropped to 500 psi within minutes, triggering an automatic shut‑in. western energy services was notified at 09:13 and emergency services arrived at 09:26. the leak was isolated and the damaged section was removed and replaced with a new 12‑inch x 80‑lb seamless pipe. the incident was reported to the nrc under incident # 2024‑0678 and a follow‑up inspection was completed on june 8.

on june 5, 2026 a subcontractor from a local utility was excavating a trench for a new water main near the 24‑inch, 1,200‑psi steel transmission line in the oak ridge area of monroe county, wisconsin. the crew failed to locate the pipeline despite a one‑call notification filed on may 28 (ticket #20260015432) and the marked stakeouts placed by the operator. while digging approximately 2 ft deep, the excavator’s bucket struck the pipe at station 12+450, creating a 3‑inch gouge that breached the coating and punctured the wall. immediate shutdown procedures were initiated; the line was isolated at the nearest block valves and depressurized to 50 psi. emergency response teams arrived within 30 minutes, installed a temporary bypass clamp, and pumped out the leaked crude (approx. 12 bbl). after confirming the pipe was stable, a hot‑tap repair was performed using a 24‑inch carbon steel sleeve rated for 1,400 psi. the repaired section was pressure‑tested to 1,300 psi and returned to service by 1900 hrs the same day. no injuries were reported. the operator filed an incident report with phmsa and updated the excavation records per regulatory guidance.

on 2/7/2024 at approximately 06:18 a.m. the southern pipeline operations center received an automated alarm indicating a sudden pressure drop on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (sp‑12345) near the red river crossing, north of cedar hill, wyoming. field crews were dispatched from the nearest maintenance yard and arrived on scene at 06:45. investigation revealed that an unprecedented ice jam caused the river to overtop its banks, exerting lateral forces that displaced the pipe support brackets and cracked the pipe wall at the riverbed sleeve. the rupture released natural gas at an estimated 785 psi, creating a visible vapor cloud that dissipated after the line was isolated at the upstream and downstream valve stations. no injuries were reported and the vapor did not ignite. emergency response costs were logged at $19,200. initial property damage, including repair of the sleeve, support structure, and 15 ft of pipe, was estimated at $87,600; final costs are pending. the incident was reported to the dot and state oil and gas commission under the required thresholds. updates: 03/02/2024 – replacement pipe segment installed and line pressure restored to 800 psi; 03/15/2024 – final cost estimate submitted, total $108,450; corrective actions include upgraded anchoring and additional river monitoring during freeze‑thaw cycles.

a severe flash flood on 07/14/2024 inundated the lower delta region of the river bend where the sunridge energy 20‑inch carbon steel transmission pipeline runs parallel to the main highway. water levels rose to 6.5 ft above the normal river stage, overtopping the earthen berm that protects the pipeline right‑of‑way. by 14:30 local time the berm failed, allowing fast‑moving water to scour the backfill and expose a 15‑ft section of the pipe. the exposed segment experienced a sudden drop in pressure from the operating 850 psig to 120 psig as the pipe sagged and the 24‑inch girth weld on the downstream side fractured. a loud “pop” was heard by nearby residents, and a visible gas plume was reported by a highway patrol officer. emergency response teams arrived at 15:10, establishing a safety exclusion zone of 300 ft. isolation valves at station a and station b were manually closed at 15:18, stopping the flow. the damaged pipe segment was excavated, removed, and a new 20‑inch x‑70 pipe with a full‑encirclement sleeve was installed. pressure testing at 950 psig was completed on 07/18/2024 and the line was returned to service at 07:45 hours. the incident caused a 3‑day unplanned outage and estimated repair costs of $2.3 million.

on monday, july 14, 2023 at approximately 09:15 am, after the passage of tropical storm marisol, field operators observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line (segment ss 312‑ss 334) from 720 psi to 140 psi. visual inspection from the aerial drone survey revealed a large shear failure in the right‑of‑way where a hillside had collapsed into the riverbed, exposing the pipe and creating a 15‑foot gash. the nrc was notified and incident # 842317 was assigned. emergency response teams were dispatched at 10:02 am, and by 11:45 am divers confirmed the pipe was severed and water was flooding the low‑pressure side. initial estimates indicated a natural gas release of 12,300 mcf before isolation. the line was shut down and isolated at the nearest valve stations, and a temporary bypass was installed on 08‑08‑2023. damage assessments show the pipe material was compromised by corrosion and the ground movement, requiring a full replacement of 2,200 ft of pipe and associated fittings. repair work is scheduled to commence on 09‑05‑2023 with an estimated completion date of 10‑12‑2023. the incident was reported to the dot and phmsa, with projected property damage exceeding $2.3 million.

a severe thunderstorm dropped over eight inches of rain in two hours, creating a flash flood across the lowland near milepost 212. the flood scoured the backfill around a 12‑inch api 5l x65 carbon steel pipeline operating at 850 psi transporting natural gas. the protective coating was stripped and the pipe experienced rapid external loading as the soil shifted, resulting in a longitudinal crack at a girth weld. gas escaped, forming a vapor cloud that ignited when it contacted a nearby power line downed by wind. the mainline pressure transducer recorded a drop from 850 psi to 120 psi, triggering an automatic shutdown. inspection later revealed a two‑foot longitudinal split and gouge in the pipe wall at the low point of the trench. the incident released approximately 3400 scf of gas and caused minor fire damage to an adjacent control house. the report notes the area’s seasonal flooding history and that the pipeline had not been upgraded with additional erosion protection measures.

a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 1150 psi, located 2 mi east of bayou city, texas, was compromised during the april 2025 tornado outbreak. the tornado produced wind speeds exceeding 150 mph and generated a 5‑foot high surge of water and debris that overtopped the low‑lying floodplain. the surge lifted a section of the adjacent earthen embankment, exposing the pipeline’s 12‑inch girth weld at a river crossing. the force of the moving debris struck the weld, shearing the surrounding pipe wall and creating a 3‑inch gash. the pipe’s automatic shut‑down valve failed to close due to water intrusion in the actuator housing, allowing gas to escape into the flooded area. initial leak detection systems did not trigger alarms because the acoustic sensors were submerged. response crews could not access the site for 72 hours because the floodwaters remained 4 ft deep and the area was declared unsafe. once water receded, divers inspected the damage, confirming a full‑depth breach and confirming that the flanged tie‑in at the downstream pigging station had been displaced. the line was isolated and a temporary bypass was installed pending repair.

march 3, 2025 – a pipeline incident occurred on line lp-57, a wellstream energy llc transmission line, in a remote class 2 location approximately two miles southeast of the town of ridgefield, columbia county, oregon. the 24‑inch, api 5l x80 steel pipe, operating at 850 psi, was traversing a narrow mountain valley when a heavy, prolonged rainstorm triggered a landslide that displaced the right‑of‑way by about three feet. the resulting ground movement exerted a lateral load on the pipe, causing a longitudinal crack near a field girth weld at milepost 112.4. operations personnel received an automated scada alarm indicating a sudden pressure drop to 420 psi and immediately closed valve lp‑57‑02 to isolate the segment. the downstream valve was also shut, and the section was depressurized and purged. field crews accessed the site, confirmed a 15‑inch crack extending 8 inches along the weld, and installed a temporary clamp. a full isolation valve was set, and a hot‑tapping unit was mobilized for repair. the line remained out of service pending excavation, pipe replacement, and geotechnical stabilization of the slope. incident reporting was completed on march 8, 2025, and a post‑incident review recommended enhanced slope monitoring and the addition of a buried flexible joint in the landslide‑prone segment.

on april 14, 2024 at approximately 06:45 central daylight time, the field operations crew received a report from the river monitoring station that the lower mississippi levee had breached following three days of heavy rain from the stationary front. water levels rose rapidly, submerging a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade b) that runs parallel to the levee at milepost 312.5. pressure sensors showed a sudden drop from 960 psig to 380 psig within minutes. the control center initiated an immediate shut‑in of the affected segment and dispatched a response team to the site. upon arrival, crews observed extensive scouring of the pipe trench and visible pipe deformation near the east anchor point. the line was isolated at valve stations 312 and 313 by 07:20 cdt. emergency services coordinated with the us army corps of engineers, the state department of environmental quality, and the local parish flood control board to secure the area and prevent further erosion. a temporary bypass using a 12‑inch flexible hose was installed to restore limited product flow while a full‑depth excavation and pipe replacement plan was developed. repairs are scheduled to begin on april 22, pending final permits, with a target re‑commissioning date of may 10, 2024.

on a february night a 24‑inch x80 grade b steel transmission line located in the foothills of the central range experienced a sudden ground shift after an intense 3‑inch rainstorm produced a rapid snow‑melt runoff. the runoff created a shallow landslide that displaced a 150‑ft section of the right‑of‑way, pulling the pipe laterally about 8 inches and exposing a 2‑inch gouge near a 3500‑psi operating pressure station. scada alarms triggered a high‑pressure differential event at 12:47 a.m., and the automatic shutdown valve (asv) at station 12‑c failed to close due to debris blockage. field operators on the night shift responded within fifteen minutes, manually isolated the segment by closing the upstream isolation valve (2500 psi rating) and the downstream valve (3000 psi rating). emergency response teams deployed a portable containment dome and vented approximately 850 mcf of natural gas to safe flare. after the area was stabilized, a temporary bypass was installed and the damaged pipe segment was replaced with a 24‑inch x100 grade b pipe. the line was returned to service at 08:30 a.m. after pressure testing at 4000 psi confirmed integrity.

a heavy rainstorm moved through the hilltop area surrounding the riverbend transmission line on march 12, 2026, producing rapid runoff that saturated the soil behind the 24‑inch, api 5l carbon steel pipeline (nominal wall thickness 0.438 in, operating pressure 820 psig) at milepost 57.3. at approximately 14:45 local time the saturated slope gave way, creating a 15‑ft deep landslide that displaced the pipe laterally by roughly 6 inches and induced a buckling deformation near the welded tie‑in at valve r‑57‑b (12‑inch relief valve). the strain caused a longitudinal crack in the pipe wall, resulting in an uncontrolled release of natural gas into the surrounding environment. the automatic shutdown system failed to isolate the line because the upstream mainline isolation valve (valve r‑56‑a) was in a failed‑to‑close condition due to the ground movement. onsite field technicians arrived at 16:10, erected a temporary containment berm, and activated the portable emergency shut‑off kit, successfully closing the downstream isolation valve (valve r‑58‑c) at 17:05. a 200‑gpm water‑based foam was applied to the leak zone to mitigate fire risk. the incident was reported to the nrc at 18:30 (incident # 1628749) and a 48‑hour update was filed on march 14, 2026 (incident # 1628893). there was no impact to any water body; the leak was contained within the land slide area. (lat/long of the breach: 40.732115, -89.645321).

on july 14, 2025 at approximately 06:12 a.m. the northland pipelines 24" x70 carbon steel main, operating at 820 psi, experienced a sudden loss of pressure alarm in the lower willow valley segment. the automatic leak detection system flagged a rapid drop of 150 psi within 30 seconds, triggering an emergency shutdown command from the central control room. field crews were dispatched from the nearby wyoming maintenance hub and arrived on site at 07:05. visual inspection revealed that the river crossing over the silver creek had been undermined by an unexpected flash‑flood event caused by an upstream thunderstorm that produced 4‑5 inches of rain in two hours. the high‑velocity water had scoured the supporting backfill, exposing the pipe and creating a 4‑foot longitudinal breach. water and gas were observed escaping from the seam, forming a vapor cloud that ignited briefly when a stray spark from a fallen tree contacted the pipe, resulting in a minor flash fire that was extinguished by the crew’s portable extinguishers. the segment was isolated, the leak was contained, and a temporary bypass was installed. a detailed damage assessment and permanent replacement of the river crossing are scheduled for early august, with additional erosion control measures to be implemented.

on 6/15/2024, during a severe thunderstorm that produced 80‑mph wind gusts and localized flooding in the lower sabine river corridor, a 24‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line operating at 850 psi experienced a ground shift that exposed a 12‑foot section of pipe near milepost 32.5. the movement caused a longitudinal crack in the pipe wall, resulting in a measurable leak of approximately 6 in³/s. scada recorded a pressure drop from 850 psi to 210 psi within minutes, triggering an automatic shut‑in and an emergency alarm to the control center. field crews arrived at the site at 09:45 am, isolated the affected segment using the nearest mainline valves, and erected a containment berm to capture escaping product. after confirming the leak, the damaged pipe section was cut out and a new 24‑inch seamless steel pipe with a matching flange connection was spliced in. the welds were pressure‑tested at 1000 psi and hydrostatic tested at 1.5× design pressure. the line was returned to service at 5:30 pm on 6/20/2024. a supplemental report will be filed once final repair costs are determined.

the 24‑inch, api 5l x70 steel main transporting sweet natural gas at 35 bar pressure across the lower mississippi floodplain experienced a sudden loss of pressure on 14 april 2024 after a prolonged heavy‑rain event raised river levels by 4.2 m. field crews observed a large sag in the right‑of‑way near milepost 112.3 where the pipe had been placed on a sand fill embankment. post‑event inspection revealed that the surrounding soil had become saturated and liquefied, causing a transverse shear failure of the fill and a 1.8‑meter vertical displacement of the pipe. the resulting buckle created a 45‑degree bend that exceeded the pipe’s allowable strain, leading to a longitudinal seam crack and a subsequent gas release of approximately 850 scf. the segment was isolated, the damaged pipe section was cut out, and a new 24‑inch x70 spool was installed with additional geotechnical reinforcement, including a concrete cradle and deeper pilings. after hydrostatic testing to 1.5 times operating pressure, the line was returned to service. the incident was documented as a natural‑force‑induced ground movement event.

the 24‑inch carbon steel pipeline belonging to western midstream, operating at 1 200 psi and transporting light crude from the rocky mountains to the coastal terminal, was impacted by a rapid snowmelt‑induced landslide on 14 january 2025. the slide occurred in a remote, steeply sloped corridor near the 62‑mile marker, displacing the right‑of‑way and shearing a 15‑foot section of pipe. an automatic leak detection system registered a sudden pressure drop of 300 psi and triggered the upstream isolation valve within 12 seconds. field crews from the emergency response team arrived the same day, confirming a 6‑inch longitudinal rupture exposing the internal coating. the breached section released approximately 9 400 barrels of crude into a shallow drainage ditch before the downstream valve closed. no injuries were reported, and fire suppression systems were not activated. containment booms and absorbent pads were deployed, and the affected segment was isolated and depressurized. a temporary bypass was installed to restore flow, while a full‑thickness replacement of the damaged pipe and a slope stabilization program are scheduled for completion by the end of the quarter.

on wednesday, october 12, 2023 at approximately 07:45 a.m., after a prolonged period of heavy rain and localized flooding in the lower mississippi valley, field operators noted a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x70) that transports sweet natural gas at 850 psig. the supervisory control system flagged a depressurization alarm at station ss‑212 and the downstream pressure transducer recorded a loss of 210 psig within minutes. aerial reconnaissance later that morning revealed a clear trench along the right‑of‑way near milepost 45.3 where the pipe had been exposed and displaced several inches downstream, creating a visible gash approximately 8 in. long and 0.75 in. wide. soil saturation from the preceding 4‑inch rain event had caused a washout of the supporting backfill, undermining the pipe’s bedding and allowing a section of the riverbank to erode into the trench. a rapid response team was dispatched, and divers confirmed the breach at 10:20 a.m. the damaged segment was isolated, and a 24‑inch repair sleeve with a 1‑inch flange was installed. the pipeline was pressure tested to 900 psig and returned to service at 18:00 on the same day. the incident was logged as case # 984321 and reported to the nrc.

during tropical storm lucas, high wind gusts and 6‑foot wave heights generated intense seabed scouring around the offshore tie‑in of the atlantic midstream 30‑inch, 40‑lb api 5l pipeline (operating at 950 psi). the scouring removed supporting sediment and caused the tie‑in assembly to settle unevenly, inducing a 12‑degree bend in the adjoining 24‑inch, 36‑lb x‑65 pipe segment. visual inspection by remotely operated vehicles showed a longitudinal crack approximately 3 inches long on the pipe’s outer wall and a gouge on the adjacent coating. immediate isolation was achieved by closing the upstream 30‑inch block valve and the downstream 24‑inch isolation valve. a pressure drop to 210 psi was recorded at the downstream gauge, confirming a leak. the damaged sections were tagged, and a hot‑tapping operation was planned for removal. replacement spools of 30‑inch and 24‑inch carbon steel pipe with 75‑mm wall thickness were mobilized, and the repaired segment was restored to service after pressure testing to 1200 psi, 25 % above normal operating pressure. the incident resulted in a 48‑hour service interruption and required additional environmental monitoring due to potential hydrocarbon release.
