on february 14, 2024 at approximately 0845 hrs a 24‑inch api 5l steel transmission line owned by midwest energy in the hills of western pennsylvania experienced a rupture after a severe ice storm. a combination of 2‑inch ice accretion on surrounding trees and a 55‑mph wind gust caused a 45‑foot ponderosa pine to fall onto the right‑hand side of the buried line, crushing the pipe at a 30‑degree bend near milepost 12.7. the line was operating at a normal operating pressure of 1180 psi and the impact created a 3‑inch longitudinal split, releasing an estimated 4,200 mcf of natural gas into the shallow soil. field crews initiated emergency shut‑in of the adjacent block valve (bv‑34) within eight minutes, and the gas was diverted to the parallel 20‑inch line. post‑incident investigation revealed that the pipe segment had not been coated with an anti‑icing epoxy, and the surrounding drainage ditch had become clogged with snow melt, increasing soil saturation and reducing pipe support. corrective actions include installing additional protective backfill, applying ice‑resistant coating to vulnerable pipe sections, and clearing drainage ditches before the next winter season.

on june 14, 2024 at 03:27 a.m. cdt a severe thunderstorm produced 4‑inch hail and gusts exceeding 55 mph over the lower mississippi river valley. the hail struck the above‑ground segment of the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (schedule 80, rated 900 psi) at milepost 212.7 near the riverbank access road. impact from multiple hailstones caused a dent in the pipe wall and displaced a 6‑inch girth weld on the east side, resulting in a slow leak of natural gas. the automatic shutdown system detected a pressure drop to 720 psi and initiated a remote closure of the upstream 24‑inch block valve at milepost 210.9 and the downstream valve at milepost 214.3. on‑call field crews arrived at 04:02 a.m., isolated the line with a 12‑inch manual valve inside the valve house, and erected a temporary bypass using a 20‑inch steel sleeve. the leak was vented safely and the affected pipe segment was removed for repair. the incident was reported to the nrc within 30 minutes of confirmation (nrc 1‑hr report #: 20240614‑01). service was restored at 12:18 p.m. after pressure testing and reinstating the mainline.

during a routine integrity check following the april 2024 river flooding, field crews discovered that a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the bend of the mississippi river had its 8‑inch lateral tee‑piece displaced and the accompanying ½‑inch isolation valve fractured. the pipe segment, rated for 960 psi, showed a longitudinal dent consistent with impact from a submerged log driven by high water velocity. visual inspection revealed that the tee‑piece flange bolts were sheared and the valve body was cracked at the seating surface, resulting in a slow gas leak that was detected by the acoustic emission monitor. the damaged tee‑piece and valve were removed, a new 8‑inch tee‑piece and ½‑inch valve were installed, and the pipe was re‑aligned using a hydraulic pull‑in tool. after hydrostatic testing to 1200 psi and confirming leak‑free operation, the line was flushed, pigged, and returned to service. post‑event analysis indicated the failure was caused by the flood‑driven debris impact, and additional riverbank stabilization measures were recommended.

on july 9, 2023, operators at the bayou city compression station observed a sudden 150‑psi drop on the 24‑inch mainline feeding the west bayou delivery corridor. an immediate inspection using a handheld gas detector at milepost 42.7 revealed a 3.2% lel methane reading and visible soil erosion exposing the pipeline. recent torrential rains from tropical storm elijah had caused a flash flood that scoured a 30‑foot section of the right‑of‑way, removing the protective backfill and striking the pipe at the 6 o’clock position. field crews confirmed a 9‑inch longitudinal dent with a 0.7‑inch deep gouge and a hairline crack at the dent’s base. the affected segment was isolated by closing valve a‑1 and valve b‑1, and the line was depressurized to atmospheric pressure. a 30‑inch stopple and a 24‑inch bypass sleeve were installed, after which the damaged pipe section was excavated and removed. a new 24‑inch x 12‑ft schedule 40 carbon steel pipe was spliced in using a double‑coupled mechanical joint, coated with a three‑layer epoxy, and backfilled with geotextile fabric. the line was pressure tested to 900 psi, purged, and returned to service at 800 psi without further incident. no injuries or fire occurred, and service to customers was maintained throughout the repair.

on september 14, 2022 at 08:42 central daylight time (cdt) western pipeline services, inc. (wpsi) monitoring center received a call from the clark county sheriff’s office reporting a sudden gas odor near milepost 112 on the 30‑inch, 2,400 psi maop, api‑5l sch‑40 carbon steel transmission line that traverses the lower clark river floodplain in missouri. wpsi field crews arrived on scene at 09:15 cdt and found the pipeline had broken open at a low‑lying culvert crossing that had been completely inundated by flash flooding from an overnight thunderstorm. the water had scoured the surrounding fill, exposing the pipe and causing a 12‑inch longitudinal split. a vapor cloud ignited briefly, burning vegetation but causing no damage to structures or injuries to personnel. the pipe segment was isolated at 09:48 cdt and the line was placed out of service. wpsi submitted a 48‑hr nrc update on september 15, 2022 (report no. 1348921). the ruptured section was recovered and sent to a metallurgical laboratory, which concluded that the failure resulted from external mechanical loading due to rapid soil displacement and hydrostatic pressure associated with the flood event. repairs involved installing a deeper reinforced concrete encasement and relocating the culvert to mitigate future flood‑related stresses. the line was returned to service on october 3, 2022.

on march 14, 2022 a routine aerial patrol identified a vapor plume emerging from a vegetated right‑of‑way near pine ridge creek, approximately 2.3 miles southeast of the marion county valve station. field crews were dispatched at 09:12 and arrived on scene by 09:46. the affected segment was a 12‑inch carbon steel pipeline (api 5l grade b) operating at 850 psi, installed in 1998. visual inspection revealed that a 30‑inch section of the pipe had been displaced vertically by approximately 18 inches, exposing a 1‑inch lateral tap that was fully exposed to the creek bank. further investigation indicated that recent heavy rainfall had caused a rapid rise in creek water level, resulting in bank erosion and a small landslide that shifted the pipe. the lateral tap, a previously decommissioned service connection, fractured under the stress of movement and debris impact, creating the observed release. the line was isolated at 10:22, depressurized, and the compromised pipe segment was excavated. a new 12‑inch welded steel sleeve was installed, and the line was returned to service at 16:05 after hydrostatic testing confirmed integrity. the incident was reported to the nrc at 12:30 and a metallurgic analysis was requested to confirm the failure mechanism.

on april 3, 2026, southern gas transmission reported a sudden loss of pressure on its 30‑inch carbon steel main (schedule 40) near the foothills of the blue ridge. a severe thunderstorm produced 6‑inch of rain in a six‑hour window, causing flash flooding that overtopped the creek crossing at milepost 142.5. field crews arrived at 0920 est and observed the downstream section of the pipe displaced laterally by approximately 18 inches, with a longitudinal seam opening visible near a girth weld. pressure had dropped from 800 psig to 420 psig before the automatic shut‑in at 0905 est. a downstream pigging station confirmed a rapid pressure surge followed by a steady decline. the floodwater had eroded the supporting sand backfill, undermining the concrete encasement and allowing the pipe to settle unevenly, resulting in a ductile rupture at the welded joint. crews isolated the line by closing the upstream isolation valve c-12 and the downstream relief valve c-14, then pumped down water to depressurize the segment. a temporary bypass was installed, and a full‑scale pipe replacement with a 36‑inch high‑strength alloy pipe and reinforced concrete bedding is scheduled for the week of april 10. the incident is being investigated for potential improvements to flood‑risk assessments.

after a severe derecho swept through the county, the 12‑inch carbon steel mainline feeding the west field experienced a sudden pressure drop from 720 psi to 380 psi on the control panel. inspection crews discovered that the 24‑inch pressure reduction valve at station 4c had been ripped from its flange, its bolts sheared by debris propelled by the high‑speed winds. the adjacent 4‑inch orifice meter housing was also torn from its foundation, leaving the 1‑inch stainless steel instrument tubing exposed. the storm surge raised water levels to 6 ft above the grade, causing the concrete pad to shift and the meter building to tilt, which in turn fractured the ¾‑inch vent line. the vent line rupture released an estimated 350 mmcf of natural gas into the atmosphere before the automatic shut‑down sequence activated. field personnel accessed the site two days later using an all‑terrain vehicle and temporary scaffolding, removed the damaged valve assembly, replaced the orifice meter housing, and installed new instrumentation. the line was hydro‑tested to 1500 psi and returned to service after confirming no further leaks.

on the evening of september 22, 2023, operators at the midwest pipeline control center observed a gradual drop in pressure on the 30‑inch api 5l x80 mainline near the foothills of the colorado front range. the pressure fell from 900 psi to 720 psi over a thirty‑minute period. the dispatcher contacted the field supervisor, who instructed the nearest crew to mobilize to the last known pressure reading location, approximately twenty‑four miles west of the small town of silver creek.

the crew arrived on site at 0200 hours on september 23 after navigating a winding, unpaved access road that had been partially obstructed by recent storm runoff. visual inspection revealed a clear scar on the right‑hand side of the pipe where the surrounding soil had been eroded away, exposing a 12‑inch section of the pipe wall. a downstream landslide, triggered by three days of intense rain and rapid snow melt, had removed supporting fill and caused the pipe to settle unevenly, creating a longitudinal seam crack that released natural gas.

containment crews erected a temporary sandbag barrier and activated the automatic shut‑off valve, isolating the segment. a hot‑tapping crew was dispatched the following day to install a repair sleeve and replace a 15‑foot pipe section. the line was pressure tested at 850 psi on september 27 and returned to service at 910 psi on september 28. the incident resulted in an estimated loss of 1,200 mcf of gas.

at 3:45 pm on april 12, 2025, a line of severe thunderstorms moved through the panhandle of texas, producing wind gusts of up to 70 mph and multiple hail events. a 24‑inch carbon‑steel transmission pipeline (api 5l sch40, rated 1 200 psi) owned by western midstream operated at a steady pressure of 950 psi when a 30‑lb hailstone struck the exposed section of the line near the hilltop valve station on county road 112. the impact caused a dent that breached the pipe wall, creating a 3‑inch opening. immediately, the downstream 10‑inch relief valve on the associated gathering system popped open due to the sudden pressure drop, venting dry natural gas at an estimated rate of 15 million cubic feet per hour. the automatic shutdown system isolated the segment within 6 minutes, but a faint odor was reported by a nearby rancher at 3:53 pm. emergency response teams arrived at 4:10 pm, establishing a safety perimeter of 500 ft and initiating evacuation of the adjacent homestead. the leak was fully contained by 5:02 pm after the field crew installed a temporary clamp and depressurized the line. the incident was reported to the national response center at 5:15 pm, and a post‑incident review cited the need for additional hail‑resistant shielding at exposed valve stations.

at approximately 7:14 am cdt on september 12, 2023, the 30‑inch, 70‑lb api 5l transmission line 22 transporting refined products from the oak ridge terminal to the glenwood distribution hub in north dakota experienced a sudden loss of pressure at m.p. 212.47. the incident was first reported by a call attendant alarm triggered by the glenwood pump station at 7:18 am cdt. field crews arrived on scene within twenty‑four minutes and observed a 4‑foot longitudinal rupture of the pipe near a steep embankment that had failed following three days of intense rainfall and flash flooding. the rupture exposed product at an estimated 920 psi operating pressure, resulting in an immediate vapor cloud that ignited upon contact with a nearby power line, creating a brief fireball that was extinguished by the automatic shut‑down of the station. crews closed the mainline block valve mlv‑22‑398 at mp 209.9 and the downstream isolation valve mlv‑22‑405 at mp 215.2, isolating the damaged segment by 7:46 am cdt. nrc notification was initiated at 8:02 am cdt after confirming the rupture and compiling initial data. a preliminary investigation indicated that the flood‑induced landslide exerted lateral forces exceeding the pipe’s design tolerance, causing the failure. further analysis will assess pipe material integrity and the adequacy of slope stabilization measures. the incident caused approximately $1.3 million in property damage and a temporary disruption of product flow for 12 hours.

on april 14, 2023 at approximately 06:30 am, the 30‑inches, api 5l x65 steel gas transmission line (nominal design pressure 1 200 psi, operating pressure 900 psi) running across the lower susquehanna valley was exposed to a sudden flash flood following a stalled thunderstorm. the floodwaters rose to a depth of 6 feet, overtopping the earthen embankment that supports the right‑of‑way. the high‑velocity water eroded the backfill beneath a 400‑ft span of the pipe, creating a 12‑ft long trench that caused the pipe to sag and eventually fracture near milepost 23.4. automatic leak detection indicated a pressure drop to 720 psi; the downstream isolation valve at station r‑12 automatically closed, while the upstream valve at station r‑10 required manual actuation by field crews arriving at 08:10 am. a total of 3 850 mcf of natural gas escaped before isolation was complete, with no ignition. the leak was contained and the affected section was capped with a temporary sleeve. subsequent investigation identified the flood as the primary trigger; soil moisture levels had exceeded design assumptions for the embankment. repair plans include installing a concrete slab under the trench, adding a 24‑inches protective berm, and replacing the damaged pipe segment with a new 30‑inch, api 5l x80 line. a supplemental report will be filed within 30 days.

on april 14, 2024, a severe thunderstorm produced 6‑inch of rain in the lower sabine river basin, causing flash flooding that overtopped the low‑lying road crossing of the 12‑inch x65 carbon steel transmission line owned by lone star pipelines. the floodwaters eroded a 30‑foot section of the riverbank, exposing the pipeline at a point where it was buried 2 feet below grade. high‑velocity water flow struck the pipe, displacing it laterally and creating a 4‑inch split at the 45‑degree weld joint near milepost 27.6. pressure in the line, normally 850 psi, dropped to 420 psi within minutes, triggering an automatic shut‑in at the upstream control station. downstream pressure sensors recorded a rapid depressurization, and a low‑pressure alarm initiated an emergency response. field crews from the incident command arrived at 08:45 am, erected a temporary berm to divert water, and installed a 24‑inch steel clamp to stop the leak. a total of 18.7 million cubic feet of natural gas were vented to atmosphere before the clamp held. subsequent hydrostatic testing confirmed the integrity of the repaired section at 900 psi. the riverbank was re‑stabilized with rip‑rap, and a geotechnical survey recommended increasing burial depth to 4 feet in flood‑prone zones. a post‑incident review identified the need for enhanced flood‑risk mapping and will be incorporated into the company’s pipeline integrity management program by the end of 2025.

on may 14, 2025, at approximately 03:27 cst, a severe thunderstorm passed over the midland compression station in jackson county, missouri. the station, operated by western gas transmission, llc (operator id 8421), is equipped with a 30‑inch carbon steel mainline operating at 720 psi and a 12‑inch downstream distribution line at 210 psi. a direct lightning strike hit the station’s primary control building, damaging the 480 v main switchgear and a 250 amp circuit breaker protecting the plc system. the loss of control power caused an automatic shutdown of the 5‑stage centrifugal compressors, but the backup diesel generators failed to latch onto the bus within the required 10‑second window due to a mis‑set voltage sensing relay. as a result, the low‑pressure safety valve on the 30‑inch line opened, releasing an estimated 3.8 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding area. emergency response teams from the local fire department and the agency for toxic substances arrived within 12 minutes. the gas plume dissipated without ignition, and no injuries were reported. restoration crews repaired the switchgear, re‑programmed the relay, and performed a full functional test of the backup generators before returning the station to service at 17:02 cst.

on 5/7/23 at 07:12 am the operations control center received a call from a local fire department reporting a sudden gush of gas odor near mile marker 42 on the east valley pipeline. the line, a 24‑in. x 0.5‑in. api 5l x65 pipe, operates at 850 psi and transports 380 mmcfd of natural gas. field crews were dispatched at 07:30 am and arrived on scene at 08:05 am to find the pipeline exposed after a flash‑flood event the previous night. heavy rain had caused the adjacent creek to overtop its banks, eroding the backfill and creating a 15‑ft section of pipe that had been displaced laterally by approximately 6 in. the displacement produced excessive bending stress at a 24‑in. girth weld located at a directional change. visual inspection revealed a longitudinal split in the weld throat and a small leak at the joint. the line was isolated at 08:45 am and the area was secured. subsequent x‑ray nondestructive testing confirmed a crack propagating through the weld root. the incident report cited soil movement from the flood as the primary force causing the weld failure. repairs were completed on 5/10/23, and the pipeline was returned to service at 13:00 hrs after hydrostatic testing at 1.5 × design pressure.

on 4 august 2022 at approximately 07:14 utc, western pipelines inc. received an urgent call from the county sheriff’s office reporting a sudden collapse of a 24‑inch, schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line crossing the south fork of the colorado river near milepost 132. the line, normally operating at 1150 psig transporting dry natural gas, had been isolated for routine maintenance two weeks prior, but the isolation valves on the upstream and downstream mainline remained closed. field crews arrived within 45 minutes and observed a deep, water‑filled trench exposing a 30‑foot section of pipe that had been ripped from its supports. investigation revealed that a rapid snow‑melt flood, intensified by a localized thunderstorm, caused scour of the riverbank, removing the bedding material and creating a free‑span condition. the ensuing vortex‑induced vibration led to a fatigue crack at the toe of a longitudinal seam, ultimately rupturing the pipe. the rupture released gas, which ignited briefly before being extinguished by the river’s flow; no fire persisted. western pipelines promptly notified the national response center, phmsa, and the state oil and gas commission, and began emergency isolation and pressure relief procedures while environmental crews monitored the river for contamination.

on june 22, 2025, at 0815 hours, field operators observed a sudden pressure drop on the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline (api 5l grade b) serving the highland valley gas gathering system. the pipeline, rated for 900 psig, was operating at 750 psig when an automatic shutdown was triggered. visual inspection revealed a 4‑foot section of the pipe exposed at the base of a steep ravine where a rapid snowmelt flood had scoured the earthen cover and deposited a thick layer of ice. ice expansion exerted lateral forces that fractured the pipe wall at the welded joint identified as tag‑34‑b. emergency response teams were dispatched, the area was isolated, and a temporary bypass valve was installed to restore limited service. after water levels receded, a crew excavated the damaged segment, removed the broken pipe, and installed a new 24‑inch x 12‑foot replacement section with a reinforced steel sleeve and additional concrete backfill to mitigate future scour. hydrostatic testing to 1200 psig confirmed integrity. the line was returned to normal operation at 1630 hours on june 23, 2025. post‑event review cited extreme melt‑water flow combined with freeze‑thaw cycles as the primary natural force contributing to the failure.

on august 14, 2026 at 03:17 central daylight time (cdt), western pipelines, inc. received an automated alarm indicating a sudden pressure loss on the 24‑inch, 80# api 5l mainline (apn‑45) near the oak ridge valve station in lewis county, kansas. field crews were dispatched and arrived on scene within twelve minutes. visual inspection revealed a gash approximately 18 inches long in the pipe wall, exposing the carrier gas to the atmosphere. the rupture coincided with a severe thunderstorm that produced 60‑mph straight‑line winds and hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter. a subsequent lightning strike ignited the escaping gas, creating a brief fireball that was extinguished by the on‑site fire‑suppression system. the incident resulted in the isolation of the affected segment, a temporary reduction of flow to 70 % of rated capacity, and a loss of 0.27 mmcfd of natural gas. initial damage assessment estimated repair costs exceeding $210,000, including replacement of the damaged pipe section, valve, and associated fittings, as well as soil remediation. the incident was reported to the phmsa under report number 20260078‑3124, and a root‑cause investigation remains ongoing, focusing on the impact of extreme weather on pipeline integrity.

on april 14, 2023 a severe thunderstorm produced localized flash flooding in the lower foothills of the san joaquin valley. by 1730 hrs the rising creek water had overtopped the culvert protecting the 30‑inch, schedule 80 steel transmission line (line 12‑c) that runs parallel to the stream at mp 42.7. the high‑velocity water scoured the embankment, exposing a 12‑inch section of pipe to direct hydraulic forces. field crews from the operations center received a leak alarm at 1805 hrs indicating a pressure drop from 1250 psig to 650 psig. a rapid response team arrived on scene at 1830 hrs and confirmed a 3‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall, with gas escaping at an estimated rate of 450 mmscfd. the valve at station v125 was closed, and the line was depressurized to atmospheric. a temporary bypass was installed using a 28‑inch stainless steel sleeve and the damaged segment was cut out. subsequent geotechnical analysis concluded that the flood‑induced scour caused the pipe rupture. permanent repairs will include a reinforced concrete retaining wall and additional backfill to protect the pipe from future hydraulic erosion. the incident was logged at 1915 hrs and a full incident report was submitted the following day.

at 06:45 on 04/12/2024 a 16‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) located in the lower meadows of the colorado river valley experienced a sudden loss of pressure. the line, operating at 850 psi, was situated near a historic floodplain. after three days of heavy rain, the river rose 5.2 ft above flood stage and breached its levee, sending a fast‑moving mudflow across the right‑of‑way. the flow eroded the soil support beneath the pipe, causing a 12‑ft section to be pulled from the trench and the pipe to separate at a welded joint. downstream pressure dropped to 150 psi, triggering an automatic shutdown of the upstream regulator. field crews arrived at 08:10, isolated the segment, and erected a temporary steel sleeve to contain the breach. a 30‑minute controlled vent relieved residual gas. the damaged pipe was removed and a new 18‑inch x70 pipe was installed with a deeper trench and reinforced concrete bedding. the line was returned to service at 14:30 on 04/14/2024 after pressure testing to 1000 psi and a full integrity inspection.

during a prolonged thunderstorm on 14 september 2023, a 30‑inch x70 steel pipeline (api 5l grade b) in the lower mississippi valley experienced a sudden loss of pressure at milepost 212.5. the storm produced unprecedented gusts exceeding 80 mph and localized flooding that raised the riverbank by more than 6 ft. high‑velocity water forced the riverbank into a rapid erosion event, exposing the pipe’s lower crown. as the soil support failed, the pipe sagged and the seam at a longitudinal weld cracked, creating a 4‑inch gash that released product at an estimated 620 psi operating pressure. operators observed a rapid pressure drop from 650 psi to 380 psi within seconds and activated the automated shutdown sequence. the affected segment was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream block valves, which were tagged out and locked per company procedure. emergency response teams arrived on scene, confirming a significant hydrostatic leak with visible oil sheen on the water surface. repairs are scheduled pending geotechnical stabilization of the riverbank.

on april 12, 2023, a severe thunderstorm moved through the foothills of the san juan mountains, dropping more than 7 inches of rain in a six‑hour period. the resulting flash flood overtopped the arroyo near milepost 214.3 of the western transmission system, a 24‑inch, 800‑psi api 5l x70 steel pipeline that transports natgas from the monterey gathering facility to the desert interconnect. high‑velocity water scoured the protective sand cover and exposed a 12‑foot section of pipe, causing the surrounding soil to shift and the pipe to bend beyond its design curvature. at 14:37 local time the pipeline integrity monitor recorded a sudden pressure drop to 420 psi, and the automated leak detection system triggered a shutdown. emergency response crews arrived within 30 minutes, isolated the line at the nearest block valves (mp 209.5 and mp 219.0), and confirmed a longitudinal rupture with a 4‑inch gash. two workers on site were treated for minor lacerations; no fatalities occurred. approximately 20 residents within a half‑mile radius were evacuated as a precaution. after water receded, a temporary bypass was installed, and a full excavation and replacement of the damaged segment is scheduled for early may.

on april 3, 2024, a severe thunderstorm produced over 8 inches of rain in a six‑hour period, causing the riverbend creek to swell beyond its banks and breach the adjacent floodplain. the resulting floodwaters eroded the soil supporting a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission pipeline (api 5l x70) operating at 820 psi near the 12‑mile marker of the hillcrest mainline. as the riverbank collapsed, a 30‑foot section of the pipe was exposed and twisted, leading to a longitudinal crack that opened a 4‑inch gash in the wall. the automated upstream valve at the hillcrest control station (valve‑h12) opened to shut in the line, but the downstream manual valve (valve‑h13) required on‑call crews to manually close it after reaching the site. personnel arrived to find natural gas escaping at an estimated rate of 250 mmcf/d, with visible vapor cloud drifting downstream. emergency response isolated the affected segment, vented the 12‑mile section to atmospheric pressure, and deployed a temporary steel containment sleeve while a replacement 24‑inch pipe section was fabricated. the incident caused a 12‑hour service interruption to 4,500 residential customers and prompted a post‑event review of flood‑risk assessments for all low‑lying pipeline corridors.

on 05-17-2024 a 24‑inch high‑density polyethylene (hdpe) transmission line operated at 720 psig located in the foothills of the sierra nevada experienced a sudden rupture after a severe thunderstorm produced flash flooding. the floodwaters overtopped the right‑of‑way berm, exerting hydraulic forces that displaced a 30‑foot section of the pipe from its supports, pulling the pipe away from a welded coupling. the resulting split released approximately 3.4 mmcf of natural gas, which ignited when it contacted a nearby power line downed by the storm. emergency response crews from the operator and the local fire department isolated the line at the upstream and downstream valves within 45 minutes, extinguished the fire, and evacuated the surrounding area. initial damage assessment indicated a 24‑inch pipe segment and associated fittings were destroyed, with soil erosion requiring extensive backfill. total repair costs are projected at $1.2 million, including replacement pipe, reinstatement of the right‑of‑way, and environmental remediation. the incident was reported to the dot and the state pipeline safety commission under the >$250,000 damage threshold. investigation remains ongoing to determine if additional protective measures are needed for flood‑prone sections.

on april 22, 2024 at approximately 1400 hours, the field operations supervisor for midwest transmission received a call from the county emergency manager reporting rapid rise in the middle fork of the silver river after an overnight thunderstorm. the 24‑inch, 70‑grade carbon steel main, operating at 960 psig, runs 0.6 miles downstream of the river crossing on a buried trench that had been installed in 2003. during the flood event, the river overtopped its banks and the high‑velocity water scoured the protective backfill, exposing a 150‑foot section of pipe. at 1435 the crew dispatched to the site observed a visible vapor plume and audible hissing from the exposed segment. an immediate shutdown was initiated; the upstream block valve at milepost 12.3 and the downstream block valve at milepost 13.0 were closed by 1442, isolating the line. the leak was measured at approximately 1,200 scfh of natural gas. the exposed pipe showed a 2‑inch longitudinal seam crack likely caused by the sudden loss of soil support and bending stress from the flowing water. emergency response teams placed sandbags and erected a temporary cofferdam to stabilize the riverbank. after securing the area, the damaged pipe was cut out and a 30‑foot replacement spool of 24‑inch x70# pipe was mobilized. the repair is scheduled for completion by april 28, pending final inspection and reinstatement of service. the incident is being coordinated with the state petroleum commission, the army corps of engineers, and the local flood control district.

on august 3 at 07:12 a.m. the operations control center received an automated alarm indicating a rapid pressure loss on the 24‑inch carbon steel main (design pressure 1250 psig) near the foothills of the san juan range. the preceding 48 hours had brought 7.3 inches of rain, triggering a series of small flash‑flood events across the right‑of‑way. a field crew dispatched at 07:45 a.m. observed a newly formed gully cutting across the trench, exposing a 30‑foot section of the pipe. visual inspection revealed that the pipe had been displaced laterally by approximately 2 inches, creating a pronounced buckle and a transverse crack roughly 3‑inches long on the lower 5‑inch schedule 40 wall. the surrounding soil was saturated, and additional mudslide material was observed moving down the slope. the segment was isolated at 08:10 a.m., pressure reduced to 300 psig, and a temporary leak clamp could not be applied due to the misalignment. emergency response coordinated with the local fire department to establish a containment berm. a replacement 24‑inch pipe segment was mobilized, excavated, and installed by 15:30 that day; the line was repressurized and returned to service at 18:05 a.m. with post‑repair integrity testing confirming no further leakage.

on april 7, 2024 at 14:22 local time, field crew for western gas transmission observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch x70 carbon steel main near the foothills of the sierra ridge. the segment, rated for 850 psig, was operating at 720 psig when the automated scada alarm indicated a rapid pressure loss of approximately 180 psig within minutes. a visual inspection confirmed that a section of the right‑hand side trench had been exposed by a flash flood that occurred overnight after a severe thunderstorm produced 4 inches of rain in the watershed. the floodwaters eroded the soil cover, causing a 15‑foot long washout that displaced the pipe and created a 2‑inch longitudinal split at md 112.4. emergency shut‑in procedures were initiated at 14:35, isolating the affected block valve and reducing line pressure to 30 psig by 14:50. a rapid response team arrived at the site at 15:10, erected temporary cofferdams and installed a clamp over the split. the damaged pipe segment was excavated and removed on april 9, and a new 24‑inch x70 pipe with internal coating was installed and pressure tested to 900 psig before returning to service at 11:45 on april 12.

on april 14, 2024, at approximately 02:18 central standard time (cst), a section of the southern ridge natural gas pipeline experienced a sudden rupture near milepost 312.7 in the foothills of the colorado front range. the pipeline, a 30‑inch schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line operated by western interstate pipelines, llc, is rated for a maximum allowable operating pressure of 1,350 psig and was transporting dry natural gas at 1,080 psig at the time of the event. heavy snowfall combined with a rapid thaw caused a shallow landslide that displaced the right‑of‑way by roughly three feet, exerting a lateral load that exceeded the pipe’s design tolerance. a low‑pressure scada alarm triggered at 02:20 cst, prompting the control center to initiate an automatic shutdown and dispatch field crews. first responders arrived at the scene at 02:45 cst and observed a gash approximately 18 inches long with visible gas release and ignition of surrounding vegetation. the impacted segment was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream valves by 03:10 cst. emergency services confirmed no injuries or property damage beyond the vegetation. the damaged pipe was excavated, removed, and replaced with a new 30‑inch api 5l x70 pipe, pressure tested to 1,500 psig, and returned to service at 15:30 cst on april 15, 2024.

on april 14, 2022 a severe thunderstorm system moved through the lower mississippi valley producing straight‑line winds exceeding 80 mph and localized hail up to 2 in. the 30‑in. api 5l sch‑40 carbon steel transmission line (design pressure 1480 psi) that traverses the north side of the oak ridge floodplain was exposed to a sudden gust that caused a 12‑ft section of right‑of‑way vegetation to be uprooted and driven into the pipe support structure. the impact sheared the 24‑in. lateral tie‑in flange and displaced the adjacent 30‑in. pipe, resulting in a full‑depth gouge and a 4‑in. longitudinal crack near the 85‑mile marker. pressure monitoring stations recorded an immediate drop from 1450 psi to 870 psi within 3 minutes, triggering the automatic shutdown of the upstream mainline pump station. field crews arrived at 07:45 cst, isolated the segment by closing the downstream block valve, and confirmed a loss of 2.3 mmcf of gas. a temporary containment sleeve was installed, and the damaged section was tagged for removal. a detailed damage assessment is underway; the pipeline will be replaced with a new 30‑in. line‑pipe and upgraded support brackets to mitigate future wind‑induced loading. the incident was reported to phmsa within the required 30‑minute window.

at 0645 hours july 14, 2022 a southern pipeline operations dispatcher received a call from a farmer who reported a large water surge flowing across his pasture near milepost 212 on the company's 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (rated 900 psi). the farmer said the ground had risen several inches after three days of intense thunderstorm rainfall, creating a visible fissure in the right‑hand side of the right‑of‑way. field crew arrived at 0730 hours, inspected the trench and observed a 12‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe with a grade‑2 leak releasing approximately 180 mmscfd of natural gas. warning tape and a 24‑hour isolation valve were applied, and the line was depressurized to 200 psi. a temporary steel sleeve was installed at 1045 hours and the affected section was excavated for full repair. by 1630 hours a 24‑inch x 30‑inch replacement segment was welded and hydrostatic tested to 1250 psi, exceeding the operating pressure by 40 %. the line was returned to service at 1915 hours. the incident was reported to the federal energy regulatory commission at 2210 hours, and a root‑cause analysis indicated that extreme precipitation caused soil erosion and loss of support, leading to pipe sag and rupture. the company will initiate additional slope‑stability monitoring along the corridor.

at approximately 0830 hours on september 12, 2023, a severe thunderstorm produced flash flooding along the lower sabine river corridor in east texas. the rising water eroded a 30‑inch, api 5l x70 steel gas transmission main operating at 950 psig near milepost 212.5 of the southern pipeline system operated by western energy services. after the flood receded, field crews discovered a 6‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall and a venting plume of natural gas detected by a portable infrared scanner. an emergency isolation valve upstream at mlv 209.8 and a downstream valve at mlv 215.2 were automatically closed, isolating a 5‑mile segment. the incident was reported to the phmsa and the texas commission within two hours. initial damage assessment estimated a release of approximately 2,200 mcf of gas before isolation. a temporary bypass using a 24‑inch flexible hose was installed to restore limited service while a repair crew fabricated a new steel insert. the damaged pipe section was removed, a new 30‑inch api 5l x70 pipe segment was welded in place, hydrostatic tested to 1,500 psig, and returned to service at 950 psig on september 15, 2023. no injuries or property damage beyond the pipeline were reported.

on april 22, 2023, field operators for western energy systems received an automated alarm indicating a rapid pressure drop on the 24‑inch, api 5l x70 carbon steel mainline (line a) at milepost 87.4 in the black hills region of south dakota. upon arrival, the response crew found a section of the pipe exposed in a freshly formed slip scar on a steep north‑facing slope. the ground had moved approximately 4 feet downhill during an overnight snow melt combined with a sudden thunderstorm, creating a shear zone that pulled the pipe away from its supports. visual inspection revealed a 12‑inch longitudinal crack and a gouge in the pipe wall where the soil had scoured the coating. the line, operating at 850 psi and transporting 750 mmcf/d of dry natural gas, was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream block valves within 20 minutes of the alarm. after depressurizing the segment, a temporary bypass was installed using a 24‑inch stainless steel sleeve and a pressure test was performed at 1.2 times design pressure with no leaks detected. the damaged pipe segment was excavated, cut out, and a new 24‑inch api 5l x80 pipe was spliced in using a welded butt joint and a full‑length external coating system. service was restored on may 3, 2023 after successful hydrostatic testing and re‑pressurization.

on april 14, 2024 a slow‑moving mesoscale convective system produced record flooding along the lower mississippi river. the 30″ carbon steel mainline (api 5l x70) operating at 870 psi experienced rapid riverbank erosion upstream of the oak ridge valve station. by 08:45 cdt the river had undercut the pipe support at station oak‑ridge‑02, causing a 12‑inch lateral bend and a subsequent longitudinal split in the pipe wall. the automatic shutdown system detected a pressure drop to 420 psi and initiated a full line isolation; however, a small leak persisted at the bend until the downstream block valve was manually closed at 09:12 cdt. field crews arrived at the site at 10:03 cdt, confirmed a 3‑inch gash in the pipe, and installed a temporary steel sleeve and a 30‑inch slip‑on coupling to stop the release. the affected segment was excavated, the compromised pipe was cut out, and a new 30″ x 11‑mm wall thickness spool was spliced using a welded butt joint. hydrostatic testing at 1000 psi was completed on 04/16/2024 with no leaks. the line was returned to service at 06:30 cdt on 04/17/2024. a supplemental report filed 04/20/2024 notes that the flood‑induced scour was the primary factor, and recommendations include additional rip‑rap and real‑time river level monitoring for future events.

on july 12, at approximately 09:43 local time, field operations received a report from the river monitoring team that a sudden flash flood had overtopped the south bend of the rutherford creek near the 34‑inch carbon steel main (segment 4‑a, api 5l) located at milepost 212.5. the surge water eroded the supporting fill and caused a 30‑foot section of the right‑of‑way to slump, exposing the pipe and creating a 2‑foot deep trench beneath it. visual inspection from the aerial drone showed a severe dent on the 12‑o’clock position of the pipe, approximately 14 inches long, 9 inches wide and 0.7 inches deep, with a longitudinal crack about 0.8 inches in length at the low point of the dent. immediate shutdown was initiated, reducing pressure from 800 psig to 250 psig, and the isolation valve at the upstream station was closed. a rapid response team mobilized to the site, installed a temporary 8‑inch stopple and bypass, and excavated the affected segment. a custom‑fabricated repair sleeve (2‑ft by 18‑in, type‑b, high‑strength alloy) was welded over the dented area after removing the damaged coating. magnetic particle and ultrasonic testing confirmed weld integrity. after hydrostatic testing to 900 psig, the line was returned to service at normal operating pressure. no injuries, fire, or loss of service to customers were reported. the incident was attributed to flood‑induced soil displacement.

on 03-22-2023 at approximately 02:17 a.m., operators observed an unexpected drop in pressure on the 30‑inch, 50‑psi class‑3 carbon steel segment of the mid‑appalachian eastward transmission line, milepost 214.7, located in a narrow valley of the greenbrier river basin, virginia. a heavy thunderstorm earlier that night produced 4.8 inches of rain within two hours, causing the river to overflow its banks and erode the embankment supporting the right‑of‑way. field crews, dispatched at 02:45 a.m., found that a portion of the pipe had become exposed and displaced downstream by approximately 15 feet, creating a 6‑inch longitudinal split near a welded girth. natural gas was venting at an estimated rate of 2,150 mcf/d. emergency shut‑in valves were manually closed by 03:12 a.m., and the area was secured. the damaged pipe section was removed, a new 30‑inch, 12‑inch wall thickness, api 5l grade b pipe was installed, and new supports were engineered to resist future fluvial forces. after hydrostatic testing at 70 psi, the line was returned to service at 10:45 a.m. on 03‑23‑2023. the incident report was submitted to phmsa and nrc as required.

on april 14, 2024 at approximately 07:45 cd t a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70, design pressure 1500 psi) located in the lower reaches of the green river valley experienced a sudden rupture. the incident occurred after an intense 4‑hour thunderstorm that produced peak runoff of 12,000 cfs, raising the river level by more than 9 ft above flood stage. the high velocity water undermined the trench supporting the line near a 150‑ft bridge crossing, causing the pipe to sag and the longitudinal seam to separate. field crews from the operating company responded within 90 minutes and found a 32‑in longitudinal split with a visible gash of approximately 6 in. downstream pressure dropped from 1200 psi to 450 psi, triggering an automatic emergency shutdown. a temporary clamp was installed and the affected section was isolated. subsequent investigation confirmed that scour and hydraulic uplift were the primary forces leading to the seam failure. a replacement 24‑inch pipe segment with upgraded corrosion‑resistant coating was installed, the trench backfilled with riprap, and a revised flood‑plain management plan was implemented to mitigate future scour risk. the line was returned to service at 22:10 cd t.

during a routine patrol on june 3, the crew observed a newly formed washout on the right‑hand side of the riverbank where the 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line crosses the floodplain. a severe thunderstorm three days earlier had produced 5.2 in of rain in 24 hours, raising the water level 3.5 ft above normal and eroding the protective berm. the pipe, normally buried 24 in deep, was exposed for approximately 18 in before the surrounding soil slumped, leaving the coating visibly damaged and the seam at 12 o’clock position gouged. pressure on the line was 850 psi at the time of discovery; the control system automatically reduced it to 450 psi and isolated the segment with a 24‑inch block valve downstream. field engineers confirmed a 0.12‑inch crack in the longitudinal seam, likely initiated by the lateral soil movement. a hot‑tap was performed to depressurize the affected section, the damaged 30‑inch pipe segment (≈ 22 ft) was removed, and a new 30‑inch x‑80‑lb/hr api 5l pipe with a 1.5‑in thick epoxy coating was installed. after hydrostatic testing to 1500 psi and a successful pigging run, the line was returned to service. the incident was logged, and a revised flood‑risk assessment was initiated for all low‑lying crossings.

on september 22, 2025, a gas transmission line experienced a rupture near the foothills of the blue ridge mountains in davis county, virginia. the affected segment belonged to the southern energy network, llc (sen) and consisted of a 30‑inch api 5l x70 steel pipe operating at a maximum allowable pressure of 1,250 psig. a severe thunderstorm passed through the area at approximately 03:45 est, delivering hail up to 2 inches in diameter and wind gusts exceeding 70 mph. high‑velocity hail impacted a previously exposed girth weld at milepost 127.4, causing a localized loss of wall thickness and subsequent axial overload. scada recorded an abrupt pressure drop to 620 psig, triggering an automatic shut‑in of the upstream valve (sen‑101) and a manual closure of the downstream valve (sen‑102) by field operators within 12 minutes. a visible gas plume was observed for 4 minutes before ignition was prevented by the rapid isolation. emergency response teams secured the site, and the damaged pipe segment was excavated and removed for metallurgical examination. preliminary findings confirmed hail‑induced impact fatigue as the primary failure mechanism. the line remains out of service pending replacement of the compromised section and a geotechnical review of surrounding terrain.

on 6/23/22 at approximately 0830 a high‑temperature alarm was logged at the greenville compression station on the h‑500 pipeline. field crew arrived at 0915 and observed a 24‑inch, sch‑40, x‑70 steel pipe with a longitudinal gouge on the north side of the right‑of‑way. the pipe was leaking a steady stream of dry natural gas. the mainline was isolated by closing valve h‑500‑02 at 0940 and valve h‑500‑01 at 0945. a rapid‑response crew erected a temporary containment bag and initiated a gas‑shut‑down. the area was evacuated and the incident command post was established at the station. subsequent investigation revealed that a flash‑flood event from a sudden mountain‑stream overflow, triggered by a 4‑inch rain event in the upper basin, caused a debris flow that impacted the pipeline, displacing the pipe laterally by roughly 8 inches and imposing excessive bending stress. the gouge coincided with a field‑welded tee located at a 45‑degree angle, which failed under the combined axial and bending loads. the pipe segment was removed and sent for metallurgical analysis; the coating (fusion‑bonded epoxy) remained intact. repairs were completed and the line returned to service on 7/5/22 after pressure testing to 900 psi.

on september 14, 2024, offshore energy services, inc. (oes) reported a loss of pressure on a 12‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas transmission line (tgp 12‑in. line no. 702‑b) operating at 825 psi between platform delta‑3 and the on‑shore processing facility at bayou city, la. the anomaly was detected during a routine pressure check by the control room when gauge readings dropped to 460 psi within ten minutes. an aerial surveillance drone dispatched from the platform captured high‑resolution imagery of the water surface, revealing a category‑4 hurricane‑generated storm surge that had passed over the area on september 12, causing extensive wave action and seabed scouring. subsea sonar scans performed on september 15 identified a 6‑foot longitudinal gouge in the pipe wall at mile‑segment 12.3, where the pipe had been displaced laterally by approximately 2.5 ft and rested partially buried in a newly formed sand channel. the damage was classified as external force damage resulting from storm‑induced seabed movement. emergency shutdown valves were actuated, and the line was isolated at both ends. a remotely operated vehicle (rov) was deployed on september 17 to install a temporary clamp and to conduct a full visual inspection. subsequent pressure testing on september 22 confirmed a leak‑free seal, and the temporary repair will remain in service while a permanent replacement section is fabricated and scheduled for installation during the winter maintenance window. the incident was reported to the phmsa national response center and the state oil and gas commission within the required 30‑minute window.

on april 17, 2025 a series of intense thunderstorms produced over 8 inches of rain in the lower san luis valley. the resulting flash flood breached the earthen embankment protecting the west side of the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade b) that operates at 825 psig. water rapidly eroded the support trench, exposing a 45‑foot section of pipe near mlv‑12.5. at approximately 1430 hrs field crews observed a sudden drop in downstream pressure from 820 psig to 410 psig and a visible gash in the pipe wall. immediate isolation of the segment was performed by closing the upstream and downstream block valves; the downstream valve was manually locked at 1410 hrs. an emergency response team was dispatched, and a temporary steel sleeve clamp was installed to contain the leak while a water‑pump system removed floodwater from the trench. a damage assessment determined that the pipe had suffered a 1.8‑inch longitudinal tear and corrosion‑accelerated thinning at the breach point. replacement of a 60‑foot pipe section with new api 5l grade b pipe, pressure testing to 1000 psig, and re‑burial of the line were completed by april 24, 2025. post‑repair monitoring with a newly installed pressure transducer and a soil moisture sensor is now in place to detect future hydrologic impacts.

incident: rupture of 20‑inch x70 steel pipeline segment at southwest block 12, gulf of mexico date: october 14, 2023 volume released: approx. 4.2 million gallons of crude oil chronology of events : weather conditions: tropical storm felix produced sustained winds of 85 mph with gusts up to 112 mph and wave heights exceeding 15 ft. 06:13 storm surge elevated water level 3.2 ft above normal, causing seabed scouring around block 12. 07:01 automated leak detection system (alds) recorded a sudden pressure drop from 1,150 psi to 620 psi on the 20‑inch line. 07:04 control room initiated emergency shutdown (esd) and closed the main block valve. 07:12 remote operated vehicle (rov) deployed to assess damage; video showed a 3‑ft gash in the pipe wall where a sand mound had been removed by scouring. 07:28 emergency response team (ert) dispatched two containment barges and a skimmer fleet. 08:02 first responders confirmed oil plume of 0.5 mile length drifting eastward. 08:45 secondary containment boom installed; pump‑off units began transferring oil to storage vessels. initial investigations indicated that storm‑induced seabed erosion compromised pipe support, leading to the rupture. response was hampered by high seas and limited visibility, extending containment efforts until 14:30 when flow was fully stopped and leak sealed.

following a severe thunderstorm on october 14, 2023, the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (apn‑112) operating at 720 psig experienced a sudden pressure loss at the south‑central valve station near the silver creek crossing. the storm produced unprecedented rainfall, raising the creek to a record 12‑foot stage and causing rapid bank erosion. field crews later discovered that a 30‑foot section of the pipe, located 300 feet downstream of milepost 42.5, had become exposed as the supporting fill material washed away. the exposed segment was subsequently displaced by the high‑velocity water flow, resulting in a full‑coupling failure at a welded girth joint and a visible gash on the pipe wall. an all‑call was issued and the line was isolated by closing block a and block b valves at the upstream and downstream stations. emergency response teams notified the national response center and phmsa regional office. no fire, injuries, or loss of service to downstream customers occurred, but approximately 1.2 mmcf of natural gas escaped before the line was shut. repairs involved excavating 350 feet of the riverbed, installing a new 24‑inch x‑70 ft spool with a reinforced coating, and re‑backfilling with engineered support material. the incident was reported on a 7100 form, and a final cause investigation confirmed that flash flooding and consequent soil washout were the primary factors leading to the pipeline failure.

on 03/22/2024 at 09:17 the incident command center received a call from a field crew operating the midwest gas transmission system reporting a sudden pressure drop on the 12‑inch carbon steel line (api 5l x70) at milepost 245.6 in the lower ohio valley. scada indicated a loss of 560 psi from the normal operating pressure of 720 psi. heavy rainfall from the stalled convective system had caused the adjacent river to overtop its levee, resulting in rapid bank erosion and exposure of the pipeline. the crew observed a 30‑foot gash in the pipe where the soil had been washed away, with gas escaping and forming a visible vapor cloud. emergency shut‑in valves on both sides were closed within 12 minutes, isolating the segment. a 45‑minute response team from the central repair unit arrived, installed a temporary steel sleeve, and restored service to a limited pressure of 300 psi for testing. a full replacement of the damaged 12‑inch section with a new 9‑% nickel alloy pipe rated for 900 psi was completed on 03/24/2024, and the line was returned to normal operating pressure after hydrostatic testing and pigging. all affected customers were restored without interruption after the repair.

on 4/12/2026, after an intense thunderstorm produced 3.2 in of rain in the lower san joaquin valley, california, the pipeline operations team received an automated high‑pressure alarm from the scada system for the 12″ carbon steel main (line‑c, nominal pressure 1000 psig) that runs parallel to the riverbank near the town of oakdale. field crews were dispatched at 14:45 local and arrived on site at 15:20 to find a section of the pipe exposed and partially washed away where the river had undercut the bank. a gash approximately 6 in long was visible on the pipe wall, and a distinct natural gas odor was detected. the a‑valve upstream and the b‑valve downstream were manually closed by 15:45 and the line was depressurized to 150 psig. initial estimates indicated a release of roughly 9.3 mmscf of gas before isolation. the incident was reported to the nrc at 16:30 and a temporary steel sleeve was installed by the crew at 18:10 to stabilize the breach. a detailed inspection later revealed that rapid erosion and soil sloughing caused by the flood event had removed the supporting backfill, leading to the rupture. permanent replacement of the damaged 30‑ft pipe segment and re‑grading of the riverbank were scheduled for 4/19/2026, with final reinstatement completed on 4/23/2026.

at 07:12 on january 14, 2025, the control center received a high temperature alarm on the 30‑inch mainline feeding the oak ridge compression station, followed by a low pressure alarm at 07:15 on the same line. a field crew located 3 mi away reported hearing a loud cracking noise near the right‑hand side of the line. the crew was dispatched and arrived on site at 07:30. inspection revealed that a 12‑inch segment of api 5l sch‑40 carbon steel pipe, buried 2 ft below the surface, had been displaced by a sudden 45‑mph wind gust that lifted a 20‑ton section of a nearby metal storage tank that had broken free from its anchorage during a severe winter snowstorm. the displaced pipe was fractured, causing an 850 psig gas release into the surrounding area. emergency shutdown (esd) vent valves opened automatically, venting approximately 4.2 mmcf of natural gas before isolation valves were manually closed at 07:45. the incident was reported to the phmsa. repair crew installed a new 12‑inch pipe splice and replaced the anchorage system for the storage tank. service was restored at 13:20 after pressure testing and re‑commissioning.

day of discovery: on 04/22/24 a field technician conducting routine cathodic protection checks on the 30‑in carbon steel main (api 5l x65) operating at 910 psi in the green valley region noted a sudden loss of pressure on the mainline pressure transmitter. the scada alarm indicated a drop from 910 psi to 210 psi within minutes. the technician inspected the right‑of‑way and observed a 25‑ft long trench exposing the pipe where the surrounding soil had been washed away by an overnight flash‑flood. the pipe segment was fully exposed, with visible buckling and a 2‑in longitudinal split near a welded girth joint. emergency shut‑in valves upstream and downstream were closed at 13:17 local time, isolating the section. response crews arrived by 13:45 and erected a temporary containment berm to divert water. a 4‑in steel sleeve was installed and the damaged pipe was cut out and replaced with a new 30‑in line pipe with a thicker wall (0.75 in) and additional concrete backfill. investigation concluded that the flash‑flood, caused by 5 in of rainfall in 12 hours, resulted in scouring that removed support and exposed the pipe to hydraulic forces exceeding design loads, leading to the rupture. corrective actions included revising flood risk assessments, increasing burial depth from 4 ft to 6 ft in the flood‑prone corridor, installing erosion control blankets, and updating the winter‑spring monitoring program to trigger pre‑emptive water‑level surveys. the line was returned to service at 07:30 on 04/27/24 after hydrostatic testing to 1500 psi confirmed integrity.

on march 14, 2025, at approximately 0845 hrs, a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 950 psig experienced a sudden loss of pressure near milepost 112.5 in the northern ridge section of the line. the incident was traced to a high‑velocity wind event associated with a severe thunderstorm that produced gusts exceeding 80 mph. the wind caused a mature pine tree to fall onto the right‑hand side of the right‑of‑way, striking the buried 24‑inch sleeve and shearing the pipe wall of the 30‑inch main. the impact created a 6‑inch longitudinal rupture, resulting in an immediate release of gas that ignited when it contacted a nearby power line that had been downed by the same storm. emergency shutdown (esd) valves at stations 112 and 113 actuated automatically, isolating the compromised segment. response crews from the regional operations center arrived within 45 minutes, erected a temporary earthen berm to stabilize the slope, and installed a 30‑inch steel repair sleeve with a double‑welded butt joint. the line was returned to service at 1730 hrs after pressure testing to 1500 psig and confirming leak‑free integrity. the event caused a temporary service interruption for approximately 12 customers downstream pending restoration.

on june 12, 2025 at approximately 1435 hrs a 30‑inch x70 carbon steel transmission line (segment mlv‑4.27 to mlv‑5.03) located in the foothills of the susquehanna river basin experienced a full‑diameter rupture. the rupture was precipitated by a rapid landslide triggered by three days of record‑breaking precipitation that raised the nearby creek to 9.2 ft above flood stage. a downstream a‑scan aerial patrol detected a sudden pressure drop from 720 psig to 380 psig and reported a large vapor cloud emanating from the right‑of‑way. operators immediately reduced line pressure to 150 psig, isolated the affected block by closing valve 12‑b and initiated an emergency leak survey. field crews arrived within two hours and confirmed a 48‑inches long gouge in the pipe wall, exposing the pipe interior to the saturated soil mass. a temporary steel sleeve was installed on july 1, 2025 and pressure was restored to 300 psig for testing. a permanent replacement of 210 ft of pipe, including new 30‑inch x70 pipe with upgraded coating, was completed on july 22, 2025. post‑repair hydrostatic testing verified integrity at 850 psig. no injuries or offsite releases were reported. the incident was logged with phmsa and the state pipeline safety office per reporting requirements.

on 4/12/2024, northern gas services crews responded to a rupture on the 24‑inch stainless steel transmission line (pipeline id nng‑5423) located near 12th street and maple avenue in the town of linden. the incident occurred during a severe winter storm that produced a sudden snowmelt event, generating a rapid runoff that eroded the surrounding soil and created a shallow landslide. the shift in ground pressure displaced the pipeline, causing a 3‑inch crack at the weld seam. the rupture released an estimated 1.2 mscfd of natural gas into the air, creating a vapor cloud that drifted eastward.

the crews isolated the line within 12 minutes of first alarm and conducted an emergency shut‑off. a 5‑minute gas pressure drop was observed at the nearest service valve. emergency responders from the linden fire department and local police assisted with securing the area and evacuating nearby residences. no injuries were reported, and no release of hazardous chemicals occurred.

an internal investigation determined that the cause was the combined effect of rapid snowmelt, resulting soil erosion, and a pre‑existing weld defect. the incident was reported to the dot and cpu c for a release of product exceeding $100,000 and potential property damage. repairs are scheduled for 5/02/2024, with an estimated cost of $87,500, including replacement of the damaged pipe section and soil stabilization. a supplemental report will be submitted once final cost calculations are available.

on 2024‑07‑13, a record‑breaking derechos event moved across the central plains, with wind gusts exceeding 90 mph. at approximately 13:30 local time, the 24‑inch carbon steel main line of the eastern distribution pipeline, located on the ridge between block 217 and block 218, was struck by a fallen pine tree that had been uprooted by the wind. the tree dropped onto the pipe near the 150‑ft vertical rise that connects to the 24‑inch high‑pressure line, causing a 4‑inch circumferential gouge in the weld joint. the pressure in the main line at the time of the impact was 1 100 psi, and the automatic pressure relief valve at the downstream terminal was not triggered due to a brief sensor fault. a burst pipe was detected by the scada alarm at 13:38, showing a pressure drop to 300 psi and a corresponding rise in the gas flow meter readings from 2 400 to 3 400 standard cubic feet per minute. immediate shut‑off at the nearest isolation valve was performed at 13:45. field crews arrived on site by 14:12 and confirmed the breach, estimating the damaged length to be 2.5 feet. the pipe was cut and a 2‑inch pipe‑to‑pipe joint was welded in the field. a 24‑hour shutdown was imposed, and the line was pressurized to 1 200 psi during the overnight repair. on 2024‑07‑14, a pressure test at 1 400 psi confirmed the integrity of the repair, and normal service resumed at 08:30. the incident investigation found that the tree fall was consistent with the wind speed and the root zone erosion measured by the county forestry office.

on 5/9/2024, after the passage of hurricane irma, the 30" mdp pipeline segment between junction 412 and junction 428 on the south side of the bay area was found depressurized. scada alerts triggered at 14:23 local time indicated a loss of line pressure from 2000 psig to 120 psig. a crew from the west coast operations team was dispatched by 15:10 and observed extensive erosion and sediment buildup on the pipeline trench, causing the pipe to shift and rupture. the rupture point was located approximately 75 meters east of the 412 junction, where the pipe, a 2/3-inch carbon steel section fabricated in 1985, was exposed to scouring by flood waters that had surged to a depth of 3.5 meters. field data showed a maximum burst pressure of 1900 psig before failure. the incident was reported to the d.b. and the d.o. within 30 minutes of discovery. a subsequent aerial inspection on 5/11/2024 confirmed that the ruptured section had been severed, with a 4.2-meter length of pipe detached and displaced downstream by the flood flow. repairs are currently underway, with a temporary pressure hold set at 1500 psig while the damaged segment is replaced with a 4-inch seamless steel pipe. no injuries were reported. the estimated property damage is under review, pending a final cost analysis.

on 08/12/2024, at approximately 04:45 am mountain time, a 12‑inch api 5l x65 natural gas transmission line (segment 42b‑68) located in the valley of the river bend experienced a sudden rupture. the line, installed in 2012 at a depth of 4.5 ft, was operating at a maximum operating pressure of 720 psig. intense precipitation had produced a rapid rise in the adjacent river, with water levels exceeding 12 ft above normal, leading to a scouring event that removed 3 ft of protective backfill. the resulting soil subsidence caused a 1.2‑inch longitudinal bend in the pipe, exceeding the 0.5‑inch allowable deformation. a pressure‑reducing valve upstream sensed a pressure drop from 720 psig to 120 psig and automatically opened a relief valve to atmosphere. the relief valve operated for 15 min, releasing an estimated 2,300 mcf of gas. the incident was classified as reportable. immediate actions included closing the upstream isolation valve, shutting the compressor unit 3‑line, and deploying a trenching crew. the damaged pipe section was cut, replaced with a new 12‑inch api 5l x65 segment, and the line was re‑injected after pressure testing to 750 psig. post‑incident monitoring installed a vibration sensor on the repaired section to detect future ground‑movement events.

on the night of september 15, 2024, hurricane iota produced sustained winds exceeding 120 mph and a 2‑ft storm surge along the coast of florida. the surge displaced a section of the 16‑inch carbon steel pipeline that ran parallel to state highway 30. the displaced earth and vegetation collided with the line, creating a gouge of approximately 3 feet in diameter in the pipe at mile marker 112.2. the gouge exposed the 800 psig operating pressure to the environment, causing a sudden pressure drop to 200 psig. the emergency shut‑off valve 1122‑3, located 12 ft upstream, closed within 0.8 seconds. however, the rapid depressurization triggered the downstream relief valve 1122‑5, which opened at 650 psig to vent the excess pressure, releasing about 15 % of the line’s contents into the surrounding floodplain. inspection revealed a 2‑inch longitudinal crack in the 16‑inch pipe that extended 18 inches along the line, likely initiated by the impact. no personnel were injured, but the incident resulted in a reportable spill of 1,200 gallons of natural gas liquids.

in the aftermath of the 6/12/2025 magnitude‑7.2 earthquake, a section of the 8‑inch carbon steel main operating at 1400 psi in the canyon foothills of the redwoods suffered a sudden fracture. the seismic event induced a 4‑foot landslide that displaced the 200‑ft horizontal run, causing the pipe to bend over 25°. the bend produced a local stress concentration that broke a 10‑inch diameter section of the pipe at the welded joint, exposing a 2‑inch diameter break. the rupture was discovered when a downstream pressure transmitter registered a sharp drop from 1300 psi to 200 psi within seconds, triggering the automatic shutdown of the upstream line. divers and a portable crane were dispatched the next morning to inspect the site; they found the fractured pipe lay in a 10‑foot deep mud pit, with surrounding soil saturated from the recent heavy rains. the damage was assessed as being caused by the combined effects of the earthquake‑induced landslide and the saturated ground conditions, which reduced the soil’s shear strength and allowed the pipe to move freely. the repair involved cutting the damaged section, installing a 8‑inch forged steel sleeve, and re‑welding the ends under pressure‑testing conditions of 1400 psi. the line was brought back online after 12 days of closure, and a post‑repair inspection confirmed no residual cracks.

on march 5, 2025, a ruptured section of the 30‑inch stainless steel segment of line 4‑b, operated by northern pipelines, llc, was reported near the raptor ridge in montgomery county, texas. the rupture coincided with a moderate magnitude 4.8 earthquake that occurred at 02:14 am local time. seismic records indicate a vertical acceleration of 0.35 g and horizontal displacement of 12 cm across the pipeline route. the affected pipe, rated for 6500 psi, had a wall thickness of 0.75 inches and a 12‑month inspection history with no previous defects. upon receipt of the alarm, field crews immediately isolated the line by closing valves 4‑b‑02 and 4‑b‑03 at the upstream control station and capping the downstream end with a temporary plug. the fracture, located approximately 0.8 miles east of the town of cullens, showed a circumferential tear 3 inches in length and a 1‑inch crack propagating along the weld seam. a metallurgical examination revealed localized plastic deformation consistent with dynamic loading from the seismic event. a pressure transient study confirmed a peak internal pressure of 6700 psi at the time of rupture, exceeding the design pressure by 300 psi due to a rapid pressure surge caused by the ground motion. the line has been placed out of service pending a comprehensive repair program that will include a 6‑month replacement of the affected 30‑inch segment and a seismic retrofit of the surrounding infrastructure. a preliminary cost estimate for the repair and associated shutdown is $3.2 million, with an expected restoration date of august 12, 2025.

during a severe thunderstorm on 12 august 2025, a 12‑inch wrought‑iron transmission line crossing the riverbank experienced an explosive failure. the line, rated for 1400 psig and made of 4130 steel, was struck by a wind‑driven debris pile that hit the support pier. the impact created a 30‑inch longitudinal crack, allowing 1500 psig gas to escape. the immediate pressure drop triggered the adjacent pressure‑recovery valve to trip, but the rupture was already beyond the relief valve capacity. fire crews were dispatched at 04:15 a.m. and used a 30‑foot ladder to reach the broken pipe. they applied a hydraulic clamp to contain the leak and deployed a 20‑meter chain‑link cage to shield the exposed line. by 07:42 a.m. the crew had stabilized the breach with a 3‑inch sleeve and restored the valve to normal operation. meanwhile, a mobile monitoring unit detected a 12

on july 12, 2024, a 24‑inch stainless‑steel natural gas transmission line operated by midwest pipelines, located in the valley of the concho river, suffered a rupture at the river crossing near mile marker 57. the incident occurred during a record‑breaking thunderstorm that produced a 5‑inch runoff, elevating the river to 15 ft above the pipe crown. high‑velocity water scoured the concrete bridge abutments, displacing the anchor bolts that supported the pipe supports. as the pipe sagged, the 3,500‑psi pressure in the line caused a sudden break at the support joint, releasing a plume of gas that ignited on the downstream side of the crossing.

system control logged a pressure drop alarm at 13:04, followed by a surge alarm at 13:06. field crews, arriving at 13:20, found the pipe severed and the downstream flare line inoperative. the ruptured section was isolated and a 48‑hour shutdown was implemented while a temporary repair was installed. subsequent hydraulic and visual inspections confirmed the failure was due to scour, not corrosion or weld defect. a temporary pipe splice was installed and the line was brought back online after pressure testing at 3,200 psi. the incident report recommended reinforcement of the abutment anchor system and installation of a scour monitoring sensor.

the 20‑inch 48‑year‑old steel pipeline crossing the river was operating at 950 psi when the region experienced a category 5 hurricane with peak winds of 165 mph. a sudden storm surge raised the river level by 6 ft and caused a large wave to impinge on the pipeline supports, resulting in a sudden deflection of the pipe. inspection crews noted a 2‑inch gouge on the pipe wall near the third support span, and subsequent pressure tests revealed a pressure drop from 950 to 380 psi, indicating a rupture. the emergency isolation valve at wellhead 12 was actuated and the line was shut off. a remote monitoring system reported a 0.5‑g pressure loss and the alarm system triggered an automatic shutdown of the compressor station. the ruptured section was isolated, and a retrieval team was dispatched to cut the pipe and retrieve the debris. no personnel were injured and the spill was contained within the riverbank. the pipeline was scheduled for a full integrity assessment and eventual repair within 48 hours.

after the passage of hurricane harvey, a 20‑inch, 2000‑psi high‑pressure natural gas line running beneath the gulf of mexico near the oilfield of atlantis was observed to have a circumferential crack in a 1‑inch weld joint of a 20‑inch carbon‑steel pipe. the damage was first noted during an automated pressure‑drop alarm triggered by the control room at 14:12 local time. subsequent inspection by a remotely operated vehicle confirmed a 3‑inch long, 0.25‑inch deep fissure in the weld, which was likely caused by a combination of wave‑induced torsional loading and the buoyant lift of a 10‑foot floating platform that had been dislodged by the storm surge. the valve at the downstream end of the segment was closed within 45 minutes of the alarm to isolate the section. divers were dispatched the next day and were able to retrieve a sample of the cracked weld material for metallurgical analysis. the pipe was replaced using a 20‑inch, 25‑mm wall carbon‑steel pipe, installed with a 1‑inch pipe‑to‑pipe butt weld, and the line was brought back to service after a pressure‑test at 1500 psi. the incident report notes that the damage was attributed to the severe wind and wave forces of the hurricane, and that no personnel were injured.

on july 15, 2024, at approximately 14:32 hrs. local time, a moderate 5.4 magnitude earthquake triggered a rapid slope collapse north of the springfield intersection. the debris avalanche struck a 24‑inch diameter, schedule 80 steel line (line 14) carrying natural gas at 9,500 psi. the impact fractured the pipe approximately 3.2 feet from the upstream pressure regulator, creating a 6‑inch circumferential breach. pressure drop at the downstream gauge fell from 9,400 to 2,600 psi within 12 seconds. the automatic control system triggered a 2‑1/2 inch shut‑off valve at the west‑bound segment, but the valve remained partially open due to the sudden load. emergency crews arrived within 4 minutes, closed the nearest 4‑inch remote shut‑off located 2.6 miles upstream, and deployed a field‑based manual shut‑off at the breach site. a 12‑mile segment of the line was vented over a controlled vent stack to mitigate overpressure. the incident was reported to the state regulator within 30 minutes; the event log number is 2024‑07‑15‑q1. inspection crews are scheduled to perform a full stress analysis and plan for replacement with a 24‑inch schedule 160 alloy line. the pipe material was carbon steel (api 5l x65).

after a severe flash‑flood event, a 16‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas line (line 23b‑405) located along the floodplain of the river valley experienced a sudden rupture. field crew reported a 2‑inch crack forming at the flange between the upstream 16‑inch section and the downstream 12‑inch extension. pipeline pressure fell from 2800 psig to near zero within 12 seconds, prompting an immediate shut‑off of the emergency isolation valve. downstream and upstream sections were isolated, and the damaged segment was isolated for inspection. divers observed that the surrounding trench had deepened to 6 feet, exposing the flange and causing a scouring failure of the weld joint. the joint was removed and a new 16‑inch forged pipe was installed, re‑flanged with a 3‑inch expansion joint and a 1‑inch anchor bolt assembly to resist future scour. pressure testing at 3000 psig confirmed integrity, and the line was returned to service after a 12‑hour shut‑down. the incident was attributed to scour and erosion caused by the flash‑flood.
