a 15‑ton bulldozer operated by a municipal road crew for lane widening struck a buried 6‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas pipeline at a depth of 3 ft. the vehicle’s hydraulic blade, moving at roughly 10 mph, displaced enough soil to fracture the pipe in a 2‑inch opening about 8 ft from the surface. the operating pressure of the line was 600 psi and the rupture caused a rapid drop to 200 psi within seconds, producing a small gas plume that was detected by the automatic shut‑off sensors. the crew immediately isolated the segment, shut the control valves, and depressurized the line to 50 psi before a 10‑ton crane was brought in to lift the bulldozer off the pipe. no fire or explosion occurred. a gas‑detection team verified that no gas escaped beyond the rupture zone. the damaged pipe section was marked and a 12‑inch steel sleeve was installed to contain the leak until a permanent repair could be performed. the pipeline operator placed a temporary bypass valve in line, re‑pressurized the system to 500 psi, and scheduled a full inspection. the incident is under investigation by the state department of transportation and the local fire department.

on february 14, 2025, at approximately 13:27 local time, a nearby construction site’s 12‑inch carbon steel pipeline, operating at a design pressure of 6000 psi, sustained a 4‑foot circumferential rupture during a sudden, severe storm event. the storm produced a rapid, 25‑inch per hour rainfall rate that triggered a mudslide on the adjacent slope of the green valley road. the resulting debris flow, estimated at 15,000 cubic meters, slammed into the pipe at a single point, lifting the pipe from its supports and causing a shear failure along the weld seam. the rupture exposed a 0.75‑inch throat of the pipe, releasing approximately 200 barrels of natural gas into the surrounding wetland ecosystem. field crews reported the pipe’s external diameter had been reduced from the nominal 12 inches to 10.5 inches due to the gouging. after initial containment, the gas flow was throttled to 200 psi, and a 10‑meter segment of the pipe was extracted for replacement. the incident was reported to the state environmental agency and the incident investigation team was dispatched at 14:30. the surrounding vegetation was cleared, and a temporary concrete berm was erected to stabilize the slope prior to pipeline restoration.

the incident occurred near the coastal ridge of the western seacoast, 12 miles offshore from the port of newport. the 48-inch steel pipeline, rated at 3000 psi, was in service transporting natural gas at 2750 psi. a 45‑tonne container ship was making a routine berth adjustment when a misaligned mooring line became entangled in the pipeline's support footing. the ship's engine was turned on to relieve tension on the line, causing a 4.5‑m swing that pulled the line 8 meters into the pipe, puncturing the outer jacket and creating a 25‑cm breach. at the time of the breach, the pipeline temperature was 120 c and the gas mixture was 75% methane with 25% ethane. pressure dropped to 1400 psi within 30 seconds, triggering the automatic shut‑off system. the crew of the ship attempted to release the line, but the weight of the anchor chain prevented immediate separation. emergency response units arrived within 15 minutes, isolated the segment, and performed a temporary repair using a 48-inch steel sleeve. the pipe was later inspected by a third‑party surveyor who confirmed that the damage was solely due to the external mooring line and not related to any internal fault or operational error. the incident was reported to the regulatory agency within 8 hours.

the incident occurred on july 5, 2024, when a 36‑inch carbon steel pipeline transporting natural gas at 1,200 psi on the north slope of the hill was struck by a large oak tree that had been uprooted by a severe windstorm. the impact severed the pipe at the flange assembly and caused a 20‑foot fracture. the gas leak was detected by the automatic shutdown system at 9:15 am, and the line was isolated within 30 minutes. emergency crews arrived by 10:00 am, used a hydraulic cutter to sever the remaining pipe, and deployed a 1‑inch steel replacement section with a 180‑degree joint. the pressure was gradually restored to 1,100 psi over the next four hours. the surrounding vegetation was inspected; a root system of the oak measured 15 ft in depth and had compromised a 4‑ft trench where the pipe lay. the incident was reported to the state regulator, and the company completed a root‑removal project and installed a root‑exclusion fence. the pipeline was back in service by 6:00 pm local time, with no injuries and $35,000 in repair costs.

on april 12, 2024, a 12‑inch steel transmission line located in the south‑west quadrant of the state’s high‑pressure corridor experienced a sudden rupture at approximately 2:15 pm. the line, operating at 2000 psi, was under a 12‑mile stretch between the town of linden and the coastal terminal. upon arrival, the field crew noted a 3‑inch diameter hole in the pipe where the outer diameter had been scored by a nearby construction excavator that had been operating a hydraulic backhoe in the right‑of‑way. the backhoe operator had been engaged in a utility relocation project that involved digging a trench adjacent to the pipeline corridor. the pipe was originally scheduled for a routine integrity assessment earlier that day; however, the excavation had inadvertently lifted a section of the buried conduit, exposing a vulnerable segment that had not yet been inspected. the damage caused an uncontrolled release of gas at the 2000‑psi operating pressure. the crew immediately isolated the section by shutting the upstream isolation valve and performed a pressure‑test of the remaining line, which confirmed that the system remained intact. a 2‑mile length of 12‑inch pipe was replaced and the line was brought back into service after a thorough inspection and a re‑insertion of the new pipe. the incident was reported to the state regulatory agency and a temporary protective berm was constructed around the damaged area to prevent future accidental contact by construction equipment.

on april 12, 2025, at 3:45 pm, the regional gas transmission company (rgtc) received a phone call from a local county sheriff’s office about a suspected collision involving a school bus on county road 27 near milepost 42.4. the bus, traveling at an estimated speed of 55 mph, had lost traction on a sudden patch of ice, veered left, and struck the buried 30-inch polyethylene mainline of rgtc’s 12-inch service line. the impact caused a 6‑inch gouge and a 2‑inch diameter rupture on the pipe, resulting in a rapid release of natural gas at a line pressure of 260 psig.

rgtc dispatch crews arrived on scene at 4:12 pm, isolated the affected segment between valve 45 and valve 48, and shut the upstream 8-inch valve to prevent further flow. pressure was reduced to 120 psig before a controlled vent was executed at 4:45 pm, relieving approximately 4.6 mmcf of gas. at 5:30 pm, an engineer confirmed that the rupture had been contained, and a temporary repair pipe was installed using a 4‑inch coupler and epoxy sealant. the line was brought back into service at 11:15 am on april 13, 2025, after a full integrity test. the county fire department noted no injuries, and the bus driver was transported to a nearby medical center for evaluation. a formal incident report was filed with the state environmental agency by april 15, 2025.

details from the operations log (12/04/2023 10:12 am to 12/04/2023 12:47 pm): at 10:15 am a municipal construction crew was excavating near the hwy 52 overpass to install a new storm drainage system. the crew was working in an area marked with temporary signage indicating proximity to a 10-inch schedule 80 steel natural gas line. at 10:28 am, a contractor’s backhoe arm struck the pipe, creating a 3/8 inch transverse breach. the breach caused an immediate drop in line pressure from 760 psig to 125 psig and a rapid gas release that produced a faint odor but no ignition. local emergency services were alerted at 10:35 am by a resident who observed the plume. within 2 minutes, the crew reported the incident to the gas company dispatch via radio. at 10:40 am, line shut‑off valves 12-0 and 12-0x were closed by remote control to isolate the segment. the gas company’s on‑site crew arrived at 10:55 am with a pressure relief valve and a portable line repair kit. by 11:20 am, the damaged section was capped with a 6-inch quick‑fit sleeve assembly, and the pressure had stabilized at 760 psig. a temporary shut‑in was maintained while the crew performed a pressure test at 11:45 am, confirming no leaks. the pipe segment was replaced on 12/07/2023 with a new 10-inch schedule 80 pipe, welded and pressure tested to 1100 psig. the incident was logged as a third‑party excavation injury, and the contractor received a safety citation.

a 30‑inch api 5l x70 steel natural gas line that runs from the east side of town a to the west side of town b experienced a rupture when a construction bulldozer struck the trench near mile marker 12.3 on 2024‑09‑21 at 11:07 a.m. est. the line was operating at 360 psi when the incident occurred. a crew from local utility company arrived within 15 minutes, isolated the affected segment, and secured the gas release. approximately 2,000 ft³ of natural gas escaped, prompting a temporary closure of the adjacent highway from 11:20 a.m. to 12:05 p.m. the utility replaced the damaged 30‑inch pipe section with a new api 5l x70 segment, welded with a 2‑inch joint, and restored service at 2:30 p.m. the post‑repair inspection found the damage caused by the bulldozer’s track digging into the pipe trench. the incident was reported to the state regulatory authority within 24 hours, and the utility issued a public safety notice to the affected community.

on the morning of march 3, 2025, a heavy construction crane operator mistakenly struck a 16‑inch carbon steel natural gas transmission line located in block 302, north of townsville. the impact created a 4‑inch radial breach in the 12‑inch casing, exposing the 950‑psi gas flow. within two minutes of the impact, the crew detected a sharp hissing sound and a faint odor of gas. the field supervisor immediately initiated a shutdown of the line by closing the nearest pressure control valve. the crew notified the local dispatch center at 09:12 and requested a rapid response from the regional gas safety team. by 09:45 the gas pipeline was fully shut down and a 1,000‑foot segment of the line was isolated. emergency responders established a 400‑foot exclusion zone and began an evacuation of the nearby residential area. by 10:30 the gas leak had stopped and a temporary sealant was applied to the damaged section. a full leak test was conducted at 14:00, confirming the leak was closed. a temporary shut‑in valve was installed until the line could be fully repaired. the repair crew began work at 18:00, replacing the damaged 16‑inch pipe segment. the line was brought back online at 23:00 after a pressure test at 800 psi confirmed integrity. the incident was reported to the regulatory agency on 04/01/2025.

on march 14, 2025, southwestern interstate energy corp (si ec) 36‑inch x 3500 psi stainless steel line #4054 in north dakota experienced an accidental break during a routine road maintenance project. the line was located beneath state highway 15, approximately 400 m east of the town of fargo. at 09:12 am local time, a heavy‑duty hydraulic excavator used by the state department of transportation was operating on the roadway shoulder. the operator inadvertently struck a 2‑foot high concrete retaining wall adjacent to the pipeline. the impact transmitted a force of approximately 2.5 kips to the wall, causing a 3‑inch diameter gouge in the pipe wall at the junction of the 4‑inch pig leg. at 09:18 am, the automatic pressure control valve (apcv) on section 4054‑01 shut in at 3 250 psi, triggering a partial loss of pressure. at 09:23 am, the pipeline monitoring system reported a drop in pressure to 2 100 psi and a rise in differential pressure across the valve. the on‑site operator crew mobilized the incident response team and notified the state emergency dispatch. by 09:45 am, a crew of 8 engineers from si ec arrived and performed a visual inspection; the gouged area was identified. by 10:07 am, the pipe was isolated, and the pig leg was sealed with a temporary weld. at 10:30 am, a 2‑ton jackhammer crew from the state department of transportation ceased all excavation operations and cleared the area. at 11:15 am, the pipe was inspected by a licensed welding inspector, who approved a 50‑ft weld repair. the repair was completed by 12:30 pm, and the line was re‑pressurised to 3 500 psi under controlled conditions. the incident was reported to the national regulator within 24 hours, and a post‑incident investigation found that the force from the excavator impact was the sole cause of the pipeline damage. no secondary failures or corrosion issues were identified.

on october 27, 2024 at approximately 0945 hours, a construction crew at the new city park expansion site inadvertently struck a buried 12‑inch schedule 40 steel natural gas transmission line located beneath the future playground area. the line was operating at 350 psi and had a 1.5‑inch internal diameter weld‑neck connection to a 12‑inch elbow that was installed in 2002. the incident occurred when a jackhammer operator used an oversized attachment to break a concrete slab that had been laid over the pipeline without prior coordination with the gas company. upon impact, the pipe cracked at the 3‑inch weld joint, causing an immediate release of natural gas into the surrounding soil. gas was detected by the pipeline operator’s pressure sensors at 100 psi loss within 2 minutes, triggering an automatic isolation of the affected segment. emergency response crews sealed the leak with a field‑rated epoxy patch and performed a full hydrostatic test on the entire 1‑mile segment. the incident was reported to the state energy regulator and the local fire department. no injuries or casualties were reported, and the pipeline was brought back to service within 7 hours after a complete leak‑repair and pressure verification.

on 14/03/2025, a sudden heavy rainfall triggered a localized mudslide that swept across the 6‑inch diameter steel pipeline carrying natural gas at 1,200 psi, causing a rupture near the 4.2‑km mark from the main valve. the pipeline, constructed of 6‑inch seamless carbon steel with a 0.045‑inch wall thickness, had been operating at 1,250 psi prior to the event. the mudslide impacted the pipe, gouging the external surface and severing the weld at a 30‑degree joint. the leak released approximately 3,000 cubic feet of gas per minute, which was immediately detected by the scada system and isolated by the pressure control valve. the incident led to a temporary shutdown and required replacement of a 50‑foot segment and rehabilitation of the surrounding right‑of‑way. the investigation revealed no corrosion or material failure; the damage was solely due to the external force of the mudslide.

on september 12, 2024, at 04:37 am, a small barge was conducting a routine dredging operation in the lower basin of the tennessee river when its propulsion system malfunctioned, causing the vessel to drift downstream. the barge's anchor chain collided with the 8‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas pipeline owned by southeastern energy, which was operating at a design pressure of 850 psi and had a nominal pipe size of 8‑inch, schedule 80. the impact severed the pipe at the 152‑meter mark from the upstream control valve. the resulting rupture caused a sudden depressurization to ambient pressure, releasing approximately 15,000 cubic feet of natural gas per minute. within 12 seconds, an audible sonic boom was detected by nearby monitoring sensors, and the gas ignited due to the presence of an open flame from a nearby construction site. the fire spread along a 10‑meter stretch of the pipeline before being extinguished by the local fire department at 04:52 am. southeastern energy dispatched a field crew at 05:10 am to isolate the damaged segment by shutting down the upstream and downstream valves; the upstream valve was closed at 05:22 am and the downstream valve at 05:29 am. the damaged section was replaced with a 4‑inch by 12‑inch welded segment and the line was placed back in service at 09:45 am on the same day. no injuries were reported, but the incident triggered a temporary shutdown of the 48‑mile corridor of the main trunkline pending a safety review.

7/22/2024 02:12 - seismic event magnitude 5.6 detected by local seismograph near ridge line. 02:15 - rockslide displaced 30 ft of 10" schedule 80 steel pipeline, causing a sudden drop in pressure gauge from 3,500 psi to 120 psi. 02:20 - field crew alerted via radio, control center receives automatic alarm. 02:25 - control center initiates emergency shutdown sequence, pipeline shut off at 02:30. 02:35 - remote monitoring confirms rupture at 30' mark, no gas detected in downstream line. 02:45 - emergency response team dispatched from nearest dispatch center. 03:05 - field crew arrives on scene, confirms rupture and gas leak near the displaced rock. 03:20 - crew deploys emergency gas containment vent, isolates the line, and begins leak suppression. 04:10 - hydrant placed for pressure relief, 5% of line temporarily shut. 05:00 - line isolated, incident investigation team begins damage assessment. 06:30 - restoration crew installs a 10" steel splice, performs pressure testing at 2,500 psi, verifies integrity. 08:45 - line brought back online at 4,200 psi, 09:30 - post-incident report filed, all personnel cleared to resume normal operations.

on 7/23/22 at around 9:15am a construction crew operating a compact excavator on the westbound side of 45th street, chicago, struck a buried 30‑inch diameter low‑pressure (12 psi) steel transmission line that had been installed in 1978. the excavator's hydraulic arm broke the trench walls and displaced the pipe by approximately 2 feet, creating a severe external gouge. the impact caused a sudden rupture of the 30‑inch line, releasing a large volume of condensate and natural gas into the surrounding area. the line's pressure monitoring system triggered an automatic shut‑off at the nearest regulator station, limiting the initial pressure to 8 psi. emergency crews from the state energy department responded within 10 minutes, evacuated the vicinity, and sealed the ruptured section with a temporary weld and pressure‑testing rig. the incident resulted in no injuries but a significant environmental release that required a 5‑mile air quality monitoring and soil sampling program. following the investigation, the pipeline operator installed a 10‑foot high steel guardrail along the street and required all future excavations within 50 feet of the line to use a pipe‑tracking device. the pipeline was repaired, re‑injected, and returned to service after a comprehensive integrity test at 15 psi.

on april 12 2025 at about 14:25 local time, a construction crew using a 20-ton crane to erect a new loading dock at the south side of the freight terminal inadvertently swung a 3-foot radius boom across a buried 36-inch diameter carbon steel pipeline carrying natural gas from the west terminal to the east terminal. the boom struck the pipe approximately 50 feet from the south terminus, creating a 4-inch longitudinal fracture at 2800 psig. a gas leak was detected by the automated pressure monitoring system at 14:28 and the emergency shutoff valve at the nearest control station was closed within 3 minutes. the pipeline was isolated at the west terminal shutoff and at the east terminal flare stack. the gas pressure dropped from 2800 psig to 0 psig within 12 minutes, and a vapor cloud was detected over a 200-acre area. emergency responders arrived within 15 minutes. the incident was reported to the state regulator at 15:02. a field crew from the gas company performed a rapid pressure test, confirming a fracture size of 4 inches. a temporary repair using a 3/4-inch weld and a 10-foot splice was installed at 16:30 and the pipeline was brought back to service at 20:15 after a pressure test of 2800 psig was successful. the company notified the local authorities and the incident was investigated as part of the annual compliance audit.

on march 12, 2024, at approximately 3:45 p.m., a 55‑tonne cargo truck lost control while turning at a grade crossing on highway 48 near the town of ridgefield. the vehicle collided with a 30‑inch carbon‑steel natural gas pipeline (material: 4340 steel, nominal wall thickness 1.25 inches) that operated at a design pressure of 3,500 psi and a flow rate of about 4,200 mmcf/d. impact from the truck sheared a 2.5‑inch segment of the pipe, creating an opening that released natural gas at the design pressure into the surrounding grassland.

energy transfer’s (et) on‑site safety team was notified at 3:48 p.m. by the local highway patrol. by 4:12 p.m. the et emergency response crew isolated the upstream section of the 30‑inch line at a 12‑inch isolation valve, and the downstream side was shut off at the nearest 8‑inch valve. a rapid pressure test confirmed a residual pressure of 1,200 psi in the upstream section.

the crews conducted a controlled blowdown from 4:30 to 5:20 p.m., venting approximately 0.85 mmcf of gas, followed by a 6‑inch trench cut to expose the damaged segment. a 2.5‑inch cut‑and‑plug repair was performed using a 30‑inch steel pipe splice, pressure tested at 3,200 psi, and the line was brought back to service at 7:15 p.m.

et submitted the incident report to the nrc and completed a 48‑hour follow‑up notification. the total gas lost was estimated at 1.12 mmcf, including 0.27 mmcf from the blowdown and 0.85 mmcf from the rupture. the incident was attributed to the external vehicle collision.

in the early hours of march 14th, a 10‑inch schedule 80 stainless steel pipeline running beneath the northbound lane of the interstate was struck by the boom of a crane operating on the adjacent right‑of‑way. the crane had been lifting a 40‑ton concrete block from a temporary support structure when a mis‑alignment in the hydraulic system caused the boom to swing 3 feet into the pipeline’s centerline. at the time of impact, the line was operating at 1,200 psi and transporting crude oil at a flow rate of 6,500 bbl/day. the collision produced a 6‑inch deep gouge along the pipeline’s outer surface, and the pipe was severed, creating a 3‑foot long fracture. the sudden loss of pressure dropped the line to 20 psi, triggering a rapid release of hydrocarbons into the surrounding soil. fire suppression crews were dispatched within 12 minutes, and the spill was contained by a perimeter of sandbags and a temporary vapor‑capture system. a field inspection revealed the steel was at 98 % of its design strength, but the impact had compromised the weld integrity, necessitating a complete pipe replacement. the incident was reported to the state regulatory agency the following day.

on july 14, 2024, at approximately 10:45 a.m., a storm‑induced landslide displaced a section of a 12‑inch steel natural gas transmission line running parallel to county road 42 in marshall county. the pipeline, rated at 4,200 psi and constructed of carbon steel with an average wall thickness of 0.5 inches, was at the time of the event carrying natural gas at 3,600 psi. a large mass of saturated soil and vegetation moved down the slope, colliding with the exposed pipe. the impact sheared a 2‑inch diameter section of the pipe, creating a 9‑inch longitudinal crack that caused a rapid release of gas into the surrounding air. emergency crews arrived within 8 minutes, isolated the damaged section by closing the adjacent 5‑and‑10‑bay valves, and evacuated the area. the leak was detected by a gas monitoring system that triggered an alarm at 10:53 a.m. after measuring 0.5% of natural gas in the atmosphere. no ignition occurred, and there were no injuries. temporary repair was performed using a welded steel sleeve and a 12‑inch pressure testing at 3,000 psi, which successfully stopped the leak. the incident was investigated by the state gas board; the cause was attributed to a sudden landslide event with no prior warning signs. no regulatory violations were identified, and the pipeline was restored to service on july 16, 2024 after a full pressure test at 4,200 psi.

on 7/28/2023, a sudden heavy rainstorm caused a flash flood in the valley where the 18‑inch api 5l grade b pipeline runs through a cut. the rapid influx of water displaced a segment of the road above the pipeline, and the weight of the moving water and debris accelerated the concrete retaining wall. when the wall failed, the sudden loss of support caused a 12‑inch segment of the pipe to pivot and contact the surrounding rock. the impact ruptured the pipe at a weld on the 12‑inch section, releasing approximately 1,200 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. field crews arrived at 09:30 a.m., isolated the section with the portable shut‑off valve, and began an inspection. hydraulic testing of the adjacent 18‑inch pipe at 380 psi revealed a crack on the upstream flange, likely from the same impact. the gas was recovered with the flaring system, and a temporary repair using a 12‑inch api 5l sleeve was installed. a full root‑cause analysis was initiated. a 30‑day report was filed under nrc reference 2023‑0045. the pipeline was back in service by 20:00 local time.

on february 3, 2023, at approximately 3:12pm, a 30‑inch carbon‑steel transmission line operating at 1,400 psi in the south‑east quadrant of the county near the intersection of county road 27 and maple avenue suffered a rupture. the line ran through a privately owned orchard when a tractor with a 12‑tonne loader jack lifted a mature oak tree that had grown too close to the pipeline. the tree limb, weighing roughly 1,200 pounds, detached and struck the pipe, causing a 4‑inch circumferential breach at the weld joint. the impact caused an instantaneous release of gas, with a burst plume traveling approximately 250 feet before being extinguished by a nearby water tower. emergency crews from the state gas authority responded within 5 minutes, shutting the valve at 6:05pm and mobilizing a containment team to the site. the incident was documented by the county environmental agency, and a preliminary report indicated no ignition and no injuries. a preliminary investigation confirmed the fault was due to the tree limb impact, not a pipeline defect. the site remains closed pending a full forensic analysis of the weld and surrounding vegetation.

a tractor operated by a local farmer crossed a section of the state highway adjacent to the 30‑inch steel gas line owned by midwest energy, causing a shallow trench to collapse onto the pipeline. the vehicle’s wheel spiked a buried metal stake that penetrated the pipe about 15 feet from the nearest inspection valve. the pipe, rated 1000 psi and constructed of carbon steel with a 3/8‑in. internal coating, was pressurized at 680 psi at the time of impact. as the pipe cracked, a burst of high‑pressure gas escaped, spraying over a 200‑foot radius. emergency crews from the county fire department and the state hazardous materials team arrived within 8 minutes, isolated the nearest isolation valve, and performed a controlled blowdown of the 30‑inch section. the damaged segment was cut out and replaced with a new 30‑inch, 1/4‑in. schedule 40 pipe, welded, and inspected using a 4‑in. inspection tool. the line was purged with nitrogen, re‑pressurized to 680 psi, and a pressure test of 850 psi was performed to confirm integrity. no injuries were reported, and the gas supply to the adjacent residential area was restored after the 2‑hour shut‑off period. the incident was reported to the phmsa under 49 cfr 191.5(a)(3).

on july 12, 2024, at 08:45 eastern standard time, midwest energy transmission, inc. dispatch center received an emergency call from local county police regarding a collision between a delivery truck and an abandoned 16‑inch carbon steel pipeline located at milepost 53.2 on the south side of the county line. the truck, carrying a load of lumber, had been diverted onto the right of way due to construction activity and lost control during a wet skid, striking the pipeline. field crew from midwest energy transmission, inc. arrived at 09:10 and observed a 12‑foot gash in the pipe, with a rupture at approximately 1470 psi operating pressure. a pressure drop to 430 psi was noted within 15 seconds, and a burst of liquid condensate was observed. the crew immediately shut down the segment using the remote shutdown valve at 09:15 and isolated the upstream line with a field‑installed 1/4 inch safety valve. a 20‑ton crane was deployed to remove the damaged section, and a temporary splice was installed to restore flow. the incident was reported to the national incident reporting system (nrc report no. 2024-07-12-001) and a 48‑hour update was filed by 10:45. engineering assessment determined the collision had breached the pipeline wall due to the high impact velocity, and a replacement of the 16‑inch pipe segment was ordered. the segment was de‑commissioned and the pipeline was scheduled for restart on july 24, 2024 after full testing.

on april 12, 2024, at approximately 9:45 am, a construction crew working on a new streetcar line across the old industrial district inadvertently displaced a 30‑foot section of a 20‑inch high‑density polyethylene (hdpe) natural gas transmission line. the line, operated by acme gas transmission company and operating at 850 psi, was buried under a 4‑foot layer of asphalt at the intersection of 5th street and river avenue. as the crew lowered a hydraulic jack onto the roadway, a section of the jack’s support beam slid and struck the pipe, creating a longitudinal crack that resulted in an immediate gas leak.

the crew shut down the line and contacted the local fire department at 9:58 am. emergency services arrived within 7 minutes, isolated the affected segment, and depressurised the line to 200 psi before the leak was fully contained. a bypass was installed while a 20‑inch replacement segment was fabricated and installed the following day. no injuries or fatalities were reported. initial agency notifications were made to the city fire marshal at 10:02 am, the state department of natural resources at 10:15 am, and the national response center at 10:45 am. investigators are reviewing the construction crew’s equipment logs to determine the exact cause of the beam displacement.

a heavy‑duty bulldozer operated by a local road improvement crew was moving through the 4100 block of river street in richmond, va, when the operator misjudged the width of the access lane and the blade struck a 20" schedule 80 steel natural gas line that had been buried 30 feet below the roadway. the impact severed the pipe at 3,500 psi, causing a rapid gas release that filled the surrounding area with a visible vapor cloud. emergency crews from the va state police and the richmond fire department were dispatched within fifteen minutes, and the pipeline operator pulled the field valve on the nearest control station to isolate the ruptured section. the gas was vented through the shut‑in valves, and the line was depressurized to 250 psi before a temporary repair collar was installed. a 12‑hour shutdown was initiated to conduct a full line inspection, replace the damaged segment with a 20” x 60 ft splice, and certify the integrity of the surrounding infrastructure. the incident was reported to the va department of natural resources and the us energy regulatory authority, and a debrief was held with the construction firm to review the incident and reinforce safety protocols.

on november 5, 2024, at approximately 7:30 a.m., a 15-tonne heavy‑duty tractor trailer traveling on county road 27 lost traction on a slick surface and collided with the 24‑inch seamless steel natural gas transmission line at 38.123456 -94.654321. the impact severed the pipe at the 12‑inch flange, exposing a 1‑inch through‑hole. the pipeline was operating at 185 psi at the time of the collision. the rupture caused an uncontrolled release of 2.4 million standard cubic feet of natural gas into the surrounding area. emergency response crews reached the site by 8:15 a.m., shut the upstream main by 9:00 a.m., and performed a blowdown of the 24‑inch line at 10:15 a.m., which resulted in the loss of an additional 1.2 million standard cubic feet. a secondary 8‑inch service tap was closed at 11:30 a.m. the incident was reported to the nrc within 24 hours, and a 48‑hour follow‑up notification was submitted on november 7, 2024. investigations are underway by the state highway patrol and the local fire department to determine the cause of the tractor trailer’s loss of control. repair and replacement work on the damaged segment began on november 15, 2024, and is expected to be completed by december 10, 2024.

on 7/12/2024 at 1135 hours, a local electrical contractor was conducting trenching work for a new power line beneath a 20‑inch cast‑iron natural gas pipeline that had been operating at 580 psig for the past 34 years. a jackhammer strike displaced the trench and fractured a longitudinal weld on the pipe, causing a sudden pressure drop to 420 psig and a noticeable gas odor downstream. the contractor immediately called the operator’s emergency line; operators at 1140 hours activated the nearest isolation valve at 1150 and shut off the main flow to the affected segment. a crew from the gas company’s rapid response team arrived by 1200 and confirmed a 3‑inch diameter gas leak at the fractured weld. a portable pressure‑relief device was installed, and a temporary repair sleeve was fitted over the breach. the leak was contained at 1230, but the loss of service extended to 42 residential customers and 3 small businesses downstream. the gas company notified the local fire department and the county health department. a 500‑meter evacuation zone was established, and the county emergency response center logged 73 evacuated households. the incident was closed on 7/13 after the temporary repair was secured and a pressure test at 530 psig confirmed integrity.

on march 14, 2026, during the excavation of a new storm‑drain system in the industrial district of san marcos, a construction crew inadvertently struck a 48‑inch diameter, 1200‑psi natural‑gas line buried 7 ft below grade. the crew employed a hydraulic jackhammer to break a concrete slab; the jackhammer’s guide rail was bent and subsequently sheared, delivering a high‑energy impact to the pipe’s outer surface. the impact created a 2‑inch diameter fissure in the carbon‑steel wall, which rapidly developed into a minor leak. within 30 seconds the line pressure dropped from 1200 psi to 500 psi, prompting automatic shut‑off of the nearby isolation valve. the incident was reported to the state regulator at 09:45, as the estimated gas loss exceeded 10 m³. an emergency crew was dispatched; the damaged section was temporarily capped, and a trench was opened to expose the compromised pipe. the pipe was replaced by welding a new 48‑inch carbon‑steel segment, which was pressure tested at 1500 psi to verify integrity before the line was returned to service. no injuries, fires, or customer outages occurred. for further details, contact james m. harris, field engineer, 415‑555‑0198.

midwestern natural gas transport reported a 20 mscp leak at their 36" 65 psi natural gas transmission line near the kansas-missouri border on tuesday evening. the incident involved a private residence where the homeowner was performing unsupervised excavation work with a mini-excavator. the operator unexpectedly struck the buried main, causing a rupture that released gas and immediately ignited due to the heat generated by the hydraulic cutting blade. the resulting fireball exposed 150 feet of the above-ground and buried pipe section, causing significant thermal damage to the x-65 carbon steel pipe and associated tie-in valves. the line was isolated at both ends by midwestern field crews within 45 minutes, utilizing the upstream check valve and downstream shutdown valve to contain the gas flow. fire department resources arrived shortly after to secure the perimeter and allow the fire to burn out safely. the damaged section, totaling approximately 300 feet of 36" pipe, was subsequently removed and replaced with new x-52 material. hydrostatic testing of the new section was completed at 1.5 times the operating pressure, and the line was returned to service the following morning. no injuries were reported to public or utility personnel, though the residence sustained minor heat damage to the exterior siding. the homeowner was counseled on the necessity of calling 811 before any digging activities to prevent future damage to underground infrastructure.

during routine routing operations, a third-party construction crew was installing water service lines adjacent to our 12-inch pipeline corridor. despite clear markings on the surface, the excavator's bucket slipped into a soft spot and struck the 12-inch a36 carbon steel pipe at approximately 19:00 hrs. the impact caused a partial wall breach on the lower side of the pipe, which was operating at 620 psig. upon realizing the damage, the operator immediately initiated an emergency shutdown protocol, resulting in a rapid depressurization of the affected segment to 40 psig within one minute. no ignition occurred due to the immediate isolation of the segment via remote-operated valves. inspection revealed a 4-inch gash in the pipe wall with no signs of further propagation. the damaged section was subsequently excavated and removed for off-site repair. a deviation from the authorized safety zone was cited in the final incident report, highlighting a failure in pre-excavation clearance verification by the contractor. no personal injuries were reported, but the incident resulted in temporary service interruptions for downstream facilities until pressures stabilized.

the incident took place on 6/14/2019 at 14:22 near milepost 45.8 of the highline natural gas transmission system. a third-party construction contractor was conducting excavation work for a private residential utility upgrade approximately 20 feet adjacent to the right-of-way. during the operation, the hydraulic boom of the excavator contacted the 24-inch api 5l x-65 buried transmission line while maneuvering over a obstructed trench. immediate leakage was reported to the control center, which initiated a full shutdown of the segment via the automatic cathodic protection monitoring system and manual valve closures. field personnel arrived on scene at 15:45 and established a cold zone with a 500-foot radius due to the significant volume of released gas, which was traveling at 785 psig at the time of failure. the gas did not ignite due to favorable wind conditions. the damage assessment revealed a multi-point puncture spanning 3.5 feet along the pipe body. repair operations began on 6/16/2019 involving a hot tap connection and the installation of a full-length repair sleeve. the line was re-pressurized in a stepwise manner beginning on 6/20/2019 and returned to full operational capacity on 6/22/2019 after successful pressure testing and leak checks.

upon routine inspection following the recent storm event, a full bore rupture was discovered in the 12-inch x-ploy steel mainline located approximately 2.5 miles northeast of the coastal processing facility. the pipeline had sustained a catastrophic failure along a 400-foot segment, with distinct scraping marks and deformation patterns indicating contact with a hard, heavy object. initial assesssment suggested the line was subjected to an external impact beyond the design limits of the surrounding soil and rock cover. further investigation of the trench area revealed large fragments of a vessel's anchor and associated chain links resting alongside the severed pipe sections. records from the local port authority confirmed that a bulk carrier had lost anchor control during high winds on the previous night. the rupture occurred at operating pressure of 650 psig, resulting in an immediate shutdown of the affected feeder line to prevent overpressurization of the downstream manifold. no fire or secondary explosion was reported at the site, though significant hydrocarbon residue was observed in the surrounding marshland. repair crews were mobilized to isolate the failure section using remote operated valves, allowing for the removal of the damaged 400 feet of 12-inch pipe. the external forces involved in this incident exceed normal operational stresses, pointing to interference from maritime traffic as the primary driver of the structural damage.

on 04.15.25, a third-party excavation operation went awry when a mechanical backhoe, operated by an unauthorized contractor, struck a buried 6-inch sch40 steel lateral line at a residential driveway crossing. the contractor had failed to obtain a locate ticket or call for utility markings prior to starting work. the backhoe bucket penetrated the pipe wall, causing immediate leakage of product gas. the operator shut down equipment immediately upon noticing the release and contacted the utility company's emergency response line. response crews arrived on site within 20 minutes and isolated the segment using remote shutoff valves located at either end of the lateral. the section was dug around, and a temporary 1/2" repair clamp was applied to stop the leak, although the damage was later found to be a 4-inch crack. the contractor removed the damaged 8-foot section of pipe and welded a new coupling into place. the area was kept clear of public traffic during the repair process. pressure testing confirmed the integrity of the new weld before the line was returned to service. no injuries or property damage beyond the pipeline itself were reported. the incident highlights the ongoing risk of failed locate procedures by third-party excavators. a report has been filed with the relevant regulatory agency, and a referral to the texas natural gas conservation board has been initiated to address the unlicensed excavation activities.

on march 12, 2023, at approximately 09:30 hours, the operations control center received an automated sensor alarm indicating a pressure drop on the 18-inch high-pressure transmission line located in rural franklin county, ohio. field personnel dispatched to the site confirmed that a third-party excavation contractor, working on a municipal water main project adjacent to the right-of-way, had inadvertently struck the pipeline with a hydraulic backhoe bucket. the impact resulted in a through-wall puncture measuring approximately 2.5 inches in diameter, causing a visible release of natural gas that formed a flammable vapor cloud around the excavation area. immediately upon arrival, the crew established a two-mile safety perimeter and ignited the pool to prevent further accumulation, simultaneously isolating the affected segment by closing the mainline block valves at mile markers 42.1 and 44.5. the section experienced a rapid pressure decay from 650 psi to atmospheric pressure within fifteen minutes. emergency response teams coordinated with local fire authorities to monitor air quality, using portable gas detectors to ensure no hazardous concentrations migrated toward nearby residential properties. the excavation site was secured, and the injured contractor equipment was moved away from the hazard zone. repair crews initiated temporary bypass operations to maintain service to downstream compressor stations while preparations were made for a full pigging operation. the damaged three-foot section of x52 seamless steel pipe was cut out, and a new spool piece was fabricated and hydrostatically tested at 975 psi before being installed using standard seam welding procedures. integrity checks, including x-ray radiography of all welds and a final hydrostatic test, were completed before the line was returned to service on march 14, 2023. a joint investigation was conducted to review excavation notification protocols and marking practices to prevent future occurrences.

on march 12, 2021, at approximately 14:30, a third-party excavation crew began work in the northwest corner of a commercial industrial site located along route 9 interchange. during the initial cut phase, the operator of a backhoe struck a buried 6-inch steel distribution line, causing a significant rupture. the immediate impact sheared the pipe open, resulting in a rapid release of natural gas. operators at the local compressor station detected a pressure drop in the zone and initiated a remote shutdown of the emergency valve at 14:45. company field technicians arrived on scene at 15:20 to confirm the leak and establish a safety perimeter. the excavation contractor remained on site pending investigation by local law enforcement. the damaged section was isolated, and trenchless repair clamps were evaluated but deemed insufficient for the extent of the rupture. consequently, the crew excavated the existing trench to expose the 6-inch pipe for a full splice repair. a new 6-inch x 10-foot stub-end was added on each side of the breach, and the line was hydrotested to 1.5 times the design pressure before being vacuum dried and re-energized. the line returned to service at 09:10 on march 14, 2021. no injuries were reported, and approximately 15,000 cubic feet of gas were released prior to isolation. the incident highlights the necessity of updated utility locates and strict adherence to strike avoidance protocols during mechanical excavation.

on tuesday morning, a heavy machinery contractor working on a nearby roadway extension attempted to maneuver a 12-ton excavator loader across a temporary access path that crossed the leased right-of-way. the operator failed to notice the buried marker flags, and the unit's front loading bucket struck the ground with enough force to puncture the 24-inch carbon steel transmission line. an immediate loud hissing sound was heard, and a visible jet of natural gas escaped the breach at an estimated 900 psi internal pressure. the contractor notified the pipeline emergency response team, who arrived within 15 minutes to shut in the isolation valves at milepoints 4.2 and 5.8, effectively isolating the damaged section. after depressurizing the segment to atmospheric levels, a leak detection team confirmed the extent of the damage, finding a 4-inch diameter puncture hole through the pipe wall and severe deformation of the adjacent 15 feet of casing. the section was excavated, and the damaged 15-foot pipeline segment was cut out and removed for disposal. a new temporary spool of schedule 40 pipe was installed and hydrostatically tested to 1330 psi to restore service capability. root cause analysis determined the incident was caused by third-party excavation negligence and lack of coordination with the pipeline company's locate line. corrective actions include requiring all future contractors in the area to obtain written permission before performing any earth-moving activities within 20 feet of the right-of-way boundary and installing additional buried warning tapes at 10-foot intervals to provide visual cues during excavation.

on october 12, 2015, the company received a notification from a local propane delivery service that their truck had struck and displaced several large concrete survey markers adjacent to the right-of-way. the vehicle's undercarriage subsequently dragged across the surface, damaging an above-ground steel transition riser connected to a 36-inch high-pressure transmission line. field responders confirmed that the impact had gouged the outer coating of the 4-inch riser pipe, exposing the carbon steel material. a hydrostatic pressure test revealed a small leak at the seam where the riser connects to the underground tee. although the main 36-inch line maintained full integrity and no significant gas release occurred, the section of the line nearest the impact had to be taken out of service for safety isolation. excavation was performed within the 24-foot wide right-of-way to access the damaged riser and the associated tap. the damaged above-ground assembly was removed and replaced with a new protected riser enclosed in a reinforced concrete vault to prevent future accidental contact. the area was backfilled and compacted, and monitoring was established for 48 hours to ensure depressurization and pressure stabilization. the incident was reported as the truck driver was unfamiliar with the specific location of the buried facility markers obscured by seasonal vegetation, highlighting the need for recurring vegetation management along this corridor.

on november 14, 2021, at approximately 0930 hours, a third-party construction contractor operating a backhoe loader for a water district in rural tarrant county struck the buried 30-inch steel transmission pipeline with a bucket while trenching for a new lateral connection. the excavator had not contacted the prior notification requirements and assumed the utility line was a water main based on prior engineering drawings. upon contact, the excavation bucket punched a 12-inch hole through the pipe wall, causing an immediate release of natural gas at 900 psi. the gas jet had a hissing sound that was heard by the operator, who abandoned the scene immediately after realizing the severity of the strike. the pipeline operator’s control room received an alarm for low pressure on section k-4 and dispatched an emergency response class vehicle to the location. engineering surveyors arrived on site at 1015 hours and verified the breach location. the section was isolated by closing the manual block valves at mileposts 42.5 and 43.1. the damaged 15-foot section of the 30-inch x 22-gauge api 5l grade x65 steel pipe was excavated and removed. repairs were completed using a full-bore weld with a short spool of new pipe. the repair site was tested helium leak detected and coated with a qualification 55,000-minute hour rating. the incident resulted in no injuries, fatalities, or fires. the estimated cost of the release and repair is calculated at $125,000. a final report was submitted to the phmsa and state regulator, noting the lack of asset tracking data for the contractor’s equipment.

during early morning operations on october 14, 2018, the control room at station north reported a sudden and significant drop in line pressure on the 10-inch distribution lateral. initial telemetry indicated the pressure fell from the standard 110 psi operating level to zero within less than sixty seconds, triggering an automatic emergency shutdown valve closure. immediate inspection crews were dispatched to the last known normal pressure location, situated approximately 0.4 miles downstream of the main interconnect. upon arrival, personnel discovered a visible rupture in the ductile iron pipe at a shallow depth crossing a disused rail spur. forensic examination of the site revealed a 2-inch diameter hole with outward deformation and metal displacement consistent with high-energy external impact. no internal corrosion, fatigue cracking, or third-party boring activity was identified in the immediate vicinity. soil disturbance patterns and scuff marks in the adjacent ballast suggested the intrusion came from a heavy, rolling object dragged across the surface. given the recent high winds and storm surge in the region, it is suspected that a dislodged section of construction fencing or heavy debris from a neighboring unsecured site was propelled by the wind into the pipeline cover. the segment was isolated, repaired with a clamped coupling, and returned to service following a successful pressure test. no injuries were reported, and the leak was contained before reaching a public roadway.

during routine maintenance operations on a 12-inch transmission line in williamson county, a heavy excavator was positioned approximately 50 feet from the right-of-way to assist with vegetation control. the pipeline, constructed of x-65 steel and operating at an internal pressure of 850 psig, runs beneath a secondary access road maintained by the local parish. on july 14 at approximately 10:15 am, while the operator was reversing the equipment toward the staging area, a hydraulic cylinder failure caused the boom to droop unexpectedly. the end of the boom struck a wooden utility pole adjacent to the right-of-way, which then leaned and made direct contact with the exposed 12-inch mainline at a shallow burial depth of 18 inches. the impact resulted in a significant deformation of the pipe wall and a subsequent rupture, releasing a high-volume stream of natural gas. scada alarms triggered at 10:17 am, and a rapid response team arrived on site by 10:45 am. the area was immediately evacuated by local emergency services, clearing a 1,500-foot radius that included a small commercial strip and two adjacent residential properties. the pipeline was isolated by closing the nearest block valve, located 1.2 miles downstream, within 15 minutes of receiving the alarm. upon full isolation and depressurization, inspection revealed a 14-inch gash in the pipe’s circumference. a temporary mechanical clamp was not feasible due to the extent of the deformation, requiring a section of pipe to be cut out and replaced with a new spool piece. a backhoe was used to repair the excavator boom damage off-site. repairs were completed and the line re-pressurized with nitrogen before being switched back to natural gas by 4:30 pm the same day. no injuries were reported, and there were no fire or explosion events associated with the initial release.

on march 12, 2023, at approximately 09:15 am, a heavy-duty excavator operated by a third-party telecommunications contractor accidentally struck an 8-inch steel pipeline while trenching for fiber optic cable installation near milepost 42 of the cedar ridge transmission line. the contractor had not obtained a pre-dig ticket and failed to identify the utility lines beneath the surface. the steel tooth of the excavator broke through the 0.375-inch wall thickness of the pipe, creating a tear approximately 18 inches in length. the impact caused a massive loss of natural gas, which was operating at 750 psig, sending a plume of gas into the trench. the operator of the equipment immediately ceased work and called the emergency response line. upon arrival at 09:42 am, it was confirmed that the leak was significant and hazardous. the crew quickly established a safety perimeter and blew down the segment between the upstream quick-closing valve at mp 41.5 and the downstream station at mp 43.2 to isolate the breach. investigation revealed that the water shutoff in the area had been marked incorrectly on the as-built drawings, leading the contractor to trench in the wrong location. the damaged section of the 8-inch pipe was cut out, and a new spool piece with welded couplings was installed to restore integrity. the line was hydrostatically tested to 1,125 psig, painted, and backfilled before being returned to full service pressure on march 15, 2023. no injuries were reported, and the fire brigade was present on scene as a precautionary measure but did not respond to an active fire.

on march 14, 2023, a 12-inch steel transmission line located in the rural area of grant county, oregon, sustained significant structural damage resulting in a minor leak of natural gas. the line, operating at 300 psig, was situated along a county access road leading to agricultural fields. preliminary site inspection by repair crews revealed deep gouges and deformation on the bottom elevation of the pipe, consistent with impact from heavy equipment. it was determined that a county-maintained gravel truck, while maneuvering a low-clearance trailer, struck the exposed pipeline section. the driver had not been aware of the pipeline's presence due to thick vegetation obscuring the right-of-way markers at that specific location. the impact punctured the pipe wall, causing a release of approximately 1.5 mmcf of gas before being detected by a nearby pressure monitoring station. upon arrival, emergency personnel established a safety perimeter and monitored air concentrations, which remained well below the lower explosive limit. no fire or ignition occurred, and no hazardous injuries were reported. a hot tap was performed to isolate the damaged section, allowing for the removal of the failed pipe segment. a compliant spool piece was installed, and the line was returned to service after passing all required pressure tests and leak checks. the gravel contractor was notified of the incident, and a joint meeting was held with the county public works department to coordinate future maintenance activities near known pipeline easements. additional signage and vegetation management were subsequently scheduled to enhance visibility for vehicle operators traversing the nearby road.

at 1430 hrs on 03/12/09, a contractor operating for an adjacent transmission line company was bucketing service drops in the corridor. the operator failed to detect the buried 10" gas transmission line beneath the vegetation cover during initial site assessment. as the bucket of the aerial lift was lowered into the trench to clear debris, it struck the pipe, causing a longitudinal tear approximately 14 feet in length at the field joint. the incident resulted in a rapid depressurization event with an audible hiss and visible misting from the damaged section, though no immediate ignition occurred due to the rain-soaked ground conditions. emergency response teams were dispatched to isolate the affected section between two existing shut-off valves located 0.5 miles apart. the leak was contained using soil backfill and natural dissipation after pressure was reduced to 50 psi in the affected block. a follow-up inspection of the 14 feet of damaged carbon steel pipe revealed significant deformation and metal loss consistent with high-impact mechanical stress. the utility has since updated its interface agreements with third-party contractors to require mandatory line locating and positive verification procedures prior to any excavation adjacent to existing right-of-ways.

on june 14, 2018, a 24-inch carbon steel transmission line located in rural oklahoma was compromised due to impact from construction equipment. crews working on an adjacent utility crossing failed to locate the underground pipeline marker, resulting in a backhoe operator digging directly into the pipe wall. initial reports indicated a significant gas leak with the area evacuated for safety. surveying the damage revealed a 12-foot section of the pipe had a longitudinal tear approximately 18 inches in length, accompanied by deep gouges on the outer surface consistent with a bucket tooth. forensic analysis of the soil displacement suggested the bucket penetrated the top of the pipe at a 45-degree angle, severing the material and creating a sharp edge around the rupture site. the pipeline was at an operating pressure of 650 psi at the time of the incident. repair crews installed a temporary bypass to restore service to downstream compressor stations before excavating the failed section for permanent repair. after removing the damaged segment, a new sleeve weld and full girth weld were performed on the replacement spool. post-incident review noted that the lack of protected markers and coordinated utility locating procedures contributed to the third-party damage event.

during routine excavation work for a new fiber optic cable installation along route 9, a contractor’s backhoe bucket inadvertently contacted the 12-inch diameter carbon steel transmission main. the pipeline was buried at a depth of 6 feet below ground in sandy loam soil. the impact from the machine caused a localized dent and subsequent fracture on the top quadrant of the pipe wall, resulting in an immediate release of medium-pressure gas. upon detecting the pressure drop via their remote monitoring system, the company’s control room initiated an emergency shutdown of the adjacent block valves to isolate the affected segment. emergency response teams arrived within 20 minutes to establish a safety perimeter and prohibit further construction activity in the area. the breach, measuring approximately 4 inches in length, was confirmed by visual inspection after the trench was carefully excavated to expose the damaged section. the fractured pipe segment was removed, and a new spool piece with matching seamless steel specifications was welded into the line using standard grooved butt welds. destructive testing and hydrostatic pressure testing were performed on the repair to ensure structural integrity and leak-tightness before the line was returned to service. the contractor was cited for failing to call the one-call utility notification service prior to beginning digging operations, which had not been properly verified for the specific location.

on august 14, 2021, an excavator operated by a third-party utility company damaged an above-ground 2-inch purger stub associated with the pacific ridges transmission line 304 during construction activities near mile post 112 in santa clarita, california. the contractor was grading a foundation for a utility pole in close proximity to the right-of-way boundary when the bucket physically struck and sheared the 2-inch pipe at the flange connection. this impact caused an immediate uncontrolled release of natural gas into the atmosphere. the 2-inch purger is typically depressurized and isolated by a manual shut-off valve located 10 feet from the main 116-inch pipeline, however, the valve was found to be frozen in the open position due to corrosion, allowing over 800 psi of pipeline pressure to flow through the damaged stub. field personnel arrived on-site within 15 minutes and were able to manually depressurize the section by closing an upstream sectionalizing valve. the damaged 2-inch stub piping and flange were removed and replaced with new carbon steel components. an analysis determined that the contractor failed to conduct required underground utility locating and failed to maintain a safe distance from visible above-ground pipeline appurtenances. the pacific ridges transmission line experienced a temporary 12% reduction in flow capacity during the 6-hour repair window. post-incident review confirmed that the main 116-inch 5/8-inch wall line pipe remained intact and unharmed. enhanced monitoring protocols have been implemented for the adjacent construction zone.

during routine excavation work for a municipal water main extension, an excavation contractor inadvertently struck a buried 8-inch sch 40 carbon steel gas distribution main. the contractor’s backhoe bucket struck the pipeline at a shallow depth of 24 inches below grade, causing a 6-inch longitudinal gash in the side of the pipe. immediate visual inspection confirmed a persistent hissing sound and the distinct odor of mercaptan, indicating an active leak. the excavation crew ceased operations immediately and notified the pipeline operator’s control center. upon arrival, operator personnel isolated the affected section by closing the nearest lateral valves, depressuring the main to ambient levels. the damaged segment was excavated, and the 8-inch gasketed joint was identified as the point of failure due to the blunt force impact. a temporary bypass was arranged to maintain service to nearby residential customers while a permanent repair crew replaced the damaged 10-foot section of pipe. hydrostatic testing of the new segment was completed to 150 psi before the trench was backfilled. the incident resulted in no injuries but required a full investigation into the contractor’s locate compliance and use of shoring protections during deep cuts.

report received from customer indicating loud bang and displaced earth near the 12-inch transmission line in rural section of county road 45. upon arrival, maintenance crew observed a third-party utility bell digger had inadvertently struck the 12-inch x 0.500 inch radius pipe buried at a depth of 24 inches. the impact caused a clean tear approximately 6 feet in length, resulting in significant pressure loss and soil erosion around the valve station. the line was immediately isolated using the upstream and downstream block valves to prevent further leakage. soil survey indicated no gas migration to neighboring properties beyond a 50-foot radius. the damaged section was excavated, and the pipe was hydro-tested to establish integrity of the remaining line. a 12-foot sleeve repair was installed over the breach area using pipe clamps and witness holes per company repair standards. following pressure testing back to 85% of maximum operating pressure, the site was backfilled and graded. final restoration work included compacting the soil in 8-inch lifts and replacing turf sod. no injuries were reported, and the emergency response team cleared the scene after verifying gas detection levels were within safe limits. the customer service was restored without interruption as the main transmission pressure held steady during the repair operation.

on march 12, 2024, a 24-inch carbon steel natural gas transmission pipeline in pinto county, texas, suffered a rupture. the incident occurred following an inadvertent excavation by a third-party contractor performing utility locating work for a local water district. heavy excavation equipment struck the buried line, causing a significant breach that released approximately 42,000 mcf of gas. the initial impact resulted in a partial wall thickness reduction, which subsequently failed under operating pressure of 550 psig. upon discovery of the gas release, the line was isolated, and an emergency response team was dispatched to the scene. no injuries were reported, and the immediate area was evacuated as a precautionary measure. the rupture was contained within an unpopulated section of right-of-way, though it severed a parallel fiber optic cable. investigation confirmed that the failure mechanism was due to external mechanical damage and subsequent ductile tearing, consistent with outside force impact. repair crews initiated spool replacement operations immediately following securing of the scene.

on september 12, 2021, a 4-inch carbon steel distribution main located along oak ridge avenue in clarion, pennsylvania, was ruptured when a landscaping contractor unknowingly used a large-scale excavator bucket to break through compacted soil next to the road. the operator failed to properly contact the one-call center prior to beginning excavation work and assumed the area contained no buried infrastructure. as the bucket made contact with the pipe, the 250 psig natural gas line was severed, creating a loud blowout and igniting a flash fire that engulfed the immediate area. emergency services were notified within minutes and established a perimeter, evacuating three nearby residential properties. the gas supply was isolated at the main shutoff valve located approximately 200 feet away, effectively stopping the flow of fuel to the leak site. fire crews extinguished the flames after approximately 40 minutes, and the contractor equipment was moved from the area. inspection of the damage revealed a clean transverse fracture across the entire diameter of the pipe, consistent with direct impact from the heavy steel bucket rather than gradual corrosion or wear. replacement pipe was installed the following afternoon, hydrotested to ensure integrity, and the line was returned to service after safety checks were completed. the contractor was issued a notice of violation for failing to comply with underground facility safety regulations prior to digging.

during early morning operations on june 12, 2024, city construction crews performing grading work for a local road improvement project inadvertently struck the right-of-way with a large hydraulic excavator bucket. the strike impacted the northbound 24-inch x 0.438-inch wall carbon steel pipeline, which was operating at a static pressure of 850 psig. the impact resulted in a longitudinal gouge approximately 3 feet in length with a maximum depth of 0.35 inches, penetrating the pipe wall and causing a continuous hydrocarbon leak into the surrounding soil. immediately upon realizing the strike, the construction contractor ceased operations and notified the pipeline operator's control center. the facility operator initiated emergency procedures to isolate the affected segment, depressurizing the line to reduce flow and contain the release. no public safety hazards or significant environmental impacts were observed at the initial scene. the incident was reported to phmsa and the state pipeline safety office within the required timeframe. repair crews mobilized to the site to excavate the exposed pipeline section for inspection and subsequent hot tap and plug repair. the pipeline segment was returned to service on june 14, 2024, following hydrostatic testing and integrity verification. a joint review with the municipality was scheduled to update construction notification procedures and right-of-way marking visibility to prevent recurrence.

inspection crew reported a distinct hum and vibration near the 12-inch vapor line at the river crossing. initial assessment indicated a breach in the pipeline, releasing product into the water. subsequent dive survey revealed a significant crushing force had been applied to the exterior of the pipe, creating an oval-shaped deformation that reduced the internal diameter by approximately 15%. further examination identified deep, parallel scoring marks on the pipe surface consistent with heavy equipment tracks. investigation traced the incident to a contractor performing shoreline stabilization work upstream. the contractor had failed to verify underground utility locations and operated a skid-steer loader directly over the buried line. the concentrated weight of the machine, combined with the shear strength of the exposed pipe wall, caused the structural failure. the leak was isolated using remote-controlled valves, allowing the section to be depressurized. repair crews replaced a 40-foot section of the piping with new material of the same specification. post-repair pressure testing confirmed the integrity of the joint and the surrounding pipeline. the incident highlights the critical need for third-party verification of subsurface utilities before heavy machinery operations commence in areas with overlapping infrastructure.

control room operators in huntington, wv detected a pressure drop in the 24-inch mainline serving the eastern ohio region. initial remote terminal unit readings showed a significant variance between upstream and downstream stations. maintenance crews dispatched to the suspect location in jefferson county discovered a rupture in the buried pipeline. excavation revealed that the ductile iron and steel transition pipe had been severed. metallurgical examination of the broken ends confirmed a clean, ductile tear consistent with an external impact event rather than internal stress or corrosion fatigue. the immediate cause was identified as the operation of unapproved heavy construction equipment by a third-party utility contractor. during the relocation of a surface gas meter, the operator’s backhoe bucket struck and penetrated the undocumented pipeline segment. no prior marking was received despite active work in the area, and the contractor had not invoked the national dial before digging hotline notification process. the release was significant, with an estimated total volume of 4,500 mcf vented during the investigation and temporary shutoff procedure. the line, which operates at a maximum operating pressure of 630 psig using astm a53 grade b steel, was fully shut in to prevent further inventory loss. all necessary notifications were made to phmsa and state authorities. subsequent review of rights-of-way records highlighted a gap in as-built drawings for this specific lateral connection. corrective actions include updated documentation, enhanced monitoring via distributed fiber optic sensors along this corridor, and additional education for local contractors regarding pipeline safety protocols and proper locate procedures to prevent future incidents caused by external mechanical damage.

at 06:45 am on october 12, dispatch received reports of a severed underground power line crossing the line 150-04 right-of-way near millersburg, tx. inspection by the on-call pipeline engineer revealed that a backhoe operating for a third-party electrical contractor had struck and fractured the 12-inch x 0.250-inch carbon steel pipe while digging a trench for the new utility conduit. the operator failed to contact utility locate services prior to excavation, placing heavy load on the already compromised connection point. due to the integrity failure, the pipeline depressurized rapidly from its operating level of 580 psig to atmosphere. no gas odor was deteected by site personnel or emergency responders upon arrival. the area was secured by local law enforcement, and the adjacent duc pipeline was shut in at the nearest valve station to eliminate upstream pressure. a full bore rupture was confirmed at the fracture site, and the leakage extended approximately 300 feet into the surrounding soil. repair crews mobilized and completed a six-foot pipe splice overnight. after hydrostatic testing and soil restoration, the segment was repressurized and returned to service at 09:15 am the following day. a formal investigation determined that the damage resulted solely from unauthorized excavation equipment striking the pipeline infrastructure without proper notification or protective measures in place.

on march 14, 2024, at approximately 09:15 a.m., geotechnical monitoring indicated a sudden displacement of the ground surface above the 30-inch carbon steel transmission line near the hwy 9 interchange. dispatch was notified and emergency response teams were deployed to the site. upon arrival, personnel observed that a third-party heavy excavation contractor had been performing utility relocation work within the right-of-way without active notice of the buried pipeline. the contractor’s hydraulic backhoe had struck the pipe, creating a transverse rupture approximately 400 feet from the nearest valve station. upon impact, the line depressurized rapidly, causing a significant release of natural gas that resulted in a visible vapor cloud. the area was immediately evacuated by county sheriff, and an exclusion zone was established extending 500 feet in all directions to prevent ignition risk. the gas release naturally dissipated without incident as the pipeline pressure dropped below operating limits. after confirming the area was toxicologically safe, repair crews installed a line stopper to isolate the damaged section. a 30-inch replacement spool was then installed, welded, and tested per api 1104 standards. the section was hydrostatically tested and returned to service at 85% of maximum allowable operating pressure at 14:30 p.m. on march 16, 2024. an investigation determined the root cause was the contractor’s failure to verify underground utility locations prior to digging, resulting in mechanical damage to the pipeline. corrective actions include enhanced real-time construction surveillance in the vicinity and coordination with the local one-call center to increase awareness of active excavation projects near critical infrastructure. no injuries were reported.

on march 14, 2023, at approximately 10:15 am, pipeline control received a report from a construction crew regarding a compromised surface casing in a residential subdivision under development. the crew had been operating compactors near a marked utility corridor when the vibratory tamping equipment struck an unshielded above-ground meter set. field operations personnel arrived on site at 11:30 am and confirmed that the 2" stainless steel service line had been partially severed at the connection point of the downstream meter valve. immediately, remote isolation valves were operated to isolate the affected tap from the main transmission line. a subsequent leak detection purge system was activated to sweep the area of any residual gas accumulation before personnel approached the immediate damage zone. upon securing the area and verifying zero gas concentrations, it was determined that the mechanical impact from the heavy construction machinery had sheared the pipe behind the meter, causing a continuous leak of natural gas. no fire or ignition occurred. the damaged section was excavated, and the compromised 2" segment was replaced with a new galvanized steel nipple and coupling. pressure tests were conducted on the repaired assembly using nitrogen prior to reintroducing product flow. service to the affected customer was restored by 2:45 pm on the same day. no injuries were reported, and the construction site was directed to cease operations in the immediate vicinity pending a final safety walk-down by pipeline engineers. the incident was classified as a significant event due to the potential for public exposure had the detection system not alerted operational staff promptly.

operator received a call from a local drilling contractor on march 14, 2013, regarding an unintentional strike on a transmission line in the willow creek area. the contractor’s heavy equipment, a 40-ton track hoe, had inadvertently excavated into the right-of-way while preparing a new access road. the incident resulted in a full-hole puncture to a 12-inch diameter, 0.500-inch wall thickness x42 carbon steel pipeline. at the time of the strike, the line was operating at 850 psig. the contractor immediately ceased operations and notified the operator’s emergency response team. upon arrival at 10:15 am, field personnel verified that the gas flow had stopped due to rapid depressurization of the immediate section, preventing a fire or explosion. the adjacent 8-inch diameter lateral, which was also damaged but not ruptured, was isolated using field weld-on blocks. mainline isolation valves were closed remotely, and the affected segment was blown down to zero pressure by 11:45 am. inspection revealed a tear approximately 18 inches in length on the south side of the 12-inch pipe, along with significant displacement of the line. repairs involved cutting out the damaged section, fabricating a short spool piece, and welding it into place. the new section was hydro-tested and subsequently purged of all liquids before being re-pressurized with natural gas. service was restored to the downstream compressor station at 4:30 pm on the same day. the damaged track hoe was removed from the site, and the contractor incurred costs for the replacement spool, welding, and labor. no injuries were reported, and there was no environmental impact as the strike occurred in a dry, rocky formations area.
