during a routine inspection of the 30-inch steel transmission main in the rural section of county route 12, a field technician observed significant displacement of the right-of-way vegetation. upon further investigation with ground-penetrating radar, it was determined that an unauthorized excavation had been conducted nearby by a third-party contractor installing a water line. the contractor's machinery had inadvertently damaged the coating and dented the pipeline wall, compromising the structural integrity. although no immediate gas release was detected, the pipeline pressure was reduced from 850 psig to 400 psig as a precautionary measure to allow for safe assessment. a temporary bypass line was installed to maintain customer service continuity while the damaged section was being prepared for repair. engineering inspectors confirmed that the dent depth met the level 2 criteria, necessitating a hydraulic expansion tool to restore the original shape of the pipe. after the repair and application of temporary cold weather coating, hydrostatic testing was performed to verify the structural soundness of the joint. no further leaks or failures were observed during a 24-hour monitoring period. the incident resulted in a two-day service interruption for approximately 450 commercial customers in the affected sector. total repair costs, including materials and labor, were estimated at $120,000. the local sheriff's department was notified, and the construction company was issued a warning regarding proper utility locates. no injuries were reported during the response and repair activities.

the incident occurred on 06/14/24 at approximately 14:30 local time involving the 36-inch x 0.500 inch carbon steel transmission line located in section 12 near milepost 45.3. during routine hydrostatic testing following a splice repair, an unexplained rapid pressure drop of 15 psi was observed from the top-of-line gauge. field crews dispatched to the location identified a sheen of brownish water migrating through the grassy right-of-way, approximately 200 feet east of the nearest access road. visual inspection revealed a bulge in the pipeline coating but no visible rupture or active leak at the surface. soil investigation on 06/15/24 indicated displacement of native sand consistent with external movement, however, no third-party equipment or obvious mechanical damage was found on the pipe surface. the section was isolated using the remotely operated valves at mp 44.0 and mp 46.5. initial gamma gauge readings showed no significant wall loss in the immediate vicinity of the sag. radiography of the affected area is scheduled for 06/18/24 to determine if internal erosion or a subsurface void contributed to the failure. the cause remains undetermined as no third-party activity was identified and internal inspection data for the last 24-month period shows no anomalies. this report is submitted as an initial notification; a supplement will be provided upon completion of the non-destructive examination and forensic review of the coating vendor records.

march 3, 2018: a 24-inch x 91.4 mm schedule 40 line pipe segment in the alder canyon section experienced a sudden pressure drop from 685 psig to 120 psig within minutes. flow balancing at the adjacent compressor station indicated a significant loss of supply, prompting operators to remotely activate the emergency shutdown (esd) valves. the line was made of x65 grade steel with an internal pipe coating. initial visual inspection by field crews revealed a 4-inch longitudinal rupture near a right-angle dogleg marker. the rupture did not result in a sustained gush of fire due to immediate depressurization and the wet soil conditions. subsequent investigation by a third-party engineering firm determined that the failure was not caused by corrosion, third-party impact, or manufacturing defects. metallurgical analysis of the fracture surface showed evidence of high-temperature combustion and localized melting inconsistent with standard operation. further review of the site's subsurface geology and utility maps identified an unmapped abandoned oil well pad located directly beneath the pipeline route. the well had been plugged using a cement seal that had degraded over time, allowing a pocket of trapped methane and other inert gases to exist under high pressure. the specific failure mechanism was attributed to this anomalous subsurface pressure differential combined with a minor coating defect that allowed moisture ingress, leading to a stress rupture event. the root cause was classified as an external geological or unknown factor requiring further hydrogeological study, distinct from the typical causes of corrosion or third-party damage. permanent rerouting of the 24-inch line was implemented to sever the path over the affected wellhead site to prevent recurrence.

on july 14, 2018, the transmission line experienced an unplanned shutdown during a routine maintenance window. field personnel were performing hydrostatic pressure testing on a newly spliced section of 30-inch xiameter p110m pipe. the test was conducted at 80% of the maximum allowable operating pressure (maop). midway through the 24-hour holding period, a minor leak was detected at a flanged connection on the spare pig receiver. while the leak was being investigated by a welder fitting a new gasket, an unsecured crane hook swung into the work area and struck the pipe support restraint. the impact caused a sudden drop in system pressure, triggering the emergency shutdown system (esd). the esd valves at the adjacent compressor stations closed automatically as designed. the event resulted in a small release of natural gas from the disturbed flange before isolation was complete. no injuries were reported, and no environmental impact was identified. a subsequent root cause analysis determined that the primary factor was inadequate securing of lifting equipment in the active work zone, which compromised the structural integrity of the temporary support. corrective actions included implementing a new hot work permit procedure, requiring independent verification of all rigging attachments before commencing any maintenance, and increasing inspection frequency for flanged connections during pressure tests. the incident was reviewed against reporting criteria, and while an internal report was filed for process improvement, it did not meet the thresholds for public notification based on the volume of release and absence of hazardous consequences.

on july 14, 2011, a 16-inch subsurface pipeline owned by gulfport energy partners suffered a partial rupture at milepost 445.2 in harry county, mississippi, approximately 400 feet south of the interstate 10 right-of-way. the incident resulted in a rapid gas release that vaporized and ignited upon reaching the surface, producing a fireball that lasted approximately forty-five seconds. no injuries were reported, but two structures within 500 feet of the rupture site sustained thermal damage to roofing and siding. the pipeline section was located in 6 feet of water at the time of the event. initial visual inspection of the exposed steel revealed a 3-foot transverse fracture across the carrier pipe. metallurgical examination indicated the failure originated from a pre-existing internal weld butt zone defect located at the 3:00 clock position. the fracture propagated rapidly under internal pressure of 850 psig, which was at the maximum allowable operating pressure for the line. subsequent non-destructive testing of the adjacent 500-foot segment found no additional indicators of fatigue or stress corrosion cracking. the removed section was replaced with a new spool piece made of api 5l x65 grade steel, complete with full-penetration welded joints. leakage tests were conducted at 120% of maximum operating pressure for a continuous duration of 24 hours. post-repair integrity checks confirmed no displacement or settlement of the surrounding riverbed silt. the restored segment returned to service on august 2, 2011, following final verification by the department of transportation pipeline safety division.

third-party excavation activity near the right-of-way severed the 24-inch x 0.500 wall seamless carbon steel main. the digging machine struck the pipe section at a depth of 6 feet below grade, causing a complete transverse break. high-pressure natural gas at 985 psi escaped immediately, creating a strong whistling sound that alerted nearby field responders. the operator initiated an emergency shutdown procedure, closing both upstream and downstream isolation valves to stop the flow. a significant gas pocket formed in the excavation pit before ignition occurred approximately 15 minutes after the initial leak was detected, likely sparked by the electric power shovel. the resulting fire was contained to the immediate vicinity of the break, but thermal damage extended to adjacent 12-inch distribution laterals, requiring full replacement of 400 feet of mainline and associated tie-ins. the area was de-energized and gas-free before repair crews could secure the wellhead connections. post-incident analysis determined that the excavator lacked adequate locate markings and failed to follow pre-dig protocols, leading to the catastrophic failure of the integrity-tested pipeline segment.

on 03/12/25, operator personnel detected an odor report near mile marker 45.2 of the 24-inch carbon steel transmission line. initial drone inspection revealed a minor seep at a crossing over a rural access road. the line was depressurized from 850 psig to 100 psig and isolated via block valves at mile markers 44.8 and 46.5 to facilitate inspection. an in-line inspection pig identified a defect consistent with accidental damage from third-party construction activity that occurred six months prior, where shield tunneling equipment had caused subtle deformation not immediately apparent. the damaged section was excavated after permitting was granted. upon exposure, a 2-inch out-of-round deformation and a hairline crack were observed. the pipe segment was removed and a new standard grade 1 pipe was hydrostatically tested and installed. all joints were coated and protected per spec. the line was backfilled, and the area was re-vegetated after environmental assessment confirmed no soil contamination. the system was returned to service on 03/28/25 after successful pressure testing to 125% of design. no injuries were reported during the response.

field personnel were dispatched to a rural area in oklahoma after a local farmer reported a hissing sound near his irrigation ditch. upon arrival, gas detection equipment confirmed a release along the 8-inch carbon steel main line, which operates at a maximum pressure of 620 psi. initial visual inspection of the exposed pipe section revealed no external corrosion or third-party damage. the line was immediately isolated and depressurized to allow for proper assessment. after dewatering the excavation, technicians noticed a small weep of gas emanating from a circumferential weld seam located approximately 4 feet from a line stop. further investigation determined that the leak originated from a hairline crack in the weld cap, likely exacerbated by cyclic thermal stresses and soil movement over time. microscopic examination of the area indicated no significant wall loss on the base metal, suggesting the failure was isolated to the weld fusion zone. a mechanical repair clamp was installed over the defect following code compliance testing. hydrostatic testing of the repaired section was conducted to confirm integrity before the line was returned to service. no other anomalies were found during the inspection of the surrounding pipe.

operating personnel detected a pressure drop of approximately 15 psi across segment 4 of the 12-inch xod 306 carbon steel natural gas line located in a high-density urban area. emergency procedures were initiated, isolating the affected section within twenty minutes. excavation of the presumed leak site revealed severe localized corrosion on the exterior surface of the pipe, approximately 0.2 inches from the nearest girth weld. the wall thickness had been reduced to near zero at the point of failure. metallurgical analysis indicated that the root cause was a combination of poor coating adhesion and the presence of chlorides in the surrounding soil environment, leading to accelerated metallic loss over an estimated five-year period. previously buried drainage tiles were found in close proximity to the pipeline, creating a persistent moisture accumulation zone that exacerbated the corrosive conditions. the incident was contained without any external fires or significant gas migration into adjacent structures due to rapid isolation. the damaged section was removed and replaced with new pipe welded according to specification. follow-up investigation focused on updating the cathodic protection monitoring interval for this specific routing segment and implementing stricter material inspection protocols for areas with known drainage complications. the facility has been returned to service following successful hydrostatic pressure testing and inline inspection of the adjacent sections.

unstable ground conditions adjacent to the 24-inch transmission line caused a lateral shift in the trench support structure during the night crew's excavation activity. the movement occurred approximately 20 feet from the mainline, which was operating at 750 psig, and resulted in the partial collapse of the shoring system into the active work zone. no direct strike or puncture to the pipeline wall was observed, but the vibration and soil displacement triggered a false pressure fluctuation reading on the in-line telemetry unit at valve station vs-09. the control room operator received an alarm indicating a rapid pressure drop of 15 psi over 30 seconds, prompting an emergency stop of the pump station. a field inspection team arrived within 45 minutes and confirmed that the pipeline integrity was maintained, with no visible deformation or coating damage on the exposed section. the incident report notes that while the pipeline remained intact, the safety barrier distance was compromised, and two workers sustained minor contusions from falling debris. the site was secured, and the trench was re-shored using steel plates before operations could resume. investigation determined that the soil saturation from the previous week's heavy rainfall had significantly reduced the shear strength of the clay layer, leading to the unexpected slip. no release of hydrocarbons or hazardous materials occurred, and local environmental authorities were notified in accordance with company policy for near-miss events involving structural integrity concerns.

on august 14th at approximately 09:30 am, an uncommanded shutdown was triggered on the 30-inch cross-country transmission line due to a sudden pressure transient. the event originated near field station fs-402, located in a rural agricultural area. monitoring systems detected a rapid drop in line pressure from 850 psig to 650 psig over a 15-second interval, activating the emergency shutdown valves at both ends of the isolation section. no external gas odor or visual release was observed by field personnel upon arrival. investigation of the historical data logs revealed that a third-party contractor conducting asphalt paving work adjacent to the right-of-way had inadvertently struck the pipeline survey marker, causing a significant ground displacement that shifted the pipe support structure. this mechanical impact likely induced a fatigue crack in the welded joint of a pre-existing repair sleeve from 2018, which subsequently wept gas internally without breaching the outer casing. the affected 2-mile segment was isolated and flared safely. excavation confirmed the damage to the welded joint, and a full replacement of the pipe spool and associated tie-ins was performed according to specification. the line was hydrostatically tested and returned to service 48 hours later. a joint meeting with the contractor was held to update underground facility marking protocols.

on august 14, 2012, at approximately 2:15 am, pipeline monitoring software flagged a deviation in the upstream pressure of the 24-inch x460 psig transmission line located at mile point 45.6. operators immediately initiated an emergency depressurization sequence, reducing the line pressure from 850 psig to 20 psig within four minutes. crew access was established via the nearest intake station, and leak detection personnel confirmed a seepage indication at the identified segment. excavation began at 4:00 am, revealing that the pipeline had sustained a longitudinal split approximately 12 inches in length. inspection of the failure site indicated that the rupture occurred at a location where the pipe had been installed over a bed of sharp, angular rock without adequate concrete encasement or protective cement coating. high soil erosion, exacerbated by recent heavy rainfall in the region, had slowly exposed the bare metal of the pipe to direct contact with the underlying gravel layer. field analysis suggested that the mechanical abrasion, combined with potential ground settling over time, compromised the structural integrity of the 3/8-inch nominal wall thickness at that specific point. the damaged span was removed, and a new section of x52 grade steel pipe was installed with proper bedding and 6 inches of sand covering. inline corrosion coupons retrieved from the segment showed no signs of external corrosion, confirming the failure was primarily mechanical in nature due to environmental factors and installation conditions rather than material degradation. the line was repressurized following hydrostatic testing and returned to service on august 15 at 11:30 am.

on 22 july 2024 operators observed an unexpected pressure drop on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) feeding the coastal processing plant. the line was normally operating at 850 psig with a design limit of 950 psig. scada alarms indicated a loss of 120 psig within ten minutes, prompting an immediate shutdown and isolation of the affected segment. a mobile inspection crew deployed a pigging unit and discovered a 15‑inch longitudinal dent spanning approximately 30 feet near milepost 42.5, consistent with ground settlement caused by recent underground excavation activities unrelated to pipeline construction. the dent had compromised the pipe wall thickness from the rated 0.75 in. to about 0.45 in., resulting in a slow gas leak that was later confirmed by portable gas detectors. the leak was contained by activating the emergency relief valve set at 900 psig, which vented to the flare system for 22 minutes. repair work involved cutting out the damaged section and installing a new 30‑inch x70 pipe with an inline coupling and additional corrosion‑inhibitor coating. after hydrostatic testing at 1200 psig, the line was returned to service. the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety board and the operator’s internal risk management team for further root‑cause analysis.

on 3/22/2024 a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (grade 53) operating at 1150 psi in the panhandle region of texas began emitting a faint vapor near a valve station #7. field crews performing a routine pressure test observed a pressure drop of 70 psi over a ten‑minute interval and reported an odor of light crude downstream of the valve. a visual inspection revealed a small, irregular rupture at the threaded connection of a pressure‑reducing regulator that had been installed two years earlier during a flow‑rate upgrade. the failure appeared to be a manufacturing defect in the thread seal, as no external damage or corrosion was present. the line was isolated with a downstream block valve, the damaged regulator was removed, and a new 2‑inch stainless‑steel reducer was installed. the released hydrocarbon vapor was captured by the onsite vapor recovery system and vented to the flare stack. after confirming line integrity with a hydrostatic test at 150 % of design pressure, service was restored. an incident report (nrc #2024‑0322‑01) was filed with the regulatory authority on 3/23/2024, and a follow‑up audit of similar regulators was scheduled for the next quarter.

the incident occurred on april 7th at approximately 14:45 local time on a 24‑inch, 1‑2‑5 carbon steel transmission line owned by transco pipelines llc. the line, which transports natural gas at a maximum allowable operating pressure of 950 psi, is situated in a remote valley roughly three miles east of the town of redfield, wyoming, crossing a seasonal creek at a depth of 18 feet. during routine pressure monitoring, operators observed an unexpected drop in line pressure from 940 psi to 620 psi accompanied by a sudden rise in downstream flow meter readings. shortly thereafter, a loud “pop” was heard and a visible plume of gas was seen venting from the right‑hand side of the crossing. emergency shut‑in valves were activated within minutes, but the gas ignited upon contact with a stray spark from a nearby wildlife‑activated solar‑powered sensor, creating a brief flame front that was quickly extinguished by the automatic suppression system. the exact trigger for the rupture remains undetermined; preliminary assessments suggest possible third‑party excavation activity or material fatigue, but no definitive evidence has been found. a full forensic investigation, including in‑situ pipe wall thickness testing and review of recent right‑of‑way permits, is ongoing with assistance from the state oil and gas commission and an independent engineering firm.

on march 12, 2025 a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the river bend gathering system experienced an unplanned shutdown after a sudden pressure drop was recorded at the mainline pressure transmitter (p‑101). the line, rated for 960 psig, was operating at 820 psig when the downstream pressure fell to 380 psig within three minutes, triggering the automated emergency shut‑down (esd) sequence. field operators opened the remote manual shut‑off valve at station r-7 and isolated the segment. a visual inspection of the right‑of‑way revealed no visible leaks, ruptures, or third‑party damage. the pigging launcher located 2.4 miles upstream was found to be partially jammed; however, the pig had been removed the previous night without incident. further investigation uncovered that the 4‑inch vent valve on the auxiliary bleed line, installed for pressure regulation during pigging, had a corroded seat that allowed a slow leak when the line pressure exceeded 600 psig. the leak persisted unnoticed until the pressure differential caused the mainline alarm. after replacement of the vent valve and a pressure test at 1000 psig, the system was returned to service at 14:45, and the incident was closed pending a root‑cause review.

midwest natural gas company’s 24″ x 30‑inch schedule 40 steel pipeline (segment 45‑b) operating at 950 psig experienced an unexpected gas release on 04/03/24 during routine pigging operations. the inline inspection pig encountered a sudden pressure drop of approximately 120 psi, triggering the automated shut‑in system. operators noted a faint hissing sound near the 12‑mile marker and observed a thin white vapor plume emerging from a low‑lying grassy area adjacent to the right‑of‑way. immediate emergency response was initiated; a 10‑percent pressure reduction was applied while a qualified crew performed a visual inspection and deployed a portable gas detector, confirming methane concentrations of 4 % at ground level. the source was identified as a 2‑inch longitudinal gouge on the outer wall of the pipe, likely resulting from a latent manufacturing defect in the weld seam that had propagated over time. the affected pipe section was isolated, depressurized, and excavated. repair involved removal of the compromised pipe segment and installation of a new 24″ double‑welded splice with a full‑encirclement welded sleeve, followed by hydrostatic testing to 1.5 times operating pressure. the pipeline was returned to service on 04/07/24 after successful re‑commissioning.

on april 7, 2025 operators at the midland compression station observed a pressure drop on the 30‑inch, 800 psi carbon steel main feeding the northern distribution network. the automatic leak detection system flagged a release near milepost 142.5. field crews accessed the site and found a 3‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall at a recent tie‑in location where a temporary flange had been installed for a pigging operation. the split appeared to have initiated without any external impact; no excavation or third‑party activity had been recorded in the vicinity. a thorough visual inspection of the adjacent 24‑inch lateral revealed no signs of corrosion or mechanical damage. the incident was reported to the pipeline safety authority (nrc #1260458) at 14:23 and a 48‑hour follow‑up (nrc #1260532) was logged at 09:15 on april 9. a multidisciplinary meeting was convened with senior maintenance engineer lisa patterson, control systems lead ryan choi, and external consultant dr. alberto silva to review installation procedures, torque specifications, and the temporary flange design. further metallurgical analysis and stress‑relief testing are scheduled before the line is re‑pressurized.

at approximately 06:17 on 03/14/2022 the central gathering station at the hillside facility detected a rapid drop in pressure on the 24" x70# api 5l carbon steel main that transports raw gas from the north field. the control system generated a low‑pressure alarm and an automatic shut‑in valve began to close, but the valve failed to seal completely and the line continued to vent. operators initiated an emergency response, dispatched the maintenance crew, and called the local fire department at 06:32. the crew arrived at the site at 06:55 and observed a steady plume of vapor escaping from a 12‑inch split in the pipe wall near a recently installed pressure‑regulating station. the split appeared to have no visible corrosion, gouge, or third‑party damage. a temporary blind flange was installed at 07:45 to stop the release, and the area was evacuated. the incident was reported to the pipeline safety authority at 08:10. a detailed investigation concluded that the failure was likely due to a manufacturing defect in the pipe material that manifested under normal operating pressures of 720 psi, but the exact origin could not be definitively determined. the pipe segment was removed and replaced with a new 24" api 5l pipe, and the station returned to service on 03/18/2022.

the incident involved a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line located in the lower bend of the red river, approximately 0.75 mi downstream of milepost 124.5 near the town of springfield, ks. on 3 april 2026 the line experienced an unplanned pressure drop from its normal operating pressure of 1 200 psi to 650 psi, triggering an automatic shutdown. field crews arrived to find a small spray of petroleum product emanating from a section of the pipe near the riverbank, but the exact origin could not be identified. visual inspection revealed no obvious gouge, dent, or third‑party activity, and the surrounding soil appeared undisturbed. the river stage was near flood level at the time, with currents estimated at 4 ft/s, which may have contributed to the difficulty in locating the breach. a temporary clamp was installed to halt the flow, and the line was placed in a non‑pressurized state for further evaluation. due to limited access and the uncertain nature of the failure, the operator elected to abandon the affected segment and construct a bypass route rather than attempt a full repair. the incident resulted in an estimated $3.2 million in operator costs, primarily for abandonment and rerouting.

during a scheduled valve replacement on the 24" x70 grade b carbon steel mainline at the mid‑river crossing, the field supervisor ordered a temporary isolation of the line and instructed the crew to vent the segment to atmosphere. the venting procedure was carried out using a 4" flanged vent stack that had been previously de‑rated for a maximum pressure of 500 psi, but the line was still pressurized to 850 psi due to an oversight in the pressure relief sequencing. when the crew opened the vent, high‑velocity gas escaped through the undersized stack, striking a nearby portable generator set that was idling for power. the generator ignited the released natural gas, producing a brief flame front that singed a section of the work platform and damaged a crew‑owned hydraulic jack. no personnel were injured, but the generator and jack were destroyed, and the incident resulted in a loss of approximately $42 000 in equipment. the line was subsequently isolated, depressurized, and repaired with a new vent stack of appropriate rating. the event was documented and reported to the phmsa under the property‑damage reporting threshold.

at approximately 0735 hours on 22 september 2025, a western gas transmission employee was conducting a routine integrity inspection of the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near milepost 57.4 in the high desert region. during the walk‑down the crew observed an unexpected settlement of the right‑of‑way caused by recent heavy rains, which had created a shallow trench approximately 3 ft deep across the pipeline corridor. the crew marked the location and proceeded to install a temporary steel plate to bridge the low spot. at 0810 hours the field supervisor directed the crew to re‑align the pipe clamp on the existing valve block, but the written work order incorrectly referenced valve‑12 instead of valve‑21. consequently, the crew opened valve‑12 while the line remained pressurized at 950 psig (maop 1200 psig). the sudden pressure drop caused a rapid decompression event; a downstream pressure relief valve opened as designed, releasing an estimated 4.2 msc­f of natural gas into the open trench. the escaping gas ignited when it contacted a spark from a nearby diesel generator, resulting in a brief flash fire that was extinguished by the on‑site fire crew. no injuries were reported, but the incident caused approximately $32,000 in equipment damage and a temporary shutdown of the affected line segment for three hours. the event was reported to the cpuc and the ferc under the required incident reporting thresholds.

on 7/14/26 at approximately 14:42 a pressure drop was observed on the 20" offshore gas pipeline (api 5l x70) located 32 ft below the seabed in the north galveston channel. the line had been operating at 850 psig with a flow rate of 1.2 mmcfd when the automated monitoring system flagged a 120‑psi differential pressure loss over a 15‑minute interval. immediate shutdown of the pump stations was initiated and the line was isolated by closing the remote operated isolation valves at stations 12‑a and 12‑b. divers were deployed the following day to inspect the pipe segment between the two valves; however, poor visibility (30 ft) and strong currents limited visual assessment. a side‑scan sonar survey conducted on 7/16/26 identified a shallow depression approximately 8 ft wide and 3 ft deep centered over the pipeline route, but no definitive breach was visible. samples of the coating retrieved from the exposed pipe showed no signs of corrosion or mechanical damage. a subsequent remotely operated vehicle (rov) inspection on 7/20/26 captured footage of a large, partially buried concrete block positioned against the pipe at a 30° angle, suggesting possible external impact, though the block’s origin and placement time remain unknown. the line remains depressurized and isolated pending further investigation; repair scheduling is contingent on weather windows and availability of a replacement pipe segment. a supplemental report will be issued once additional evidence is collected and analyzed.

june 3, 2024 at 14:27 hrs, a 24‑in. x70 carbon steel transmission line operated by transco midwest was scheduled for routine pigging at 850 psi (gauge). during the pig launch at the westfield terminal, the control operator observed an unexpected pressure surge to 1050 psi and a rapid drop in downstream pressure to 300 psi. the automated safety shutdown (esd) system engaged within 2 seconds, isolating the affected segment with the nearest isolation valves. onsite crew arrived within 12 minutes and confirmed a sizable release of natural gas from a 1‑ft. longitudinal crack located near the 15:30 o’clock position of the pipe, adjacent to a recently installed 30‑ft. splice sleeve. initial inspection indicated the crack originated from a stress concentration caused by a misaligned pipe joint that had been welded during a third‑party construction activity three weeks earlier. the gas plume was ignited by a passing maintenance vehicle, resulting in a brief flame front that was extinguished by the emergency response team without injuries. the incident was reported to the nrc and the ferc. a full root‑cause analysis was later completed, noting inadequate weld inspection procedures and recommending enhanced non‑destructive testing for all third‑party work on high‑pressure lines.

on april 7, 2022, at 14:22 local time, the midland compression station experienced an unexpected release from the 30‑in. x65 carbon steel transmission line that was operating at 870 psig. a contractor from a nearby road widening project had been using an excavator to remove fill material when the machine struck a 12‑in. buried service line adjacent to the mainline. the impact displaced the protective concrete encasement and caused a gouge in the pipe wall approximately 18 inches long. the resulting breach allowed natural gas to escape at a rate of roughly 1,200 mmscfd. the station’s automatic shutdown (esd) system detected the pressure drop and initiated a safe shutdown sequence, closing the upstream isolation valve within 5 seconds. however, the downstream shut‑off valve failed to seal completely due to debris lodged in the actuator, allowing a secondary leak that persisted for another 22 seconds before the valve was manually secured by onsite personnel. emergency response crews were notified, the area was evacuated, and the gas was vented to a flare stack. an investigation determined the primary cause to be third‑party excavation damage and secondary cause to be valve actuator obstruction. the damaged pipe segment and affected valve assembly were replaced, and additional underground utility mapping protocols were implemented. the incident was reported to phmsa under the applicable reporting thresholds.

on 14 april 2025 a 16" x70 mil carbon steel transmission pipeline operating at 720 psig experienced an abrupt pressure drop while transporting sweet natural gas in the lower galveston bay area, approximately 0.9 nautical miles east of the shoreline near the mariner’s point. the line had been isolated from the main system at the nearest valve station and depressurized to 150 psig for initial assessment. a side‑scan sonar sweep performed on 16 april by deepwater surveys inc. identified a 9‑foot long, 1‑2‑foot deep depression in the seabed directly above the pipe alignment; the pipe was not visible due to sediment cover. a remotely operated vehicle (rov) inspection on 18 april revealed a clean external surface with no visible coating breach, corrosion, or impact damage, but a 10‑foot section of the pipe wall appeared to be missing, creating a gap consistent with the sonar crater. the surrounding sub‑sea terrain showed recent displacement, possibly from a low‑frequency acoustic event, yet no definitive source was identified. subsequent magnetic flux leakage (mfl) scanning on 22 april detected no wall loss outside the gap area. the pipeline remains isolated and a temporary bypass was installed on 25 april to maintain service. further forensic analysis of recovered pipe fragments, seabed samples, and acoustic recordings is pending; the exact mechanism that caused the wall loss remains undetermined.

a subcontractor hired to install a drainage ditch near the right‑of‑way unintentionally struck a buried 12‑inch schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line with a backhoe while excavating the trench. the impact created a 3‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe, causing a sudden release of natural gas at the line’s normal operating pressure of 620 psi. the automatic shutdown valve failed to close because the control cable had been routed through the same trench and was severed in the same incident. gas migrated into a nearby low‑lying depression where a crew was performing hot‑work on a valve box, using an oxy‑acetylene cutter. the escaping gas ignited, producing a fireball that engulfed the cutter and set fire to the surrounding vegetation. emergency response teams arrived within 8 minutes, isolated the section with a portable blind‑flange, and vented the remaining gas. the damaged pipe segment was later replaced with a 12‑inch api 5l x80 line, and the control cable was rerouted to a protected conduit. the incident prompted a review of excavation permits and underground utility mapping procedures.

on 5/16/24 at approximately 0830 hrs a routine aerial survey over the 24" x65# api 5l pipeline in the hillcrest valley identified a faint hydrocarbon sheen approximately 0.3 miles downstream of the valve station 12‑b. the line had been operating at 95 psig with a steady flow of 820 mmbtu/d. ground crews were dispatched and confirmed a small venting source at a welded joint near milepost 42+15. the joint exhibited a circumferential hairline crack likely initiated by stress corrosion, though no definitive cause could be established. immediate response actions included isolating the affected segment by closing the upstream and downstream block valves, depressurizing the isolated loop to 5 psig, and installing a temporary steel clamp to stop the release. a 24‑in. full‑encirclement welded sleeve was fabricated on site and installed the following day, after which the line was pressure‑tested to 110 % of operating pressure and returned to service at 90 psig. environmental monitoring over the next 48 hours showed no detectable increase in soil or water contaminants. the incident was logged per 49 cfr part 191, and a root‑cause investigation was opened to evaluate coating integrity and cathodic protection performance along the affected stretch.

upon routine patrol on april 22, 2026 a field crew observed a faint odor of natural gas emanating from the right-of-way near milepost 47.6 of the 20‑inch, x70 steel transmission line operating at 800 psi in the black hill valley, colorado. the crew deployed a calibrated cg4 detector and recorded a continuous reading of 12 % lelev. a quick visual inspection revealed a small, wet patch on the vegetation adjacent to the pipeline trench. excavating a 2‑ft radius around the wet spot uncovered a ¼‑inch pinhole breach on the outer longitudinal seam of the pipe, located just below the riverbank. the seam appeared to have been compromised by corrosion that was not evident in the last inline pig run performed six months earlier. after confirming the leak, the line was isolated and depressurized to 150 psi. a hot‑tapped repair sleeve, 24‑inch long and rated for 900 psi, was installed over the damaged area and the joint was back‑filled with sand and a protective geomembrane. post‑repair pressure testing reached 900 psi without any detectable emissions. the line was returned to normal service at 750 psi, and the incident was logged for further corrosion monitoring.

the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 910 psi experienced an unexpected pressure drop at the mid‑segment monitoring station. initial diagnostics showed the automatic shut‑in valve (asn‑12) failed to close fully, allowing approximately 4 % of the nominal flow to escape into the surrounding right‑of‑way. the valve actuator was reported to have received a spurious signal from the distributed control system (dcs) at 14:23 local time, but the root cause of the signal anomaly could not be identified on site. a downstream pressure relief valve, set at 950 psi, opened briefly for about 22 minutes, venting natural gas at an estimated rate of 450 mmscfd before the system was manually isolated. local fire‑rescue units were dispatched, and a shelter‑in‑place order was issued for the adjacent residential community of 78 households. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission within 30 minutes and to the national response center within 45 minutes. damage assessment indicated minor soil contamination and a need to replace the asn‑12 valve assembly, as well as a thorough review of the dcs firmware to prevent recurrence. the exact trigger for the actuator signal remains undetermined.

on april 22nd 2024 at approximately 07:40 am, field operations responded to an unplanned release on the central hub line, a 24‑inch api 5l steel pipeline transporting 1250 psig natural gas from the western processing complex to the downstream distribution hub. the incident was first detected by an automatic gas detection sensor located near milepost 312.5, which triggered an alarm and a visual vapor cloud was observed by the on‑site crew. initial isolation procedures were executed, shutting down the upstream block valve and bleeding the affected segment to a safe pressure of 200 psig. investigation of the site revealed that a recently installed fiber‑optic cable trench had unintentionally intersected a buried valve manifold, causing a partial breach in the valve body. the breach measured approximately 4 inches in diameter and released an estimated 8,500 mcf of gas before isolation was complete. emergency services were notified, a perimeter was established, and the area was evacuated. the damaged valve was removed, the trench backfilled with protective padding, and a new valve assembly was installed per the manufacturer’s repair standards. after hydrostatic testing at 150 % of design pressure, the line was repressurized and returned to service at 1200 psig. no injuries were reported.

on october 4, 2023 at 07:45 am the operations control center received an alarm indicating a sudden rise in pressure to 845 psig on the 30‑inch mainline feeding the eastward transmission station. the line, a seamless api 5l x70 grade b pipe, normally operated at a maximum of 800 psig. the automatic pigging sequence had been initiated at 06:30 am to clean residual wax buildup, but the pig failed to clear the 1,200‑ft section near milepost 112. field crews dispatched from the maintenance yard arrived at 08:10 am and observed a localized bulge on the external coating approximately 15 ft downstream of a previously installed girth weld. visual inspection revealed a small crack in the weld throat, likely induced by the pressure spike when the pig became lodged and the downstream relief valve opened. the segment was isolated and depressurized to 10 psig by 09:05 am, and the pig was recovered using a retrieval tool. a 22‑ft pipe section was removed, sent to the fab shop for repair, and reinstalled with a new welded joint, coated, and hydrotested to 1,100 psig before returning to service at 03:20 pm. post‑incident review identified the root cause as an unexpected debris accumulation in the pipe that was not detected during routine inline inspection, prompting a revision of the pigging schedule and the addition of an ultrasonic inspection pass after each cleaning run.

during a routine hydrostatic test of a 24‑inch api 5l x65 pipeline operating at 1 250 psi, a sudden pressure drop of 150 psi was observed at station 12‑b. the line was immediately isolated and depressurized. a crew of four performed a surface inspection and identified a narrow, crescent‑shaped seam opening approximately 4 inches long on the lower flange of a valve block that had been installed during the 1998 expansion project. the opening was not visible during previous pigging runs because the defect was internal to the valve body. the valve assembly was removed, and the damaged flange was sent to an external metallurgical laboratory for fracture analysis. preliminary visual examination suggested a possible manufacturing lapse in the heat‑treatment of the flange material, but no definitive conclusion could be drawn. the valve was replaced with a new 24‑inch forged carbon steel unit rated for 1 500 psi, the section was leak‑tested for 3 hours at operating pressure, and the line was returned to service. final laboratory results are pending to confirm the exact origin of the seam failure.

on april 14, 2025 at approximately 1430 hrs a field maintenance crew was conducting a routine pressure verification on the ab‑12 mainline (24‑in. x 30# api 5l) near milepost 112+45. the line had been isolated with block valve a (bv‑a) and block valve b (bv‑b) and pressurized to 850 psig using a portable pump. during the test the crew observed a gradual pressure loss of about 120 psig over a ten‑minute interval. the on‑site gauge on the pump read normal, however a handheld digital transducer on the downstream side showed 730 psig. the crew immediately closed bv‑a and opened the emergency vent to bleed the line to 600 psig while notifying control. after venting, a small spray of natural gas was detected at a splice near the eastward turn of the line. the area was evacuated and a fire‑watch team was deployed; no ignition occurred. the splice was later excavated and the gasket was found to be displaced, allowing a micro‑leak that escaped detection during previous inspections. the line was depressurized, the splice repaired, and the system restored to service at 820 psig after a 4‑hour shutdown. the incident was reported to the nrc as a non‑significant event pending further metallurgical analysis of the splice material.

10/14/2024 06:42 am – field crew conducting a routine cathodic protection survey on the 24‑inch, 720 psig main (segment km 12‑15) observed a faint odor of natural gas near the right‑of‑way at milepost 13.4. handheld detector confirmed presence of hydrocarbon vapors emanating from a vented casing vent pipe. 07:10 am – operations dispatched a leak response team; the area was cordoned off and emergency response was notified. 07:35 am – isolation valves upstream (station a‑102) and downstream (station a‑108) were closed, reducing line pressure to 150 psig. 08:00 am – a temporary plug was installed on the affected pipe section while the leak was assessed. visual inspection after exposing the pipe revealed a 0.8‑inch longitudinal split in the lower 5‑inch wall, likely initiated at a weld overlay. 08:45 am – the compromised segment was cut out and a 24‑inch splice sleeve was fabricated on‑site; the splice was welded and hydrostatically tested to 1.5 × working pressure. 10:20 am – the line was repressurized and product flow resumed. 11:00 am – a third‑party metallurgical lab was engaged to examine the failed pipe fragment. their preliminary report indicated a combination of material contamination and stress‑corrosion cracking, but a definitive root cause remains pending further analysis. the incident was reported to the national response center (nrc# 202411014).

on 03/14/26 at approximately 14:42 while conducting a routine valve inspection on the 24" x70# api5l mainline near station r-12, the field crew noted an unexpected drop in pressure from 860 psig to 410 psig after closing the upstream block valve. a subsequent leak detection survey with a portable acoustic sensor identified a faint hiss at the junction of a 24" tie‑in branch that had been installed two years prior. the branch had a 20" x60# api5l sleeve welded onto the mainline using a field‑fabricated grooved connection. further inspection revealed that the sleeve’s external coating had delaminated, allowing moisture ingress which corroded the grooved coupling. the corroded area measured approximately 3 in. in length and was the source of the pressure loss. the leak was isolated by opening the downstream isolation valve and depressurizing the segment; a temporary clamp was installed to stop flow until a permanent repair could be scheduled. the incident was reported to operations control, safety manager r. delaney, and maintenance supervisor k. mendoza. a corrective action plan was issued on 03/18/26 requiring replacement of the sleeve and a review of all similar field‑fabricated connections. the line was restored to service at 78 psig on 03/20/26 after successful repair and hydrostatic testing. the incident report was closed on 04/02/26 with no injuries reported.

on september 12, 2023 a routine pigging operation was initiated on the 30‑inch, sch40 carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade x70) operating at 720 psi. the pig was launched from the western launch bay and after traveling 6 miles the downstream receiver was found to be pressurized despite the isolation valves being fully closed. an immediate manual vent was attempted using the two 2‑inch ball valves located on the receiver vent manifold, but the valves failed to open due to a seized stem caused by corrosion buildup. pressure in the receiver built to an estimated 450 psi before a secondary safety vent on the sidewall ruptured, releasing a jet of natural gas that ignited from a nearby hot work torch used by maintenance personnel. the flame was extinguished by the onsite fire suppression system, but the incident resulted in minor burns to two technicians and a temporary shutdown of the line for repair. subsequent investigation revealed that the vent manifold had not been inspected in accordance with the 5‑year maintenance schedule, and the corrosion on the valve stems was documented in a previous audit but never addressed. corrective actions included replacing the vent manifold, updating the maintenance tracking system, and conducting a root‑cause review of the inspection compliance process.

pipeline control noticed an unexplained drop in pressure from 1,200 psi to 800 psi on the 24‑in. carbon steel mainline feeding the south field processing plant at 03:12 am. scada alarms triggered a high‑low pressure event and the operator immediately opened the emergency shutdown panel. after a brief investigation, it was discovered that a temporary bypass valve installed for a downstream pigging operation had not been fully closed after the pig passed. the valve, a 10‑in. flanged gate valve with a known history of seat wear, was left in a semi‑open position, allowing the line to vent to the atmospheric vent stack at a rate of approximately 850 mmscfd. operations isolated the affected loop at the nearest block valve at 03:28 am and depressurized the segment to 0 psi by 04:02 am. a site walk‑down confirmed the valve position and a missing lockout tag. the valve was secured, the lockout/tagout procedure was re‑implemented, and a replacement valve was ordered. the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety board under report number tx‑2026‑0456. no injuries or releases beyond the vented gas were recorded, and service to customers was restored by 07:15 am after pressure was rebuilt to normal operating levels.

on september 12, 2026, operators of the midwest gas transmission system observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch, 2.5‑inch wall thickness carbon steel line designated as the h‑210 segment. the line, which normally operates at 950 psig, fell to 620 psig within 12 minutes while transporting sour natural gas at a flow rate of 6.4 mmcf/d. a downstream isolation valve was closed and the section was depressurized to 0 psig by 19:45 local time. field crews arrived at the site and identified a small venting plume near a river crossing. excavation revealed a 3‑inch longitudinal crack near a previously installed expansion joint. the cause of the crack is under investigation; preliminary review suggests possible ground movement or a manufacturing defect, but no definitive conclusion has been reached. the affected portion of the pipe was cut out and replaced with a new 24‑inch seamless steel segment, and the line was re‑pressurized after hydrostatic testing to 1200 psig. there were no injuries, and no property damage was reported beyond the immediate excavation area. regulatory notifications have been submitted and a supplemental incident report will be filed pending final root‑cause analysis.

on 8/2/2026, midwest interstate gas transmission observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 30‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x70) at mile marker 127. scada alarm triggered at 09:14 indicating a 15‑psi differential loss. operations dispatched a field crew who arrived at the site at 09:42 and noted a 3‑inch gouge in the pipe wall with visible soil intrusion. the breach was isolated by closing the upstream block valve (bv‑127‑up) and the downstream block valve (bv‑127‑dn) at 09:55, halting gas flow. the area was secured and a hot‑tapping unit was positioned to install a temporary steel sleeve. emergency response was coordinated with the state fire marshal and the incident was logged with the phmsa at 10:30. a replacement 30‑inch segment was fabricated and installed on 8/4/2026; hydrostatic testing confirmed 1.5 × design pressure integrity before reinstating service at reduced pressure on 8/6/2026. a root‑cause investigation is underway to determine why soil erosion had exposed the pipe, and a supplemental report will be filed pending completion of the analysis.

during a routine maintenance shutdown of the midwest transmission line, the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline (schedule 40, api 5l) was isolated with a 24‑inch block valve that had been serviced two weeks earlier. after the line was depressurized to 50 psig, a subcontractor crew began welding a new pressure regulator onto the downstream pig launcher. the welder inadvertently struck the adjacent 2‑inch vent line with the torch, causing the vent line to develop a pinhole leak. the pinhole allowed natural gas at 250 psig to escape into the surrounding soil. because the vent line was buried only 12 inches deep and not equipped with a leak detection sensor, the release went unnoticed for approximately 45 minutes. the escaping gas accumulated in a nearby low‑lying area and was ignited by an unrelated spark from a diesel generator, resulting in a brief fireball that damaged a section of the earthen berm. emergency shutdown procedures were initiated at 14:32, the fire was extinguished by 14:38, and the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety office at 15:10. subsequent investigation identified the accidental torch contact as the primary cause and prompted a revision of welding clearance protocols.

on april 14, at approximately 07:45 a maintenance crew was conducting a routine cathodic protection survey on the 30‑in. api 5l x70 steel pipeline (design pressure 1500 psi) that traverses the pine ridge conservation area. while lowering the voltage probe into the right‑of‑way, the crew observed an unexpected voltage drop and a faint hiss of gas near the 12 mile marker. the operator immediately isolated the section by closing the downstream 30‑in. isolation valve (isolation point a) and opened the upstream 30‑in. bypass valve (bypass point b) to maintain service to downstream customers. a visual inspection revealed a 6‑inch long longitudinal crack in the pipe wall, with a low‑temperature hydrocarbon vapor plume escaping into the surrounding wetland. the leak released an estimated 0.8 bbl of natural gas condensate before the line was fully depressurized at 09:12. emergency response teams erected a containment berm and deployed absorbent pads; the affected area, approximately 0.4 acre, was later surveyed for soil contamination. the incident was reported to the nrc (incident #20241178) at 09:45 and a follow‑up report (incident #20241205) was submitted on april 16, 2024. the pipe segment was excavated, removed, and sent for metallurgical analysis to determine the root cause.

during a routine cathodic protection inspection on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) operating at 960 psi, field crews observed a persistent sheen of petroleum‑like liquid on the grass adjacent to the right‑of‑way, approximately 0.8 mi southeast of the nearest valve station. excavation of the wet ground revealed a 6‑inch long longitudinal seam split in the pipe wall, located just downstream of a 30‑year‑old 24‑inch inline valve that had been de‑energized for a previous maintenance outage. the split appeared to have originated at a corrosion pit that had penetrated through the pipe wall and then propagated laterally under the coating. the pipe segment, measured at 1 520 ft, was removed and replaced with new 24‑inch x70 pipe, spliced using 24‑inch 150‑degree grooved couplings and backed‑filled with a 0.125‑in. thick epoxy‑based sealant. a new inline valve with a dual‑seal arrangement was installed, and the restored section was pressure tested to 1.2 × design pressure (1152 psi) for 48 hours with no leaks detected. post‑repair monitoring indicated normal operating parameters, and the incident was logged for future corrosion mitigation planning.

at approximately 06:37 on 03/11/2022 a pressure surge alarm was triggered on the 24‑inch api 5l x65 steel transmission line feeding the north ridge gathering system. the control room operator noted a sudden rise to 1450 psig in the downstream pressure transmitter, exceeding the design limit of 1350 psig. an automatic shutdown (esd) was initiated at 06:38 and the main isolation valve at milepost 12.4 closed within 3 seconds. field crews were dispatched and arrived on scene at 07:02. visual inspection revealed a small spray of oil‑free gas emanating from a weld joint on a 6‑inch tie‑in branch line near the valve station, but the source could not be pinpointed due to ice accumulation on the pipe. the gas was isolated, vented to a flare pit, and the line was depressurized to 200 psig for further examination. a preliminary investigation ruled out external interference and confirmed that the pressure relief valve functioned correctly. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission via after‑hours voicemail at 07:45 and a formal report was filed with the nrc at 11:30. a full root‑cause analysis is underway, with recommendations to review weld inspection procedures and temperature monitoring protocols.

on 3/18/2024 at approximately 09:45 a.m. a routine pressure test was being conducted on the 30‑inch x70 mil carbon steel main (segment 12‑b) to verify integrity after a recent pigging operation. the automatic pressure control valve (apcv‑04) at the northbound station malfunctioned and failed to modulate, causing the line pressure to rise from the scheduled 550 psig to 720 psig within two minutes. operators observed a sudden pressure spike on the control panel and initiated an emergency shutdown. the high pressure caused a minor crack to develop at the heat‑affected zone of a previously repaired girth weld near milepost 215. a small hydrocarbon vent was detected by the continuous emission monitoring system (cems) and a faint sheen was observed by the aerial surveillance team over the adjacent wetland. the section was isolated, depressurized to 30 psig, and a field repair crew installed a 24‑inch steel slip‑on sleeve with a backing ring. the repaired area was pressure‑tested to 650 psig and held for 24 hours. an incident notification (nrc# 1456789) was submitted at 12:30 p.m. central time, and a detailed root‑cause analysis will be completed pending metallurgical lab results. the line was returned to service at 14:15 on 3/20/2024.

during a routine inline inspection on 03/14/24, a 30‑inch x70 grade b pipeline carrying 720 psi of natgas experienced an unexpected pressure drop of approximately 180 psi over a 2‑mile segment near milepost 145. the pigging crew reported a sudden increase in pig resistance and audible grinding noises as the tool passed the location. immediate isolation of the line was performed using the nearest upstream and downstream shut‑in valves, and the affected section was depressurized to 50 psi for safety. first responders from the site emergency team arrived within ten minutes, establishing a 100‑ft perimeter. a small venting plume of natural gas was observed, but no ignition occurred. after a thorough visual inspection, a 2‑inch longitudinal split was identified in the pipe wall, likely caused by a combination of thermal fatigue and stress corrosion cracking, though the exact initiating factor could not be conclusively determined. the incident was reported to the pipeline safety authority, and a temporary bypass was installed while a detailed metallurgical analysis is underway. recommendations include revising integrity management intervals for high‑risk segments, implementing enhanced corrosion monitoring, and reviewing recent temperature cycling data for similar pipe sections.

on april 17, 2025 at approximately 14:35 hrs a maintenance crew was performing a scheduled valve replacement on a 24‑in carbon steel pipeline transporting 650 psi natural gas near the river bend segment. the valve was isolated with a lock‑out/tag‑out procedure and a portable gas detector was positioned upstream. while the crew removed the 12‑in gate valve, the supervisory control system automatically initiated a pressure reset on the main line after a transient loss of signal from the remote transmitter. the sudden pressure increase to 720 psi propagated through the isolated section before the valve was fully sealed, causing a rapid surge that ruptured a 6‑in branch pipe that had been previously cut for pig launcher installation. a high‑energy jet of gas escaped, igniting when it contacted a nearby welding torch that had been left on standby. the flash resulted in minor burns to two technicians and a small fire that was extinguished by the on‑site fire suppression system within five minutes. an investigation team was convened on the same day; findings highlighted a lack of coordination between the control system reset and the manual isolation work, an outdated pressure relief setting on the branch line, and the presence of an active ignition source in the immediate vicinity of the isolated pipe. corrective actions include revising lock‑out/tag‑out protocols to require system interlock verification, updating relief valve setpoints to 800 psi, and implementing a hot‑work clearance checklist for all maintenance zones. the incident was reported to the pipeline safety authority and is pending final review.

on july 3, 2024 a routine pig run on the 24‑inch, 70‑grade carbon steel main (design pressure 1 250 psig) detected an unexpected pressure drop to 820 psig at mile‑12. field crews were dispatched and used handheld gas detectors, confirming a faint methane plume near the right‑of‑way. the segment was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream block valves and the area was secured with a 30‑meter exclusion zone. investigation of the exposed pipe revealed a localized gouge approximately 2 inches deep and 4 inches long on the external coating, likely caused by a recent heavy‑equipment maneuver that displaced a backfill rock. the damaged section was cut out and a 24‑inch, 70‑grade steel replacement spool was welded in place, followed by non‑destructive testing of the welds and reinstatement of the coating system. additional bracing was installed around the pipe at the site of the incident to prevent future mechanical impact. a temporary increase in patrols of the right‑of‑way was ordered, and the maintenance schedule for coating inspections was revised to include quarterly visual checks in high‑traffic zones.

on august 14, 2025, western pipelines received a telephone alert from a local landowner reporting a possible oil seepage near milepost 112.3 of the 24‑inch api 5l carbon steel main that traverses the foothills of the green ridge. western field operations dispatched a leak detection crew at 06:45 am. upon arrival, the crew observed a thin sheen on the grass approximately 15 ft downstream of a recently installed road crossing. pressure at the upstream station was 850 psi, while downstream pressure read 430 psi, indicating a pressure drop of roughly 420 psi. the crew isolated the segment by closing the upstream block valve at milepost 111.9 and the downstream valve at milepost 112.7, and subsequently depressurized the isolated section to 5 psi. a visual inspection revealed a 0.4‑inch crack in the pipe wall at the point where the crossing’s concrete encasement had been repaired three months earlier. the cause of the crack is under investigation; possible factors include improper backfill compaction or residual stress from the recent repair. the affected pipe section was excavated, removed, and replaced with a new 24‑inch api 5l pipe coated with a three‑layer polyethylene system. the line was reinstated and pressure restored to normal operating levels at 15:20 hrs. the incident was logged as case number 842761 and reported to the nrc.

on 03/15/2024 a low‑pressure leak was identified on a 24‑inch api 5l x65 carbon steel transmission line operating at 850 psi near the riley ridge valve station in north dakota. the leak was first observed during a scheduled aerial patrol when a faint vapor plume was noted approximately 0.6 mi east of the station. ground crews were dispatched and, after confirming gas odor, commenced excavation. exposure revealed a 0.35‑inch longitudinal crack at the toe of a girth weld on a recently installed pipe segment that had been placed in 2019 during a capacity expansion. visual inspection showed no obvious corrosion, impact damage, or external stress. the affected pipe section was isolated, the cracked weld cut out, and a 15‑foot splice was installed using a reinforced sleeve. the removed pipe and weld coupon were sent to an independent metallurgical laboratory for failure analysis. preliminary reports indicate the fracture surface exhibits intergranular features suggestive of a possible hydrogen‑induced cracking mechanism, though no definitive source of hydrogen has been identified. the investigation remains open pending full laboratory results. meanwhile, the operator has initiated a review of recent welding procedures and post‑weld heat‑treatment records to mitigate any similar occurrences.

the 20" carbon steel pipeline, grade api 5l x70, operating at 950 psi, was being cleared with a foam pig when the pigging crew noticed an abnormal pressure drop of 120 psi over a 3‑minute interval. further inspection revealed that a previously installed temperature sensor housing had become dislodged during a recent unrelated subsea inspection by a third‑party contractor using a remotely operated vehicle. the housing struck the pipe wall at station 14‑b, creating a 0.75‑inch gouge that compromised the pipe wall integrity. the breach allowed a low‑density natural gas release into the surrounding water column, which was quickly detected by the pipeline’s emergency shutdown system. the e s d system isolated the section at valve stations 13‑a and 15‑c, and the area was declared a hot work zone. divers were deployed to assess the damage, and a temporary clamp was installed to stop the leak until a replacement pipe segment could be fabricated. the incident required a 48‑hour shutdown of the line, resulting in an estimated loss of 1.2 mmcfd of gas throughput. the root cause was determined to be unintended equipment impact by an external contractor during non‑pipeline‑related activities.

04/03/2025 – 08:42 am – field operations received a call from the contract maintenance crew working on a nearby utility easement about a sudden hiss and visible vapor plume near the 30‑inch, 7‑inch wall thickness, api 5l grade b steel pipeline (line c‑12) located at milepost 12.5. the line is rated for 950 psi operating pressure and transports 70 % propane‑rich natural gas. at 08:46 am the site supervisor instructed the crew to clear the area and established a 300‑ft exclusion zone. at 08:52 am the regional emergency response team was dispatched; hazmat units arrived at 09:07 am and began atmospheric monitoring. by 09:22 am the pipeline control center initiated an automatic shut‑in of line c‑12 and isolated the affected segment using valve c‑12‑sv‑02 and the upstream isolation station. the leak was confirmed at a weld seam on a recently repaired splice, but no immediate mechanical failure was observed. approximately 3,200 mcf of gas were released before the shut‑in was complete. at 10:15 am the state environmental agency was notified, and at 10:38 am the incident commander declared the situation “contained” and lifted the evacuation order for the surrounding residential area. the cause of the rupture remains under investigation pending metallurgical analysis and review of recent weld inspection records.

04/22/2025 - at approximately 1430 hrs utc, a release was observed on the 24‑inch, 600‑psi x70 carbon steel mainline (segment a‑b) of the mid‑state transmission corridor, located near milepost 112.3 in the oak ridge valley. the incident was initially detected by the scm system, which recorded a sudden drop in downstream pressure from 598 psi to 432 psi and a corresponding increase in acoustic emission signals. field crews arrived within 45 minutes and confirmed a visible plume of natural gas emanating from a ~3‑inch longitudinal crack in the pipe wall, approximately 12 feet below the ground surface. the line was isolated using the nearest mainline isolation valve (valve 4‑a) and depressurized to 0 psi before a hot‑tapping operation was performed. divers were deployed to expose the damaged section, and a plidco repair clamp was installed on 04/24/2025. the pipe was returned to service on 04/26/2025 after pressure testing to 650 psi. because the pipe segment had been in service for 18 years and no recent excavation activity was reported, the exact initiation mechanism of the crack could not be determined. further metallurgical analysis is pending. for further information contact jason murray, pipeline integrity manager, 816‑555‑0198, jason.murray@midstatepipelines.com.

while conducting a scheduled inline inspection on the 30‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x70) the pig became lodged near station 412+18 after encountering a buildup of scale and a small piece of corrosion product. the crew attempted to push the pig forward using the launch pump at 1 500 psi, but the pressure downstream rose to 2 200 psi and the pig remained immobile. a decision was made to open the vent manifold on the adjacent pig trap to relieve pressure. the vent valve was manually opened, but the release line was partially obstructed, causing a rapid pressure drop in the main while residual gas remained trapped behind the pig. when the clamp securing the vent manifold cover was loosened, the vent housing swung open with enough force to strike a technician standing on the platform, causing a bruised rib and minor lacerations. after the incident, the pig was recovered using a back‑pull unit, and the obstructed vent line was cleared. the main was depressurized to 600 psi, inspected for damage, and returned to service after confirming no breach. the event was logged as incident #2026‑1123 and reported to the safety office.

on 14 august 2024 a 30‑in. api 5l x65 transmission pipeline located in western karnes county, tx experienced a rapid pressure surge that resulted in a gash approximately 0.75 in. in diameter on the mainline at station mr‑12. the line, installed in 2005, operates at a maximum working pressure of 900 psi and is coated with three‑layer polyethylene for corrosion protection. during routine maintenance, a subcontractor was tasked with cleaning the valve pit at the downstream pressure‑reduction station. the crew inadvertently installed a temporary sandbag seal on the isolation valve instead of the specified steel block. when the control system commanded a normal blow‑down to 400 psi, the valve remained partially closed, causing a sudden pressure differential of roughly 500 psi across the downstream section. the resulting water hammer induced a high‑frequency stress wave that exceeded the pipe’s fatigue limit, tearing the steel wall at a weld joint that had previously undergone a hot‑tap installation. natural gas escaped for approximately six minutes before the automatic shut‑down system isolated the segment. emergency responders evacuated a nearby mobile home park of 22 units as a precaution, and a 0.5‑mile stretch of county road was closed pending repair. subsequent investigation highlighted the improper temporary seal as the primary factor, prompting a revision of field‑procedure checklists.

incident description: on september 12, 2024 at approximately 07:42 local time, a venting event was reported at the silver creek gathering station on the 24‑inch, 900‑psig mainline serving the northern field. a 911 call from a nearby ranch indicated a strong odor of natural gas near the south‑side pig trap. operations personnel arrived on site at 08:10 and observed continuous venting from the pig trap vent valve, which displayed a closed position on the hmi but was releasing gas at an estimated 4.8 mmscfd. the vent valve was manually isolated at 08:23, and the associated line was purged and depressurized by 09:01. the incident resulted in a total loss of approximately 6,120 mcf of gas before isolation. initial inspection revealed an unexpected fracture in the vent valve stem, likely caused by a foreign object that had entered the valve housing during a recent pigging operation. the object was identified as a piece of pigging sleeve metal that had broken off downstream. to mitigate future occurrences, a supplemental seal inspection program has been scheduled for all vent valve assemblies on the line, and an additional pressure‑differential alarm will be added to the scada to detect abnormal vent flow. the root‑cause investigation remains ongoing, and a supplemental report will be filed upon completion.

on 7/12/25 at approximately 08:45 a maintenance crew began pigging the 24‑inch api 5l x65 line to clear accumulated sand from the recent hydraulic fracturing operation. the pig was launched from the western pig trap at a line pressure of 120 psig, which was within the operating range for the segment. during the run, the control system recorded a sudden drop to 45 psig and a brief surge to 150 psig when the pig encountered a previously undocumented 2‑inch reduction fitting that had been installed during a field modification three months earlier. the reduction was not reflected in the as‑built drawings because the installation was recorded only in a field log that never made it to the central database. the pig became lodged at the fitting, causing a localized over‑pressure that ruptured the surrounding carbon‑steel sleeve, resulting in a small hydrocarbon seep that was observed by the aerial surveillance team at 09:10. the leak was isolated by closing the nearest valve, pressure was bled, and a temporary clamp was installed. a full inspection later confirmed the sleeve failure and the missing drawing amendment. corrective actions include updating the engineering database, revising the pigging procedure, and adding a pressure relief valve downstream of the reduction. the line was returned to service at 14:30 after a pressure test at 130 psig.

on 15 april 2026, at approximately 0830 hrs, a routine pigging operation was initiated on the 30" api 5l x80 carbon steel transmission line (segment id 8421) transporting 1400 psig natural gas from the hillcrest compression station to the midriver delivery point. the pigging crew observed an unexpected rise in back‑pressure to 1650 psig and a sudden loss of pig velocity near milepost 12.4. field personnel halted the run and performed an external visual inspection, noting a faint hiss of gas and a small vapor cloud emanating from a joint near the right‑hand side of the pipe. a handheld ultrasonic thickness gauge indicated a localized wall thinning to 0.30 in., well below the nominal 0.48 in. wall thickness. further investigation revealed that a previously installed temporary steel support bracket, added during a third‑party construction activity three months earlier, had been improperly bolted, causing a stress concentration that led to micro‑cracking and eventual breach of the seam. the line was isolated, the damaged section was cut out, and a 12‑in. splice sleeve with a full‑penetration weld was installed. the incident was reported to the regulatory authority as a significant event due to the unanticipated failure mode and the potential for downstream service interruption. the support bracket was removed, and a revised installation procedure was issued to prevent recurrence.

on july 14, 2025 at 0830 hrs, a routine high‑pressure integrity test was being conducted on the western segment of the riverbend transmission line, a 30‑inch api 5l x70 carbon steel pipeline rated for 1050 psi operating at 720 psi. the test involved raising the line pressure to 950 psi while monitoring with a portable electronic pressure transducer mounted on the mainline pig launcher. the transducer, calibrated six months earlier, drifted and displayed a pressure reading 80 psi lower than the actual line pressure. unaware of the discrepancy, operators maintained the test pressure for the prescribed 45‑minute hold period. after the hold, the line was depressurized, but a sudden pressure spike of approximately 150 psi occurred as the pig valve on the downstream side snapped shut unexpectedly due to a latch malfunction. the combined over‑pressure exceeded the pipe’s maximum allowable stress, resulting in a longitudinal rupture near the 12‑mile marker. the rupture released a high‑energy jet of natural gas, igniting upon contact with a nearby diesel‑powered generator. the fire burned for roughly 12 minutes before being extinguished by onsite fire‑suppression crews, causing damage to the generator, a 5‑ton steel gantry, and three adjacent service trailers. the incident was logged and a detailed root‑cause analysis initiated.

on june 14, 2025 maintenance crew was performing routine pigging on a 24‑inch x70 steel pipeline transporting 720 psi natural gas in the panhandle region. after the pig passed a recently installed 90‑degree bend, operators noticed a sudden pressure drop of 85 psi and an audible hissing at the bend location. field inspection revealed that the new flange installed two weeks earlier had been torqued with a standard carbon steel bolt instead of the specified high‑strength alloy bolt, resulting in bolt stretch and loss of seal integrity. a thin film of corrosion product was observed between the flange faces, further compromising the joint. the line was isolated and depressurized, and a temporary stainless‑steel split sleeve rated for 1 200 psi was placed over the compromised flange while a full replacement was scheduled. a leak check was performed for 3 hours at the line’s operating pressure, and divers performed a visual inspection of the joint from the interior. the incident caused a brief service interruption but no injuries or environmental release beyond the immediate area.
