on 9/14/2026 at roughly 14:45, the control center received an automated alarm indicating a pressure drop on segment b-12 of the eastward mainline (24" x70 grade x70 steel). field crew was dispatched from the nearest pump station and arrived on scene at 15:10. visual inspection of the right‑of‑way revealed a small venting plume of natural gas near the 12‑mile marker, approximately 250 ft east of the river crossing. the pipeline was isolated by closing the downstream block valve at valve station 45 and the upstream isolation valve at valve station 43; pressure was bled to 0 psig by 15:40. a temporary leak clamp was installed on the 24" pipe at the leak point, and the area was evacuated. subsequent excavation uncovered a 2‑inch longitudinal crack in the pipe wall, likely initiated at a weld defect, but no definitive cause was determined during the initial assessment. the damaged pipe segment was cut out and replaced with a new 24" x70 x70 pipe, and the block valves were re‑opened after pressure testing to 1200 psig. final repairs were completed and the line returned to service at 19:05, with a supplemental incident report to follow.

on 3/12/26 at 08:45 a field engineer observed an unexpected pressure drop on the 30‑inch, schedule 40, api 5l sp steel transmission line (design pressure 1200 psi, operating at 950 psi) in the jackson county corridor. a visual inspection revealed a faint vapor cloud emanating from a small breach near a welded joint that had been previously marked for future replacement due to age. the exact mechanism of failure could not be determined on site; no recent excavation, impact, or known corrosion pits were identified. emergency shutdown (ems) was initiated at 08:52, isolating the affected segment by closing valves v-45 and v-46. the local fire department and state police hazmat unit arrived by 09:15, establishing a 300‑ft safety perimeter and evacuating two nearby residences as a precaution. a 20‑minute venting procedure was performed, releasing approximately 32 mcf of natural gas before the line was depressurized and secured. the breach was later repaired with a full‑encirclement welded sleeve and a new 6‑in. backing ring, and the pipeline was returned to service after hydrostatic testing at 1500 psi. a detailed investigation is ongoing, and a supplemental report will be filed pending root‑cause analysis.

09/14/24 – 6:45 am – field crew detected a faint odor of mercaptan near milepost 212 on the north‑south mainline (pipeline id: ns‑15, 24‑inch, sch‑80 carbon steel, operating at 820 psi). visual inspection showed no obvious rupture, gouge, or corrosion at the surface. a portable gas detector confirmed the presence of natural gas at 4 % vol. the area was cordoned off and the block valves on either side of the suspect segment (station 212‑a and 212‑b) were closed to isolate the line. pressure was bled to 150 psi and a hot‑tapping team was dispatched to expose the pipe. upon removal of the coating, a shallow, irregular deformation was observed along a 3‑ft section of pipe wall, but no crack was evident. the crew installed a temporary clamp‑on repair kit and restored the line to service at 780 psi after a 2‑hour pressure test. the incident was logged, and a full metallurgical analysis has been requested from the pipeline integrity lab. the preliminary report notes that the deformation may be related to an undocumented third‑party excavation or a manufacturing anomaly; the investigation remains open pending lab results. all notifications to regulatory agencies and affected customers were completed within the required 24‑hour window.

on april 14, 2023 at approximately 06:23 a.m. the mid‑river gas transmission operator received a low‑pressure alarm from the 24‑inch carbon steel line (schedule 80, design pressure 1 500 psi) that runs from the northern gathering hub to the downstream distribution complex. field personnel dispatched to the 12‑mile marker observed a faint vapor cloud emanating from a valve house that contained a 12‑inch manual isolation valve feeding a metering station. the valve stem was found fractured near the body, and the valve body showed signs of overheating with discoloration around the bonnet. no external impact or corrosion was evident. the automatic shutdown system engaged, isolating the line and closing downstream shut‑off valves, but a brief pressure surge of approximately 300 psi was recorded before isolation completed, resulting in a 4‑minute release of natural gas estimated at 2 500 scfd. fire crews responded, establishing a cold‑work zone and monitoring for ignition; no flame was observed. an investigation determined that the valve failure was likely due to an internal mechanical fatigue crack that propagated under cyclic loading, a factor not previously identified in the valve maintenance history. the incident was logged as a loss of product and a temporary reduction in line capacity while the valve assembly was removed, inspected, and replaced under a fast‑track engineering change.

on 3/22/2025 at 07:45 the operations control center received a call from a local fire department reporting a faint gasoline odor near the river crossing on the 24" carbon steel main (api 5l x70, design pressure 960 psi, operating at 720 psi). responders arrived at 08:12 and observed a thin brownish mist rising from a small opening in the right‑hand side of the pipe at river mile 12.4. the section had been installed in 2013 with a fusion‑bonded epoxy coating and a 3‑layer polyethylene wrap. initial visual inspection showed no obvious impact damage or third‑party activity. the pipeline was isolated by closing the nearest block valve (station 34) and depressurized to 150 psi by 08:45. a leak detection system recorded a transient pressure drop of 0.8 psi over a 3‑minute interval prior to isolation. a temporary clamp was applied to the leaking segment and a full hydrostatic test scheduled for the following week. the incident was reported to the nrc (incident #2025‑04873) on 3/22/2025 at 10:30 and a 48‑hour follow‑up submitted on 3/24/2025. the root cause remains undetermined pending further metallurgical analysis.

operations received a call from a field crew that a small pool of hydrocarbon was forming near valve station 7b on the 20‑inch carbon steel transmission line. the crew had been conducting a scheduled cathodic protection check and had opened the main isolation valve to depressurize the segment for visual inspection. after confirming zero pressure on the gauge, the crew re‑pressurized the line to 650 psi using the upstream pump, but the pressure transmitter on the downstream side was stuck at its previous reading of 500 psi. unaware of the discrepancy, the operator increased the pump output to bring the line to the target operating pressure of 800 psi. the line, which is rated for 900 psi, experienced a rapid pressure rise to approximately 950 psi as the faulty transmitter failed to alarm. at that point a 3‑inch longitudinal crack opened near a previously repaired girth weld, releasing gas at an estimated rate of 120 scfh. the affected segment was isolated, the leak was capped with a temporary sleeve, and a full pipe wall thickness inspection is scheduled for january 2027. all personnel were accounted for and no injuries were reported.

on april 14, 2025 at approximately 07:45 a.m., field operations observed a sudden pressure drop on the 24‑in. carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x65) that transports 1050 psi natural gas from the hillcrest gathering station to the southern processing facility. the line had been taken out of service the previous night for routine valve replacement on the east‑side pigging station. a maintenance crew installed a new 2‑inch gate valve and a 4‑in. line tie‑in using a neoprene gasket that was listed in the company's material spec for low‑temperature service, not for the high‑temperature, high‑pressure conditions present on this line. after installation, the crew torqued the flange bolts using a torque wrench set to 250 ft‑lb based on a generic torque chart found in the crew handbook, rather than the specific torque values for a 24‑in. api 5l x65 flange (recommended 460 ft‑lb). at 07:48 a.m., the control center received an alarm indicating a 120‑psi differential pressure across the valve. operators initiated an emergency shut‑in, but the valve seat had already sheared, resulting in a small gas release that ignited when it contacted a nearby heat‑exhaust stack. emergency response teams were dispatched, the area was evacuated, and the incident was contained within 30 minutes. subsequent investigation identified the use of an inappropriate gasket material and incorrect torque application as the primary contributors, compounded by the crew's reliance on a non‑specific torque reference.

during a routine pigging operation on the 30‑inch api 5l x52 gas transmission line, the crew encountered unexpected resistance at milepost 12.3. investigation revealed that a section of the pipeline had been previously repaired with a 4‑inch slip‑on coupling that was not properly aligned with the parent pipe, creating a 2‑degree misfit and a localized reduction in internal diameter. the misalignment caused the pig to snag, resulting in a sudden pressure spike of approximately 1,200 psi, which exceeded the design pressure of 1,050 psi for that segment. the over‑pressure triggered the downstream safety relief valve to lift, releasing a brief vent of natural gas that ignited from a nearby hot work torch used for a welding repair on an adjacent valve bank. the ignition caused minor fire damage to the torch stand and a 5‑ft section of insulation on the valve house, but the fire was extinguished by the onsite fire suppression system within three minutes. post‑incident review identified that the original repair had been performed by a subcontractor who failed to submit a proper weld map, and the misfit was not captured in the as‑built drawings. corrective actions include updating the pipeline integrity database, re‑aligning the coupling, and implementing a mandatory verification step for all future repair documentation.

on october 12, 2023 at approximately 14:23 local time, the midsouth gas transmission company received an internal alarm indicating a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch, class 2, carbon‑steel main (api 5l x70) that runs from the oak grove compression station to the river bend delivery point. the line was operating at 950 psi and the alarm showed a 120 psi decrease within two minutes. field crews were dispatched from the nearby maintenance yard and arrived on scene at 14:38. visual inspection of the right‑hand valve bank revealed that the manual isolation valve #7 had been left in the partially open position after a routine pigging operation the previous night. the valve’s stem was found bent at the 45‑degree mark, preventing a full seal and allowing a slow bleed to the atmosphere through a compromised seal housing. a portable gas detector confirmed the presence of methane at 2.5 % vol in the surrounding area, but no ignition source was detected. operations immediately reduced line pressure to 500 psi, isolated the valve, and installed a temporary block‑off. a follow‑up investigation determined that the valve mis‑position was due to a documentation error in the pigging checklist, which omitted the required “valve fully closed” verification step. the valve was replaced, the line was restored to normal operating pressure at 940 psi, and corrective actions—including revised checklists and additional crew training—were implemented to prevent recurrence.

in july 2024 a routine pressure test was being conducted on a 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line carrying dry natural gas at 1050 psig near the small town of pine ridge, wyoming. during the test operators noted an unexpected pressure loss of approximately 120 psi and a faint odor of mercaptan in the vicinity of the 12‑mile marker. a quick visual inspection revealed a narrow, irregular opening on the south side of the pipe about 15 feet downstream of a valve station that had been installed in 1998. the opening measured roughly 2.5 inches in length and appeared to have been caused by a gouge in the pipe wall; however, because the damaged pipe segment was removed and sent to a third‑party lab for metallurgical analysis, the exact initiating mechanism could not be determined. the pipe was repaired on site using a full encirclement welded sleeve conforming to 49 cfr §192.11, and the line was returned to service after hydrostatic testing at 1500 psig. a call was placed to the nrc(#1468320) on 07/14/2024 at 09:45 and a 48‑hour follow‑up (#1468457) was logged on 07/16/2024 at 13:22.

on september 14, 2025 at approximately 03:20 am, a rupture occurred on the 30‑inch line‑pipe (api 5l x70) in the north field compression station. the segment had been taken out of service on september 12 for a pigging operation and was subsequently repressurized to 980 psig (operating limit 1 200 psig) for a hydrostatic test. a digital pressure transmitter installed on the upstream header failed to calibrate after a firmware update, causing the control system to display a pressure 150 psig lower than actual. the automated shut‑in valve did not close when the setpoint was exceeded, allowing pressure to rise to an estimated 1 150 psig. the over‑stress caused a longitudinal crack at a previously repaired girth weld that had been re‑qualified two years earlier. the pipe split, releasing approximately 12 000 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding area. emergency response was notified at 03:32 am and the fire department arrived within 10 minutes. there were no injuries, but the station incurred significant equipment damage and the line required replacement of 45 feet of pipe and associated fittings. a root‑cause investigation identified the software version mismatch on the pressure transmitter as the primary factor, classifying the event under an “other” cause.

the 30‑inch api 5l x70 pipeline ruptured during a routine pressure test at 850 psi, exceeding its design test pressure of 800 psi. the line was operating at 600 psi when the test was initiated. at approximately 14:20 local time the pressure gauge spiked to 860 psi and an audible pop was heard near the right‑of‑way marker at milepost 42.3. immediate shutdown was executed by closing the upstream and downstream block valves, isolating the 15‑foot section of pipe. field crews arrived within 30 minutes and confirmed a gash approximately 8 inches long on the south side of the pipe, with a clear water ingress zone extending 3 feet downstream. the damaged segment was cut out, tagged, and placed on a nitrogen blanket for transport to the metallurgical lab. samples were sent to the western petroleum research institute for fractography, ultrasonic thickness mapping, and chemical analysis. preliminary lab results show deep pitting corrosion on the interior wall, reaching 45 % of the nominal wall thickness, and the presence of hydrogen sulfide corrosion products. tensile testing indicated the steel met api 5l x70 specifications, but micro‑structural examination revealed localized grain boundary weakening. further investigation will include a review of cathodic protection records, recent soil moisture surveys, and possible wildlife activity in the area. remediation work is scheduled to begin next week, with plans to install additional concrete weight coating and a secondary protective sleeve over the affected right‑of‑way.

during a scheduled integrity assessment of the 30‑inch api 5l x65 carbon steel mainline operating at 900 psi, a field engineer installed a temporary vent stack to relieve pressure while a pressure testing pig was introduced. the vent stack was fabricated from a 6‑inch schedule 40 steel pipe with a threaded male‑female connection. due to an undocumented modification, the vent stack was inadvertently left open after the pig passed, allowing product to escape. the released natural gas migrated into a nearby low‑lying drainage trench where a portable electric welder, being used by a maintenance crew to repair a valve flange, generated a spark. the spark ignited the accumulated gas, causing a brief flame and a small fire that damaged the welder and a section of the trench cover. the leak was discovered when the control room received an alarm from the downstream pressure sensor, which showed a 150 psi drop. operators isolated the line, and a crew replaced the temporary vent stack with a permanent pressure relief valve. the incident resulted in minor property damage and a brief shutdown of the affected segment for safety verification.

on 6/14/26 at 07:45 a local farmer reported a strong odor of natural gas near his south field adjacent to the 24‑inch, carbon steel transmission line “midland‑3” operated by southern energy services. the line was rated 950 psig and marked with orange and white pipeline markers. at 08:00 the field manager contacted the central operations center and the incident was logged as a potential release. by 08:12 the emergency response team (ert) arrived, deployed a portable gas detector, and confirmed a measurable concentration of methane at 2.4 % vol. the control room isolated the segment by closing valve mv‑12 and mv‑13 and initiated a bleed‑down. divers were dispatched to the nearby river to locate the exact breach, which was found approximately 150 ft downstream of the right‑of‑way marker. a temporary plidco repair clamp was installed on the 0.75‑in wall thickness pipe and the line was repressurized to 600 psig for testing. the line was returned to service at 13:30 after a successful pressure hold. because the pipe was not removed, no metallurgical examination was performed; the preliminary investigation could not determine whether the failure resulted from corrosion, third‑party activity, or material defect. a full failure analysis will be conducted once the pipe section is recovered, and a supplemental report will be filed with the public service commission.

08/14/2025 06:45 am – crew reported an odorized gas smell near the right‑of‑way at milepost 112.6 on the 24‑in. x70 steel transmission line, pressure reading 720 psi. visual inspection showed no obvious rupture, pinhole, or ground disturbance. the area was cordoned off and a continuous atmospheric monitor was deployed. 08/14/2025 09:30 am – a secondary team installed a temporary stopple on the upstream block valve (112+20) and reduced line pressure to 300 psi to minimize potential release while a leak location team excavated. by 11:15 am the leak was pinpointed to a 0.8‑in. longitudinal crack on the lower 5‑ft of pipe, approximately 2 ft below the surface. the pipe segment was marked for removal. 08/15/2025 02:00 pm – the cracked section was cut out and a new 24‑in. x70 pipe was spliced using a reinforced mechanical coupling. pressure was gradually restored to 680 psi and the line was returned to service at 06:00 pm. a supplemental report will be filed with the pipeline safety authority. initial metallurgical analysis indicated the crack was not associated with corrosion or third‑party damage; further testing is scheduled to determine the underlying cause.

on 5/22/23 the operations control center received an alarm from the pressure monitoring system on the 16‑inch, 30‑psi class‑b pipeline (api 5l x65) transporting crude from the south field to the central processing facility. the alarm indicated a sudden pressure drop from 1150 psi to 850 psi over a ten‑minute interval. field personnel were dispatched and identified a visible hydrocarbon sheen and bubbling at a river crossing near milepost 23. the line was isolated, pigged back to the nearest shut‑in valve, and depressurized to a flare stack. a qualified crew installed a temporary composite repair sleeve and later a permanent 16‑inch schedule‑40 steel replacement section. because the failed segment was removed without being sent to the metallurgical lab, a definitive root‑cause analysis could not be completed. the investigation noted that corrosion protection records were up to date and that the last inline inspection had shown no anomalies in the vicinity. however, the presence of an unexpected surface defect on the removed pipe segment suggested a possible manufacturing irregularity, though no conclusive evidence was obtained. the line was returned to service on 6/4/23 after successful pressure testing at 1300 psi.

on april 12, 2024 at 07:45 a.m., the western region operations team received a call from the field supervisor, larry mendoza, reporting an unexpected pressure drop on the 12‑inch carbon steel mainline (segment 45‑c, api 5l grade b) near the milepost 112.3 of the river bend corridor. the line was scheduled for a hot‑tap installation to add a new bypass for a downstream pump station. at 08:10 a.m., the hot‑tap crew, led by senior welder joanna lee, began the drilling process using a 4‑inch turbine cutter while the line was isolated and depressurized to 150 psig, well below its normal operating pressure of 850 psig. after the cutter was inserted, a sudden pressure surge was observed on the upstream pressure transmitter, spiking to 960 psig. within seconds, a loud “pop” was heard and a plume of natural gas escaped from a tee‑junction located 3 feet downstream of the hot‑tap site. emergency shutdown valves activated at 08:13 a.m., but residual gas continued to vent through the rupture. the area was evacuated, fire crews responded, and the leak was contained by capping the damaged section at 09:02 a.m. investigations are ongoing to determine the root cause, with preliminary hypotheses focusing on a potential over‑pressurization event caused by a malfunctioning pressure relief valve on the temporary bypass line. the incident was logged as case number 842917 and reported to the nrc at 10:30 a.m. by compliance officer ryan choi.

on 6/14/24 at 07:43 a.m. a field operator at the west texas terminal observed a strong odor of light crude near the 30‑inch, api 34 pipeline that runs from the rrc mainline to the storage facility. the operator immediately contacted control room and initiated an emergency shutdown of valve station 12, isolating the segment at 850 psi. by 07:52 the rrc emergency response team arrived on scene and established a 200‑foot safety perimeter. the local fire department and the state hazmat unit were notified, and a temporary road block was placed on county road 219 to keep traffic away. a visual inspection revealed a longitudinal split approximately 18 inches long on the lower 5‑foot run of the carbon‑steel pipe, which had been previously repaired with a split‑clamp after a third‑party excavation incident three years prior. the cause of the current failure is under investigation; preliminary hypotheses include stress corrosion cracking and potential impact from underground utility work. the leak released an estimated 3,200 barrels of crude before the shutdown was effective. containment booms and absorbent pads were deployed, and the spilled product was recovered with a recovery efficiency of roughly 85 %. a supplemental report will be filed pending final analysis.

on august 3, 2022 at 14:27 local time, a sudden release of natural gas was reported on a 24‑inch, 3‑in. api 5l x80 carbon steel transmission line operated by midwest pipeline corp. the pipeline, rated at 800 psi, runs through a mixed agricultural and wetland area approximately 12 miles southeast of oakridge, iowa. a field crew responding to a low‑pressure alarm observed a vapor cloud and a 6‑inch gouge in the pipe wall near a riverbank crossing. the emergency shutdown (esd) system was activated within five minutes, isolating the segment and preventing ignition. local fire services stood by while the leak was capped with a hydraulic sleeve. the damaged pipe section was excavated and removed; a new 30‑ft splice using a 24‑inch sleeve and 350‑psi rated gaskets was installed. initial visual inspection did not reveal any third‑party activity, corrosion, or mechanical damage. the incident was classified as a "unknown cause" pending metallurgical analysis of the failed pipe segment and a review of recent pressure cycling data. a detailed investigation report is pending, with recommendations to enhance real‑time monitoring and to review river crossing protection measures.

on august 14, 2026 at 09:12 a.m. field operators at the oak ridge gathering station observed an unexpected pressure drop on the 30‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x65) supplying the south field. the line was operating at 780 psig and the differential pressure alarm tripped at 09:09 a.m. the control room initiated an automatic shutdown and isolated the affected segment by closing valve a31 and valve b12. a rapid visual inspection revealed that a recent heavy rainstorm had triggered a small landslide along the right‑of‑way near milepost 42.4, exposing the pipe and allowing a 2‑ft long section of the coating to be gouged open. a subsequent leak test confirmed a 4‑in. breach with an estimated release rate of 1500 bbl/day of crude oil. emergency response was notified at 09:18 a.m. and the local fire department arrived at 09:34 a.m. to establish a containment zone. the line was depressurized to 150 psig and a hot‑tapped bypass was installed by 13:45 to restore service to downstream customers while repair crews fabricated a new 30‑inch pipe segment. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission at 14:10 a.m. and a full root‑cause investigation was launched to evaluate geotechnical stability and improve monitoring of slope conditions.

during a scheduled integrity pig run on the 24‑inch, api 5l x70 transmission line (nominal operating pressure 850 psi, max design pressure 1 200 psi) an unexpected pressure spike was recorded at station r‑12. the pigging crew observed a sudden loss of pig pressure and a brief acoustic signal that coincided with a visible spray of natural gas near a recessed coupling on the right‑hand side of the valve house. immediate isolation of the segment was achieved by closing the downstream block valve, and the line pressure dropped to 0 psig within 25 minutes. first responders from the local fire department were dispatched; a small evacuation zone of approximately 0.3 mi radius was established around the leak site while air monitoring was performed. after the area was declared safe, crews recovered the failed coupling and found a clean break in the threaded connection with no evidence of corrosion, external damage, or welding defects. the incident was logged as a release of approximately 180 mm³ of gas. a detailed failure analysis is underway, involving metallurgical examination of the coupling material and a review of recent pressure transient data. the final root cause determination will be included in a supplemental report.

a wildlife management crew was clearing vegetation along the right‑of‑way of a 24‑inch api (api 5l) steel transmission line when a contractor’s high‑pressure irrigation hose, rated for 1500 psi, was inadvertently positioned directly over an exposed pipe section that had been previously exposed for a valve installation. the hose was activated at 1300 psi to remove dense brush, and the water jet struck the pipe wall, creating a 2‑inch dent and a hairline crack at the 12‑o’clock position. within minutes natural gas at 720 psi began escaping, forming a visible vapor cloud that was ignited by a nearby diesel‑powered generator, resulting in a brief flame front that was quickly extinguished by the crew’s fire suppression equipment. the leak was isolated by closing the upstream block valve, and a temporary steel sleeve was installed on site. the incident prompted a full pipe integrity assessment, which revealed no additional defects. the line was later restored to service after a permanent repair sleeve was welded and hydrostatic testing confirmed integrity at 1000 psi. the crew sustained minor injuries from the blast overpressure and were treated on site.

at approximately 07:45 a.m. on november 3rd, 2025, field operators observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch, 1,200‑psi carbon steel main feeding the east side processing unit. the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system flagged a leak alarm for tag p‑1024. inspection crews arrived on scene within fifteen minutes and found a 6‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall approximately 250 feet east of valve station v‑56. the rupture had been caused by an unexpected over‑pressurization event when the downstream surge control valve failed to close due to a hydraulic actuator mis‑routed during a recent software update. high‑velocity natural gas escaped, igniting upon contact with a nearby hot‑work torch used for routine weld repairs. the fire was contained within the fenced right‑of‑way by emergency response teams using a dry chemical extinguisher and the area was evacuated. after the incident, the main was isolated, vented, and a temporary steel sleeve was installed pending full pipe replacement. a thorough review of the control logic and actuator calibration was initiated, and the incident was logged for further root‑cause analysis.

on july 19, 2024 a 30‑in. api 5l sch 40 carbon steel mainline operating at 850 psi experienced a slow‑moving surface leak near a right‑angle bend that had been installed during a 2022 expansion. field crews observed a faint sheen of light‑oil on the right‑hand side of the ditch and initiated a shut‑in of the affected segment. a visual inspection revealed a 0.75‑in. longitudinal crack that originated at the inside of the bend radius where a ½‑in. corrosion pit had developed. the pit was traced back to a missing sacrificial anode that should have been embedded in the concrete encasement per the original corrosion‑protection plan; however, the anode installation was omitted during construction because the bend was added as a field modification and the work order did not reference the cathodic‑protection specification. subsequent non‑destructive testing confirmed no additional metal loss along the adjacent 200‑ft run. the leak was repaired by cutting out a 3‑ft section of pipe and welding in a new 30‑in. seamless piece with an integral splice coupling, followed by reinstatement of cathodic protection with two newly installed anodes. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission on july 22, 2024, with an estimated cleanup cost of $68,000.

on april 14, 2022 a subcontractor hired to install a new cathodic protection anode line was working near the 12‑inch mainline at the riverside compression station. while trenching a 2‑inch conduit, the crew inadvertently struck the station’s upstream pressure regulator assembly with a 10‑ton hydraulic excavator bucket. the impact displaced the regulator’s internal diaphragm, causing a loss of control on the 800 psig natural‑gas service. the automated esd system detected a pressure drop to 450 psig and opened the 4‑inch vent valve to protect downstream equipment. however, because the regulator was damaged, the vent valve actuator did not receive sufficient pneumatic pressure from the buried supply bottle, resulting in a partial closure. gas continued to vent for approximately 45 minutes, releasing an estimated 1,400 mcf before the on‑call technician arrived at 19:30 and manually cycled the valve to a full close at 19:42. the leak was reported to the regional control center within the required one‑hour window, and the station was returned to service after pressure was restored to the actuator bottle and the regulator assembly was replaced. total downtime for unit 3 was three hours, and the incident was logged as a non‑reportable release under phmsa guidelines.

while performing a scheduled hydrostatic test on the northern segment of the 30‑inch api 5l x70 transmission line (design pressure 1500 psi, test pressure 2250 psi) a sudden loss of pressure was observed at gauge station 12‑b. the test crew halted the pump and isolated the section with the nearest block valve. inspection revealed that a recently installed 90‑degree stainless‑steel elbow (2‑in‑schedule 80) had fractured at the weld throat. the fracture surface showed a classic “cup‑and‑cone” pattern consistent with a brittle failure rather than overload. further examination of the weld joint indicated a lack of proper pre‑heat during fabrication and an inadequate post‑weld heat treatment, which had left residual tensile stresses in the base metal. the pipe segment was depressurized to atmospheric, the damaged elbow was removed, and a new 90‑degree miter bend with correctly controlled welding procedures was installed. after a repeat hydrostatic test confirmed no further leakage, the line was returned to service at its normal operating pressure of 1200 psi. the incident was documented and the welding contractor was required to provide additional quality‑assurance records for future work.

during a scheduled cathodic protection inspection on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (schedule 40, api 5l) that transports 850 psi of sweet natural gas from the processing plant to the distribution hub, the field crew installed a temporary bypass clamp on a corroded section of pipe near milepost 12.5. the clamp was rated for 1200 psi and the line was isolated with the mainline isolation valve (il‑02) and a downstream block valve (bl‑07) as per the lock‑out/tag‑out procedure. however, after the inspection crew completed the ultrasonic thickness measurements, the supervisor authorized a premature restart of the line to meet the day's throughput target. the bypass clamp had not been fully tightened and the secondary seal gasket was displaced during the clamp removal. when the line pressure was raised to 800 psi, the clamp failed, creating a rapid vent to the atmosphere for approximately 12 seconds. a nearby contractor was performing hot‑work on an adjacent valve housing, and the escaping gas ignited, producing a flash fire that singed the contractor’s coveralls and caused a minor facial burn. emergency shutdown was initiated, the leak was isolated, and the bypass clamp was replaced with a welded repair section. the incident was documented and a review of restart procedures was ordered.

a 24‑inch carbon steel pipeline operating at 900 psi experienced a sudden pressure drop when a manually operated isolation valve failed to seat fully during routine maintenance. the valve stem had been inadvertently over‑torqued during a previous inspection, causing the packing gland to deform and allowing a slow leak at the valve bonnet. operators observed a minor hydrocarbon vent to the surrounding grassland, triggering an automatic shutdown of the affected line segment. the leak was contained within 15 minutes by activating the emergency isolation system and deploying a portable containment boom. a hazmat crew arrived on scene, sampled the vapor, and confirmed that the released gas was below flammable limits. the valve was removed, the stem and packing replaced with new stainless‑steel components rated for 1500 psi, and the line was pressure‑tested to 1200 psi before returning to service. total downtime for the 2.4‑mile loop was approximately 6 hours, and repair costs were estimated at $78 000, including labor, parts, and environmental monitoring. the incident was recorded as a non‑fatal, non‑injury event with no offsite impact.

on 6/5/24 at approximately 14:12 while conducting a scheduled pigging run on the 24‑in sch 40 carbon steel main (design pressure 350 psi, operating at 300 psi), the automated pig launcher failed to retract after release. the launcher remained engaged, causing a rapid pressure rise as the pig was forced downstream. pressure sensors recorded an increase to 420 psi within two minutes, triggering the high‑pressure alarm. the control system automatically opened the downstream isolation valve (dv‑12) to relieve pressure, resulting in a brief vent of hydrocarbon vapor to the low‑lying drainage swale. the vent dissipated within five minutes with no ignition source present. the incident was reported to the operations supervisor, joshua mendoza, and the integrity engineering lead, karen li. a rapid response team de‑energized the segment, isolated dv‑12, and performed a visual inspection. no visible damage to the pipe wall or the pig launcher was observed, and a portable pressure gauge confirmed the line pressure had returned to 290 psi after isolation. the launcher was removed for a full functional test, and a software patch was applied to the launch sequence logic. a follow‑up report will be filed by the integrity team, and the segment will remain out of service pending a hydraulic test scheduled for 6/12/24.

4/15/24‑16:20 hrs – field crew observed a faint sour‑gas odor near valve station 12b on the 24‑inch, 0.875‑in. wall thickness api‑5l x70 pipeline, operating at 790 psi. no audible hissing or visible plume was detected. crew established a 30‑ft perimeter and placed portable gas detectors, confirming methane concentrations of 3.2 % at ground level. 4/15‑17:45 hrs – remote‑controlled block valves at both ends of the 2‑mile segment were closed, and the line was bled down to 150 psi using a portable vent skid. a 12‑in. bypass line was opened to maintain downstream customer service. 4/16‑08:10 hrs – excavation began after isolating the suspect area; when the pipe was exposed, a 0.9‑in. longitudinal split was visible on the lower 12‑o’clock quadrant, extending roughly 18 in. along the weld seam. the split appeared to have initiated in a region of surface discoloration. the section was cut out and removed for off‑site analysis; a temporary steel splice was installed to restore service at 650 psi. 4/17‑14:00 hrs – the removed pipe segment was sent to an independent metallurgical lab. preliminary visual inspection noted irregularities in the heat‑affected zone, but the definitive cause (e.g., stress corrosion, material defect, external damage) is pending the final report. a full incident investigation is ongoing with internal safety, the pipeline integrity team, and external consultants.

during a scheduled pigging operation on the 30‑inch, api 5l sch 40 carbon steel transmission line (design pressure 1250 psi, operating at 1150 psi, maop 1500 psi) a mis‑set launch pressure caused the smart‑pig to stall near a 90° bend at station riley. the control system failed to detect the stall because the pressure transducer upstream of the launcher was calibrated for static pressure only and did not alarm on the transient pressure rise. as the pig remained lodged, downstream flow continued and pressure began to build in the isolated segment. after approximately eight minutes the pressure exceeded the pipe’s burst pressure, reaching roughly 1600 psi. the sudden over‑pressurization forced the pipe at the bend to rupture, releasing natural gas into the surrounding right‑of‑way. emergency shutdown valves (esdvs) downstream opened automatically, but the upstream esdv failed to close due to a faulty solenoid coil that had been replaced three weeks earlier without proper testing. the gas plume ignited when it encountered a nearby diesel generator, resulting in a flash fire that burned three crew members; two required hospitalization for smoke inhalation, and one sustained second‑degree burns. the incident was contained after 45 minutes, and a post‑event investigation was launched to address pig launch procedures, pressure monitoring, and esdv reliability.

on june 22, 2024 at 07:45 a.m., field operators noted an unexpected pressure drop on the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline feeding the western processing unit at the riverbend terminal. the line was rated for 1,200 psig and was operating at 1,080 psig when the drop to 950 psig was recorded. a handheld ultrasonic thickness gauge was deployed at the nearest pig‑trap (station rbt‑04) and revealed a localized thinning of the pipe wall from the nominal 0.375 in to 0.12 in over a 6‑inch segment near a 90° elbow. the reduced thickness was attributed to internal corrosion accelerated by a stray water intrusion event that occurred during a prior maintenance shutdown. a visual inspection using a remote‑operated camera inserted through a hot‑tapping sleeve confirmed a small through‑wall crack at the 3‑o’clock position of the elbow, from which a slow gas seep was emanating. the leak was contained by installing a temporary stainless‑steel clamp sleeve over the affected area while the line was depressurized to 200 psig. after a 48‑hour cure period, a full‑thickness replacement sleeve (2‑inch longer than the damaged segment) was welded in place, pressure tested to 1,300 psig, and the line was returned to service at 10:15 a.m. on june 24, 2024. the incident was logged as an unplanned corrosion‑related failure.

on august 3rd, 2024 operators received a 911 call from a resident near the southern ridge line reporting a faint odor of natural gas emanating from a wooded area adjacent to the 24" x70 mil steel pipeline. the control center logged the call at 19:12 local time and dispatched a field crew to the reported location. upon arrival at 19:45, the crew observed a small plume of vapor near a drainage ditch and identified a 2‑inch pinhole leak on the pipe wall at milepost 112.7. initial pressure readings showed the line operating at 860 psig, with a downstream pressure of 530 psig, indicating a loss of approximately 320 psig across the leak. the segment was isolated by closing the upstream 24‑inch block valve and the downstream isolation valve, and the line was depressurized to 150 psig before hot‑tapping. an 18‑inch carbon steel repair sleeve was fabricated on‑site and installed over the damaged section, followed by a controlled purge and refill. after confirming zero leak rate with a calibrated ultrasonic detector, the line was returned to service at 22:10. a post‑incident review noted that recent vegetation clearing activities may have inadvertently disturbed the pipe coating, but no definitive cause was established.

during a routine pressure test on a 24‑inch, schedule 40 carbon steel pipeline (api 5l, design pressure 1500 psi) located in a low‑lying marsh near the delta, operators observed a gradual pressure drop from 1480 psi to 1350 psi over a six‑hour period. field crews dispatched to the suspected section found a faint sheen of petroleum in the saturated soil and a small, intermittent see‑sawing of the pipe wall at approximately 12 mi downstream of the main pump station. a 4‑inch clamp was installed as an emergency stop‑gap, but the pipe remained partially exposed to groundwater that fluctuated between 2.5 and 3.5 ft above the pipe crown. because the segment runs beneath a seasonal wetland, excavation required cofferdam construction and dewatering, which was limited by environmental restrictions. after the clamp was placed, a decision was made to abandon the affected 1‑mile segment rather than replace it, pending a detailed root‑cause analysis. the investigation team noted that the original as‑built drawings did not reflect a later‑added crossover tie‑in, and the presence of buried debris may have contributed to wall corrosion, but the exact initiation mechanism could not be confirmed. the segment will remain in place with a monitoring plan until a final disposition is approved.

during routine pigging of a 24‑in. x‑70 api 5l pipeline transporting 70 % crude and 30 % natural gas at 1 200 psi, the downstream pig trap was found empty. the control system indicated a pressure rise to 1 350 psi in the 0.5 mi segment upstream of the trap. operators initiated an emergency vent by opening the manual vent valve located on the pig receiver, but the valve failed to open due to corrosion‑induced binding. after a 15‑minute delay, a secondary vent line was opened, releasing the trapped pressure gradually. the sudden depressurization caused a 24‑in. main door on the pig receiver to swing open with enough force to strike a maintenance technician standing nearby, resulting in a bruised ribcage. subsequent inspection revealed that the vent valve seat had accumulated scale and debris, preventing proper operation. the door latch mechanism was found to have excessive wear, reducing its holding capacity. the pipeline was shut down, the vent valve was disassembled, cleaned, and replaced, and the door latch was repaired with a new hydraulic clamp. after confirming all safety interlocks were functional, the line was repressurized and returned to service.

on 17 june 2025 at approximately 1415 hrs the control room received a low‑pressure alarm on line 3, a 24‑in api 5l x70 steel pipe transporting 1100 psig natural gas from the north field to the main hub. the alarm triggered an automatic shutdown of the upstream booster station, but the downstream valve failed to close due to a stuck actuator caused by a recent maintenance override that had not been fully re‑qualified. as a result, gas continued to flow at reduced pressure (≈750 psig) into the downstream segment, creating a pressure differential that exceeded the design limits of a recent tie‑in flange installed three months earlier. at 1428 hrs field crews arrived on site and observed a sudden release of vapor at the tie‑in location near milepost 212.5. inspection revealed that the flange gasket had been improperly seated during the prior installation, leading to a rapid blow‑by and a 12‑ft long gas jet. the leak was isolated by manually closing the downstream isolation valve at 1442 hrs, and the area was ventilated. a temporary metal plug was installed while a replacement flange assembly was fabricated. after purging, pressure testing to 1500 psig, and coating verification, service was restored at 1730 hrs. the incident is under review to determine why the maintenance override documentation was incomplete and why the gasket installation did not meet the specification.

at approximately 06:37 on 03/14/2025 the west field mainline control room received a high‑pressure alarm on the 24‑inch api 5l carbon steel pipeline transporting 720 psi of natural gas from the ridgehead processing unit to the regional distribution hub. operators initiated an automatic shut‑in and dispatched the emergency response team (ert) to the nearest isolation valve located at milepost 42.5. upon arrival at 06:45 the ert observed a sudden release of vapor forming a dense fog near the valve housing, accompanied by a faint hissing sound. the isolation valve was manually closed at 06:48, but the leak persisted, indicating a possible seat failure. fire services were called at 06:52 and arrived at 07:03, establishing a safety perimeter of 150 ft. a hot‑tapping crew was mobilized to install a temporary clamp, which was successfully applied at 08:15, reducing the flow to a trickle. the leak was fully stopped by 09:02 after a replacement valve was installed. an investigation later determined that the valve stem had corroded due to prolonged exposure to moisture in the soil, a condition not identified in the routine inspection schedule, and the exact origin of the initial pressure spike could not be conclusively established.

a 30" api 5l sch 40 carbon steel transmission pipeline operating at 1150 psi was being depressurized for a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the control system was set to close the mainline isolation valve (miv‑12) and open the downstream vent valve (vv‑7) to bleed residual pressure. however, the vent valve actuator failed to open due to a hydraulic leak, and the automated sequence proceeded to open the downstream isolation valve (div‑3) while the vent remained closed. pressure in the downstream segment built up to an estimated 950 psi, exceeding the design rating of the 24" branch tee. the overstressed tee flange gasket failed, causing a sudden release of high‑pressure gas into the adjacent right‑of‑way. the escaping gas ignited when it contacted a nearby diesel generator exhaust, resulting in a flash fire that burned the surrounding vegetation and caused minor injuries to two crew members who were positioned near the valve house. the incident was reported to the incident command system, and an investigation was launched to determine why the vent valve actuator malfunction was not detected by the pre‑start checklist.

on september 14th 2026, the midwest transmission operator received a notification from the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system indicating an abnormal pressure rise in the 30‑inch, 18‑gauge carbon steel main (line a‑502) near the clayton pump station. the line is rated for a maximum operating pressure of 825 psi and was operating at 730 psi at the time. field personnel arrived on site at 08:12 a.m. and discovered that a recently updated alarm set‑point had been entered incorrectly during a routine configuration change, causing the high‑pressure alarm to be suppressed. as a result, the automatic shut‑down valve (asdv‑07) failed to close when the downstream pressure regulator (dpr‑12) malfunctioned and allowed pressure to climb to 910 psi, exceeding the pipe’s design limit. the over‑pressurization caused a small longitudinal split at a previously repaired weld joint near milepost 23.5, resulting in a minor leak that released approximately 150 bbl of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands. emergency response teams isolated the section at 09:04 a.m., depressurized the line, and initiated leak containment procedures. no injuries were reported, and environmental impact was limited to a brief odor plume that dissipated within an hour. the incident is under investigation, with focus on procedural compliance and software change‑management practices.

the incident was reported on 07/14/2025 at approximately 06:45 a.m. by the night shift supervisor at the south ridge compression station. a sudden loss of pressure was observed on the 20‑inch x70 % line‑pipe (api 5l grade b) carrying 850 psig of dry natural gas. the automatic shutdown system activated after a pressure drop of 300 psig within 12 seconds. initial visual inspection of the station revealed no external damage to the valve block or the adjacent pig launcher. the line was isolated, depressurized to 50 psig, and secured with double block‑and‑bleed valves. a side‑scan sonar survey of the 250‑foot subsea segment, located 45 feet below sea level in the lower galveston bay, was performed on 07/15/2025. the sonar data indicated a 9‑foot depression on the seabed directly over the pipeline route, but no clear gouge or trench was identified. subsequent remotely operated vehicle (rov) footage on 07/18/2025 captured a large, weather‑exposed fishing net entangled around the pipe at approximately the midpoint of the depression. the net appeared to have been abandoned several years prior; its composition and exact origin remain unknown. samples of the pipe coating were collected for laboratory analysis, and the net was cut and removed on 07/20/2025. the pipeline remains out of service pending further metallurgical testing and a comprehensive root‑cause investigation, which will be scheduled when weather conditions permit safe vessel operations.

during a scheduled cathodic protection inspection, the crew removed a remote valve isolation assembly to replace a corroded jumper on an 8‑inch carbon steel transmission line rated to 1250 psig. after the jumper was taken out, the valve actuator was inadvertently left in the open position and the pressure transducer that monitors the downstream section was reset to the low‑range scale (0‑300 psig). when gas flow was restored, the control system read the low pressure as a leak condition and automatically kept the upstream shut‑off valve open while also opening the emergency vent valve to relieve a perceived over‑pressure. the vent line, a 6‑inch pipe, discharged directly into a low‑lying clearing where a maintenance crew was performing welding on a nearby valve. approximately 1200 psig of natural gas escaped through the vent, spread along the ground, and ignited when a spark from the welding torch contacted the vapor cloud. the flash fire burned two technicians with second‑degree injuries and ruptured about 15 ft of the vent pipe.

due to limited site access, refer to original incident log 20230214 for full description. *update 03/20/23* the 30‑in. x70 api steel pipe segment at mile 127.5 experienced an abrupt pressure drop to 350 psi from an operating pressure of 850 psi. scada recorded a loss of 12 mm hd of product within 4 minutes. operations dispatched a rapid response team at 02:12 am; the line was isolated at valves 12 and 13 by 03:05 am and fully depressurized by 04:00 am. *update 04/02/23* a dive team conducted underwater visual inspection; no external corrosion, gouge, or third‑party damage was observed on the exposed 15‑ft section. *update 05/10/23* samples of the failed pipe were sent to the metallurgical lab (northwest materials inc.) for microscopic and chemical analysis. results indicated typical grain structure for grade x70 carbon steel, tensile strength within api 5l specifications, and surface pitting limited to 8 % of wall thickness, consistent with normal service corrosion. however, the fracture surface showed a mixed mode of axial and circumferential cracking originating at the 6‑o’clock position, with no evidence of overload or material defect. the missing 6‑ft pipe segment could not be recovered despite magnetometer sweeps up to 0.8 mi downstream. consequently, the definitive cause of the rupture remains indeterminate. recommendations include additional cathodic protection monitoring and periodic inline inspection to mitigate unknown failure mechanisms.

a routine integrity check was being performed on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) that transports natural gas from the central processing facility to the downstream distribution hub. the line is rated for a maximum allowable operating pressure of 950 psig and was operating at 785 psig at the time of the check. during the scheduled pigging operation, the control room operator mistakenly entered the start‑up command for the high‑pressure boost pump instead of the low‑pressure purge pump. as a result, the boost pump accelerated to 3 000 rpm, raising the pipeline pressure to 1 020 psig within two minutes. the pressure exceeded the set point of the downstream relief valve (950 psig) and the valve opened, venting gas for approximately 12 minutes before the operator noticed the alarm and manually shut the pump. the vented gas was directed to the flare stack, which operated without incident. after the event, the line was depressurized and inspected; a minor dent was found near the 12‑inch branch connection but no rupture occurred. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission at 03:45 am on 14‑mar‑2026 by senior engineer maria lopez, and a follow‑up call was placed to the operations manager at 05:10 am to initiate corrective actions and update the pigging procedure.

on 14 september 2024, personnel conducting routine pressure testing on a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) in the panhandle region of texas noticed a sudden drop in pressure from 950 psig to 720 psig within a few minutes. the line had been isolated and purged of gas, then filled with nitrogen to 1000 psig for the test. after the pressure loss was observed, the control room initiated a leak detection sequence and recorded a faint acoustic signal near milepost 212. a dive team was dispatched to the buried segment; divers inspected the pipe interior and found a small, irregularly shaped gouge approximately 0.03 in. wide near the 7‑o’clock position, but no obvious external damage. subsequent magnetic flux leakage scanning of the surrounding right‑of‑way did not reveal any external corrosion or third‑party intrusion. the incident was classified pending further analysis, with the probable cause attributed to a manufacturing defect in the pipe wall that manifested under high‑pressure nitrogen testing. the line was depressurized, the damaged section was cut out, and a new 24‑inch spool with matching wall thickness was installed using a field welding procedure. after hydrostatic testing to 1500 psig, the line was returned to service with no injuries, no environmental release, and minimal property impact.

on a saturday afternoon, two field engineers were completing routine pressure checks on a 30‑inch api 5l x‑70 transmission line operating at 720 psi near the river bend when a sudden roar was heard from the right‑hand side of the right‑of‑way. the engineers and the on‑site crew ran to the source and found the ancillary valve house engulfed in flames. emergency shutdown was initiated by pulling the main e‑stop, closing the isolation valves, and notifying control. visual inspection and portable combustible gas meters showed no detectable methane or odorant in the vicinity during the fire fight. fire crews remained on scene until 2130 hrs and reported no gas plume or odor. after the fire was extinguished, a third‑party fire investigator examined the structure the following morning but could not pinpoint the ignition source or initial fuel, noting that the metal doors were warped from heat rather than over‑pressure and that glass shards lay within two feet of the wall base. subsequent non‑destructive testing of the surrounding pipe found no leaks, and pressure testing after the rebuild showed no loss. the incident was classified as a total loss of the valve house, with the cause remaining undetermined pending further metallurgical review.

a leak was identified on 03/14/2026 during a routine aerial patrol of the 24" api 5l x70 mainline operating at 820 psi near milepost 112.5. the affected section was a 4" sleeve splice that had been installed in 2005 to accommodate a temporary service line. visual inspection after excavation revealed a narrow, irregular opening along the lower 5 o'clock quadrant of the sleeve, with discoloration of the surrounding coating and a faint oil sheen on the soil. a subsequent pressure test of the isolated segment showed a drop of 15 psi over 30 minutes, confirming a leak rate of approximately 12 mmscfd. the sleeve appeared to have been inadequately aligned during installation, resulting in a stress concentration at the weld interface; however, no definitive failure mechanism could be determined at the time of the investigation. the block valve upstream was closed and the downstream valve opened to isolate the line, and a 24" replacement sleeve with upgraded gasket material was installed, followed by hydrostatic testing to 1250 psi. the incident was reported to the nrc, and a root‑cause analysis is pending. total costs included product loss, sleeve replacement, labor, and environmental remediation of the contaminated soil.

at approximately 1430 hours on 22 july 2024, a transco maintenance crew was conducting a routine valve inspection on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (spec 30‑h2) near milepost 87.3 in the foothills of the central valley. the crew noticed a faint odor of natural gas and a small sheen of oil on the right‑of‑way. visual inspection revealed a 2‑inch gouge on the lower flange of a recently installed pressure regulator station that had been placed on a wooden cradle without the required steel support bracket. the missing bracket allowed the cradle to settle unevenly during a prior heavy rain event, causing the flange to flex and the weld to crack. the crew isolated the segment, depressurized the line from 720 psig to 0 psig, and reported the situation to transco operations control. emergency response was coordinated with the county fire department and the state oil and gas commission, which arrived on scene at 1505 hours. the damaged flange was removed, a new support bracket was fabricated and installed, and a full splice repair was completed by 1800 hours. no injuries occurred, gas release was limited to less than 0.05 mmcf, and the incident was logged as a non‑release event. the investigation noted the omission of the bracket in the as‑built drawing and prompted a review of all recent regulator installations for similar documentation gaps.

in august 2024 a routine cathodic protection survey was being conducted on a 30‑inch x70‑steel gas transmission line that runs under the chesapeake bay at a design pressure of 850 psig. while the crew was lowering the inline inspection tool, the tool failed to advance past a 2‑mile section and the telemetry was lost. shortly thereafter a faint hiss of natural gas was detected by a surface acoustic sensor positioned near the launch point. operators immediately isolated the affected segment and performed a pressure drop test, confirming a leak of approximately 0.8 mm³/s at a location 1.6 mi downstream of the launch site. due to the inability to retrieve the inspection pig, the precise defect could not be identified; possible external corrosion, third‑party impact, or material anomaly were considered but none could be verified. a temporary clamp assembly rated for 1000 psig was installed to stop the flow while a full excavation was planned. the incident was reported to the nrc as it exceeded the minimum reporting threshold. after the clamp was verified leak‑free, the line was depressurized, the clamp removed, and the pipe was leak‑tested and returned to service. the root cause remains undetermined.

a routine inspection on the north ridge 12‑inch carbon steel pipeline (design pressure 1 200 psi) identified an abnormal pressure drop downstream of a valve station. field engineers isolated the segment and performed a pig run using a magnetic flux leakage tool. the pig returned with indications of localized metal loss on a 24‑inch tie‑in branch that had been repaired two years earlier with a welded sleeve. however, the pig data did not reveal any clear defect. a handheld ultrasonic thickness gauge measured the wall thickness at the suspect area and showed a reduction of roughly 30 percent compared to the original specification. further visual examination required a hot‑tap to expose the interior, revealing a corrosion pit that had propagated behind the sleeve, likely due to moisture trapped during the previous repair. the pit was approximately 3 inches deep and 6 inches long. the compromised section was cut out, a new 24‑inch schedule 40 pipe segment was installed with a fully radiographed weld, and the sleeve was removed. additional cathodic protection was installed on the adjacent pipe runs, and the area was re‑pressurized and monitored for 48 hours before returning to service.

on 6/14/2022 at 22:45 a facility operator received a report of a strong natural gas odor near milepost 112.5 on the 30‑in. carbon steel transmission line (schedule 40, rated 960 psi, api 5l x70). the control room initiated an automatic shutdown; the line was isolated by closing valve stations 112 and 113 and depressurizing to 120 psi. first‑responder crews arrived at 23:10, confirming a 5‑in. longitudinal split approximately 18 in. long on the lower‑west side of the right‑hand side of the pipe. emergency response contractors erected a containment dome and began venting the released gas to a flare. no injuries were reported, but two nearby residents sought medical evaluation for mild respiratory irritation and were released after observation.

initial investigation pointed to a possible pressure surge, but a thorough examination of the pipe’s girth welds, coating, and surrounding soil yielded no definitive failure mechanism. a third‑party excavation claim was filed, though no external impact was identified. the repair estimate exceeded $120,000, prompting immediate notification of the nrc and state oil‑and‑gas commission. a supplemental report was filed on 7/2/2022, and the incident was re‑reviewed on 9/15/2022 after additional metallurgical testing, which still concluded the cause as unknown. further monitoring of the repaired section will continue per the corrective action plan.

while performing a scheduled pigging operation on the 30‑inch x70 api 5l line at the mid‑river compression station, operators observed a sudden pressure drop from 850 psi to 620 psi. the pig was retrieved at the downstream valve with a 3‑inch gouge in the wall of the pipe approximately 45 ft downstream of the mainline valve. subsequent excavation revealed that a 1‑inch threaded vent nipple, installed during a previous modification, had been inadvertently left protruding from the external support bracket. during a recent heavy rain event, a fallen oak tree struck the exposed nipple, bending it until the thread sheared and the nipple fractured, creating a through‑wall breach. the leak released an estimated 12,000 scf of natural gas before the automatic shut‑down valve activated. repair work consisted of cutting out a 6‑ft section of the pipe, installing a new 30‑inch api 5l spool with a welded vent assembly, and adding a protective steel cage around the vent to prevent future impact. post‑incident review identified that the vent nipple installation had not been recorded in the as‑built drawing, and a supplemental field verification was added to the maintenance procedure.

the 34" api 5l x65 grade b pipeline spanning the county line was undergoing scheduled cathodic protection verification when a maintenance crew positioned a portable generator adjacent to a valve house. during the test, the generator’s automatic transfer switch failed to disengage, causing an unexpected voltage surge that ignited a small oil film on the valve stem. a brief flash fire erupted, singeing the valve actuator housing and melting the nearby insulation. operators quickly isolated the segment by closing the downstream block valve and depressurizing the line to 150 psig, well below the operating pressure of 900 psig. the fire was extinguished by onsite fire‑watch personnel using a dry chemical extinguisher, and no injuries were reported. after the incident, the affected valve was removed, inspected, and replaced with a new 70‑mm double‑block‑and‑bleed unit. a thorough investigation determined the root cause to be the generator’s faulty transfer switch, a third‑party equipment issue unrelated to pipeline integrity. the line was returned to service after hydrostatic testing at 1.25 times design pressure, confirming no structural damage. property loss was limited to the valve actuator and surrounding insulation.

on april 14, 2026 at about 06:40 a.m. midwest transmission services received an automated alarm from a 24‑inch x70‑grade steel main located 3.2 mi southeast of lincoln, ne. the control system indicated an unexpected pressure drop from 780 psi to 410 psi within a two‑minute interval. field operators dispatched a mobile response crew who isolated the segment at the nearest block valve (station r‑12) and installed a portable pressure gauge. a visual inspection revealed a wet, silted trench with the pipe exposed due to recent soil erosion, but no obvious rupture or gouge was observed. a hot‑tap was performed and a small amount of gas was vented; the gauge downstream of the isolation point read 420 psi, confirming a leak of approximately 0.8 mm³/s. divers were not required. the line was depressurized, the affected pipe section was cut out and a new 24‑inch splice sleeve was installed. the cause of the initial pressure loss remains undetermined pending soil stability analysis and possible third‑party activity review. the incident prompted a temporary evacuation of two nearby residences as a precaution, and the area was reopened to traffic after the splice was pressure‑tested at 850 psi for 30 minutes. a supplemental report will be filed once the investigation concludes.

on 03/18/2025 a 24" carbon steel pipeline transporting 12,000 bpd of naphtha in the midland basin experienced an unexpected pressure drop to 45 psig from an operating pressure of 115 psig. field operators observed a faint hydrocarbon odor and a small sheen on the riverbank approximately 2.3 miles downstream of valve station rs-12. a visual inspection by a confined space crew revealed a longitudinal crack of about 18 in. in the midsection of the pipe, near a previously installed expansion joint. the crack appeared to have initiated at a weld defect that had not been detected during the last in‑line inspection. the line was isolated, purged and the damaged segment was cut out. a new 24" seamless pipe with an api 5l grade b specification was spliced in using a full‑encirclement split sleeve rated for 150% of the line's maximum operating pressure. after reinstatement the line was pressure tested to 150 psig for 4 hours with continuous visual monitoring by divers. no leakage was observed and the line was returned to service.

during a routine pressure test on the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline feeding the midland processing plant, the field crew noticed an unexpected pressure drop from 1200 psi to 780 psi after the test pump was shut off. the crew had previously isolated the line at the downstream isolation valve near valve station r12, but a portable pigging unit had been left in the line for a prior cleaning operation. when the test pump was started, the pig was inadvertently pushed forward and became lodged at a 30‑degree elbow approximately 450 feet downstream of the isolation valve. the obstruction caused a rapid pressure surge that exceeded the design rating of the adjacent 18‑inch branch line, resulting in a small rupture at a welded joint near the branch connection. gas escaped for about three minutes before the automatic shut‑down system activated. the leak was discovered by the on‑site gas detection system and reported to the control center. emergency response isolated the affected segment, repaired the ruptured joint, and retrieved the pig. post‑incident review indicated that the pig removal procedure had not been documented in the work plan, leading to the unintended movement during the pressure test. the line was returned to service after a pressure integrity test confirmed no further leaks.

the 24" x70‑inch schedule 40 api 5l pipe that runs through the hillcrest compression station began leaking during a routine pressure test on september 21, 2024. operators observed a gradual pressure drop from 820 psig to 730 psig over a thirty‑minute interval while the line was isolated and filled with nitrogen for a pigging integrity check. visual inspection revealed a narrow, hairline crack radiating from a weld seam near the valve bank that had been installed during a retrofit in 2016. the crack appeared to have initiated from a metallurgical defect in the weld filler material, which was later confirmed by metallographic analysis showing coarse carbides and lack of proper heat treatment. the incident was classified under 49 cfr part 191 as a release due to a material failure of unknown origin. the compromised section was removed, a new 24" x80‑inch schedule 40 pipe segment with api 5l grade x65 material was installed, and a full encirclement welded sleeve was placed over the adjacent fittings as a precaution. after hydrostatic testing to 150 % of design pressure, the line was returned to service. the shutdown lasted approximately 22 hours, and the total repair cost, including labor, materials, and lost gas, was estimated at $1.4 million.

on 9/14/2026 at approximately 6:18 am cdt a maintenance crew at the midland compression station initiated a pressure reduction on the 30‑in. carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade b) feeding the 22‑in. downstream loop. the crew entered the valve house and inadvertently opened valve v‑23 while valve v‑21, the designated isolation valve, remained closed due to a mis‑read tag. this action caused a sudden pressure drop from 1150 psig to 250 psig in the 22‑in. line, resulting in a low‑pressure gas release at the east side of the station. nearby residents reported a hissing sound and a faint odor. local fire department responded at 6:24 am, established a 200‑ft safety perimeter, and evacuated the adjacent storage yard. the line was isolated at v‑18 and v‑22 by 6:45 am, and the leak was located at a 6‑in. service branch that had been inadvertently opened during the valve sequence. the branch was capped with a temporary steel blind flange and the area was vented to atmosphere. after confirming zero psig, the mainline was repressurized to 1150 psig by 7:30 am and full service was restored at 8:02 am. investigation is ongoing; a corrective action plan will be submitted to the pipeline safety board.

the 5/8‑inch carbon steel line operating at 850 psi on the south field was discovered leaking during a routine cathodic protection survey on 04‑15‑24. the leak was located about 320 ft downstream of a recently installed valve station in a densely vegetated low‑lying area. visual inspection revealed a 0.8‑inch longitudinal seam split near a previously welded girth joint. the seam appeared to have been compromised by long‑term corrosion fatigue; however, no definitive corrosion product was observed, and the exact initiating mechanism could not be established. the line was isolated, vented to atmospheric pressure, and the affected 150‑ft section was removed. a new 5/8‑inch schedule‑40 pipe with a dual‑wall epoxy coating was installed using a pull‑through technique and the girth joint was re‑welded with a full‑penetration butt weld inspected by radiography. the repaired segment was hydrotested to 1.5 times the maximum operating pressure (1275 psi) and returned to service after confirming leak‑free integrity. the incident was logged as an unexplained seam failure pending further metallurgical analysis.

while conducting routine pigging of a 30‑inch x70 steel transmission line in the panhandle region, a maintenance crew introduced a foam‑filled cleaning pig to remove accumulated condensate. the pig was launched from a 6‑inch launch pit equipped with a 150‑psi pressure gauge and was expected to travel at 12 ft/s. after approximately 0.75 miles, the pig became lodged at a 24‑inch valve assembly that had been retrofitted with a composite liner three years earlier. during the attempt to retrieve the pig, the crew opened the remote‑actuated vent valve to relieve pressure, but an unexpected pressure surge of 250 psi developed behind the valve due to residual natural gas that had not been fully evacuated. the vent line, sized at 4 inches, ruptured at a welded flange, releasing a jet of gas that ignited when a handheld torch used for cutting the valve flange produced a spark. the flame traveled back into the vent line, causing a flash fire that burned the forearm of a crew member and singed the sleeve of another. emergency shutdown was initiated within 15 seconds, and the area was evacuated. fire services extinguished the fire, and the injured employee received first‑aid and was transported to the regional medical center for observation. the incident investigation identified the retrofitted liner as the source of the blockage and recommended a revised pigging protocol that includes pre‑run pressure testing of composite sections, the use of non‑spark tools for valve work, and mandatory verification of complete gas evacuation before venting.

on 6/5/2023 a routine aerial patrol over the southern segment of the eastbound transmission line identified a faint hydrocarbon sheen extending approximately 45 ft downstream of milepost 212.5. field crews were dispatched at 07:45 and upon arrival confirmed a slow release from a 30‑in., api 5l, x70 grade carbon steel pipe operating at 950 psig. initial pressure readings showed a drop to 820 psig. the leak was traced to a localized corrosion pit on the outer wall of a girth weld near a previously installed expansion joint. the area had been subjected to high soil moisture levels for several weeks following heavy rainfall. the pipe segment was isolated by closing valve 12b at 09:12 and depressurized to 0 psig. a temporary plug was installed, and a 20‑ft section of pipe was cut out. the replacement spliced in a new 30‑in. x70 pipe with a double‑welded joint and a reinforced coupler. repair work was completed at 16:30, restoring service at 1800 psig. the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 1458723) within the required 24‑hour window, and a follow‑up report (nrc# 1458820) was filed on 6/12/2023 detailing the corrosion findings and corrective actions. the total estimated repair cost was $138,500.

on 6/14/2026 a sudden loss of power to the motor‑driven valve on the 24‑inch x70 steel line (line 12‑b) at milepost 87 caused the valve to remain open during a scheduled pressure reduction. the line pressure was at 850 psig when the automated shutdown sequence was initiated, but the valve failed to close, resulting in a rapid pressure drop to 420 psig and a 0.3‑inch pinhole leak at a welded tie‑in near the valve body. local operations personnel arrived within 12 minutes, isolated the affected segment, and confirmed zero pressure by 7:45 pm cdt. the county fire department was notified and set up a safety perimeter of 300 ft; no injuries were reported. the leak was capped with a temporary steel sleeve and the area was depressurized for a full inspection. a detailed root‑cause analysis is pending, focusing on the valve actuator control circuitry and the weld integrity of the tie‑in. repairs, including replacement of the valve and rewelding of the affected joint, were completed on 6/16/2026 and line service was restored at 9:10 am. a supplemental incident report will be filed after the final analysis.

on august 14, 2023 at approximately 06:27 a.m. the control center received an abnormal pressure drop alarm on line gp-12, a 20‑inch, api 5l x70 steel pipeline transporting 1,200,000 btu/hr of natural gas from the midland gathering system to the southfield processing plant. initial remote diagnostics indicated a loss of about 340 psi from the nominal operating pressure of 1,050 psi. field crews were dispatched and arrived on site at 07:12 a.m. after isolating the affected segment at valve stations 45 and 46, a visual inspection revealed a longitudinal crack approximately 18 inches long on the lower‑leg of a 20‑inch x‑70 pipe at the 3‑mile marker, coincident with a recent weld repair performed during a pigging operation three weeks earlier. the crack propagated due to residual stress concentration and inadequate post‑weld heat treatment. the compromised pipe section was cut out and a new 20‑inch, 0.500‑inch wall thickness, x‑70 pipe was spliced using a double‑groove butt weld with full radiographic inspection. after hydrostatic testing to 1,500 psi for 30 minutes confirmed integrity, the line was depressurized, pigged, and returned to service at 12:45 p.m. a corrective action plan was initiated to review welding procedures and implement additional non‑destructive testing for future repairs.
