on 6/14/2024 operators observed a sudden pressure drop from 850 psig to 420 psig on the 24" carbon steel main that transports sweet natural gas between the houston hub and the galveston processing plant. the automatic shutdown system activated and the segment between milepost 12.3 and 13.7 was isolated within 12 minutes. visual patrols the following morning identified a small wet area on the right‑hand side of the right‑of‑way approximately 150 ft downstream of a recent utility easement excavation. the ground surface appeared disturbed, but no obvious third‑party damage to the pipe was visible. a hydrostatic test was performed on 6/16/2024 at 1500 psig and held for 2 hours with no leakage. a portable ultrasonic thickness gauge measured wall thickness values within 5% of design specifications, and the coating appeared intact. the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 1487623) as a non‑release event. a detailed investigation is ongoing to determine whether subsidence, groundwater infiltration, or an undisclosed third‑party activity contributed to the pressure loss. further sub‑surface imaging is scheduled for 7/2/2024 pending weather clearance, and a supplemental report will be filed once the root cause is confirmed.

on monday, june 3, 2025 at 07:45 a.m., the west valley operations supervisor, larry f. harris, received a call from the field crew stationed at mile marker 112 on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l grade b). the crew reported an unexpected pressure drop from 950 psi to 620 psi while conducting routine pressure testing after a recent valve replacement. harris instructed the crew to shut in the line at the nearest isolation valve (valve id 112‑b) and to begin a leak detection survey using an acoustic emission monitor. the monitor indicated a faint signal approximately 350 ft downstream of the isolation valve, near a recently installed 12‑inch lateral that had been pigged earlier that week. a visual inspection revealed a small gouge in the main pipe wall, likely caused by a stray piece of equipment that had slipped during the lateral tie‑in, but no definitive source could be identified. the line was depressurized, a temporary clamp was installed, and a hot‑tapped repair was scheduled for june 10. the incident was logged under case number 874321 and reported to nrc at 11:20 a.m. the cause remained undetermined pending further investigation.

during routine pressure testing of a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line at the north field interchange, the field crew observed an unexpected pressure drop from 950 psig to 720 psig over a ten‑minute interval. the crew halted the test and isolated the segment by closing the upstream 30‑inch block valve and the downstream 24‑inch isolation valve. visual inspection of the exposed pipe revealed a small, crescent‑shaped crack near a previously welded tie‑in for a pressure‑reducing station. the crack was not apparent during the pre‑test ultrasonic thickness survey, which showed wall thickness of 0.625 in. the crew notified gas control and the incident response team. a hot‑tapping unit was dispatched to attach a temporary bypass and relieve the line. subsequent leak detection using a combustible gas indicator confirmed a slow gas release at the crack location, but no odorant was detected by personnel on site. a third‑party fire investigator was engaged; their preliminary report indicated that the failure could be attributed to thermal fatigue from repeated temperature cycling during previous startup events, though the exact initiation mechanism could not be conclusively determined. the affected pipe section was cut out and replaced with a new 30‑inch x 0.75‑in. schedule 40 steel pipe, and the line was returned to service after pressure re‑commissioning at 960 psig. the incident resulted in a brief service interruption and a loss estimate of $120,000 for repair and downtime.

a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 1,200 psi was scheduled for a routine pigging operation at station 7. the line had been isolated with a 20‑inch block valve (bv‑12) and a pressure safety valve (psv‑4) set to open at 1,350 psi. during the pig launch, a temporary 6‑inch bypass line, installed the previous week for a downstream tie‑in, was inadvertently left open after the tie‑in crew completed their work. the bypass was connected to a low‑pressure drainage system (≈150 psi) and lacked a check valve. as the pig accelerated, back‑pressure built up in the main line and forced fluid through the open bypass, creating a sudden surge that caused the bv‑12 to slam shut. the rapid closure generated a water hammer wave that exceeded the design surge pressure, rupturing a nearby 12‑inch branch tee (tag‑c‑34) and releasing approximately 450 bbl of crude oil onto the surrounding right‑of‑way. emergency shutdown was initiated within 45 seconds, fire‑water monitors contained the spill, and the leak was capped after 2.5 hours. the incident was reported to the incident command team, the bypass line was removed, and a review of temporary line lock‑out procedures was ordered.

on september 14, 2024 at approximately 07:18 am a routine aerial patrol observed a plume of vapor emanating from a 24‑inch carbon‑steel transmission line owned by northern midstream, inc. the line, operating at 720 psig and transporting dry natural gas, runs across a privately owned meadow near mile‑post 212.5 in columbia county. the leak was traced to a 12‑inch coupler that had become partially detached from the main pipe after a recent landowner‑requested excavation to install a new irrigation well. the excavation crew, unaware of the buried pipeline, had inadvertently applied lateral force to the coupling during back‑fill, causing a misalignment that resulted in a small but continuous release. emergency response teams from the county fire department and the company’s incident command unit arrived within fifteen minutes, establishing a safe isolation zone and venting the line to a downstream shut‑in valve. the affected segment was depressurized to 30 psig, the coupler was removed, inspected, and replaced with a reinforced flange assembly. post‑incident analysis indicated that the lack of a recent “one‑call” notification and inadequate pre‑excavation coordination were primary contributors. a corrective action plan now includes enhanced stakeholder outreach and the installation of additional surface markers along the corridor.

on april 5, 2022, at 14:37 utc, the control room of the silver creek transmission line observed an unexpected pressure drop on line 12b, a 24‑inch carbon steel pipe rated at 1,440 psig transporting sweet natural gas from the north field to the main hub. the automated leak detection system triggered an esd and isolated the segment by closing the mainline isolation valve. field technicians arrived within 12 minutes and discovered a 4‑inch longitudinal split near milepost 87.5, approximately 250 ft downstream of a recent right‑of‑way clearing. preliminary inspection indicated that the split was caused by a buried steel reinforcement rod that had migrated into the pipe wall during a prior road resurfacing project, an external factor not anticipated in the original design. the incident resulted in a temporary loss of 18 mmcf/d of gas and a minor release of gas that was safely vented to flare. after the event, a root cause analysis was performed, leading to corrective actions: 1) implement a subsurface utility mapping verification protocol for all future right‑of‑way activities, 2) install pressure monitoring transducers at 10‑mile intervals on all 24‑inch lines, and 3) update the emergency response plan to include rapid mobilization of a mobile containment unit. all corrective measures have been completed and the line was returned to service on april 19, 2022.

05/22/2023 - during a routine pigging operation on a 24‑inch, 70‑psi carbon steel transmission line (design pressure 1 200 psi) a sudden pressure surge was observed at the downstream pig trap. the operation was being performed by pipelineco field crew led by john doe, operations supervisor (555‑123‑4567, john.doe@pipelineco.com). the line had been isolated, depressurized to 20 psi, and then re‑pressurized to 650 psi prior to pig launch. after the pig entered the 18‑inch crossover section, a section of the internal coating had delaminated due to an undocumented third‑party excavation that had left a shallow trench directly beneath the pipe. the trench reduced soil support, allowing a minor sag that caused the pig to snag on a weld protrusion. the snag induced a localized high‑velocity impact, rupturing a 2‑inch vent connection that had been previously installed for pressure testing. approximately 1 850 mcf of natural gas escaped, igniting briefly before the emergency shutdown system isolated the line. post‑incident investigation identified the undocumented trench as the primary contributor, while the vent connection failure was attributed to age‑related corrosion. corrective actions include updating excavation permits, re‑coating the affected pipe segment, and replacing the vent assembly.

the 30" x80 api 5l carbon steel transmission line crossing county road 112 experienced a sudden loss of pressure during a scheduled pigging run. the control room noted a drop from 840 psig to 610 psig within minutes and an automatic alarm triggered. field crews dispatched to the incident zone confirmed a faint hissing sound near the right‑of‑way, and a small vapor cloud was observed downwind. the segment was isolated by closing the nearest block valve at the 12.4 mile marker and the downstream valve at the 15.2 mile marker; the line was depressurized to atmospheric and purged with nitrogen. a visual inspection revealed a longitudinal crack originating from a girth weld on a 12‑in schedule 40 elbow that had been installed two years earlier. the weld defect was attributed to a non‑conforming filler material identified during post‑weld radiography review. the affected section was cut out, a new 30" x80 api 5l pipe splice was fabricated and welded in place, and the weld was heat‑treated in accordance with api 1104. after hydrostatic testing to 1.2× the maximum operating pressure (1000 psig), the line was returned to service. no injuries were reported, and the surrounding property owners were evacuated for 45 minutes as a precaution. the incident was logged with the state pipeline safety board and a corrective action plan was issued to audit all recent girth welds on similar segments.

at approximately 07:45 a.m. on october 3, 2021, field operations observed an unexpected pressure drop on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) located near the old miller crossing, milepost 152.4. scada indicated a loss of 18 psi from the normal operating pressure of 720 psi, triggering an automatic alarm. operators initiated an emergency shutdown (esd) and isolated the affected segment by closing the remote mainline valve (rmv‑12) and the downstream block valve (bv‑7) from the control center. the area was evacuated and a muster point was established at the nearby maintenance yard. after confirming the leak, a crew dispatched from the central repair hub arrived on site at 08:22 a.m. and identified a 4‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall, likely caused by a manufacturing defect that had propagated under cyclic stress. the crew installed a 30‑inch composite repair sleeve with epoxy bonding, performed hydrostatic testing to 1.5 times design pressure, and restored service at 11:15 a.m. following a full system integrity verification. a preliminary investigation was opened, and a third‑party inspection firm was engaged to perform non‑destructive testing of adjacent pipe sections. the incident was reported to the nrc and state regulators on october 4, 2021, under case no. 2021‑4529.

a crew from the operations center was performing a scheduled integrity check on a 20‑inch, api 5l x65 transmission line located in the hill country of west texas. the pipeline, rated for 950 psi, had been operating at a steady 820 psi delivering sweet natural gas to a downstream processing plant. during the check, a portable pressure gauge was attached to a manual isolation valve at milepost 12.7 while a field technician was preparing to conduct a smart‑pig run. the valve had been partially opened for venting purposes earlier in the day, but the technician failed to close the vent bleed line after the pressure relief test. later, when the pig was launched, the partially closed valve created a sudden restriction, causing a pressure surge that exceeded the pipe’s design limit. the surge propagated upstream, and at a nearby girth weld that had been repaired after a previous excavation, the overstress caused a brittle fracture. natural gas escaped from the rupture, forming a visible vapor cloud that ignited when a spark from a handheld radio ignited the mixture. emergency shutdown was initiated within three minutes, but the fire caused extensive damage to the surrounding vegetation and the nearby valve house. the incident was reported to the state pipeline safety board for investigation.

the field crew was dispatched after a farmer reported a sudden wet spot and a faint odor near a rural crossing on the 24" api 5l x70 pipeline that transports crude at 650 psi. upon arrival, operators confirmed a small seepage at the right-of-way at milepost 12.4, adjacent to an old drainage ditch. the segment was isolated by closing the upstream and downstream block valves and the line was depressurized to atmospheric pressure using the automatic blowdown system. a quick visual inspection revealed a 3‑inch longitudinal crack near a previously repaired girth weld, but the surrounding soil showed no evidence of recent excavation or external impact. the pipe was cut out, removed, and a new 24" spool with a full‑face gasketed flange was installed. the repaired section was hydrostatically tested to 1.5 times operating pressure and returned to service. a detailed failure analysis has been scheduled; samples will be sent to an external metallurgical lab for scanning electron microscopy, hardness testing, and residual stress evaluation. the investigation team noted that the pipe material met api 5l x70 specifications, but the presence of a stress corrosion cracking pattern could not be ruled out. further data collection, including in‑line inspection tool runs, is planned for the next quarter.

release on 4/12/2026 at approx. 18:45 utc on the 24" line (api 5lx grade x70, nominal wall thickness 0.375 in). the segment between milepost 212+15 and 212+42 was isolated; pressure was reduced to 0 psig by 19:10 and confirmed by field gauge. local emergency services responded to reports of a strong odor of natural gas near a residential subdivision; 9 homes were evacuated as a precaution. initial visual inspection on 4/13 revealed a shallow surface gouge on the south side of the pipe, approximately 12 in. long, with no obvious puncture. the area was depressurized to 150 psig and the pipe was vented to a nitrogen blanket for safety. a diversion line was installed using a 20" steel spool piece to maintain product flow while the investigation continued. samples of the pipe steel and surrounding soil were sent to the western petroleum laboratory for metallurgical and geotechnical analysis; results are pending. a third‑party construction crew reported heavy equipment activity in the vicinity the previous night, but no direct contact with the pipeline was documented. a follow‑up field survey with ground‑penetrating radar is scheduled for 4/20 to assess possible subsurface movement. further updates will be posted as the root cause assessment progresses.

on april 14, 2026 at 0735 hrs a pressure drop was observed on the 30‑inch, api‑5l x70 steel main transporting 850 psi natural gas between the midland gathering hub and the oak ridge processing plant. the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system recorded a 120‑psi loss within five minutes and automatically isolated the affected loop. field crews arrived at the 12‑mile‑south segment near milepost 57.3 and identified a 4‑inch rupture in the pipe wall of the 30‑inch line, with a visible jet of gas escaping into a low‑lying meadow. no recent excavation, third‑party activity, or known corrosion was reported for the area; the pipe had been pigged two months earlier with a smart‑pig indicating only minor wall‑thickness loss. the cause of the rupture could not be determined on site; investigators noted a possible stress‑corrosion cracking initiation at a weld seam but required further metallurgical analysis. the transportation safety board and state petroleum commission were notified at 0800 hrs, and the national response center logged the incident at 0805 hrs (call reference 842‑726). evacuation orders were issued for the nearby farmhouse complex, and temporary shelter was provided for twelve residents. initial damage estimates are $1.2 million, covering pipe replacement, site remediation, and emergency response costs. further investigation is pending.

on 9/14/2026 at 04:17 a.m., the 24‑inch api 5l x70 carbon steel mainline transporting sweet natural gas at 850 psig from the east field to the processing plant experienced an unplanned vent due to a malfunctioning pneumatic isolation valve at station bravo. the valve's solenoid coil had been inadvertently wired to the shutdown control panel during a recent retrofit of the supervisory control and data acquisition system, causing the valve to receive a false open command when the emergency shutdown sequence was initiated for an unrelated pressure rise upstream. as a result, the valve opened fully, allowing approximately 3.2 million scf of gas to escape into the surrounding low‑lying meadow before the automated emergency shutdown system detected the loss of pressure and closed the upstream block valve after 42 seconds. emergency response teams were dispatched, the area was evacuated, and the vent was isolated with a temporary clamp. no fire or injuries occurred, but the incident prompted a review of wiring practices and an update to the valve testing procedures. a supplemental report will be filed per phmsa guidelines.

the incident investigation determined that on 14 september 2025 a 30‑inch x70 steel transmission line, operating at 825 psi (57 bar) and coated with three‑layer polyethylene, experienced an unexpected pressure spike during a scheduled cathodic protection verification. a field technician had connected a portable dc power source to the test electrodes but inadvertently reversed the polarity, creating a localized galvanic surge that induced a short circuit at a junction box near valve station 12‑b. the resulting arcing ignited residual hydrocarbon vapors present in the valve pocket, causing a brief flash fire that damaged the valve body, adjacent hand‑hole cover, and a nearby service truck. no personnel injuries were reported, and the pipeline itself remained intact with no leak detected. after the event, the line was isolated, the affected valve was removed and replaced with a new 150‑lb forged carbon steel unit, and the surrounding area was vented and inspected. the incident met phmsa reporting thresholds due to equipment loss exceeding $150,000. a corrective action plan was issued, requiring revised polarity check procedures for all future cathodic protection tests and mandatory verification of electrode connections by a second qualified crew member.

on 03/18/06 a 20" x 0.375" api 5l sp steel pipeline transporting 68% propane/32% butane at a max allowable operating pressure of 960 psig experienced an unplanned venting event. the incident occurred near mile marker 124.7 in a remote desert segment of the line that is buried 4 ft deep beneath a compacted sand fill. initial operator logs show that the automatic shut‑in valve failed to close when the upstream pressure spiked to 1015 psig during a transient pump start‑up. the downstream relief valve opened at its set point of 970 psig and released gas for approximately 42 minutes before the control system forced a full line isolation. field crews arrived on site at 2130 hrs and found the vent line damaged with a 6‑inch gouge, but no obvious mechanical failure could be identified. a subsequent non‑destructive examination of the pipe wall revealed no corrosion, dents, or coating defects. a ground penetrating radar survey conducted on 03/22/06 detected a minor subsidence zone adjacent to the pipe alignment, possibly related to recent seasonal rain runoff, but the correlation to the venting event remains inconclusive. further metallurgical analysis of the valve seat and a review of pump surge controls are pending, and a supplemental report will be issued once additional data are available.

on may 3, 2025 at approximately 1435 hrs a low‑frequency acoustic sensor on the 24‑inch x‑70 steel main of the western interregional gas corridor (wigc) registered an abnormal vibration signature near milepost 112.7. field operators initiated an emergency shutdown, reducing line pressure from the normal 1050 psi to 620 psi. visual inspection by the maintenance crew revealed a faint oil sheen on the right‑hand shoulder of the right‑of‑way, approximately 15 ft downstream of a recently installed cathodic protection anode. no third‑party activity was reported in the vicinity and the pipeline had passed its most recent inline inspection (ii) run without recorded anomalies. the incident was escalated to the pipeline safety board, which convened an investigative team led by senior analyst maria lopez. weather conditions at the time were clear with wind from the northwest at 8‑12 mph, eliminating precipitation as a factor. the line remained out of service while a temporary bypass was installed and the suspect section was excavated. preliminary findings suggest an unidentified external force may have compromised the coating integrity, but the definitive cause remains under review. a supplemental report will be issued pending further metallurgical analysis.

on 22 september 2023 a field crew observed a sudden drop in pressure on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) that transports refined natural gas at 850 psi from the central processing unit to the regional distribution hub. the automatic shut‑in system activated after a 12‑psi differential was detected, isolating the segment between milepost 45.2 and 48.7. initial visual inspection revealed a small wet spot on the right‑hand side of the right‑of‑way, approximately 15 ft downstream of a recently installed telecommunications conduit. a side‑scan sonar sweep of the adjacent creek showed no obvious gouge or external impact on the pipe, but the surrounding soil appeared disturbed, likely from erosion during a recent heavy rain event. the exact mechanism that caused the pipe wall breach could not be determined from the available data. the line was depressurized, the compromised section was excavated, and a 24‑inch replacement pipe was spliced in on 30 september 2023. a 48‑hour notification update was submitted to the regulatory authority on 2 october 2023, detailing the volume of gas released (estimated at 3.2 mmcf) and the remedial actions taken.

on 8/2/2026, midwest transmission company detected an abnormal pressure rise on the 30‑in. carbon steel mainline (api 5l x65) at milepost 112.5 via the scada system. the alarm indicated a pressure of 1020 psig, exceeding the maximum allowable operating pressure of 950 psig. field technicians were dispatched and arrived at the site at 1430 hrs. they discovered that the upstream isolation valve (valve‑15) had failed to fully close due to a seized actuator, allowing downstream pump‑station‑4 to continue feeding gas into the line. the team manually opened the bypass line and used a handheld pneumatic wrench to force the valve shut, then vented excess gas to a low‑pressure flare. after stabilizing the line at 870 psig, the segment was isolated and the compromised valve was removed for replacement. a temporary bypass was installed to restore service while the replacement valve (api 6d‑type) was fabricated. the pipe segment was tested for leaks on 8/6/2026 and cleared for service on 8/9/2026 after a phmsa restart approval. a root cause investigation is ongoing to determine why the actuator seized and why the condition was not flagged by the preventive maintenance schedule.

a routine pressure test was performed on the 24‑inch, schedule 80, x‑70 carbon steel main at station 12b on june 3, 2025. the line is rated for 1,200 psig and was being pressurized to 1,050 psig with nitrogen. during the test, the control system recorded a rapid drop to 730 psig and automatically initiated an emergency shutdown. operators inspected the isolation valves and found them in the open position, consistent with normal operation. a field crew dispatched to the 12b site examined the line for signs of leakage but observed no wet spots, rust stains, or audible releases. the downstream pressure transducer indicated a stable 1,050 psig, while the upstream gauge remained at 730 psig. further diagnostics revealed that the upstream pressure transmitter had been inadvertently calibrated to the wrong span during a recent preventive maintenance visit on may 28, 2025. the mis‑calibration caused a false low‑pressure alarm, triggering the shutdown sequence. a corrective action plan was drafted, including re‑calibration of the transmitter, a review of maintenance documentation procedures, and a training session for the maintenance crew led by senior instrument engineer lisa mcfarland. the incident was logged as a non‑release event and the line returned to service after verification testing on june 7, 2025.

during a scheduled integrity verification on 04/22/2024, a 24" api 5l x65 carbon steel transmission line operating at 950 psi was isolated and depressurized to 150 psi for inline inspection using a smart pig. after the pig was retrieved at the downstream pig trap, maintenance personnel opened the isolation valve to re‑pressurize the line. an unexpected valve seat fracture occurred on the newly installed 1‑inch manual shut‑off valve, causing a rapid pressure surge that blew the valve body off its bonnet. a 3‑inch vent stack released a white vapor cloud composed of residual natural gas and condensate, which drifted across the adjacent grassland and entered a nearby cattle feedlot, coating equipment and livestock pens. emergency shut‑down was initiated within 45 seconds and the affected section was isolated. response teams contained the spill, removed the vapor‑soaked feed, and decontaminated the area. the incident was reported to the nrc (event #1260457) at 13:22, with a 48‑hour follow‑up (event #1260602) logged at 15:48. investigation identified a manufacturing defect in the valve seat as the root cause and recommended replacement of all similar valve assemblies on the line, revision of post‑pigging pressurization procedures, and additional non‑destructive testing of valve components.

on september 3, 2025 at approximately 07:42 a.m., field operations received a low‑pressure alarm from the 30‑inch api 5l sch 40 steel main located 2.3 miles north of the silver ridge pumping station in cheyenne county, wyoming. the alarm was triggered after a routine pressure test on the adjacent 24‑inch gas‑oil pipeline, which was being pressurized to 950 psi. at 07:50 a.m. the control center dispatched a field crew and initiated an automatic isolation of the affected block valve (bv‑12) and the upstream valve (bv‑9). by 08:05 a.m. the crew arrived on scene, observed a small spray of natural gas near a weld joint at the 12‑o’clock position of the pipe, and confirmed a leak rate of approximately 150 mcf/hr. emergency services were notified, and a hazmat team was on site by 08:30 a.m. the leak was contained by fully closing bv‑9 and bv‑12, and a hot‑tapping crew installed a temporary repair clamp at 09:15 a.m. the pipeline was depressurized to 0 psi, purged, and later re‑pressurized to 200 psi for testing. the incident was reported to the nrc and the state oil and gas commission. full restoration of service was achieved on september 5, 2025 at 14:20 after a permanent weld repair was completed and the line was pressure tested to 900 psi. the exact trigger for the weld failure remains under investigation.

on 3/7/25 at approximately 0830 hrs a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) located at milepost 112.4 experienced a sudden pressure drop from 820 psig to 340 psig during routine pigging operations. the pigging crew reported hearing a metallic “ping” as the smart pig entered the high‑point section near the river crossing. visual inspection by the field team revealed a 4‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall just downstream of the cathodic protection anode ring, which had been installed three years earlier. the split correlated with a previously undocumented change in pipe coating thickness; the original coating spec called for a 2‑mil epoxy, but field notes indicated a 1‑mil coat was applied during the 2022 retrofit. immediate isolation of the segment was achieved by closing the adjacent isolation valves (isolation valve a‑112 and b‑112). emergency response crews erected a temporary steel containment box and installed a 24‑inch steel repair sleeve, secured with 4‑bolt flange connections, to restore line integrity. after pressure testing to 900 psig, the line was returned to service at 750 psig. the incident was logged, and a review of all coating records was initiated to prevent recurrence.

on august 22 2023 at approximately 07:45 utc, a routine patrol crew on the 24‑in. x65 carbon steel main in the lower susquehanna valley observed a faint vapor cloud near milepost 112.7. the crew recorded gps coordinates 40.8753° n, 77.1239° w and reported a pressure drop from the nominal 1 200 psi to 1 050 psi on the supervisory control and data acquisition system. an immediate isolation valve was closed, and the line was depressurized to 200 psi for safe access. a 12‑in. access sleeve was cut downstream of the suspected zone and a small pinhole leak was found in the longitudinal seam of the pipe. the leak emitted an estimated 3 500 scf/hr of natural gas. the cause could not be identified because the pipe segment was not removed for metallurgical examination; no recent stress events, third‑party activities, or corrosion anomalies had been logged for that section. a temporary repair clamp was installed, the line was flushed, and pressure was gradually restored to operating levels. the incident was logged with the national incident database and a full root‑cause investigation was scheduled.

on april 14, 2026 at 0725 hrs a routine integrity inspection was being performed on the 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line (design pressure 1050 psi, operating pressure 720 psi) near the roanoke county, va right‑of‑way. the inspection crew had installed a temporary bypass valve to isolate a 300‑ft section for ultrasonic thickness testing. during the bypass installation a sudden thunderstorm produced a lightning strike that hit the grounding electrode of the nearby substation. the resulting surge caused a momentary over‑pressurization of the bypass valve assembly, forcing the 1‑inch vent port to rupture. a high‑velocity jet of natural gas escaped through the vent and ignited when it encountered a nearby power line that was still energized, creating a brief flash fire. the fire was self‑extinguished within seconds as the gas supply was automatically shut off by the pipeline control system after detecting a 15 % pressure drop. emergency response teams were dispatched, but no injuries were reported. the incident was classified as an “other” cause after investigation revealed the lightning‑induced surge as the primary trigger. corrective actions included upgrading surge protection on all remote valve stations and revising bypass procedures during adverse weather.

on 6/3/24 at approximately 09:45 am the crew was performing a routine pressure test on a newly installed 30" api 5l x70 carbon steel line (design pressure 1500 psig) in the northern segment of the gulf coast mainline. after the line was pressurized to 1400 psig, a low‑frequency vibration was noted at the 12‑mile marker. inspection revealed that a 24‑inch expansion joint installed two weeks earlier had been incorrectly oriented, causing the joint bellows to be exposed to axial load beyond its rated limit. the mis‑alignment produced a hairline crack in the bellows housing which was not detected during the initial hydrostatic test. the line was immediately depressurized to 200 psig and isolated with a double block and bleed. the expansion joint was removed, the bellows replaced, and a proper torque sequence was applied per the manufacturer’s installation guide. the incident was reported to the operations manager, j. rodriguez, and the engineering lead, s. patel, who initiated a design review of all recent expansion joint installations. a corrective action plan was issued on 6/5/24 requiring additional verification steps for joint orientation and a supplemental training session for field crews. the line was returned to service at 1200 psig on 6/7/24 after successful leak‑free testing.

on 9/14/24 at 07:45 a.m. the control room received an alarm from the south field compressor station indicating a sudden pressure drop on the 20‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l grade b) transporting sweet natural gas at 900 psig. operators isolated the line by closing valve ml‑15 and ml‑16 and initiated an emergency vent on the downstream pig trap. field crews arrived at the site at 08:10 and observed a small plume of natural gas near the right‑hand side of the pipe support at station 12‑b. the vented gas was directed to a flare stack and burned off safely. initial inspection revealed a gouge approximately 4 in. long on the pipe wall, but no obvious third‑party activity or corrosion patterns. the line was depressurized to 100 psig and a hot‑tapping team was dispatched to remove the damaged section for further metallurgical analysis. the incident resulted in a loss of 12,300 mcf of gas and a brief evacuation of the adjacent maintenance yard as a precaution. the root cause remains under investigation pending laboratory results and a review of recent pigging operations.

on august 14, 2023, at approximately 18:45 local time, the oak ridge compression station experienced an unplanned vent of natural gas from unit three. the station was operating at a discharge pressure of 960 psig on a 24‑inch api 5l carbon steel pipeline, with unit three running at 78% turbine speed. a routine pressure check by the control room operator showed a gradual rise in suction pressure to 420 psig, exceeding the normal range of 350‑380 psig. the alarm for high suction pressure triggered, and the operator initiated an immediate shutdown sequence. however, the suction vent valve remained partially open, resulting in a continuous low‑rate release estimated at 1.8 mmscfd. emergency response crews were dispatched at 19:10 and arrived on site at 19:45, where they confirmed a visible gas plume extending approximately 150 feet downwind of the station. the vent valve was manually closed, and the station was placed in a safe state. gas loss calculations later indicated that the 3‑hour release threshold of 3 mmscfd had been exceeded. a preliminary investigation revealed that the valve actuator had suffered corrosion damage to its hydraulic piston seal, likely due to prolonged exposure to moisture during recent rain events. the seal failure prevented the valve from fully seating. the incident was reported to the nrc, and a corrective action plan was issued to replace the affected actuator, install additional moisture monitoring sensors, and update maintenance procedures to include quarterly hydraulic seal inspections.

on july 14, 2024 at approximately 07:45 am a field crew was conducting a scheduled pigging operation on the 30‑inch carbon steel pipeline (grade x65, api 5l) that transports 850 psi of sweet natural gas from the marion gathering system to the central processing facility. the pig launcher was equipped with a temporary bypass valve to allow depressurization of the launch section. after the pig entered the line, the crew initiated closure of the bypass, but a mis‑rigged hand‑wheel was left in the half‑open position. by 08:12 am the pressure downstream of the bypass began to drop, and a low‑pressure alarm triggered at the control center. operators observed a sudden vent of gas at the launch site; a white plume was seen emanating from the valve housing. the crew immediately activated the emergency shutdown and isolated the 30‑inch line at the nearest mainline shut‑off valve (station 12‑b). the leak was confined to the bypass valve assembly, which had a 2‑inch orifice due to the incomplete seat closure. after confirming the area was safe, a replacement valve was installed, the line was purged, pressure tested to 900 psi, and returned to service at 14:30 hrs. the incident was recorded as a non‑corrosion, non‑third‑party event and reported per the operator’s incident notification procedure.

on 4/22/2025 a routine inline inspection was scheduled on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70, design pressure 1500 psi) that runs from the petrochemical complex near houston to the coastal storage terminal. the pigging crew had completed the launch when a subcontractor’s back‑hoe, working on a nearby storm‑drain project, inadvertently struck a buried fiber‑optic cable that was co‑located with the emergency shutdown (esd) valve actuator. the impact sheared the cable, causing a short circuit that forced the esd valve to open automatically. natural gas at approximately 1300 psi was released from the 24‑inch main into the surrounding low‑lying grassland. at the same time, a welder from the same subcontractor was performing hot‑work on a steel support structure 30 ft away. the released gas found the ignition source and a brief flame front developed, producing a visible fireball that burned for about 30 seconds before being extinguished by the facility fire‑water system. local fire‑rescue units arrived within 8 minutes; no injuries were reported, and the fire was fully contained. the incident was logged as a “significant event” and reported to the phmsa and ferc under the appropriate reporting thresholds.

on october 22, 2024, during routine pigging of a 30‑inch, api 5l x70 steel transmission line operating at 1150 psig, the pig became lodged near a 12‑inch reduction valve at milepost 57. after attempts to retrieve the pig with a push‑through tool failed, the control system automatically opened the downstream emergency shut‑off valve, causing a pressure surge that exceeded the valve’s set‑point of 1200 psig. the surge resulted in a short‑duration vent of approximately 350 scfd through the vent stack before the valve closed. the vent was detected by the remote monitoring system, and operators initiated an emergency response. a subsequent inspection revealed that a corrosion‑induced wall thinning of the reduction valve body had reduced its structural integrity, allowing the over‑pressure condition. the valve was replaced, the affected pipeline segment was hydrostatically tested to 1300 psig, and normal service was restored after a 48‑hour outage. no injuries or third‑party damage were reported, and the incident was logged with the ferc and state pipeline safety board for further review.

on 9/14/2023 at 08:45 a.m. field crews observed a faint hissing sound near milepost 212+30 on the 30‑in. api 5l x70 steel line (design pressure 1 200 psi) transporting sweet natural gas at 980 psi. initial visual inspection revealed a small, wet area on the north side of the right‑hand side girth weld, but no obvious puncture. a portable gas detector confirmed elevated methane concentrations (≈12 % vol) at the site. the line was immediately isolated by closing the upstream block valve at station 212+45 and the downstream valve at station 212+15, reducing pressure to 150 psi to prevent further release.

maintenance personnel erected a temporary containment dome and began depressurizing the isolated segment. after 30 minutes the pressure dropped to 45 psi and the hissing ceased. excavation uncovered a hairline crack, ~0.8 in. long, propagating through the weld throat. metallurgical analysis later indicated the crack originated from an incomplete fusion defect left from the original fabrication, which was aggravated by cyclic pressure fluctuations during peak demand periods.

the compromised section was cut out and a new 30‑in. spool with full‑penetration welds was installed. post‑repair hydrostatic testing was performed at 1 200 psi for 30 minutes with no leaks detected. the line was returned to service at 09:30 a.m. on 9/15/2023.

on august 14, at approximately 0930 hrs, a residential contractor was excavating a backyard for a new septic tank on county road 12, near milepost 27.5. while using a compact excavator, the operator struck a 24‑in. carbon‑steel natural gas transmission pipe (api 5l grade b) buried at a depth of 4 ft. the pipe, part of the central valley mainline, was operating at 900 psig and transporting dry natural gas at a flow rate of 1.2 mmcf/d. the impact caused a 3‑in. longitudinal gouge, resulting in an immediate gas release. nearby residents reported a strong odor of natural gas. the contractor halted work and called emergency services; the utility’s emergency response team arrived at 0945 hrs and initiated an emergency shutdown by closing the upstream and downstream isolation valves located at the nearest valve stations (stations 14‑a and 14‑b). a temporary blind was installed at the damage site, and the leak was contained within 30 minutes. the incident was reported to the nrc (event #2026‑01873) within the required 30‑minute window, and a detailed investigation was launched to determine why the pipeline marker signs were not visible and why the contractor’s one‑call notification was not logged. the pipeline segment was taken out of service for repair and pressure testing before reinstatement.

while conducting routine pressure testing on a 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel pipeline at milepost 42.7 in the pine ridge area, field crew observed a sudden drop in pressure from 960 psig to 720 psig within two minutes. the crew immediately halted the pump and initiated an emergency shut‑in. visual inspection revealed a small venting plume of natural gas near the right‑of‑way adjacent to an abandoned well pad. a handheld gas detector confirmed methane concentrations of 12 % in the immediate vicinity. the segment between milepost 42.2 and 43.0 was isolated using the nearest block valve and the line was vented to atmosphere. a 12‑hour leak‑rate estimate was calculated at approximately 350 mmscfd. the incident was reported to operations and to the state oil and gas commission within 30 minutes. an excavation performed the following day located a 4‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall about 15 feet below the surface, likely caused by corrosion pitting that had progressed undetected. the damaged pipe section was cut out and a new 30‑inch × 0.5‑in wall‑thickness api 5l pipe was installed and hydrostatically tested to 1500 psig before return to service. additional corrosion monitoring was ordered for the surrounding line.

on october 14, 2022 a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the riverbend processing plant experienced an unscheduled shutdown after a sudden pressure drop to 380 psig from its normal operating pressure of 720 psig. the line, installed in 1998, is equipped with a remotely operated mainline valve (mlv‑3) that is normally held closed by a pneumatic actuator supplied from a 150‑psi air reservoir. during the event, the control system logged an automatic open command to mlv‑3 at 02:17, followed by a rapid depressurization and an estimated 4,200 mcf of natural gas released before the valve was manually closed at 02:45. investigation revealed that a recent software patch to the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system had inadvertently re‑mapped the alarm clearance signal to the valve open command. the misconfiguration was not documented in the change control log, and the field technician who applied the patch was unaware of the valve’s critical safety function. the primary cause was identified as an undocumented software change resulting in an inadvertent valve opening, with a contributing factor of inadequate change management procedures. the incident was reported to the appropriate regulatory agencies within the required one‑hour window.

on april 12, 2023 a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (line # 84) operating at 720 psig was being re‑pressurized after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the segment runs through the foothills of the sierra and has a max allowable operating pressure (maop) of 850 psig. during the restart, the field supervisor instructed the crew to close the downstream isolation valves and increase the line pressure to 800 psig to meet downstream demand. however, the control room operator, unaware that a new high‑pressure relief valve had been installed at the mountain ridge station with a set pressure of 770 psig, approved the increase. the line pressure continued to rise and at 2:45 pm the relief valve opened, venting approximately 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere for about ten minutes before the control system automatically reduced pressure. the release triggered a reportable event to the state and phmsa. investigation found the root cause to be a failure to update the pressure operating limits in the central control database after the valve replacement and a miscommunication between field operations and gas control that led to an unauthorized pressure increase beyond the relief setting.

(on april 12, 2025, a maintenance crew performed a planned pigging operation on section 14 of line # 472, a 10" stainless steel transmission conduit with a 530# maop, operating at 470# during normal service). the line had been scheduled for a pig pass to clear accumulated debris that had been identified during a routine inspection on march 28, 2025. at 02:15 am local time, the crew positioned the pigging head at the upstream valve station and closed all downstream isolation valves. a field engineer, jr. m. harris, was assigned to monitor the pressure transducer while the pigging crew, led by contractor l. t. singh, performed the purge sequence. however, due to a misread of the operating manual, the engineer mistakenly set the upstream pressure limit to 520# instead of the required 480#, believing the line was still at a reduced operating pressure. once the pig passed and the purge valve was opened at 02:45 am, the upstream pressure spiked to 525#, exceeding the set limit of the upstream relief valve calibrated at 520#. the relief valve opened to atmosphere at 02:47 am, releasing approximately 8.2 mmcf of natural gas. the incident was reported to phmsa within 24 hours, and the operator conducted a root‑cause analysis that identified the incorrect pressure setting as the primary operational error.

on march 15, 2024 at 09:42 am (est), compressor station 312 in virginia experienced an unscheduled shutdown (uss) after a 10‑inch carbon steel line (bwp 1400 psi) began to vent through a partially open cross‑over valve (cv‑312). the valve was located in the high‑pressure section of the main transmission line and was operated manually by a field crew using a handheld remote. during the routine pressure‑drop test, the crew opened the valve to 10% of its travel to check for leaks, but the operator did not verify the valve position with the station’s hmi or the position sensor. the valve remained in an open state when the compressor was brought online, causing a rapid pressure decline to 650 psi. as the line pressure dropped, the downstream relief valve (rv‑312) operated at 650 psi setpoint and opened, discharging 4,200 mcf of gas to the atmosphere. the event caused a 120‑minute outage of the compressor. post‑incident investigation found that the operator had used a portable battery‑powered test lead to energize the valve actuator instead of the scheduled hmi control sequence. the valve actuator was also missing a calibrated limit switch, which prevented the system from automatically shutting the valve when the compressor returned to normal pressure. corrective actions include retraining of crew on valve‑operation protocols, installation of a redundant position indicator, and revision of the daily pressure‑drop test procedure to require hmi verification before any manual valve operation.

on august 5 2024 at 14:32 (pst), the eastern interconnect line 42kpsi, 24‑inch schedule 80 steel, experienced a rapid depressurization event following an incorrect manual override of the automatic pressure relief valve (aprv). the operator mistakenly set the aprv setpoint to 45 psi instead of the required 15 psi while attempting a routine pressure test. within 12 seconds the line pressure surged to 48 psi, causing the downstream flare stack valve to trip and the line to vent 2.3 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. emergency responders were dispatched to the site; two employees sustained minor skin burns from the hot gas and were treated at the local clinic. the incident prompted an immediate shutdown of all downstream pumps and a full inspection of the aprv system. the root cause analysis identified a training gap and a missing lockout tag during the pressure test. corrective actions include updated operating procedures, mandatory lockout/tagout, and a refresher training program for all field operators.

on wednesday, october 3 2023 at 1030 hours, an 8‑inch 10,000 psi natural gas transmission line experienced a sudden pressure surge. the control valve was mistakenly set to open during routine maintenance. the operator did not verify the valve position before starting the test. as the line pressure exceeded 12,000 psi, the high‑pressure relief valve opened to the atmosphere. the rapid venting produced a fireball that ignited flammable vapors in the surrounding vegetation. emergency crews were dispatched; the fire was extinguished within 20 minutes. no injuries were reported. the incident was reported to the nrc and the state energy regulator. investigation found that the operator used a faulty pressure gauge and misinterpreted the alarm signals. corrective actions included retraining the crew, replacing the gauge with a digital pressure transducer, and updating the operating procedures to require a two‑person verification for valve operations.

on april 3, 2024, during a routine pigging operation on the east‑canyon natural gas pipeline, the field crew mistakenly set the pig‑gate valve to a 30‑psi differential pressure limit instead of the required 120‑psi. the 16‑inch schedule 80 steel line was operating at 210‑psi mean operating pressure (mop), and the pigging vessel was filled with a 200‑psi purge gas. because the valve was set too low, the pigging pressure dropped to 40‑psi, triggering the pig‑gate alarm and causing the downstream pressure regulator to trip. the regulator’s bypass line was opened automatically, allowing 1,200 mcf of gas to flow into the safety relief system, which then opened at 150‑psi to protect the line. the relief valve vented to atmosphere, creating a visible vapor plume. a post‑incident review revealed that the valve technician had used the wrong reference manual and had not verified the set point against the operating procedure. the incident caused a minor environmental release and a temporary shutdown of the 18‑mile segment while the crew recalibrated the valve and updated the field operating instructions.

on march 14, 2024, at 08:23 am cdt, the central region gas transmission line 5-4-2, a 26‑inch schedule 80 stainless steel pipe, experienced a sudden pressure spike following an operator error during a routine valve test. the line, operating at 850 psi maop, had its main isolation valve 4‑4‑2‑3 inadvertently left in the open position while the crew was verifying the pressure relief valve settings. at 08:27 am, the pressure sensor registered 1,100 psi, exceeding the line’s maximum allowable operating pressure by 30%. the crew immediately initiated a manual shut‑down; however, the high pressure had already forced the 12‑inch downstream service line 5‑4‑2‑6 to rupture, releasing 3,200 mscf of natural gas into the atmosphere. the incident was reported to the control center at 08:35 am, and the emergency shutdown system activated, stopping the flow within 45 seconds. post‑incident review showed that the operator had misread the valve indicator light and failed to verify the valve position with the lockout/tagout procedure. corrective actions include revising the valve operation training program, adding a secondary visual check for isolation valves, and installing an automated valve position sensor on the 4‑4‑2‑3 isolation valve.

on 7-12-2025, a contractor was performing a line‑to‑line pigging operation on a 36‑inch, 4‑mm‑thick stainless steel pipeline running 150 miles between the north distribution hub and the east storage complex. the pipeline was rated for 7500 psi and operating at 6800 psi during the scheduled work. the contractor’s pigger crew had received a brief refresher on the pigging procedure but had not reviewed the latest operating manual update that reduced the allowable pigging pressure to 6000 psi after the installation of a new high‑temperature pigging valve. the crew selected the wrong pigging fluid and set the back‑pressure gauge to 7200 psi, believing it to be within safe limits. as the pig entered the pipe, the pressure sensor read 7200 psi, and the pigger operator, noticing the reading, increased the back‑pressure by adding more fluid until the pressure reached 7900 psi. the pipe’s pressure‑relief valve, calibrated for 7500 psi, was tripped, venting the line and causing a sudden pressure drop that triggered a rapid depressurization shock wave. the shock wave cracked a 4‑mm weld seam near the pigging valve, producing a small gas release that ignited in the presence of residual hydrocarbons. the contractor’s incorrect pressure operation was determined to be the primary cause of the incident, and the company has revised the pigging procedures to require pre‑job confirmation of pressure limits and re‑training of all pigging personnel.

on 08-15-2024 at 10:27 am, a 36‑inch schedule 80 api 5l x‑70 natural gas transmission line near the ridgeview compressor station experienced a rapid pressure surge to 1,200 psi. the line, operating normally at 850 psi and 260 °f, was subjected to an abrupt shutdown of the upstream 4‑inch isolation valve by a field technician. the valve had been incorrectly set to the "closed" position while a maintenance crew was performing a pig‑sweep operation. the technician had previously set the valve to "open" for the pig but forgot to reset it before leaving the control room. the pressure increase was detected by the differential pressure transmitter on the main line, which tripped the downstream 8‑inch relief valve at the ridgeview substation. however, the relief valve remained latched due to a mechanical fault; the operator failed to manually trip the valve because the alarm was misinterpreted as a false signal. as a result, the mainline ruptured at a weld on the 12‑inch pressure‑rated section, releasing a cloud of gas that ignited when a portable welder was brought to the site to repair the weld. the incident caused a 4‑minute fire, burned two crew members, and temporarily shut down the entire ridgeview block. investigations showed the root cause was an operator error in valve positioning and inadequate alarm verification protocols.

on 03/15/2024 at 02:30 pm, a maintenance crew performing routine line cleaning on the 6-inch schedule 80 steel natural gas transmission line at the el paso hub inadvertently opened a 3/8-inch safety relief valve that had been incorrectly labeled as a test valve. the valve, rated 5000 psi, was supposed to remain closed during the operation. the opening caused a rapid drop in system pressure from 850 psi to 120 psi over 4 minutes and a gas loss of approximately 3.2 mmscf as measured by the flow monitoring system. the crew immediately shut down the adjacent 4-inch isolation valve, isolated the line segment, and activated the emergency shutdown procedure. the incident was reported to the regional control center within 5 minutes, and the field operations team arrived on site at 02:48 pm. upon inspection, the relief valve had been set to open due to a misconfigured handle orientation during the previous year’s calibration. the valve was reinstalled in the correct position, a locking collar was installed to prevent accidental operation, and the maintenance protocol was revised to include a double-check of valve identifiers before any field work. a follow-up audit confirmed no further incidents. no personnel injuries were reported.

on april 10, 2025 at approximately 10:22 a.m., workers at the midwest compression station performed a scheduled maintenance check on the 8‑inch line feeding the 1100 psi section of the western pipeline. the crew intended to shut down the line by closing valve 701, the downstream isolation valve, before isolating the upstream pressure source. however, following a misread of the control panel, they first closed the upstream control valve 700, which left the downstream valve 701 open to the high‑pressure line. when the crew opened the relief valve 702 to relieve pressure in the downstream line, a surge of 1100 psi gas accelerated through the open valve 701, causing a rapid venting of 2.3 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. the resulting flash fire ignited at the valve seat, damaging the 8‑inch carbon steel pipe (api 5l x42) and the surrounding equipment. the incident was recorded in the incident log and the field crew was retrained on the proper isolation sequence and the importance of verifying the closed status of all valves before initiating pressure relief. the internal investigation concluded that the crew’s failure to follow the lockout/tagout procedure and the incorrect sequencing of valve closures were the direct causes of the event.

on february 9, 2024, a field crew at the alameda transmission station performed a routine maintenance on the 30‑inch mainline. during the inspection, the crew inadvertently left the 12‑inch isolation valve in the closed position while the pressure control unit was set to high pressure mode. as the compressor spool accelerated to 1200 rpm, the upstream pressure rose to 1350 psig, exceeding the valve’s burst pressure of 1200 psig. the sudden pressure surge caused the valve to fail, releasing a jet of natural gas into the surrounding area. the crew was immediately notified by the facility’s gas detection system, and an emergency shutdown was triggered. the gas plume traveled 50 yards, igniting a small flame when it contacted a spark from a nearby welding torch. the fire was contained within 4 minutes by the station’s automatic fire suppression system. two crew members sustained minor burns and were treated on site before being transported to the local hospital. the incident investigation concluded that the valve had been improperly positioned due to a miscommunication during the shift change, and procedural revisions were implemented to prevent recurrence.

at 09:12 am, the northwest energy transmission, l.l.c. (ne) dispatch office received a notification that the emergency shutdown system had tripped at node 22 in central arkansas. at 09:25 am, the shift supervisor instructed a field crew to open valve v‑5 on the 12‑inch carbon steel line 22‑a to relieve pressure and restore flow after a scheduled inspection of the pressure‑regulating unit. the crew, unaware that the valve had a default “pressure‑down” operation, incorrectly commanded the valve to open fully. the valve failed to close during the subsequent pressure‑sweep test at 09:48 am, and the 1500‑psi pressure spike in the 12‑inch line caused the downstream rupture of a 300‑mm diameter welded flange. the rupture released approximately 2,500 cubic meters of natural gas, which escaped into the surrounding farmland and was detected by the air‑quality monitoring stations at 10:02 am. the incident triggered an emergency response call at 10:15 am and a containment team was dispatched. the field crew shut the line at 10:30 am, and a pressure‑relief valve was installed at 12:10 pm. after the event, ne conducted a root‑cause analysis that revealed the operator had omitted the required change‑management checklist. ne retrained all line operators on the correct valve‑operation procedures and updated the standard operating procedures to include a mandatory verification step for any valve that controls a pressure‑regulation line.

on april 12, 2025 at 07:30 am, the westcoast gas transmission team inadvertently opened the isolation valve on the 24‑inch, 16‑mm‑dia high‑strength steel line (segment 14‑23) that was scheduled for a routine pressure test. the valve was mistakenly turned to the open position while the line was still pressurized to 540 psig, a level well above the 30‑inch line’s maximum allowable operating pressure of 500 psig. the resulting pressure rise of approximately 80 psi triggered the over‑pressure relief valve on the adjacent 30‑inch line to open at 07:32 am. the relief valve vented 2,200 mcf of natural gas to the atmosphere over a period of 5 minutes, until the line pressure dropped below 450 psig. the incident was discovered when an on‑site engineer noticed the alarm log and inspected the valve. the company performed a full gas‑loss calculation and estimated a loss of 2.2 mcf, which exceeded the 1.0 mcf reporting threshold, and the event was reported to the national response center at 08:15 am. the investigation concluded that the operator had not followed the correct valve‑handling procedure and had omitted the required lock‑out tag‑out before manipulating the valve.

on march 15, 2026, at approximately 02:30 am (est) a crew at the oak ridge compressor station was performing a routine pressure test on an 8‑inch schedule‑80 steel line (mp 23.5) after a repair of a previous burst. the crew had to shut the mainline valve and operate the safety relief valve to relieve pressure before reconnecting the line. however, the operator mistakenly selected the 4‑inch high‑pressure shut‑off valve instead of the 8‑inch main line valve, isolating the line from the relief system. as a result the line pressure rose to 480 psi, exceeding the design limit of 400 psi. the operator then tried to relieve the pressure by opening the safety relief valve, but the valve was installed at a 30‑degree angle and was not oriented correctly, so it did not open. pressure continued to climb until the line burst at 02:55 am, releasing approximately 0.6 mmcf of natural gas. the burst line ignited and burned for 45 minutes. one operator suffered severe burns and was hospitalized. the incident was reported to the nrc at 04:20 am and to the dot within 8 hours. the root cause was identified as incorrect valve operation during a pressure test. corrective actions include a revised standard operating procedure for valve selection, additional operator training, and installation of a redundant check valve. the affected system was shut down, the line repaired, and operations resumed at 09:15 am after testing.

on thursday, april 18th, two technicians were performing a routine integrity check on the 6‑inch high‑pressure natural gas line that runs from the east processing unit to the main compressor. technician b, who had been on duty for 5 hours, decided to bypass the isolation valve on the line to speed the test. he opened the 6‑inch isolation valve while the upstream pressure remained at 250 psi. the sudden opening caused a pressure surge that blew the downstream 6‑inch fitting, sending a jet of gas and metal fragments into the bay. the fragment struck technician a, breaking his left wrist, and the gas jet caused a small explosion that ignited the spilled lubricant. both technicians were taken to the on‑site medical bay for treatment; technician a had a fractured wrist and required a cast, while technician b received a minor burn on his left hand. an investigation found the crew had skipped the required procedure of closing the isolation valve before testing, and a new training program was implemented.

at approximately 10:15 a.m. on 12 february 2024, operators at the elmsfield transmission corridor inadvertently set the 18‑inch steel line to 3000 psi, exceeding the design limit of 2500 psi for the 15‑year‑old carbon‑steel pipe. the valve that normally throttled the surge during temperature excursions was left in the fully open position because the operator mis‑read the manual, assuming the pressure control loop had already compensated. the resulting pressure spike reached 3200 psi, causing the flange on section 5‑12‑b to fail and a 2‑inch longitudinal crack to propagate in the 304‑steel isolation valve. gas escaped, igniting a small flare that was extinguished automatically by the flare‑gas system. no injuries were reported and the area was quickly sealed. a 3‑hour shutdown of the adjacent 12‑inch line was executed to remove the damaged section and replace the valve. the incident was logged as a significant event, and an investigation found that the operator had omitted a required safety interlock check during routine startup. a supplemental report was filed with the regional regulatory office, documenting corrective actions including revised operator training and an updated operating procedure that mandates a double‑check of pressure settings prior to valve operation.

on august 9, 2025, around 10:45 a.m. mountain time (mt), a pressure excursion and subsequent pipe failure occurred during routine pressure test operations on the 20‑inch, 4,000‑ft segment of the 35b natural gas line located near the cedar grove compressor station, colorado. the failure resulted in a 15‑foot rupture, spraying high‑pressure gas into the surrounding vegetation and injuring a field technician who was performing valve checks on the adjacent 5‑inch service line. the technician sustained a severe burn on his left forearm and required emergency treatment at the nearest medical facility.

the incident was initiated when the operator misread the downstream pressure gauge, believing it indicated normal operating pressure, while the upstream pressure had been inadvertently set to 2,200 psi due to a software glitch in the pressure regulator controller. the excessive pressure exceeded the design limit of 1,800 psi for that pipe section, causing the wall thickness to yield. the operator failed to activate the automatic pressure relief valve and did not verify the system pressure using a calibrated manometer prior to proceeding with the test.

investigators found that the operator’s failure to cross‑check pressure readings and the absence of a written procedure for verifying regulator settings contributed to the event. the company is suspending the operator’s qualifications for pressure‑control tasks and will implement mandatory refresher training on pressure‑management protocols.

on march 15 2025, a field crew at the oak ridge natural gas processing facility performed a pressure test on a 16 inch stainless steel line segment. the crew was not following the approved procedure because the line had been previously shut down for maintenance and the lockout tag had been removed by an engineer in the control room. the crew operator mistakenly opened the 20 inch gate valve using the quick‑disconnect handle rather than the hand lever, causing a sudden pressure surge of 920 psig into the upstream manifold. the downstream 10 inch flared pipe was not equipped with an inline pressure relief device at that point. the pressure spike triggered the built‑in pressure‑switch on the 20 inch valve, which partially opened and allowed high‑temperature gas to flow into the 8 inch flare. the flare was not rated for the temperature of the gas, leading to a flare line rupture that released 4.2 mcf of natural gas over a period of 35 minutes. the release was detected by the scada alarm after 12:45 a.m. the crew attempted to shut the valve, but the valve had already been partially opened and the gas had escaped. after the incident, the company revised the operating instructions for gate valve operation and instituted a mandatory lockout‑tagout verification step for all pressure tests.

on february 10, 2025 at 09:12 a.m., operators at the rogers field gas transmission line experienced an unplanned release when a 30-inch, 3% stainless steel segment of the main line was incorrectly shut down by a field crew during a pressure test. the crew had set the line to 1,200 psi for a diagnostic run but forgot to open the isolation valve on the pressure monitoring loop. as a result, the upstream 1,800 psi pressure built up in the test section. the downstream relief valve, which had a trip set at 1,600 psi, began cycling but did not open because the line was blocked by the closed isolation valve. the crew misread the scada alarm, assuming it was a transient pressure spike, and did not take corrective action. at 10:45 a.m., the pressure reached 1,950 psi and the main line ruptured at a weld joint, releasing approximately 45,000 cubic meters of natural gas. emergency shutdown was initiated at 10:57 a.m., and the gas was vented to the atmosphere until the line was secured at 11:20 a.m. investigation revealed the crew had followed a legacy operating procedure that no longer applied to the upgraded control system, and the training program had not been updated. corrective actions included revamping the operating manual, re‑training all field personnel, and installing an automated pressure interlock on the isolation valve.

on march 12, 2024 at about 09:45 local time, a 36‑inch api 5l steel mainline at the northbridge compressor station was scheduled for a pigging operation. the operator assigned to the job, john doe, had not yet completed the required valve closure checklist. during the start‑up of the pig run, the high‑pressure shut‑off valve (hp‑sv‑04) was left in the open position, while the downstream pressure relief valve (prv‑08) had been set to 1200 psi instead of the approved 600 psi. as a result, the 150‑bar (2175 psi) pipeline section experienced an uncontrolled pressure surge that exceeded the material yield strength. the valve stem fractured, releasing a sudden burst of natural gas that ignited at the flare stack. the incident resulted in a small explosion, a fire that burned for 12 minutes, and damage to the adjacent 12‑inch gas distribution line. immediate action was taken: the site commander shut down the entire field, isolated the affected section, and called the fire department. an investigation revealed that the operator had misread the pressure gauge, and the valve position indicator was not calibrated. corrective actions included retraining all shift operators on pressure relief procedures, installing a secondary visual alarm for the high‑pressure valve, and implementing a mandatory double‑check protocol before any pig run. the mainline was repaired with a 40‑inch api 5l replacement fitting and returned to service on march 28, 2024 after a full integrity review.

on monday, april 10, 2025 at 14:20 hours, xyz utilities was notified of a gas release at the intersection of main street and river avenue in townville. during routine maintenance on a 30‑inch natural gas transmission line (mdr 1200 psig, pipe material 316l steel) a field crew was performing a pressure test on a 2‑inch safety relief valve that had been scheduled to be shut in as part of a scheduled pressure reduction. the crew incorrectly opened the valve to allow a flow test, disregarding the valve isolation procedure documented in the field operations manual. the relief valve opened at 1200 psig, releasing approximately 3.2 mmcf of gas into the atmosphere over a period of 45 minutes. the release triggered a hazardous gas alert on the local fire department. no injuries were reported, but a small residential property adjacent to the pipeline sustained minor fire damage. the incident was reported to the state regulator and the incident cost exceeded $90k due to cleanup and property damage. the investigation concluded that the crew failed to follow the prescribed procedure for valve isolation and pressure testing, leading to an uncontrolled release.

at 10:17 a.m., western energy pipeline company, l.l.c. received a low‑pressure alarm on line 300‑5, a 24‑inch schedule 80 steel pipe operating at 1,200 psig. the operator on the control room decided to open relief valve 3b to 50 % to relieve the alarm, but the valve was incorrectly installed with a “low‑pressure” setpoint of 1,500 psig. as a result, relief valve 3b stayed closed and the upstream pressure rose to 1,500 psig. at 10:23 a.m., the system automatically triggered an emergency shutdown (esd) on section 300‑5. the operator, in an attempt to restore service, manually opened downstream isolation valve 7c, which was rated for 600 psig. the valve failed to close, causing a rapid depressurization and a 0.3‑inch diameter hole in the 300‑5 pipe. the loss of 5,000 mcf of gas was vented to the atmosphere. the operator had previously replaced valve 3b without a management‑of‑change (moc) and had not verified the pressure setpoint after installation. corrective actions included revising the moc procedure, re‑training operators on valve setpoint verification, and installing a secondary alarm for relief‑valve status.

on 12-02-2023, at approximately 10:15 am, the westbound gas transmission line 58‑th street gate station in new york city was undergoing a scheduled pressure test. the gas control supervisor, j.d. smith, initiated a remote closure of rov 74321 while the station was still in production. the procedure called for a gradual valve closing in 20% increments, but the supervisor mistakenly set the command to full closure instantaneously. the station's outlet pressure, which was 275 psig at the time, spiked to 510 psig within 30 seconds, triggering the high‑pressure protection system. the remote operation alarm was not acknowledged until 10:17 am, by which point the valve had already been fully closed and the downstream line was at 540 psig. the pipeline operator activated the emergency relief valve at the 51‑st street junction, which opened to 350 psig, relieving the pressure but causing a surge back into the upstream line. the surge forced the upstream relief valve to close, trapping a pressure wave that persisted until 10:45 am when the gas control crew manually opened rov 74321 in 10% steps. the incident resulted in a temporary shutdown of the gate station and a pressure excursion of 265 psig above the maximum allowable operating pressure of 300 psig. the company documented the event in part e3.g and notified the state regulatory agency.

on april 12, 2023, at approximately 14:35 h, the west coast transmission pipeline, owned by energyflow corp., experienced a sudden loss of pressure in the 24‑inch stainless steel section near the mile marker 132.3. the incident occurred during a routine pigging operation when the pig was commanded to reverse for a diagnostic run. the pig operator inadvertently set the command to full reverse, causing the pig to collide with the downstream pig trap and forcefully disengage the 8‑inch isolation valve (i‑v‑132) that had been opened for maintenance. the collision led to a rapid vent of the 2000‑psi line, and the valve stem failed to seat, creating a 60‑second pressure drop that caused the downstream flare system to trip. emergency shut‑in of the adjacent 30‑inch section isolated the fault, but the flare had to be temporarily disabled while the valve was replaced. post‑incident review revealed that the pig operator had not followed the established pig‑traverse procedure, which requires a 10‑second wait after reverse command before applying force. the training record for the operator showed a gap in the pig operation refresher. corrective measures include updating the pig‑operation sop to include a mandatory stop‑and‑verify step, installing an interlock that prevents reverse command until the valve is fully closed, and scheduling a quarterly refresher training for all pig operators.

on friday, march 15, 2025, at approximately 14:23 hours, an operator at the east county gas transmission facility mistakenly opened a 30‑inch, 350‑psi, stainless steel line segment to conduct a maintenance purge without first verifying that the upstream isolation valves were closed. the operator, following a routine checklist, incorrectly identified a 10‑inch isolation valve (model pv‑109) as the correct valve for shutdown, when in fact the correct valve was a 12‑inch, double‑acting, hydraulically actuated valve (model dv‑213). because the isolation valve remained open, the purge air entered a pressurized section of the line, raising the local pressure to approximately 450 psi. the excess pressure caused the line’s expansion joints to fail, resulting in a sudden release of natural gas along a 200‑meter section of the right‑hand side of the line. the gas plume ignited at a nearby weld repair site where a maintenance crew was using a cutting torch, producing a small explosion that caused a fireball. two crew members were burned, one sustained third‑degree burns and required surgical intervention, and the other suffered second‑degree burns and was hospitalized for 48 hours. the incident was reported to the state energy regulator and the federal pipeline safety administration, and an emergency shutdown of the entire line was executed within ten minutes of the release. the operator’s failure to properly identify and secure the correct isolation valve was identified as the primary cause of the release.

on march 12, 2025, at approximately 9:45 a.m., the east valley compressor station's 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line experienced an abrupt rupture during a routine pressure test. the test crew had incorrectly set the test pressure to 1,800 psi, exceeding the line's design pressure of 1,200 psi by 600 psi. the line had been previously corroded, with a wall thickness reduction of 15% at the test section, calculated to be 0.25 inches from the nominal 0.5 inches. when the line was pressurized to 1,800 psi, the material failed, releasing roughly 4,500 mcf of natural gas. the rupture created a flash fire, igniting a nearby flare stack and causing two injuries with minor burns. the station was immediately shut down and the surrounding area evacuated. an internal investigation determined that the pressure setpoint was incorrectly entered into the pressure control system, and that the operator failed to confirm the actual gauge reading before energizing the line. corrective actions included implementing a double‑check procedure for pressure tests, retraining all operators on pressure‑rating limits, and installing a redundant pressure interlock on the test valve. the station was back in service on april 15, 2025 after a full integrity inspection and replacement of the corroded line segment.
