on february 12, 2026, at 14:03, a crew of three supervisors and two field technicians were conducting routine inspection and pigging on the 16-inch, 304 stainless steel, high‑pressure section of the sierra canyon natural gas pipeline located near the coyote ridge service valve. the line was operating at 4,800 psi with a gas flow rate of 1.2 million standard cubic feet per day. the crew had received a brief refresher on the pigging procedure but had not yet confirmed the isolation of the 6‑inch isolation valve that had been marked “closed” on the control panel. while attempting to open the isolation valve to allow the pig to pass, the first technician inadvertently released the valve fully while the pipe remained at operating pressure. a sudden pressure spike occurred, causing the valve flange to fail and eject a 0.5‑inch fragment that struck technician b on the right shoulder. technician b suffered a moderate fracture and was transported to the local hospital for orthopedic evaluation; he was discharged after 72 hours. technician a was uninjured but the pipe section sustained a 3‑inch breach that was immediately shut down by the field crew. the post‑incident investigation found the primary root cause was the crew’s failure to follow the lock‑out/tag‑out procedure for the isolation valve, resulting in the release of high pressure while the valve was still closed.

on july 12, 2023 at 3:45 a.m. cdt, the riverside regulating station (mr 45218) experienced a sudden overpressure event during a routine pressure test. the 48‑inch schedule‑80 steel pipeline was operating at 950 psig, with a maop of 1000 psig. the upstream control valve had been inadvertently left in the closed position during the previous week’s maintenance on mr 45218. when the operator began the test, the valve knob was turned to the open setting without verifying its actual position on the control panel. the result was a rapid drop in upstream pressure and a corresponding spike to 1120 psig in the downstream 48‑inch section. the overpressure forced the relief valve at the downstream 36‑inch junction to open at 5:02 a.m. cdt, releasing 4.3 mmcf of natural gas through the vent line, exceeding the 3‑mmcf phmsa reporting threshold. scada logs recorded the anomaly, and an emergency shutdown of the 48‑inch segment was initiated at 5:07 a.m. cdt. the investigation determined the incident stemmed from the valve being left in an incorrect position during maintenance and the operator’s failure to confirm its status before proceeding. training updates and a double‑check procedure have been added to the operating manual to prevent recurrence.

on may 2, 2024 at approximately 10:15 a.m. cst, the central valley gas transmission line was undergoing a scheduled pressure test of the 12‑inch, x‑46, carbon steel mainline located in dallas county, texas. the test involved isolating a 250‑foot segment of the line by operating the isolation valve at the remote control station. however, the on‑site engineer mistakenly selected the wrong valve position and opened the high‑pressure shut‑off valve instead of the designated isolation valve. as a result, the 12‑inch line, operating at 350 psi, experienced an uncontrolled pressure spike that exceeded the design pressure by 80 psi. the excessive pressure forced the upstream 90‑degree elbow, a 0.300‑wall, grade a, to shear, releasing approximately 5,000 cubic feet of natural gas into the atmosphere through the emergency blow‑off stack. the gas was detected by the gas detection system within 12 seconds, and the system automatically activated the emergency shutdown (esd) sequence, venting the remainder of the line. operations personnel were dispatched at 10:28 a.m. and isolated the damaged section at 10:42 a.m. the line was capped with a temporary welded plug, and a new 12‑inch x‑46 pipe was installed and tested. the line was returned to service on may 4, 2024 at 1:15 p.m.

at approximately 9:37 am edt on march 12, 2024, the southern interstate gas pipeline company's (sigtc) unit 12 experienced an unintended release during a routine line maintenance operation. the maintenance crew had been scheduled to perform a pigging operation on the 30‑inch, 2‑inch, schedule 80 carbon steel pipeline running at 350 psig. prior to pigging, the crew closed valve 5b on the suction side and valve 5c on the discharge side as part of the isolation procedure. however, a mis‑click on the control panel caused valve 5b to remain in the open position, while valve 5c was inadvertently set to “hold open” for a later scheduled pig. the pigging line was then inserted, and the pressure differential caused gas to flow through the unclosed valve 5b, creating a pressure surge of approximately 200 psig that the pressure relief valve on the suction line could not handle. the relief valve opened and vented 1,200 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere over a 12‑minute period before the operator noticed the abnormal pressure gauge reading. the incident was reported to the state regulatory agency, and an investigation revealed that the operator had not performed the required lockout/tagout check before closing valve 5b. the operator was retrained on the valve isolation checklist, and sigtc updated its procedure to include an automated confirmation step for valve status before any pigging operation.

on march 15, 2025, during routine maintenance on line 3 of the south valley pipeline, a senior operator mistakenly set the downstream pressure setpoint on the main control valve to 2000 psi instead of the scheduled 1200 psi. the line was rated at 3000 psi with a 16‑inch schedule 80 steel pipe. the valve was manually opened 30 percent during the pressure rise. within 4 minutes the upstream pressure climbed to 2600 psi, causing the pressure relief valve at the upstream flange to open. the relief valve discharged 450 mcf of natural gas into the adjacent safety isolation loop. the discharge vent opened at 12:03 pm, releasing gas into the surrounding vegetation, where a spark from a nearby welding activity ignited the gas plume. the resulting fire burned for approximately 10 minutes, causing smoke and heat damage to the nearby storage tank. no personnel were injured, but the incident prompted a shutdown of line 3 and a review of operator training. an internal investigation revealed that the operator had misread the pressure gauge because of a recently installed digital display that had not yet been calibrated. corrective actions included installing a redundant analog gauge and revising the operating procedure to require dual confirmation before valve manipulation.

on 5/14/2023 at 09:43 a.m., an operator at the midwest regional pipeline facility in dallas, texas, performed routine pressure checks on the 30-inch carbon steel line 7‑b. the line carried natural gas at 7,500 psi and was scheduled for a scheduled maintenance outage. the operator opened valve 7‑b‑01 to relieve pressure for a diagnostic test but failed to close the downstream isolation valve 7‑b‑02 after the test was complete. as a result, the line remained under full operating pressure while the upstream pressure regulator was bypassed. at 10:12 a.m., a burst occurred at the 12‑inch flanged joint on pipe segment 7‑b‑04, causing a rapid release of gas into the surrounding soil and igniting a localized fire. emergency shutdown procedures were initiated within 45 seconds, and the fire was contained by the fire suppression system. the incident was reported to the regional operations center, and the pipeline was isolated for a full investigation. the root cause analysis concluded that the operator had not followed the standard operating procedure for valve isolation and had not documented the valve status in the logbook. corrective actions included mandatory re‑training on valve isolation procedures, implementation of a double‑check system for valve status verification, and the installation of a real‑time valve position monitor on the 7‑b line. the line was restored to service on 6/02/2023 after all corrective actions were verified.

at 2:41 pm on april 15, 2024, the western pipeline company (wpc) received a radio call from a remote monitoring site reporting a sudden pressure spike in the 10‑inch line connecting the central compressor station to the downstream processing plant. the wpc engineer on duty, mr. alvarez, arrived within 8 minutes and found the 10‑inch schedule 80 steel line under 1,200 psi, 400 psi above the normal operating set‑point of 800 psi. after consulting the operating manual, he mistakenly selected the high‑pressure relief valve (hprv) setting of 1,400 psi, assuming it was the normal set‑point for emergency blowdown. the valve opened, releasing approximately 1,200 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. a nearby residential property reported a hissing sound and subsequent evacuation. an erl conference call was initiated at 2:55 pm to coordinate the response. the incident was classified as a gas release exceeding 1,000 mcf, triggering a notification to the state regulatory agency. the investigation revealed that the valve operator had been re‑programmed last month to a higher set‑point to accommodate an upcoming line maintenance, but the operator’s manual was not updated. the wpc subsequently revised its operator training to include a double‑check step for valve set‑points during emergencies.

pipeline segment # 412, a 36‑inch schedule 80 steel pipe on the interstate corridor, operating at 950 psi with a 550 psi design pressure. the line was being tested for leak integrity after a 22‑inch flared fitting replacement at the upstream pressure test station. on april 17, 2024, at 14:30, the operator engaged the 22‑inch isolation valve for the test section. due to a misinterpretation of the valve position indicator, the valve was closed fully while the test section remained at full line pressure. the pressure transducer at the test manifold showed a spike to 1200 psi, but the operator, assuming a normal test pressure rise, left the valve closed for 45 minutes to “confirm pressure stability.” during this interval, the pressure‑rated flanged joint failed, rupturing the pipe and releasing approximately 1.2 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding area. the incident was detected by the remote gas‑detection system, which triggered a fire alarm in the nearby storage building. emergency responders were dispatched, and the area was evacuated. the valve was manually opened after the incident, allowing the line pressure to drop to 300 psi. subsequent investigation revealed that the valve position indicator was faulty and the operator’s training documentation did not emphasize the need to de‑pressurize the test section before closing the isolation valve.

on january 15, 2024, at approximately 09:30 a.m., the west‑field gas compression station 5270 reported an abnormal rise in the discharge header pressure of the 8‑inch gas header. the station control room operator observed the pressure gauge reading 515 psig, 20 psig above the set‑point of 495 psig, and noted that the high‑pressure alarm at the 12‑inch safety relief valve had not been triggered. the operator mistakenly believed the relief valve had been bypassed for maintenance and therefore left the valve open to allow for pressure buildup during the scheduled back‑flush of the associated 4‑inch regulator. after noticing the pressure trend, the operator immediately applied a remote shut‑down command to the gas‑turbine compressor, which was in normal run mode, and closed the upstream isolation valve (v‑402) to isolate the 8‑inch header. the pressure subsequently fell to 480 psig over the next fifteen minutes. field personnel discovered that the safety relief valve had been improperly set to a 530 psig set‑point during the recent calibration, causing it to remain inactive during the pressure excursion. an investigation determined that the operator had incorrectly referenced the wrong operating manual during the shift handover, leading to the misinterpretation of the relief valve configuration. corrective actions included updating the operator training manual, installing a lock‑out tag on the safety relief valve during maintenance, and implementing a cross‑check procedure for relief valve set‑points. no injuries or product loss were reported.

on september 12, 2023 at 10:43 a.m., a crew operating the western energy transmission line at mile marker 284.6 in texas performed a valve isolation procedure on the 40‑inch schedule 80 steel line to prepare for a downstream pressure test. the crew, led by engineer r. harris, mistakenly selected the wrong isolation valve (valve 5) instead of valve 3, which controls the section under test. while the valve was being opened, the line pressure rose to 1150 psig, exceeding the design pressure of 1100 psig for that segment. the relief valve on the line opened at 1120 psig, causing a rapid gas release of approximately 18,000 standard cubic feet over 6 minutes. no personnel were injured, but the release triggered a fire alarm in the nearby facility, forcing evacuation of three adjacent buildings. after the release, the crew shut down the main line, performed a pressure purge, and restored the valve to its correct position. a post‑incident review found that the operator had not cross‑checked the valve number against the schematics, and that the valve indicator lights were not calibrated for the 40‑inch line. corrective actions included a revised training program on valve identification, installation of a second visual confirmation system, and a quarterly audit of valve labeling accuracy. the incident was reported to the nrc within 24 hours under the 8‑hour reporting threshold.

on may 14, 2021 at approximately 10:12 am, a remote operation of rov 42315 at the loma city gate station was performed during a scheduled shutdown of the upstream 30‑inch, 960‑lb/ft steel line. the gate station was delivering 11,200 dekatherms per hour to the city of loma with an outlet pressure of 260 psig. at 09:58, all personnel had assembled and confirmed that the gate station was in a safe operating condition. at 10:00, the control group received a notification that the remote valve was scheduled to be cycled for a brief testing interval. however, the operator mistakenly selected the "close" command instead of "open" on the control console, resulting in the rov 42315 closing while the downstream line was still pressurized. the downstream pressure rose rapidly, reaching 385 psig within 30 seconds, exceeding the line’s 350 psig maximum allowable operating pressure. at 10:02, a high‑pressure alarm tripped on the gate station's pressure relief valve, which opened at 10:03 to vent 4500 cfm of natural gas into the atmosphere. the incident caused a temporary loss of gas service to loma and required a full containment procedure. a post‑incident review determined that the operator had incorrectly interpreted the command menu due to a recent software upgrade that changed the command labels. corrective actions include retraining of all control operators, installation of a lock‑out/tag‑out system for remote valve operation, and revision of the operating procedures to include a mandatory two‑person confirmation for remote valve status changes.

on january 12, 2026, at 7:32 a.m. mountain daylight time, a temporary line 45a underwent a planned pressure test following a 4‑day outage. the line was a 12‑inch schedule 80 carbon steel segment with a maop of 580 psig. during the pre‑job the crew did not verify that valve v3 on the interconnection yard was closed, nor did they set the pressure control valve to the required test setpoint of 150 psi. at 7:45 a.m. the field crew opened valve v3 to allow flow into the test section, assuming the pressure controller had already been set. because the controller remained at the default 0 psi setpoint, the upstream pressure surged to 615 psig within 45 seconds. the pressure relief valve on the test section, with a setpoint of 620 psi, opened at 7:46 a.m., releasing 1,200 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. the rapid release triggered a secondary rupture in pipe 45a at the 3‑inch weld throat, causing a 0.3‑mile section of line to fail and a plume of gas to ignite in the adjacent grassland. emergency shutdown was executed at 7:48 a.m., but the ignition spread before the flares could be engaged, resulting in a fire that burned for 12 minutes and caused a $70,000 loss. after the incident, the company reviewed the pressure test protocol and required a two‑person verification for valve operations before any test is conducted.

on monday, april 22, 2024, a 12‑inch schedule 80 carbon steel natural gas line operating at 2,500 psi experienced a sudden rupture during an unscheduled pressure test. the line was in the middle of a routine high‑pressure integrity check after a routine maintenance shutdown of the adjacent 10‑inch flare stack. operators were instructed to close the remote‑operated isolation valve (v‑102) before applying test pressure, but a mis‑read on the control panel led to the valve being left partially open at 0.2 inches. as the test pressure reached 2,400 psi, the valve’s ball failed to seat fully, allowing a flash of gas to escape through the valve’s clearance gap and ignite in a nearby ventilation shaft. the resulting blast tore a 2‑inch hole in the pipe wall, causing an immediate loss of pressure and a 400‑foot plume of flammable gas. emergency crews shut in the line within 12 seconds, but the explosion caused a localized fire that damaged a 1‑inch steel support bracket and ignited a nearby stack of maintenance rags. the incident was reported to the state energy agency and the national response center under report number 1129345. an internal investigation revealed that the pressure test procedure was not followed correctly; the operator had bypassed the required two‑person lock‑out and the test pressure gauge was miscalibrated. corrective actions included re‑training operators, updating the pressure test checklist, and installing a secondary pressure‑sensing alarm on the valve actuator.

on march 3, 2024 at 07:45 am, the 20-inch trans‑state transmission line # 12, rated at 950 psi, was scheduled for a pig run to clear a 12‑inch weld. the operator mistakenly closed the main isolation valve on the upstream line instead of the pig‑run valve. during the purge, the line pressure rose to 1120 psi and the valve seat failed. the sudden pressure drop released a large volume of natural gas into the surrounding work zone. a nearby welding torch ignited the gas, producing a flash fire that burned the operator's protective gear. two workers sustained second‑degree burns and were airlifted to the regional medical center. emergency responders were called at 08:02 am. the gas control system was immediately shut down and a pressure test of 1200 psi for 12 hours was conducted to confirm integrity. the valve was replaced with an industrial‑grade stainless steel seat and an interlock system was installed to prevent accidental closure during pigging. the pipeline was restored to service on 04/05/2024 after a full inspection and verification of all safety interlocks.

on april 12, 2023 a 20" x70″ api 5l carbon steel transmission line (line # 412) was being recommissioned after a scheduled bypass for a downstream compressor tie‑in. the line’s maop was 950 psi and the operating limit for the new downstream regulator was 880 psi. during the start‑up the field supervisor instructed the control room to “bring the line up to normal pressure” without specifying the regulator set point. central gas control, assuming the regulator had been pre‑set to 820 psi per the recent engineering change notice, increased the line pressure to 910 psi. the on‑site operator, noticing the high gauge reading, attempted to open the manual bleed valve at the 12‑mile marker to relieve pressure, but the valve was misidentified as a low‑pressure vent and was actually the upstream isolation valve. the isolation valve was opened, causing a rapid depressurization that exposed a section of recently installed girth welds still under residual stress. the sudden pressure drop caused a 0.6‑inch longitudinal crack to propagate, releasing an estimated 3.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere before the crew could reseal the line. the incident was later classified as a procedural lapse in communication and pressure set‑point verification.

on august 14, 2025 at 06:42 (cst), the westfield compression station on the 24‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x65) experienced an unintended pressure surge. the station control engineer initiated a manual start‑up of the downstream booster compressor while the upstream inlet valve was still partially open from a previous maintenance cycle. the inlet pressure was 820 psig, and the booster was set to increase downstream pressure to 1050 psig. because the inlet valve had not been fully closed, the sudden addition of compressor flow caused a rapid pressure rise to 1320 psig, exceeding the design limit of the 24‑inch pipe segment. a section of the pipe near the valve manifold, which had a previously repaired girth weld, ruptured, releasing approximately 12,400 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands. emergency shutdown was manually triggered at 06:48, and the area was isolated. no injuries were reported, but local wildlife was impacted. the incident investigation concluded that the engineer failed to verify valve position before compressor start‑up, and that the station’s standard operating procedure for sequential valve closure was not followed. corrective actions include revising the start‑up checklist, implementing an interlock to prevent compressor activation with inlet valve partially open, and retraining all operators on valve sequencing.

on october 14, 2024 at 09:45 mst, the south ridge compression unit 12 experienced an unscheduled vent. the unit was being brought back online after a maintenance shutdown when the operator manually opened the suction isolation valve using a handheld key switch instead of the hmi command. the valve was intended to remain closed until the downstream pressure reached 550 psig, but the manual actuation allowed gas at 720 psig to flow into the 20‑inch carbon steel suction line. a downstream pressure transducer was out of calibration, reading 480 psig, so the automatic shutdown logic never engaged. the vent valve opened when the unit pressure exceeded its high‑pressure alarm setpoint of 800 psig, releasing approximately 12,416 mcf of natural gas to the atmosphere over 18 minutes. investigation revealed that the portable key switch had been left energized from a previous test and that the operator was not aware of the pending high‑pressure condition because the scada display was offline for a software upgrade. corrective actions include reinstating lockout‑tagout procedures for handheld switches, recalibrating all pressure transmitters, and updating the start‑up checklist to require verification of the scada communication status before valve actuation.

on april 14, 2024 at 08:43 local time, the mainline of the northern transmission system (24‑inch x80 api 5l carbon steel) experienced a rapid pressure rise to 1250 psig, exceeding its design limit of 1100 psig. the incident was traced to an operator at the regional control center who manually opened the intertie valve between the 16‑inch lateral (rated 1050 psig) and the mainline to compensate for a perceived flow shortfall. the valve was opened beyond the recommended 30 % opening, allowing an uncontrolled surge from the downstream compressor station operating at 1150 psig. as a result, a 4‑inch split in the mainline near milepost 212 released approximately 2.8 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands. nearby vegetation ignited, prompting an automatic shutdown of the downstream compressors and activation of the emergency isolation valve. emergency response teams arrived within fifteen minutes, secured the leak, and conducted a hot‑work permit for repair. no injuries were reported, but the incident caused a temporary shutdown of 12 hours and a loss of revenue estimated at $450,000. a root‑cause analysis recommended revising operator training on intertie valve usage and implementing automated flow‑balancing controls.

on september 14, 2026 at approximately 0735 hrs a field operator at the north ridge gathering station initiated a manual isolation of the 30‑in. carbon steel transmission line feeding the west field processing unit. the line was operating at 720 psig and the operator, believing the downstream valve was fully closed, opened the upstream isolation valve to perform a pigging operation. however, the downstream 24‑in. block valve had only been partially seated due to a missed visual inspection step. when the upstream valve was opened, high‑pressure gas surged downstream, causing the partially closed valve to slip open and release a sudden jet of natural gas at an estimated 650 psig. the gas ignited when it contacted a hot surface on a nearby heat‑exchanger manifold, resulting in a flash fire that injured two technicians and damaged a section of the 30‑in. line. emergency shutdown was initiated by the control room after the automatic high‑pressure alarm triggered, but the delay in confirming valve positions prolonged the event for roughly three minutes. post‑incident review identified that the standard operating procedure for valve verification was not followed, and that the lock‑out/tag‑out process for the downstream valve was omitted, leading to the unintended gas release.

on april 14, 2022 at 03:12 am, western energy services, inc. (wes) detected a sudden pressure drop on its 24‑inch, api 5l x70 steel main (line 12‑b) near the houston, tx compression station. the control system logged a drop from the normal operating pressure of 960 psig to 620 psig within seconds. operators initiated an emergency shutdown and dispatched a field crew to the suspected leak site. upon arrival at the valve yard at 03:38 am, the crew found the mainline isolation valve 12‑b‑02 in the manual open position, contrary to the standard operating procedure that requires the valve to be set to automatic after any routine test. the valve had been manually opened earlier that week for a pigging operation, but the required step to re‑engage the automatic actuator was omitted. because the valve remained manual, the downstream pressure regulator failed to receive the proper signal, allowing the pipeline to depressurize while the upstream compressor continued to feed gas at full flow. the resulting pressure differential caused a 3‑inch longitudinal split in the pipe wall, releasing an estimated 250 mmcf of natural gas before the valve was finally closed at 04:05 am. no fire or injuries occurred, but the incident exceeded the 200 mmcf reporting threshold. wes has since revised its valve‑operation checklist, added a lock‑out tag‑out requirement for manual positions, and mandated additional training for personnel performing pigging and maintenance activities.

the 24‑inch carbon steel main feeding the east processing hub was scheduled for a pressure increase after a routine maintenance shutdown. the control room operator entered the new setpoint as 1350 psi, believing it to be the maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) for the line, but the actual maop for the 24‑inch segment is 1200 psi according to the design specification. the operator also failed to verify the upstream 30‑inch isolation valve position, which had been left closed for a previous line test. as a result, the downstream pump surge pressed the gas against the closed valve, causing a rapid pressure spike to 1520 psi at the downstream pressure regulator. the over‑pressure triggered the high‑pressure safety valve on the regulator, which released gas directly to the vent stack. the vent stack was partially obstructed by debris, leading to a back‑pressure that forced gas out of a nearby flange connection, creating a jet that ignited when it contacted a hot surface on the adjacent compressor skids. the flash fire damaged the vent pipe, melted surrounding insulation, and resulted in a temporary shutdown of the east hub. the investigation cited the operator’s entry of an incorrect setpoint and failure to confirm isolation valve status as the primary contributors.

on monday, july 8, 2025 at 0837 hrs, field operators initiated a pigging run on the 12‑inch x70 mil carbon steel main (segment a‑23) without first confirming the downstream valve isolation. the downstream block valve remained partially open, allowing 720 psi natural gas to flow while the pig was being launched. the pig struck the valve stem, causing the valve to snap shut abruptly. the sudden pressure surge, estimated at 1150 psi, exceeded the design limit of the 12‑inch line and resulted in a longitudinal split approximately 18 inches long near the 4‑mile marker. gas escaped at an estimated rate of 350 mmscfd, forming a vapor cloud that ignited when a nearby diesel generator back‑fed into the line during an unrelated maintenance activity. the ignition produced a visible flame front of about 30 ft, but fire crews contained the blaze within ten minutes. no injuries were reported, but the incident caused a temporary service outage for 3,200 customers and repair costs exceeded $210,000. the incident was reported to the nrc as a significant event due to the operational oversight. corrective actions included revising pig launch procedures, adding a mandatory valve isolation verification step, and retraining all shift personnel on the updated protocol.

on october 3, 2022 at approximately 08:17 cst, western midstream's 24‑inch, api 5l x70 transmission line near houston, tx experienced an unplanned vent to the atmosphere. the line’s maop is 1,200 psi and the downstream relief valve is set at 1,050 psi. during a scheduled pressure boost to increase throughput for a downstream processing unit, the control room operator entered a setpoint of 1,080 psi, mistakenly referencing the previous day’s test values. the field crew, following the electronic setpoint, increased the line pressure to 1,080 psi, which exceeded the relief valve’s opening pressure. as a result, the relief valve opened, releasing approximately 2,400 mcf of natural gas before the crew manually closed the isolation valve. the release triggered an automatic shutdown of the compressor station’s esd system and prompted an evacuation of nearby personnel. investigation determined that the error stemmed from an incorrect input of the pressure setpoint and a lack of verification against the valve’s rating. western midstream has revised its setpoint entry procedures, added a secondary confirmation step in the control system, and conducted refresher training on valve rating awareness for all operators.

on august 3, 2024 at 07:22 cdt a maintenance crew was performing a pigging operation on the southern pipeline company's line 12, a 30‑inch api 5l sch40 carbon steel pipe transporting sweet natural gas at a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 850 psi. the crew had been instructed to close the downstream isolation valve (isolation valve b‑12) before inserting the pig, but the valve was inadvertently left open due to a mis‑read of the valve position indicator. as the pig entered the line, it created a localized pressure surge of approximately 1.15 times the maop, raising the pressure in the 5‑mile segment to about 980 psi. the overpressure caused a 0.25‑inch longitudinal crack in a corroded section of the pipe at milepost 42.7, resulting in an immediate gas release of an estimated 4,200 mscf before the automatic shutdown (esd) system activated at 07:31 cdt. personnel evacuated the area and initiated emergency response procedures. post‑incident review indicated that the operator responsible for valve control lacked recent refresher training on pigging protocols and failed to verify valve position using the manual lockout tagout checklist. corrective actions include updating the pigging procedure, mandating double‑check verification of isolation valves, and conducting additional competency training for all field operators.

on 3/14/2023 at 07:42 am cdt, western interregional pipelines (wip) received an alarm from the control room indicating an unexpected pressure rise in the 24‑inch mainline feeding the desert ridge compression hub, located in el paso county, texas. the line, a 2‑1/2 in api 5l x70 carbon steel pipe, was scheduled for a routine start‑up after a 48‑hour maintenance shutdown. during the start‑up, the field operator manually opened the upstream isolation valve (valve‑b13) to 75 % instead of the prescribed 25 % open position, causing a rapid influx of gas from the upstream storage cavern at approximately 1150 psig. the sudden surge exceeded the design set‑point of 1000 psig and triggered the downstream safety relief valve (sr‑v07). the relief valve lifted, but due to an improperly seated o‑ring, it failed to reseat, allowing a continuous release of gas through the vent stack. emergency services were dispatched at 07:55 am cdt and arrived on site at 08:12 am cdt. the release was isolated by closing the downstream isolation valve (valve‑c21) at 08:20 am cdt. a total of 3500 scf of natural gas was vented before the situation was stabilized. the incident was reported to the nrc at 09:05 am cdt. subsequent investigation identified the incorrect manual valve opening as the primary operational error; wip revised the start‑up procedure and added interlock verification to prevent manual override beyond 30 % opening.

on july 14, 2022, at 03:12 am, midwest pipeline corporation (mpc) received an automatic shutdown alarm from its 20‑inch carbon steel transmission line (schedule 80, s355) at the riverbend compression station, nebraska. the line was being pressure‑tested at 1,150 psi after a recent weld repair on a 30‑ft segment. a technician used the handheld esd controller to isolate the test section, but inadvertently pressed the “open bypass” key instead of “close bypass.” this action opened valve rb‑12a, a 4‑inch bypass valve that diverts flow to the downstream relief manifold. the bypass opened while the test pump continued to increase pressure, causing an uncontrolled surge that exceeded the pipe’s design limit of 1,200 psi. within seconds the pipe’s longitudinal seam cracked near the weld, releasing approximately 8 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding yard. the emergency shutdown system engaged at 03:16 am, limiting the release. investigation revealed that the handheld controller’s key layout was not intuitive and the operator had not been retrained on the updated bypass procedure after the recent software upgrade. mpc has since revised the controller interface, instituted mandatory quarterly refresher training for all esd operators, and installed a physical key interlock on bypass valves to prevent accidental activation during pressure testing.

a 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 820 psi was scheduled for a routine restart after a planned shutdown at the marisol gas gathering station. the line had been isolated with a 24‑inch block valve and a 4‑inch bypass valve was left open for pigging. during the restart, the station operator manually opened the bypass valve to re‑pressurize the line but failed to verify that the block valve had been fully closed. as the 1500 hp centrifugal compressors came online, pressure built up rapidly behind the partially closed block valve, creating a pressure surge of approximately 1500 psi at the upstream end. the surge exceeded the design rating of a recently welded girth joint near milepost 27.5, causing the weld to fail and a 6‑inch rupture to open. natural gas escaped, forming a vapor cloud that ignited when a nearby hot‑work torch was used for a maintenance cut. the flash fire burned a crew of three, causing second‑degree burns to two workers. investigation revealed the operator had not followed the standard operating procedure for valve sequencing and had not performed the required pressure check with the handheld gauge before initiating compressor start‑up. corrective actions included revising the valve‑lockout checklist, retraining all operators on sequential valve operations, and installing an automated interlock to prevent compressor start when the block valve is not fully closed.

on 09/14/2025 at 22:07, the crew performing routine pigging on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (rated 1200 psi) at the riverbend compression station opened the bypass valve without confirming that the line isolation clamps were fully engaged. the isolation clamps had been manually tightened earlier in the shift, but the lockout tag was never placed. after the bypass valve was opened, gas from the 1150 psi mainline entered the pigging loop, raising the pressure in the 24‑inch pig trap to approximately 950 psi, well above its design limit of 750 psi. within three minutes the pig trap’s relief valve lifted, releasing a high‑velocity jet of natural gas into the adjacent yard. the release ignited when a nearby welding torch, being used for a scheduled flange repair, struck an exposed gas plume, producing a flash fire that damaged the torch stand and caused minor burns to two technicians. post‑incident review showed the operator had relied on a handheld pressure gauge that was still calibrated for the low‑pressure pigging circuit and failed to verify the mainline pressure before opening the bypass. corrective actions included revising the pigging standard operating procedure to require dual‑point pressure verification and retraining all field personnel on lockout‑tagout compliance.

on july 14, 2024 at 06:42 am, the western ridge compression station reported an unexpected pressure rise in line 24, a 20‑inches carbon steel main feeding the northfield gathering system. the control room had just completed a scheduled startup of compressor c‑3 after a three‑month maintenance outage. an operator manually opened the inlet isolation valve (13‑inches) to restore feed gas while the automatic shutdown interlock on the suction‑side pressure sensor was still active. the valve was left fully open for approximately 7 minutes, causing the suction pressure to climb to 1 800 psig, well above the design limit of 1 200 psig. the over‑pressure triggered the high‑pressure vent valve, releasing an estimated 12 mmscf of natural gas through the 6‑inch vent stack before the emergency shutdown (esd) was initiated at 06:52 am. field crews arrived on site at 07:10 am, isolated the inlet valve and confirmed that the compressor surge valve had sealed. post‑incident analysis indicated the operator had not verified the interlock status in the start‑up checklist. corrective actions included revising the start‑up procedure, adding a visual lock‑out on the inlet isolation valve when the suction‑side interlock is engaged, and conducting a refresher training on manual valve operations.

on april 7, 2023, maintenance crew at the midstream gathering station were executing a scheduled pigging operation on the 24" carbon steel transmission line that transports wet natural gas from the field hub to the processing plant. the line was isolated by closing the upstream isolation valve 12‑45 (rated 1200 psig) and the downstream block valve 12‑48. after confirming lockout/tagout, operators opened the pig trap vent valve to depressurize the segment. however, the crew mistakenly opened the pig trap vent valve with the pneumatic actuator set to “open‑fast” instead of using the manual hand wheel, causing the valve to snap open beyond its design travel. this created an unintended large opening to the vent stack, which was equipped with a 90‑degree elbow and a 10‑inch flare tip intended for low‑flow venting.

simultaneously, a downstream pressure regulator failed to seal, allowing line pressure of approximately 950 psig to surge through the vent stack. the high‑velocity gas struck the elbow, generating a force that fractured the vent stack flange and ejected the flare tip. approximately 18 mmcf of gas escaped before the emergency shutdown system isolated the line by automatically closing valve 12‑45. the incident was attributed to the operator’s incorrect use of the pneumatic actuator and failure to follow the standard manual venting procedure. subsequent corrective actions included retraining on valve actuation methods and reinstalling a reinforced vent stack with a pressure‑rated design.

on 02/14/2025 at 07:45 am, the 16‑inch mainline feeder at the riverbend compression station experienced an unintended pressure rise to 1 250 psi, exceeding its design limit of 1 100 psi. the station control room logged that the high‑pressure alarm triggered shortly after the crew initiated a start‑up sequence on compressor c‑7. during the start‑up, the operator inadvertently left the upstream isolation valve (size 12‑inch, carbon steel, sch 40) in the open position while the downstream automatic shut‑off valve remained closed for maintenance. this configuration allowed gas from the upstream 24‑inch pipeline (rated 1 300 psi) to flow directly into the compressor suction line, causing a rapid pressure buildup in the 16‑inch discharge header. the pressure surge persisted for 42 minutes before a field technician arrived at 08:27 am and manually closed the isolation valve, then opened the downstream shut‑off valve to restore normal flow. investigation revealed that the valve handle had not been secured with the standard lock‑out tag, and the start‑up checklist was not completed. corrective actions included installing a secondary mechanical lock on the isolation valve, revising the start‑up procedure to require dual‑operator verification, and retraining personnel on lock‑out/tag‑out compliance.

on september 22, 2023, a maintenance crew was conducting a pigging operation on the 24‑inch, schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line that transports natural gas from the ryan field to the central processing hub. the line is rated for a maximum operating pressure of 900 psi and was operating at 750 psi at the time of the run. after the pig cleared the 12‑inch reducer at milepost 45, the crew mistakenly left the isolation valve on the downstream side of the reducer in the open position while the control system automatically increased line pressure to 850 psi to resume normal flow. the open valve caused a rapid pressure surge that exceeded the design rating of the 12‑inch segment, resulting in a circumferential rupture approximately 200 ft downstream of the valve. the release ignited a nearby vegetation fire, prompting immediate evacuation of the adjacent ranches and the temporary shutdown of county road 12. emergency response teams arrived within 15 minutes, isolated the affected section, and applied a temporary clamp. the incident caused no serious injuries, but resulted in $250,000 in equipment damage and $75,000 in environmental remediation costs. the investigation identified the failure to close the isolation valve after pigging as the primary operational error.

on october 3, 2024 at 14:27 the midland gas processing plant began a scheduled pigging operation on the 24‑inch, 7‑cr steel transmission line that carries sweet natural gas at a design pressure of 950 psig. the isolation procedure required the mainline isolation valve (mlv‑12) to be closed and locked out before the pig launcher could be depressurized. the field crew, under time pressure, failed to verify that the lockout/tagout devices were fully engaged on mlv‑12 and proceeded to open the vent valve to purge residual gas from the pig launcher. the vent valve was opened while the mainline remained pressurized, allowing gas at approximately 870 psig to flow through the 12‑inch vent stack for roughly six minutes before the operator noticed the abnormal pressure drop on the control panel. a downstream pressure sensor recorded a rapid decrease from 945 psig to 420 psig, triggering the emergency shutdown system which automatically cycled the upstream shutdown valve. the incident resulted in an unplanned release of an estimated 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere and a brief plant shutdown. the subsequent investigation cited failure to follow the lockout/tagout protocol and premature venting as the primary operational errors. corrective actions include a mandatory lockout/tagout verification checklist and additional hands‑on training for all pigging crews.

on monday, july 14, 2023 at 0430 hours, the southern gas transmission company (sgtc) received a call from the field crew reporting a sudden release of natural gas at the intersection of highway 15 and county road 22, near the el dorado valley. the crew was performing a hot‑tap insertion on a 24‑inch, schedule 40 carbon steel transmission line that was operating at 860 psi (59 bar). the hot‑tap valve had been manually opened after a lock‑out/tag‑out procedure, but the pressure gauge on the line was inadvertently set to the low‑range scale, causing the operators to believe the line pressure was below 200 psi. consequently, the crew proceeded with cutting the pipe using an oxy‑acetylene torch without confirming the actual line pressure. as the torch arc contacted the pipe wall, a high‑energy jet of gas escaped from the partially opened valve and ignited, producing a flash fire that engulfed the torch holder and nearby equipment. the incident triggered an automatic shutdown of the line, activation of the nearby emergency shutdown valve, and a 911 call. fire crews arrived within ten minutes, establishing a safety perimeter and extinguishing the fire. no fatalities occurred, but two workers sustained second‑degree burns. the incident was reported because the repair costs exceeded $150,000 and the line was out of service for 48 hours. an investigation later identified the misinterpretation of the pressure gauge reading and failure to verify line pressure before hot work as the primary contributors. corrective actions included retraining on gauge calibration, mandatory double‑check of pressure readings, and revision of hot‑work procedures for high‑pressure pipelines.

on april 7, 2024, lincoln pipelines crew was conducting a routine restart of the oak ridge mainline at the clarkson pump station. the line is a 30‑inch carbon steel pipe operating at a maximum pressure of 950 psig. during the startup sequence the lead operator inadvertently opened the isolation valve downstream of the 24‑inch bypass loop to the full open position instead of the prescribed 30 % opening. this caused an unexpected surge in flow, raising the pressure in the bypass loop to approximately 1 050 psig, exceeding the design limit of the 24‑inch line. within minutes the bypass loop flange failed, resulting in a release of about 850 mcf of natural gas that ignited, creating a flash fire that burned three crew members. two workers suffered second‑degree burns and were treated on site before being transferred to a regional trauma center; the third escaped with minor injuries. the incident was reported to the incident command system, and emergency shutdown procedures were initiated, isolating the line within 4 minutes. post‑incident investigation revealed the valve position error stemmed from an outdated operating checklist that did not reflect the recent modification of the bypass loop. the company has since revised the startup checklist, implemented a digital valve position confirmation step in the control system, and retrained all operators on the revised procedure.

at 07:45 am the control room at northern midwest pipeline operations received a low‑pressure alarm on the 30‑in. × 0.375‑in. api 5l x65 carbon steel mainline feeding the antrim compression station. the operator, following the standard start‑up checklist, manually opened valve b12 to increase flow from the downstream regulator. the valve was a motor‑driven, double‑block & bleed unit rated for 850 psi, but it had been recently serviced and the actuator limit switch was inadvertently set to a “full‑open” position rather than the required “partial‑open” for start‑up. as a result, the line pressure spiked to 960 psi, exceeding the design limit of 900 psi. the pressure surge triggered the automatic shut‑down (esd) at the station, but valve b12 failed to close because the actuator limit switch prevented the closure sequence. gas was forced through a relief vent on the antrim side, releasing an estimated 1 200 mcf to the atmosphere before the crew could manually isolate the valve at 08:12 am. the incident was reported to the nrc and phmsa. investigation revealed the operator had not consulted the recent change notice documenting the actuator adjustment, and the moc procedure had not been followed for the hardware modification. corrective actions included revising the start‑up procedure, retraining operators on limit‑switch verification, and tightening moc enforcement for all actuator changes.

on september 14, 2025, at approximately 08:42 mountain daylight time (mdt), a routine restart of the east ridge gas gathering station was underway following a scheduled valve inspection. the station’s mainline consisted of a 24‑inch carbon steel pipeline rated for 1200 psig, feeding into a 12‑inch downstream distribution line rated for 800 psig. after confirming isolation of the upstream isolation valve, the control operator manually opened the downstream transfer valve to re‑establish flow, but inadvertently opened the bypass valve that feeds the high‑pressure vent line instead. the vent line, a 10‑inch schedule 40 carbon steel pipe designed for emergency pressure relief only, was left open while the mainline pressure began to rise. within minutes the upstream pressure reached 1150 psig, exceeding the vent line’s design limit of 900 psig. the vent line ruptured at a welded tee near the station’s flare header, releasing an estimated 4.7 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding scrubland. emergency shutdown (esd) signals activated at 08:48, and the station crew isolated the vent line and closed the bypass valve by 08:55. first responders arrived on site at 09:12, establishing a safety perimeter and monitoring for ignition. the gas release was contained, and the rupture was repaired with a new 10‑inch pipe section and reinforced flange connections. a post‑incident review identified the incorrect valve sequencing as the primary cause, leading to revised operating procedures and additional operator training on bypass valve management. the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 2025‑0914‑07) and the state oil and gas commission.

10/05/24 update: at approximately 06:42 am local time, the north field gas gathering station experienced an unintended release of natural gas from the 24‑in. carbon steel transmission line feeding the east‑bound loop. the release was traced to the mainline isolation valve (valve 12‑b) which had been left in a partially open position during a routine pigging operation. the pig crew had manually opened valve 12‑a to allow the pig to pass, but mistakenly rotated valve 12‑b only three turns instead of the required six, leaving the valve 50 % open. as a result, the downstream pressure regulator, set for 750 psi, received only 380 psi and began venting excess gas to maintain downstream pressure. the station control system logged an over‑pressure alarm at 06:45 am, and operators initiated an emergency shutdown (esd) at 06:48 am. the esd suction and discharge valves functioned correctly, but the partial opening of valve 12‑b prevented full isolation, allowing approximately 0.85 mmcf of gas to escape before the line was fully closed at 07:12 am. investigation revealed that the pigging procedure checklist was not followed, and the valve position indicator was not cross‑checked with the visual tag. corrective actions include retraining crew on valve sequencing, installing a position‑feedback sensor on valve 12‑b, and revising the pigging work‑order to require a second‑person verification of valve positions.

on monday, june 3rd, a field operator was instructed to restart a 10‑inch mainline after a scheduled maintenance shutdown at the ridgeview compression station. the line, a carbon steel pipe rated for 1200 psig, had been isolated with a 4‑inch isolation valve and a 6‑inch bypass valve that had been left open for pigging. the operator, believing the bypass valve to be the isolation valve, turned the 4‑inch isolation valve to the open position while the bypass remained open and the line was still pressurized from the upstream compressor at 950 psig. as the isolation valve opened, high‑pressure gas rushed into the work area, striking the operator’s left forearm and forcing a section of the bypass valve handle into his chest. the sudden surge also caused a metal plug to be expelled from the line, damaging a downstream pressure regulator. the operator was transported to the regional trauma center with a punctured lung, fractured ribs and a lacerated forearm. after the incident, the station was depressurized, the bypass valve was closed, and a lock‑out/tag‑out procedure was added to the standard operating checklist to prevent future confusion between isolation and bypass valves.

on august 22, 2025, at approximately 06:17 hrs, the western pipelines midcontinent control center authorized a restart of line c‑12 after a scheduled maintenance outage. the line, a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission pipe rated for 1 200 psi, had been depressurized to 250 psi for valve replacement at mile‑112. the field crew installed a new 24‑inch gate valve (tag gv‑112‑a) and performed a hydrostatic test at 1 500 psi, confirming seal integrity. after test completion, the crew closed the isolation valve on the downstream side (tag iv‑112‑b) and opened the upstream isolation valve (tag uv‑112‑c) to re‑pressurize the segment. however, the operator mistakenly entered “open” for iv‑112‑b in the distributed control system, bypassing the required lock‑out/tag‑out verification step. the segment was re‑pressurized to 1 050 psi while the downstream isolation remained open, causing a sudden surge that exceeded the design surge limit of 1 100 psi at the adjoining 18‑inch tie‑in. the surge ruptured a weakened flange at mile‑113, releasing an estimated 3.2 mmcf of natural gas. nearby personnel detected the odor and initiated emergency shutdown; the gas ignited after 2 minutes, producing a flash fire that burned one employee and caused minor injuries to three others. the incident was reported to the nrc and state oil and gas commission. the post‑incident review identified the incorrect valve command entry and failure to follow lock‑out/tag‑out procedures as primary contributors.

on august 3, 2022, the east valley compression station experienced an unintended release of natural gas while operators were performing a routine pressure‑decrease on the 30‑inch mainline serving the southern delivery zone. the mainline, a carbon‑steel pipe rated for 1 200 psig, was scheduled to be isolated using a 28‑inch block valve that had been manually locked open for a previous maintenance job. during the pressure‑decrease, a shift supervisor instructed the control room to close the downstream isolation valve, but the operator mistakenly engaged the automated actuator on the upstream block valve instead of the downstream isolation valve. the block valve, which was equipped with a pneumatic hand‑pump, was opened further by the operator using the power‑assist control, inadvertently allowing upstream pressure to rise to approximately 1 050 psig while the downstream valve remained open. this pressure differential caused a 12‑inch pig‑receiver vent valve to lift, releasing gas into the atmosphere for roughly 45 minutes before the error was recognized. the release amounted to an estimated 2.4 mmcf of gas. investigation later identified that the operator misread the valve position indicator and that the procedural checklist did not require a double‑check confirmation for valve actuation during pressure‑decrease operations. corrective actions included revising the checklist to mandate visual confirmation of valve status and installing a lock‑out tag on the block valve during maintenance.

on 15 may 2024, at 0830 hrs, a southern california gas transmission operator reported a sudden pressure rise in the 30‑inch carbon steel mainline near the silverado interchange. the line, rated for 1 500 psig, was operating at 1 350 psig when a field supervisor instructed the control room to close valve b‑23 to isolate a downstream maintenance crew. the supervisor failed to verify that valve b‑23 was a double‑block‑and‑bleed configuration and inadvertently opened the adjacent isolation valve b‑24 without confirming its status. this action allowed high‑pressure gas to bypass the intended shutdown point and flow into the maintenance section where a temporary vent stack, installed for a pigging operation, was only rated for 800 psig. within minutes the vent stack failed, releasing a jet of natural gas that ignited from a nearby spark source, creating a brief flame front. emergency shutdown (esd) was initiated at 0845 hrs, and the mainline pressure was reduced to 1 200 psig by 0902 hrs. the vent stack rupture caused a minor property loss and two crew members sustained second‑degree burns; both were treated on‑site and released. post‑incident review identified the lack of a written procedure for confirming valve configurations during isolation as the primary factor in the incident.

on april 14, 2023 at 02:17 a.m. the ridgeview gas gathering station, located near wyoming, wy, initiated a routine pressure reduction on the 28‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the downstream metering skid. the field operator entered the manual override on the mainline isolation valve (valve id #12‑b) using the handheld touchscreen panel, intending to close the valve fully for the scheduled maintenance. however, due to a mis‑read of the valve status indicator, the operator only partially closed the valve to approximately 45 % open, leaving a restricted flow path. the reduced aperture caused an unexpected pressure buildup upstream, increasing the line pressure from the normal 850 psig to 1 180 psig within ten minutes. the high‑pressure condition triggered the automatic shut‑in on the downstream pressure safety valve (psv‑04), which opened to vent gas to the atmosphere at a rate of roughly 2.8 mmcf/d. the vent remained open for 4 hours and 23 minutes before the on‑call supervisor arrived, identified the mis‑set isolation valve, and manually returned it to the fully open position, allowing the psv to reseat. the incident resulted in an estimated release of 6 mmcf of natural gas and prompted a revision of the valve status verification procedure, adding a secondary visual confirmation step for all manual overrides.

on 16 august 2024, western midstream operators were conducting a routine pigging operation on the 30‑inch, 20‑year‑old carbon steel mainline (schedule 80, 1 200 psi design pressure) that transports 850 mmscfd of sweet natural gas from the south field to the central processing hub. the crew had scheduled a downstream isolation of valve‑45‑c, but due to a miscommunication the field technician mistakenly opened valve‑45‑c instead of closing it while the pig was in transit. as the pig passed the valve, the premature opening allowed gas to surge into a dead‑leg section that had been depressurized for maintenance. the sudden pressure differential caused a rupture at a corroded weld joint near the valve, releasing approximately 3 500 mcf of gas into the surrounding wetlands. the incident was reported to the national response center (report #2127469) at 14:22 local time. emergency response teams sealed the leak and evacuated the immediate area. the pipeline segment was shut down, the damaged pipe and valve assembly were removed, and a new 30‑inch seamless pipe with upgraded corrosion‑inhibitor coating was installed. after hydrostatic testing to 1 500 psi, the line was re‑pressurized and returned to service on 22 september 2024 at 09:15 cst. a root‑cause investigation concluded that the operator failed to verify valve position in the control log before initiating the pig run, prompting a revision of standard operating procedures and additional training on valve‑status verification.

on september 3, 2024 at approximately 08:45 a.m. central time, the oak ridge compression station on the northern loop of the transtar 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line was performing a scheduled pressure relief valve test. the line, which normally operates at 840 psi and transports dry natural gas at a flow rate of 1.2 billion ft³/d, had been placed in manual mode after a recent compressor trip. the relief valve (tag rlv‑112) was manually opened to verify spring set‑point compliance, but the operator inadvertently left the valve fully open for the duration of the test instead of the prescribed 10‑second open interval. as a result, gas escaped from the downstream side of the valve into the ambient environment for an estimated 4 minutes, creating a vapor cloud that drifted toward the nearby maintenance yard. two maintenance technicians, who were unaware of the open valve, entered the yard to perform routine valve lubrication and were exposed to the gas cloud; one suffered a brief loss of consciousness and was treated on‑site, while the other experienced minor respiratory irritation. emergency response teams were dispatched within 12 minutes, the valve was closed, and the gas release was contained. a post‑incident review identified the root cause as failure to follow the standard operating procedure for relief valve testing, specifically the omission of the timed closure step. corrective actions include retraining all station personnel on valve test protocols, installing a timed interlock on rlv‑112, and updating the station’s operating checklist to require a second‑operator verification before manual valve operations. the line was returned to normal service at 13:20 after a pressure verification test confirmed system integrity.

on monday, may 6, 2023 at 1430 hrs, transco inc. initiated a restart of the mainline 24-in. carbon steel pipeline (schedule 40) after scheduled maintenance on the river bend station. the control room operator entered the restart sequence but omitted the step to isolate the upstream pressure reducing valve (prv) that had been left open for pigging. as a result, when the compressor station 5 increased line pressure to 720 psig, the downstream segment, rated for a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 650 psig, experienced an immediate pressure surge. the automatic shut‑in valve (asv) at milepost 102 failed to close due to a mis‑set setpoint, and gas began venting through a 4‑inch bypass line that was not equipped with a flare. approximately 12 mmcf of natural gas escaped to the atmosphere over a 45‑minute period before the field crew manually blocked the line at the nearest isolation valve. no injuries were reported, but the release triggered a reportable event to the state and phmsa. post‑incident review identified that the operator had not followed the revised start‑up checklist and that the asv setpoint had not been updated after the recent pressure rating change. corrective actions include retraining, checklist revision, and recalibration of the asv.

at 07:45 on 22 august 2024, western energy services (wes) control room received a low‑pressure alarm on the 30‑inch mainline feeding the canyon compression station (csp). the alarm triggered an automatic shutdown (as) at 08:02. field operators arrived at 08:15 and initiated the manual isolation procedure. during the isolation, the crew mistakenly opened the bypass valve b‑42 instead of the designated isolation valve i‑42, allowing gas from the downstream 24‑inch line to flow back into the mainline. the unintended flow caused the station’s relief valve to lift at 08:38, venting approximately 1,200 mcf of natural gas to atmosphere. the as sequence was prolonged because the operators also left the station loading valve in the “open‑load” position, contrary to standard operating procedure. the incident was reported to the nrc at 09:30. investigation revealed that the valve operator panels had been recently upgraded, but the new panel layout was not reflected in the station’s lockout‑tagout checklist, leading the crew to select the wrong valve identifier. corrective actions included revising the checklist to reference the updated panel schematics, conducting a refresher training on valve identification for all csp personnel, and implementing a peer‑verification step for all manual isolation actions.

on april 12, 2024 a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line at the milford compressor station was being returned to service after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the line had a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 720 psig and was normally pressurized to 680 psig during normal operation. the start‑up procedure required the isolation of the downstream 12‑inch relief valve (set at 560 psig) and the verification of the bypass block valve position before re‑pressurizing the main line. due to a misinterpretation of the written procedure, the control operator closed the bypass block valve but failed to confirm that the relief valve had been fully blocked in. after the compressor ramped up, the line pressure rose to 690 psig, exceeding the relief valve’s set point. the relief valve opened unintentionally, releasing an estimated 4.3 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding area for approximately 45 minutes before the field crew arrived at 02:15 am and manually shut it in. the release triggered a state report and a phmsa 30‑day filing. investigation later determined the root cause to be inadequate procedural adherence and insufficient verification steps in the return‑to‑service checklist. corrective actions included revising the checklist, adding a mandatory double‑sign‑off for relief valve isolation, and conducting refresher training for all shift supervisors.

at approximately 09:17 a.m. cdt on april 3, 2024, the midwest gas transmission company's oak ridge compressor station experienced an unintended gas release during a routine start‑up of unit 2. the unit, a 70 mw centrifugal compressor equipped with a 36‑inch carbon steel suction line rated to 1 500 psig, was being brought online after a scheduled shutdown for valve maintenance. the start‑up procedure called for the manual isolation valve m‑sv‑014 on the discharge line to remain closed until the automatic shut‑off valve (aso‑dv‑021) had verified pressure stabilization. however, the on‑duty operator, attempting to expedite the process, manually opened m‑sv‑014 before pressure reached the required 800 psig. this premature opening caused the discharge line to depressurize rapidly, resulting in a vent of approximately 1 200 standard cubic feet per minute of natural gas through a pressure relief vent on the downstream 30‑inch pipeline. the emergency shutdown system (esd) activated within seconds, isolating the affected segment. investigation revealed that the operator misinterpreted the control panel readout, and the lockout‑tagout (loto) procedure for the manual valve had not been properly enforced after the previous maintenance. the company is revising start‑up checklists, reinforcing training on pressure set‑points, and updating the loto protocol to include a secondary verification step for all manual discharge valves.

on friday, september 13, 2024, at approximately 14:27 hrs, a pacific gas transmission crew was performing a scheduled pigging operation on a 30‑in. api 5l sch 40 pipeline carrying 720 psig of sour natural gas from the northfield processing facility to the south ridge delivery point. the work plan called for a two‑stage pressure reduction: first isolate the line at valve‑45 using a manual ball valve, then depressurize to 150 psig before inserting the pig. however, the field supervisor instructed the operator to keep valve‑45 open to maintain line pressure for downstream customers, contrary to the written procedure. as a result, the line was only partially bled, leaving residual pressure of about 420 psig when the pig launcher was actuated. the pig struck a partially closed gate valve‑38 downstream, causing the valve stem to shear off and the pipe to rupture at a nearby girth weld. a sudden release of high‑energy gas created a jet that ignited when it contacted a hot work torch being used for a nearby valve repair. the flame traveled back into the trench, causing a fire that burned three crew members; two required hospitalization for second‑degree burns, and one suffered a minor inhalation injury. emergency shutdown of the mainline was initiated by the control room, isolating the segment within 3 minutes. fire crews arrived within 10 minutes, extinguished the fire, and performed a controlled vent of the remaining gas. the incident resulted in a loss of service for 12 hours and estimated repair costs exceeding $2.3 million.

a maintenance crew was conducting a pigging run on a 30‑inch, api 5l carbon steel transmission line operating at 1150 psi downstream of a city plant. the pig launcher was set to a 5 psi differential pressure relief, but the operator mistakenly entered 15 psi into the control panel while configuring the pig tracker. after the pig entered the line, the launcher valve was opened wider than intended, causing a rapid pressure surge that pushed the pig past the downstream pressure regulator. the surge increased the line pressure to approximately 1380 psi, exceeding the pipe’s design limit of 1300 psi. within seconds, a section of the 24‑inch branch at the 12‑mile marker ruptured, releasing a high‑velocity jet of natural gas into a low‑lying valley. the gas ignited when it contacted a nearby power line, resulting in a flash fire that damaged a maintenance trailer and caused minor injuries to two technicians. post‑incident analysis revealed that the operator had not verified the differential pressure setting on the handheld gauge and had overridden the automatic shut‑off without confirming real‑time pressure readings. corrective actions now require a dual‑verification step for all pressure entry fields and mandatory use of calibrated pressure transducers during pigging operations.

on april 3, 2024 at approximately 09:14 the western ridge compressor station experienced an uncontrolled release of natural gas while operators were executing a routine start‑up of unit 2. the station’s 12‑inch carbon steel mainline, rated for 1,200 psi, had been isolated for maintenance, and a 10‑inch tie‑in line was scheduled to be depressurized and purged prior to re‑pressurization. due to an incorrect valve sequencing, the isolation valve on the mainline was reopened before the purge valve on the tie‑in line had fully closed, allowing residual air to be forced into the freshly pressurized gas stream. the combination of elevated temperature from compression and the remaining oxygen caused a flash fire at the downstream pressure regulator, releasing an estimated 1,200 mcf of gas. two employees sustained second‑degree burns, and the incident triggered an automatic shutdown and fire‑gate activation. an internal investigation determined the root cause to be deviation from the approved start‑up procedure and lack of verification of valve positions. corrective actions included revising the start‑up checklist, retraining personnel on lockout/tagout practices, and installing a valve position interlock to prevent premature opening of isolation valves. the station returned to normal operation on may 15, 2024 after completion of all remedial measures.

on march 4, 2024, at approximately 08:37, a crew from southern midstream was conducting a scheduled valve turn‑down on the 24‑inch x70 carbon steel mainline (api 5l gr b) near the marshall county pump station, texas. the line was operating at a normal working pressure of 960 psig and was to be isolated for a downstream pressure‑test. the standard operating procedure required the line to be depressurized to 150 psig, a lockout/tagout applied to valve 12‑b, and a hydrostatic test performed on the downstream segment. instead, the operator opened valve 12‑b while the line was still at 850 psig, bypassing the required depressurization step. the sudden pressure surge caused a catastrophic rupture of a nearby 12‑inch branch connection that had been welded for a temporary bypass. a 1‑inch gash was torn in the pipe wall, releasing a high‑velocity jet of natural gas that ignited when it contacted a nearby hot‑work torch used for a separate maintenance task. two crew members sustained second‑degree burns and were transported to the regional medical center; a third worker suffered a concussion from the blast. the post‑incident investigation determined the primary cause to be non‑adherence to the valve turn‑down and lockout procedures, compounded by insufficient verification of line pressure before valve actuation. the line was shut down for repairs and returned to service on march 18, 2024.

on september 5, 2023 at approximately 04:27 am cdt the midwest 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (mr 84231) experienced an unexpected emergency shutdown (esd) while the line was being cycled from idle to full load. the line normally operates at a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 850 psi, with a design limit of 1150 psi. during the start‑up sequence, the operator manually opened the upstream 30‑inch block valve (bv‑12) and the downstream 36‑inch control valve (cv‑7) without confirming the position of the auxiliary gas‑supply valve (agv‑3). agv‑3 had been left in the open position from a prior maintenance activity intended to purge the line, allowing additional supply gas to enter the system. as a result, line pressure rose to 940 psi, exceeding the maop by 10 %. the high‑pressure alarm triggered the esd system, closing the 30‑inch emergency shutdown valve (esd‑30) and venting gas to the nearby relief vent. subsequent investigation showed no equipment failure; the fire detector and pressure transmitters functioned correctly. the root cause was determined to be the failure to reset agv‑3 to the closed position after maintenance, a procedural oversight that will be addressed with revised lock‑out/tag‑out procedures and additional operator training.

on september 12, 2025 at approximately 09:45 cdt a maintenance crew was performing a scheduled valve replacement on the midsouth mainline, a 24‑inch x70 api 5l carbon steel pipeline operating at a design pressure of 850 psig near columbus, missouri. the line was isolated using the upstream isolation valve (tag 13‑01) and downstream isolation valve (tag 13‑02) which were both confirmed closed on the handheld pressure transducer. after the old valve was removed, a temporary bypass line consisting of a 10‑inch steel pipe and two 2‑inch ball valves was installed to allow pigging operations to continue. the control system was inadvertently set to keep the downstream isolation valve open, and the bypass line was not pressure‑tested before restarting flow. at 10:12 cdt the mainline pump started, raising pressure to 780 psig. the 2‑inch ball valve on the bypass failed under the unexpected load, causing a rapid release of natural gas into the surrounding area. the gas vented through the nearest vent stack and ignited when it reached the hot exhaust manifold, producing a brief flame front. emergency shutdown was initiated at 10:15 cdt, isolating the line and extinguishing the fire. the incident resulted in a release of approximately 4.7 mmcf of gas and minor injuries to two crew members from the blast overpressure. repairs included replacing the failed ball valve, resealing the isolation valves, and conducting a full hydrostatic test before returning the line to service at 16:30 cdt.

on april 3, 2022, the hillcrest gathering system experienced an unplanned release of natural gas from a 24‑inch carbon steel main that transports gas from the riverbend field to the processing plant. the main is normally operated at 1,200 psig and is equipped with a series‑rated valve at milepost 12.5 that is controlled by the central control room via scada. during a scheduled pressure reduction to 950 psig, the control operator entered the wrong setpoint for the valve actuator and inadvertently commanded a slow open instead of a close. the valve remained partially open for approximately 45 minutes, allowing gas to escape through a 0.5‑inch leak that had developed at a previous repair weld that was not fully re‑qualified. field personnel first noticed a faint odor at the south‑east perimeter of the valve house at 14:22 local time and reported it to the control room. the control room operator, believing the valve had been fully closed, did not dispatch a response team. by the time the leak was visually confirmed at 14:58, the pressure in the main had dropped to 820 psig and an estimated 2,800 mcf of gas had been released to the atmosphere. after the incident, the company revised the valve‑actuation procedure to require a dual‑confirmation step in scada and instituted a mandatory on‑site visual verification for any pressure‑setpoint changes exceeding 150 psig. additional training on setpoint entry and a lock‑out verification for critical valves were also implemented.

during a scheduled integrity test on the 24‑inch, 970 psi carbon steel transmission line (segment a‑12) near the hillcrest regulator, the field crew was instructed to isolate the line by closing the upstream mainline isolation valve (mliv‑01) and opening the downstream test bypass valve (tbv‑07). the crew used a hand‑held portable controller to energize the tbv‑07 solenoid, believing the mliv‑01 was fully seated. however, a recent maintenance log indicated that mliv‑01 had been replaced with a new double‑block‑and‑bleed valve but the position indicator on the hmi had not been calibrated. the crew did not verify the valve position on the control panel and instead relied on a visual check of the valve stem, which appeared closed but was actually 15 % open. when the test pressure was increased to 850 psi, gas began leaking from the junction between tbv‑07 and the downstream pig launcher, creating a venting plume that triggered the emergency shutdown (esd) system. the esd valve failed to close because the power‑gas supply to the esd network was offline for a scheduled upgrade, a condition not communicated to the crew. the leak persisted for 12 minutes before the manual shut‑in was performed, releasing approximately 3,200 mcf of natural gas and causing a brief service interruption to two downstream customers. investigation highlighted the lack of verification of valve position on the hmi and the failure to coordinate the power‑gas outage with field operations.
