on september 3, 2022 at approximately 07:45 a.m. central pipeline corporation (cpc) began the routine restart of its 24‑inch carbon steel mainline (line 12) located near oak hill, texas. the line operates at a design pressure of 825 psig and transports dry natural gas from the western gathering system to the downstream processing plant. during the start‑up sequence, the control room operator manually opened the upstream isolation valve (valve a‑3) and the downstream relief valve (valve b‑7) without first confirming that the automated lock‑out‑tag‑out (loto) procedure for the recent valve replacement had been completed. as a result, the newly installed motor‑operated valve on the downstream side was still in a partially open position from its previous maintenance check. when the compressor station brought the line up to pressure, gas surged through the partially closed valve, causing an over‑pressurization condition that triggered the emergency shutdown (esd) system at 08:02 a.m. the esd isolated the line, but the upstream valve remained open, allowing high‑pressure gas to escape through a vent stack, releasing an estimated 2,400 mcf of gas to the atmosphere before the vent was capped at 08:15 a.m. investigation determined that the operator had bypassed the required management‑of‑change (moc) review and failed to verify valve position after maintenance. cpc has since revised its start‑up checklist, reinforced moc training, and updated the control system interlocks to prevent manual valve actuation until a confirmed closed status is logged.

on july 13, 2025 a tgs transmission line operating at 720 psi experienced a rapid depressurization event near the oak ridge compression station in kentucky. the incident originated when the field operator manually opened a 24‑inch low‑pressure bleed valve to purge air from a downstream pig launcher without first confirming that the isolation block valve on line‑c had been fully closed. the block valve was left partially open due to a mis‑read of the digital position indicator, allowing high‑pressure gas to flow through the bleed line. when the bleed valve was opened, approximately 3,200 mcf of natural gas escaped through the vent stack, igniting after contacting a hot surface on the nearby flare header. the flame was extinguished by the automatic shut‑down system within 45 seconds, but two technicians in the vicinity sustained second‑degree burns and were transported to the regional medical center. the incident prompted an immediate shutdown of the 12‑inch downstream line for inspection. investigation revealed that the operator had not followed the revised standard operating procedure that requires a visual confirmation of block‑valve closure before any bleed operation. corrective actions include retraining on valve‑position verification and updating the control system to provide an audible alarm when a high‑pressure line is open while a bleed valve is activated.

on september 3, 2025 at approximately 0415 hrs the western field gathering station, operated by frontier energy, observed a sudden pressure drop on the 30‑in, 20‑psi rated carbon steel main feeding the raptor processing unit. the station supervisor instructed the control room operator to manually close the upstream isolation valve (isolation valve‑12) using the handheld hydraulic wrench, bypassing the automated valve control sequence. the operator failed to verify valve seat integrity and did not log the manual actuation per standard operating procedure. after 20 minutes the valve was reopened without conducting a pressure test, and gas flow resumed at 850 psi, exceeding the design rating of the downstream 24‑in, 600‑psi service line. within five minutes a loud “pop” was heard and a 12‑in split occurred at a welded junction near milepost 142.5, releasing approximately 4500 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding prairie. emergency shutdown was initiated at 0435 hrs, and the area was evacuated. first‑responders arrived at 0440 hrs; no injuries were reported. the incident investigation determined that the manual closure and premature reopening of isolation valve‑12, without required verification and documentation, directly led to over‑pressurization and the pipe rupture. corrective actions include retraining on valve lock‑out procedures and reinforcement of electronic interlock safeguards.

on friday, september 13, 2022, at 0830 hours, the western interconnect pipeline operating company (wipoc) received a call from the field crew at the marlboro valve station reporting an unexpected pressure rise. the crew had been performing a scheduled pigging operation on a 24‑inch, api 5l x80 carbon steel transmission line that transports 720 psig natural gas from the north field to the downstream distribution network. after the pig passed the mainline, the operator manually opened the isolation valve 12‑b (a 12‑inch full‑port gate valve) to re‑establish flow without first verifying that the downstream block valve 12‑a was fully open and that the pressure relief system was armed. the valve was opened to 70 % travel while the unit pressure transducer still displayed 530 psig, causing a rapid pressure surge to 820 psig downstream of the station. the surge forced the relief valve on the downstream side to lift, releasing approximately 150 scfd of gas into the ambient atmosphere for about three minutes before the automatic shutdown sequence engaged. one crew member sustained a minor hearing injury from the loud vent noise; the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 2245789) and the state oil and gas commission. emergency services, the local fire department, and the media (local tv) were notified on‑site. the leak was isolated at 0905 hours, and repairs to the mis‑operated isolation valve and the relief valve were completed by 1210 hours. the investigation identified a lack of lockout‑tagout procedure and failure to follow the standard operating protocol for valve sequencing as the primary contributors.

at approximately 02:45 am on september 14, 2025, a field operator at midwest transmission services (mts) initiated a restart of the mainline pump station 7b after a scheduled maintenance outage. the pump, a 1500 hp vertical turbine, was brought online without verifying that the downstream isolation valve 12‑c had been fully closed. at 02:58 am the isolation valve was observed to be partially open, allowing gas to flow into the 24‑inch carbon‑steel mainline that was still depressurized from the outage. the sudden influx raised line pressure from 0 to 740 psig within seconds, exceeding the design limit of 720 psig. the over‑pressurization caused a longitudinal crack to develop near the 5‑mile marker, resulting in a release of approximately 850 mcf of natural gas that ignited after a nearby lightning strike. emergency response teams evacuated the area, sealed the leak with a quick‑connect clamp, and vented the remaining gas. a post‑incident investigation determined that the operator had skipped the required lock‑out/tag‑out verification step in the restart checklist and had not consulted the real‑time pressure display before energizing the pump. mts revised its standard operating procedures to require a secondary electronic confirmation of valve position and added a mandatory pause of five minutes with pressure monitoring before any pump start‑up. training modules were updated to emphasize lock‑out/tag‑out compliance for all pump station personnel.

on september 14, 2025, at approximately 08:46 mt, a rupture and subsequent fire occurred on the western interconnect 12″ carbon‑steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the river bend tie‑in station, located about 3.2 mi southeast of blackrock, wy. the line had been isolated for a scheduled valve replacement on segment 4b, and after the work crew removed the old 24‑in in‑line isolation valve, the system was to be repressurized using the mainline packer. the operations technician manually opened the downstream block valve (bv‑12) before the packer pressure had been equalized, resulting in a rapid pressure differential of roughly 950 psi (design pressure 800 psi, surge pressure 1200 psi) across the newly installed valve. the sudden surge caused a tensile overload at a previously repaired girth weld near milepost 12.4, leading to a circumferential rupture and immediate release of high‑pressure natural gas. an ignition source from a nearby hot‑work torch ignited the escaping mixture, producing a fireball that burned for approximately three minutes before emergency shutdown systems engaged. one crew member sustained second‑degree burns and was transported to the regional medical center; the incident caused a temporary loss of service to 2,300 customers downstream. post‑incident investigation cited the premature valve actuation and inadequate verification of pressure equalization as the primary operational errors.

pipeline segment 14, a 20" api 5l carbon steel pipe installed in 1992, rated for 900 psi, was operating at 720 psi when maintenance crews began a pressure reduction test on july 14, 2023. the procedure called for closing valve 14‑22‑a on the east side, then opening the downstream bleed valve 14‑22‑b to vent gas while the main line pressure was stepped down. the crew mistakenly opened valve 14‑22‑c, a 6" isolation valve on a parallel service line, instead of the intended 14‑22‑b. this caused a sudden pressure differential that forced gas from the main line into the service line, exceeding its 500‑psi design limit. within seconds a loud pop was heard and a flash fire erupted at the valve rack, igniting a nearby fuel oil hose. two technicians received second‑degree burns to their arms and a third‑degree burn to one forearm; both were treated on‑site and later transported to a regional burn center. the incident was reported to the operator and phmsa, and an investigation revealed that the valve tag plates were outdated and the crew relied on handwritten notes, leading to the incorrect valve operation. corrective actions included updating the valve identification system, retraining staff on isolation procedures, and revising the pressure reduction work plan.

on july 13, 2024 at approximately 14:20 local time, the control room at the riverbend gas processing facility observed a gradual rise in downstream pressure on the 30‑inch carbon steel mainline feeding the eastbound distribution network. the scheduled increase in gas injection from the 24‑inch upstream gathering line was initiated to meet a peak demand contract. the operations engineer entered a manual set point of 950 psig for the inlet regulator, exceeding the line’s maximum allowable operating pressure of 900 psig. because the pressure relief valve at the downstream pigging station was still set to its default 880 psig opening pressure, the valve never opened. at 14:35 the supervisory control system generated a high‑pressure alarm, but the engineer, assuming a sensor glitch, acknowledged the alarm and delayed corrective action. by 14:50 the pressure reached 1,018 psig, causing the low‑temperature vent valve on the 30‑inch line to lift, releasing an estimated 3,200 mcf of natural gas to atmosphere over the next 12 minutes. field crews arrived at 15:05, manually closed the vent valve, and initiated an emergency depressurization. post‑incident analysis identified the incorrect manual set point entry and failure to verify relief valve settings as the primary contributors. corrective actions include revising the standard operating procedure for pressure set point changes and re‑calibrating all downstream relief devices.

on august 14, 2022 at approximately 03:12 am local time, a maintenance crew was performing a pressure test on a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the northfield compression station. the line was rated for 1500 psig and contained dry natural gas at 1450 psig. the crew intended to isolate a 12‑inch pig trap downstream by closing the pig‑trap isolation valve (tag p‑124) and then opening a bypass valve (tag b‑87) to reroute flow through a temporary test loop. due to a mis‑read of the valve position indicator, the operator opened the bypass valve while the pig‑trap isolation valve remained partially open. this resulted in an uncontrolled surge of gas into the test loop, exceeding the design pressure of the temporary steel fittings (rated 1200 psig). a 4‑inch relief valve on the loop lifted at 1300 psig, but the sudden release caused a high‑velocity jet to escape from a loosened coupling, striking a technician standing on the platform. the technician sustained second‑degree burns to the forearm and was evacuated to the nearest hospital. the incident was halted after the mainline was shut down and the bypass valve was closed. post‑incident investigation revealed the error stemmed from an outdated valve‑status board and lack of a lock‑out/tag‑out procedure for the isolation valve. the operator’s workstation software has been updated to display real‑time valve positions, a lock‑out/tag‑out protocol has been instituted for all isolation points, and the temporary test loop fittings have been replaced with components rated for the full line pressure. training sessions on valve‑operation sequencing are being conducted for all field personnel.

on september 3, 2022 at 0837 local time, a utility technician from western pipelines was conducting a routine pressure test on a 20‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x65) that transports natural gas at a design pressure of 900 psi near the hillcrest interchange. the test procedure called for increasing the downstream regulator set point from 650 psi to 720 psi while monitoring the isolation valve. the technician mistakenly entered the new set point on the upstream station controller instead of the downstream regulator, raising the upstream pressure to 820 psi. this caused the automatic shut‑in valve to open partially, and the 12‑inch bypass line, which was still connected to the high‑pressure side, released gas into the surrounding easement. the vent persisted for approximately 12 minutes before the operator recognized the discrepancy, isolated the line, and closed the bypass. emergency services were notified at 0845, and a 3‑person fire crew established a hot‑work exclusion zone. no injuries or ignition occurred, but an estimated 18 mmcf of gas escaped, exceeding the dot reporting threshold. western pipelines filed a 24‑hour report with the ferc, conducted a root‑cause analysis, and instituted a dual‑confirmation protocol for all set‑point changes. corrective training for all field personnel was completed by october 15, 2022.

on july 14, 2022 at approximately 04:12 a.m., a routine maintenance crew arrived at the silver creek city gate station in columbia county, ne. the station feeds a 24‑in. dsu carbon steel transmission line that normally operates at 560 psig delivering 22,000 dekatherms per hour. at 04:18 the crew began a scheduled isolation of the primary meter run to perform a pressure‑drop test on the downstream regulator set. the technician manually closed the primary run valve (prv‑03) and opened the bypass valve to maintain service. after completing the test at 04:33 the technician failed to close the bypass and, instead of re‑opening prv‑03, he mistakenly left the bypass fully open while simultaneously closing the auxiliary isolation valve that isolates the downstream line. this sequence caused the line to run unattended with the bypass in service, dropping the station outlet pressure to 210 psig, well below the under‑pressure protection set point of 250 psig. the protection system automatically shut the downstream regulator, resulting in a loss of gas service to the city of silver creek. at 04:36 a high‑low pressure alarm sounded; operators attempted to restore flow but could not re‑open the primary valve because it remained locked in the closed position. the incident was reported internally at 05:10 and subsequently notified to the state pipeline safety commission and the national response center at 05:45. corrective actions include revising lockout/tagout procedures and implementing a dual‑confirmation checklist for valve isolation steps.

on october 12, 2024, at approximately 06:42 am central time, a release event occurred on the western midland transmission system (wmts) while a routine line‑swap was being performed on the 30‑inch, carbon steel segment spanning the high plains interconnect. the work crew had been instructed to isolate valve b‑2155 and open valve b‑2158 to divert flow to the parallel 24‑inch loop. due to an oversight, valve b‑2155 remained fully open and valve b‑2158 was only partially opened (≈30 %). as a result, the flow rate in the 30‑inch line spiked to 2 500 mmcf/d, raising the pipeline inlet pressure from its normal 720 psig to 815 psig, exceeding the maop of 800 psig. at 06:48 am the high‑pressure relief valve on the 30‑inch suction header lifted (set point 800 psig), venting approximately 1 200 mcf of gas to the atmosphere over the next ten minutes. the downstream pressure reduction triggered a secondary relief valve on the 24‑inch line (set point 650 psig) at 06:55 am, releasing an additional 850 mcf. emergency response was initiated at 07:03 am, and the control center isolated the affected segment by closing valve b‑2162. investigations later determined the incident stemmed from the operator’s failure to verify valve positions during the line‑swap pre‑job checklist and an ambiguous work instruction that did not require a second visual confirmation. corrective actions included revising the line‑swap procedure to require dual‑operator verification of all valve statuses, retraining crew members on the updated checklist, and installing a lock‑out tag‑out device on valve b‑2155 during future swaps. the total gas loss was estimated at 2 050 mcf, surpassing the 3 000 mcf reporting threshold, and a phmsa 191.25(b) report was filed.

on september 14, 2023 at approximately 03:45 a.m. a field crew from western pipelines was performing a scheduled depressurization of a 24‑inch, 75 psi carbon steel transmission line (segment id wp‑12‑b) to allow installation of a new pressure regulator station. the crew manually opened isolation valve iv‑2143 upstream of the regulator without first confirming the downstream block valve bv‑5678 was fully closed. the block valve had been left in a partially open position from a previous maintenance activity, resulting in residual pressure of 42 psi remaining in the line. when the crew released the isolation valve, gas escaped through a vent line that was only rated for 10 psi, creating a vapor cloud that ignited when a nearby hot‑work torch was used for pipe coating preparation. the incident caused a flash fire, minor injuries to two crew members, and a temporary loss of service for 3 hours. investigation determined the root cause was a failure to follow the standard operating procedure for sequential valve isolation and to verify valve positions via the control system read‑back. corrective actions included revising the depressurization checklist, adding a mandatory electronic lockout confirmation for block valves, and conducting a refresher training on valve sequencing for all operations personnel.

on august 14, 2025, at approximately 07:45 cdt, the west ridge compressor station was undergoing a routine start‑up after a planned maintenance outage. the station operator manually opened the low‑pressure suction governor valve (lp‑gv‑214) to initiate the compressor start‑up sequence, but inadvertently bypassed the interlock that requires the downstream suction pressure transmitter (pt‑305) to be in the ready state. as a result, the compressor reached a surge pressure of 1,250 psig, exceeding the design limit of 1,150 psig for the 30‑inch carbon steel suction line. the surge caused the suction line’s pressure relief valve (prv‑07) to lift, releasing approximately 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere through the vent stack. the operator noticed the high‑pressure alarm, shut down the compressor, and isolated the suction line. emergency response was dispatched at 08:12 cdt and arrived on site at 08:46 cdt. an investigation later revealed that the operator had not updated the start‑up procedure after a recent modification to the pressure control logic, which now required a digital lockout that was still active. corrective actions included revising the standard operating procedure, retraining all start‑up personnel on the new lockout requirements, and implementing a software check that prevents manual valve opening when the interlock is engaged.

on monday, september 9, 2024, at approximately 14:27 hrs, operators at the riverbend gathering station initiated startup of the 24‑inch api 5l x65 transmission line after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the procedure required a staged purge of air from the line using three portable air‑movers rated at 250 cfm each, followed by a gradual re‑pressurization to 1200 psig with natural gas from the downstream metering skid. during the purge, valve v‑23, a 24‑inch gate valve controlling flow to the mainline, was mistakenly left in the partially‑open position from a prior stem‑seal replacement, a condition not recorded in the clearance checklist. consequently, when v‑45—a 20‑inch control valve upstream of v‑23—was opened to admit gas, the flow was forced through the restricted opening of v‑23, creating a localized pressure surge of approximately 1850 psig, well above the design limit of 1500 psig for the pipe segment. the over‑pressure caused a rapid rupture of the pipe near the v‑23 flange, releasing an estimated 1,800 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding low‑lying terrain. the gas cloud ignited when it encountered a spark from a nearby diesel generator that had been inadvertently left running. the resulting fire damaged the station control building and caused two personnel injuries, one requiring hospitalization. post‑incident investigation identified the failure to verify valve positions and the omission of the valve‑status entry in the electronic work permit as the primary operational errors. corrective actions include revising the startup checklist, implementing automated valve‑position monitoring, and retraining all shift supervisors on clearance documentation compliance.

on april 22, 2024 at approximately 06:45 local time, the river bend transmission line was being depressurized for a scheduled valve replacement at station 12b. the line, an 18‑inch carbon steel pipe installed in 1978 with a maximum allowable operating pressure of 960 psi, was operating at 720 psi. the crew initiated the purge using nitrogen, but inadvertently opened the main isolation valve on the west‑bound feeder before the nitrogen supply had been fully established. as a result, high‑pressure natural gas at 720 psi surged into the line, displacing the nitrogen and creating a rapid pressure rise to 840 psi. the pressure exceeded the temporary bypass valve rating, causing the valve seat to lift and release a jet of gas into the adjacent yard. three workers in the vicinity were exposed to the gas flash; one suffered second‑degree burns to the forearms, and another experienced a panic‑induced asthma episode. emergency shut‑down valves were manually engaged at 06:48, and the line was isolated. after a thorough inspection, the compromised bypass valve was replaced and the isolation procedure was revised to require a confirmed nitrogen flow reading before opening any main line valves. service was restored on may 2, 2024.

may 3, 2022, at 06:12 a.m., the control room at the east ridge compression station observed a rise in line pressure on the 24‑inch mainline feeding the mid‑state delivery system. the downstream delivery pressure was setpoint at 720 psig, but the station’s supervisory control system displayed a pressure of 782 psig. in an effort to quickly reduce the pressure, the operator manually entered a turbine speed reduction command intended for the 4‑inch bypass line, but inadvertently applied the command to the primary 24‑inch turbine. this caused the main turbine to drop from 12,500 rpm to 9,800 rpm within seconds, resulting in a rapid pressure surge downstream. the surge triggered the glenwood relief valve (rated 25 mmcf/d at 795 psig) to open at 794 psig, releasing gas into the atmosphere for approximately 7 minutes before the valve automatically reseated at 782 psig. field personnel arrived on scene at 06:25 a.m. and manually closed the relief valve at 06:31 a.m. the incident resulted in an estimated 6.2 mmcf of gas released, exceeding the 3 mmcf reporting threshold. an internal investigation later determined the incident was caused by the operator’s incorrect input of the turbine speed command into the wrong control channel.

on august 3, 2022, the riverbend gathering system experienced an unintended release of natural gas at the hillcrest pump station. the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline, rated for 1100 psig, was being operated at a scheduled pressure of 950 psig when the upstream booster compressor was manually set to 1150 psig to compensate for a downstream flow restriction. the field operator failed to update the pump control panel and inadvertently opened the 18‑inch isolation valve downstream of the pressure regulator, allowing the over‑pressurized gas to bypass the regulator and enter the low‑pressure distribution network. the gas escaped through a 4‑inch relief vent stack for approximately 92 minutes before the alarm was acknowledged at 14:07 local time. during the incident, the scada system had generated a warning tag to alert operators to verify valve position after any manual pressure change, but the tag had been cleared during a recent software patch without proper documentation. after the release, the operator manually closed the isolation valve at 15:39 and the system was depressurized to 800 psig. subsequent investigation identified the lack of a lock‑out procedure for manual pressure adjustments and the removal of the scada warning tag as root causes. corrective actions included reinstating the warning tag, implementing a mandatory lock‑out/tag‑out protocol for manual pressure changes, and revising the operator training program to emphasize verification of valve positions after any manual override.

on 06/12/2024 at 07:45 a.m., the 24‑inch mainline feeding the east field was scheduled for a routine pressure increase to accommodate higher demand. the control operator mistakenly entered 1,600 psi as the target set point instead of the approved 1,200 psi. the automated pressure regulator responded by opening the upstream booster pump, and the line pressure climbed to 1,640 psi within eight minutes, exceeding the design limit of 1,550 psi for the carbon‑steel pipe. pressure relief valves on the downstream metering station opened at 1,600 psi, venting natural gas into the surrounding low‑lying area. field personnel observed a hissing sound and reported a gas plume to the control center. the incident command team was alerted, and an emergency shut‑in was initiated; the downstream block valve was closed manually while the upstream booster pump was tripped. the gas release was contained within 12 minutes, but a section of the 24‑inch pipe showed signs of strain and a small leak was detected at a girth weld 0.3 mile downstream of the metering station. the line was isolated, depressurized, and the compromised pipe segment was replaced. the root cause was identified as an incorrect set‑point entry by the operator, and a software lockout was added to prevent future manual overrides beyond the 1,250 psi limit.

on march 3, 2022, a maintenance crew was performing a pressure reduction on a 24‑inch api 5l x65 carbon steel transmission line near the edwards county pump station. the line was operating at 850 psig and was to be isolated for valve replacement on the mainline. at 08:15, technicians opened the upstream isolation valve and began venting to atmosphere using a 2‑inch vent stack rated for 500 psig. the vent stack was installed without a required pressure‑relief snubbing device, and the crew failed to verify the vent stack’s rating against the line pressure. as the pressure dropped, a sudden “pop” was heard and a jet of natural gas erupted from the vent stack, projecting approximately 30 feet downwind. operators on the control room observed a rapid pressure drop to 120 psig on scada, but did not immediately initiate an emergency shut‑in. the gas plume triggered an automatic isolation of the downstream segment at 08:22, and the area was evacuated. two crew members suffered minor injuries from the blast; both were treated on site and released. investigation later determined that the vent stack installation procedure was not followed, the incorrect venting equipment was used, and the required pressure‑relief device was omitted, leading to the uncontrolled release. the line was fully depressurized and repaired, and service was restored on march 5, 2022.

(on october 12, 2023, at approximately 06:45 a.m., a maintenance crew at the riverside compression station began a scheduled restart of the 30‑inch, api 5l x70 carbon steel main after a three‑day outage for valve inspection. the station control system was set to bring the line back to service at a target downstream pressure of 650 psig. the operating procedure required a step‑wise pressure increase, pausing at 550 psig to verify the integrity of the newly installed 24‑inch bypass loop. however, the shift supervisor mistakenly entered “550” as “5500” in the programmable logic controller, causing the compressor to accelerate to 950 psig within minutes. the bypass loop, rated for a maximum operating pressure of 720 psig, was exposed to excessive pressure, resulting in a seam failure at a girth weld near milepost 45.5. gas escaped through the breach, releasing an estimated 9.3 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands before the automatic shut‑in valve finally closed at 07:12 a.m. the release was reported to the state environmental agency and phmsa as a reportable event. investigation later determined the root cause to be incorrect data entry and failure to follow the required pressure verification step in the restart procedure.

at the ridgecrest compression station, operators were preparing for a scheduled hydrostatic test on the 30‑inch mainline (api 5l x80 carbon steel, operating at 1150 psi). the procedure required isolation of the downstream block valve (valve b‑45‑02) and opening of the test isolation valve (valve t‑45‑07). due to a misinterpretation of the work order, the control console was used to open valve t‑45‑07 before valve b‑45‑02 was fully closed. the downstream block valve remained partially seated, allowing gas from the 24‑inch feeder (operating at 1050 psi) to flow into the test section. as the test pump began pressurizing the isolated segment, the unintended flow caused the relief valve on the test manifold (relief‑t‑45‑03, set at 1300 psi) to lift. approximately 4 500 mcf of natural gas escaped through the vent stack before the operator realized the error and manually closed the relief valve at 02:17 a.m. the incident triggered an emergency shutdown, the test was aborted, and the vented volume was reported to the regulatory authority. corrective actions included revising the isolation checklist, adding interlock logic to prevent opening of test valves until block valves confirm closed status, and retraining personnel on procedural sequencing.

on 09/14/2023 at 07:22 am, the field operator at the riverbend compression station initiated a manual start‑up of the 24‑inch mainline suction pump without verifying the upstream isolation valve position. the isolation valve on the southbound feeder line was inadvertently left open, allowing product from the adjacent 20‑inch gathering line to flow into the suction inlet at an unexpected temperature of 140 °f. the pump, rated for 120 °f inlet, experienced a rapid rise in bearing temperature and tripped its high‑temperature shutdown at 07:35 am. meanwhile, the downstream pressure transducer on the 24‑inch discharge header read 1150 psig, exceeding the design limit of 1050 psig, and the automatic relief valve at the downstream metering station began to lift at 07:38 am. the operator, focused on the pump alarm, failed to notice the rising pressure on the control screen and did not close the feeder isolation valve until 07:50 am after a secondary alarm sounded. the delayed isolation caused a brief over‑pressurization event that resulted in a small vent to the atmosphere at the metering station, releasing approximately 15 scf of natural gas. the incident was logged in part e5.f and a corrective action was issued to require a double‑check verification of isolation valve status before any manual pump start‑up.

on june 14, 2025 at 08:42 a.m. central standard time, the midwest north gas transmission facility experienced an unplanned release of natural gas near the hickory ridge metering station. the facility consists of a 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line rated for 720 psi operating pressure, feeding a downstream 24‑inch line through a dual‑block valve assembly. during a scheduled pressure test, the field operator opened the upstream isolation valve (valve‑a) to isolate a 3‑mile section for inspection, but mistakenly left the downstream block valve (valve‑b) closed. after the test, the operator re‑pressurized the upstream line to 650 psi without first opening valve‑b, causing pressure to build in the isolated segment. the built‑up pressure exceeded the design limit of the temporary pig‑in‑place barrier (rated 600 psi) and forced the barrier open, ejecting a 2‑foot section of 6‑inch pigging pipe into the surrounding right‑of‑way. the release was detected by the scada alarm from a sudden drop in downstream flow and a rise in acoustic emission sensors. emergency shutdown procedures were initiated within 25 seconds, and the line was isolated with the emergency shut‑off valve. there were no injuries, but the incident resulted in a loss of product estimated at 4.2 mmcf and required repair of the pig‑in‑place barrier and replacement of the ejected pipe segment. the operator’s procedural checklist was revised to require verification of downstream valve status before re‑pressurization.

at 07:42 am mst on october 3, 2022 the austin‑hutto pipeline mainline (24‑in. carbon steel, design pressure 1500 psi, operating at 820 psi) was scheduled for a pigging run to remove accumulated paraffin. the pig launcher was manually set to a low‑pressure purge of 150 psi, but the field operator mistakenly keyed the pig‑in‑line valve to the high‑pressure service position (800 psi) while the purge was still active. as the pig entered the high‑pressure segment, the sudden pressure jump caused a rapid increase in line pressure to 1050 psi, exceeding the rated limit of the downstream pressure regulator (rated to 950 psi). the regulator failed to close, and the over‑pressurized gas opened a relief valve on the 12‑in. downstream branch, venting natural gas to the atmosphere for approximately 6 minutes before the operator recognized the abnormal pressure reading on the scada display. the venting released an estimated 3.2 mmcf of gas, which was reported to the nrc at 10:15 am mst the same day. corrective actions included retraining all personnel on pig‑launch procedures, installing a lock‑out interlock that prevents high‑service valve actuation during purge, and conducting a pressure‑test of all downstream regulators. a supplemental report was filed on october 7 to amend the initial incident description and to document the lock‑out implementation.

on friday, september 14, 2022, at approximately 0830 hours, the field crew of western midstream began a scheduled maintenance shutdown on a 24‑inch api 5l x70 carbon steel transmission line (maop 800 psi) that was operating at 560 psi transporting dry natural gas from the hillcrest gathering system to the southfield processing facility. the work plan called for a full isolation of the 3‑mile segment between milepost 12.4 and 15.7, followed by a hot‑tapping operation to install a new pressure‑taker valve. the crew mistakenly opened the downstream isolation valve before confirming that the upstream valve had been fully closed and that the line was depressurized. as a result, a sudden surge of gas at 520 psi escaped through a partially opened vent valve that had been left connected to a temporary pig launcher. the gas accumulated in a low‑lying trench where a diesel generator was being pre‑heated. an ignition source from the generator’s exhaust ignited the gas cloud, producing a flash fire that burned three workers; two suffered second‑degree burns to their arms and were transported to the regional burn center, while the third sustained a first‑degree burn to the face. the fire was extinguished by onsite emergency response within ten minutes. the incident was reported to the phmsa, the nrc (incident # 2022‑0187), and the state oil and gas commission. the line was purged, inspected, and returned to service on september 18 after replacement of the vent valve and a revised lock‑out/tag‑out procedure was implemented.

on april 12, 2025, at approximately 07:46 a.m., a crew was performing a hot‑tap on the 24‑inch, carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) at the ridgeview junction in west texas. the line was scheduled to be isolated at 1500 psi and purged with nitrogen to a residual pressure of less than 5 psi before the tap. the isolation valve on the upstream side was manually turned half‑closed by the rig operator, believing the automatic valve had already sealed the line. after confirming nitrogen flow, the operator engaged the tapping hammer and began drilling into the pipe wall. within seconds, a sudden surge of natural gas escaped from the incomplete seal, forcing the nitrogen purge to reverse direction. the escaping gas ignited when the spark generated by the hammer struck a metal fragment, producing a flash fire that singed the operator’s jacket and caused minor burns to a nearby technician. post‑incident analysis revealed that the operator had incorrectly assumed the automated isolation sequence had completed, failed to verify full closure with the pressure gauge, and did not follow the required lock‑out/tag‑out procedure. corrective actions included retraining on valve position verification, reinforcement of lock‑out/tag‑out compliance, and installation of a secondary visual indicator for isolation status.

on april 7, 2022 a scheduled integrity check was performed on the east valley 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the meadow ridge pump station. the line was operating at 950 psig with a flow of 4200 mmscfd. at 08:14 the control system set point for rov‑7423 was changed from 100% open to 0% to initiate a full‑closure test. the operator omitted the required 12‑minute flow‑reduction step, leaving the line at full throughput while the valve began to travel. at 08:18 the valve was 45% closed when a high‑pressure alarm triggered at 1020 psig, exceeding the maop of 1000 psig. the downstream pressure transducer, which had been calibrated six months prior, reported a false low reading, causing the control algorithm to command additional closure. by 08:20 the valve was stuck at 70% open and the upstream pressure spiked to 1085 psig, breaching the over‑pressure protection set point of 1050 psig. an automatic shut‑down valve downstream failed to open due to a missed maintenance check, resulting in a release of approximately 1800 scf of natural gas through a ruptured flange at the 30‑inch segment. emergency response was activated at 08:23, and the incident was reported to the state commission at 09:05. the post‑incident review identified the operator’s deviation from the standard operating procedure and the lack of a real‑time pressure verification step as root causes.

on july 7, 2023, at approximately 1515 hours, a crew from western pipeline services was conducting a scheduled tie‑in of a new 12‑inch carbon steel transmission line to the existing 24‑inch mainline at the pine ridge junction, located near milepost 112.5 in central texas. the tie‑in required the temporary isolation of the mainline using a double block and bleed (dbb) arrangement. the field supervisor instructed the operators to close the upstream block valve (valve a‑12) and depressurize the section before removing the downstream block valve (valve b‑12). however, the operator mistakenly opened valve a‑12 instead of closing it, while valve b‑12 remained fully open. as a result, the mainline pressure of 850 psig was allowed to flow directly into the isolated segment, causing a rapid pressure surge. within seconds, a 1‑inch relief vent on the tie‑in manifold lifted, releasing a visible plume of natural gas. the crew activated the emergency shutdown (esd) at 1520 hours, but the delayed recognition of the valve mis‑positioning caused a 4‑minute exposure. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission at 1545 hours and to the pipeline safety authority at 1550 hours. the post‑incident review identified incorrect valve operation and lack of a verification checklist as the primary root cause.

on 07/04/2022 at 14:20 hrs, the southern pipelines control center initiated a scheduled pressure increase on the 24‑inch carbon steel main that runs from the rutherford gathering station to the eastfield processing plant. the intended operating pressure was to be raised from 720 psig to 750 psig to accommodate a temporary surge in production. however, the field operator at the rutherford station mistakenly entered 790 psig into the manual override panel while confirming the setpoint. the high‑pressure alarm on the scada display was acknowledged as a transient event and the operator cleared it without verifying the actual valve positions. as a result, the upstream isolation valve on the 24‑inch line remained fully open while the downstream pressure reduction valve at the eastfield plant was still set to its normal 730 psig limit. the over‑pressurization caused a 2‑inch polyethylene sleeve on a lateral tee near milepost 112 to fail, releasing approximately 3.8 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands. the leak was discovered when a downstream pressure drop was recorded at 15:05 hrs and a field crew observed a vapor cloud. emergency shutdown was initiated, the damaged sleeve was replaced, and the operator received additional training on manual entry verification procedures.

on june 14, 2025 at 07:23 am cdt, a maintenance crew arrived at the river bend compression station to perform a scheduled vent and bleed of the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline after a pigging run. the crew was instructed to close the upstream isolation valve (tag b‑101) and open the downstream vent valve (tag v‑202) to release residual pressure before removing the pig launcher. the technician mistakenly opened the isolation valve instead of the vent valve, allowing line pressure of approximately 1 450 psi to flow directly into the vent stack. the sudden pressure surge forced the vent stack’s 2‑inch stainless steel relief pipe to rupture, releasing high‑pressure natural gas into the surrounding yard. emergency shutdown was initiated by the control room within 45 seconds, and the automatic block valve downstream (tag b‑303) closed, isolating the segment. the rupture was patched and the vent stack replaced. two crew members sustained minor injuries from the blast wave and were treated on site. investigation revealed the valve tag numbers were reversed on the field panel, leading to the operator’s error. corrective actions include relabeling all valve panels, revising the standard operating procedure to require a double‑check verification, and conducting a refresher training on valve identification for all field personnel.

at 07:45 am on 15 august 2024, the western interregional gas transmission system control center received a low‑pressure alarm on line w‑212, a 30‑in. api‑5l x80 carbon steel pipeline operating at 850 psig. the alarm triggered an automatic shutdown of the upstream regulator station r‑47. an on‑site operator proceeded to isolate the line for maintenance, but inadvertently opened valve v‑3212, a 24‑in. isolation valve on the downstream side, while the regulator remained in a closed “maintenance” position. this created a pressure differential that forced gas to bypass the regulator and flow through an unused bypass loop that had not been purged. the gas entered a 12‑in. vent line terminating at a temporary vent stack that had been removed for welding work two days earlier. as a result, high‑energy natural gas escaped to the atmosphere at an estimated rate of 2,400 mcf/d. the released gas accumulated in a low‑lying ditch, ignited by a static discharge from a nearby diesel‑powered pump, causing a flash fire that burned three crew members, one of whom required hospitalization. after the event, investigators determined that the operator had not consulted the revised bypass‑operation procedure and had failed to verify the valve position against the electronic log. corrective actions included retraining on bypass protocols, updating the standard operating procedure, and implementing a dual‑approval step for any valve changes during maintenance.

on may 5, 2022 the operators at gathering station r-12 were completing a routine pigging operation on the 30‑inch mainline that carries raw natural gas from the shale field to the processing plant. after the pig passed, the crew began repressurizing the line using the 10‑inch loading arm attached to the south side gate valve. the supervisor instructed technician j. williams to close the isolation valve on the north side before opening the loading arm, but he mistakenly thought the valve was already closed and opened the loading arm while the north isolation valve remained open. the line pressure rose quickly to 740 psig, exceeding the design limit of 700 psig for the downstream segment. within minutes a gash appeared at a previously repaired weld on a 24‑inch carbon steel pipe near milepost 12.3, releasing an estimated 5.2 mmscf of gas into the surrounding wetlands. emergency shutdown (esd) was initiated by the control room after the pressure alarm tripped, and the line was isolated by closing the mainline valve and the emergency vent. response crews evacuated the area, installed a temporary blind flange, and later replaced the damaged pipe section and re‑torqued all adjacent flange bolts to meet api 6d specifications. a post‑incident review cited the failure to verify valve position as the primary operational error.

on 3 july 2024 at 06:45 cst a field crew began a planned isolation of the 24‑inch mainline at the midland valve station to perform a pigging operation. the isolation procedure required closing valve a‑101 and opening bypass valve b‑202. the crew consulted the isolation checklist but mistakenly recorded the bypass valve position as “closed” and proceeded to open the downstream isolation valve c‑303 without first opening bypass b‑202. at 07:02 cst the mainline compressor station increased delivery pressure to 720 psig to meet downstream demand, unaware that the bypass remained closed. the closed bypass caused pressure to rise in the isolated segment, exceeding the maop of 690 psig. at 07:09 cst a high‑pressure relief valve on the 24‑inch line (set point 710 psig) lifted, venting natural gas to the flare system. the flare stack ignited and a secondary relief valve on the adjacent 12‑inch service line (set point 650 psig) also opened, releasing gas to the atmosphere for approximately 12 minutes. the crew re‑opened bypass b‑202 at 07:18 cst, isolated the segment, and closed the relief valves. a post‑incident review identified the root cause as failure to follow the isolation checklist and verify valve positions before pressurization, resulting in an inadvertent over‑pressure release and a reportable release of ~4 mcf.

on august 14, 2021 at approximately 07:18 am, a routine restart of the 24‑inch high‑pressure natural gas transmission line on the riverbend compression station, located near springfield, il, resulted in an unplanned release of gas. the line, rated for 1,200 psi and operating at 950 psi, was being brought back online after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the field operator opened the mainline isolation valve (tag b‑12) before confirming that the downstream 30‑inch shut‑off valve (tag c‑07) was fully seated. a pressure differential of 300 psi caused the downstream valve to fail to close completely, allowing gas to vent through a vent stack designed for low‑flow relief. within seconds, a jet of gas ignited when it contacted a nearby hot‑work torch used for a separate welding task, producing a flash fire that burned the operator’s forearm and singed a nearby control panel. emergency shutdown was initiated at 07:22 am, and the fire was extinguished by 07:26 am. the incident investigation determined that the operator’s sequence of valve operations was contrary to the approved start‑up procedure; no equipment malfunction was identified. the company has since revised the start‑up checklist and provided additional hands‑on training for all station personnel.

after routine pressure testing of the 24‑inch, schedule 40 carbon steel main at the midstream processing facility, the operator received a scada alarm indicating a pressure drop from the set point of 950 psi to 820 psi. believing the drop was due to a transient pump start‑up, the technician manually opened the bypass valve (bv‑12) without confirming that the primary pump had reached full speed. the bypass valve was left fully open for approximately five minutes while the primary pump was still throttling down. during this interval the downstream line pressure spiked to 1 120 psi, exceeding the design limit of 1 000 psi. the excessive pressure caused a girth weld failure at the 3‑mile marker, resulting in a 6‑inch rupture that released approximately 340 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding low‑lying terrain. after the incident, investigators found that the operator had not followed the standard operating procedure requiring verification of pump speed and pressure stabilization before bypass actuation. the bypass valve was also found to be incorrectly labeled, contributing to the mis‑operation. corrective actions included re‑training staff on pump‑bypass sequencing, updating valve identification signage, and installing an interlock to prevent manual bypass opening until pump speed is confirmed.

on august 9, 2024 a field operator at the midland east gas compression station began a scheduled restart of compressor c-3 after a routine maintenance shutdown. the unit, a 4‑stage centrifugal compressor rated for 1200 psi inlet pressure, was tied to a 30‑inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line carrying dry natural gas at a nominal flow of 7500 mmscfd. the standard restart procedure required the inlet pressure regulator to be set at 950 psi before the compressor could be brought online. the operator mistakenly set the regulator to 1150 psi, a value reserved for peak summer demand, and failed to verify the setpoint on the handheld digital gauge. within three minutes of startup the compressor surged, increasing line pressure to 1380 psi, exceeding the line’s maximum allowable operating pressure of 1300 psi. the over‑pressurization triggered the high‑pressure safety valve at milepost 12.4, which released approximately 450 mcf of gas to the atmosphere before the valve reseated. alarms sounded, the operator shut down c‑3, and the control room isolated the affected segment. post‑incident review identified the incorrect regulator setpoint and lack of a dual‑verification step as the root causes, leading to an update of the restart checklist and additional training for all station personnel.

on 5 october 2023 at approximately 04:23 utc a maintenance crew was performing a routine pigging operation on the north ridge transmission line (segment b-12, 24‑inch carbon steel, design pressure 1 200 psig) near the hillcrest compression station. the crew isolated the line at valve a‑34 and b‑56, but failed to verify the lock‑out of the downstream control valve c‑9 after completing the pig run. at 04:38 the control system automatically opened valve c‑9 to restart flow, unaware that the line remained partially depressurized from the pigging. gas velocity surged to 3 500 ft/s, exceeding the safe operating limit, and the sudden pressure spike caused a rupture at a corroded girth weld located 0.6 mi downstream of the station. approximately 420 mmcf of natural gas ignited, producing a flame extending 120 ft. the incident triggered an automatic shutdown and was reported to the national response center (incident #2104875). investigation determined the primary cause was the technician’s omission to confirm the valve lock‑out status before re‑pressurization. corrective actions included revising the lock‑out/tag‑out checklist, retraining all field personnel on valve verification procedures, and installing a secondary interlock on valve c‑9 to prevent inadvertent opening during maintenance. the line was repaired and returned to service on 23 november 2023 after hydrostatic testing at 1 300 psig.

on 7 august 2022 at 14:12 local time a maintenance crew was performing a routine pressure test on the 24‑in. carbon steel line feeding the lakeview compression station. the crew was instructed to isolate the line by closing the upstream isolation valve (tag 12‑45) and to open the downstream test valve (tag 12‑52) to vent the segment to the atmospheric vent stack. due to a mis‑read of the valve tag plates, the technician inadvertently opened isolation valve 12‑45 instead of 12‑52, allowing high‑pressure gas at 1,200 psig to flow directly into the vent stack. the control system generated an immediate high‑pressure alarm, but the operator at the control room assumed the alarm was a transient from the pressure test and acknowledged it without dispatching field personnel. the vent remained open for 8 hours, during which approximately 54,000 mcf of natural gas were released to the atmosphere before a field supervisor noticed the discrepancy during a routine walk‑around at 22:15. the vent valve was finally closed, and the line was depressurized. subsequent investigation identified the root cause as incorrect valve operation stemming from inadequate verification of valve identification and a failure to follow lock‑out/tag‑out procedures. corrective actions included revised valve labeling, mandatory two‑person verification for isolation steps, and an update to the scada alarm response protocol.

on april 12, 2025, a crew from western energy services was conducting routine valve isolation on the 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the midland interchange station, operating at 720 psig. the line was temporarily taken out of service for a scheduled pigging operation, and the crew was instructed to close the upstream block valve (b‑v‑12) and open the downstream bypass valve (b‑v‑14) before depressurizing. due to a misinterpretation of the valve identification tags, the operator closed the downstream bypass valve instead of the upstream block valve, leaving the line still pressurized while the pigging crew proceeded with the purge. shortly after the pig was introduced, a sudden pressure surge of approximately 950 psig was recorded, and a loud pop was heard near the bypass valve assembly. a gash of about 4 inches was exposed on the valve body flange, releasing natural gas into the surrounding area. emergency shutdown was initiated at 1432 hrs, and the line was fully isolated by 1505 hrs. no injuries occurred, but the incident resulted in a loss of service to 2,300 residential customers for 4 hours and repair costs estimated at $78,000. an investigation determined the release was caused by the operator’s incorrect valve operation during the isolation procedure.

at 07:45 am on 3/22/2025, the crew at the oak ridge mainline performed a scheduled valve change on a 24‑inch, api 5l x70 steel pipe rated 1200 psi. the isolation valve on the east side of the tie‑in station was a 4‑inch ball valve that had been left in the open position after a prior test. the technician, believing the valve to be closed, proceeded to depressurize the line by opening the downstream vent without first confirming the valve position. the line remained pressurized at approximately 950 psi, causing a rapid pressure surge when the vent was opened. the surge forced the valve seat to lift, and the 4‑inch valve stem sheared off, allowing high‑pressure gas to escape. a bright orange jet was observed for about 45 seconds before the automatic shutdown system activated. the gas, primarily methane, escaped at an estimated rate of 650 mscfd, resulting in a total loss of roughly 12 mmscf before isolation. post‑incident investigation revealed the operator had not followed the lock‑out/tag‑out procedure and had misread the valve indicator. the valve was replaced, the lock‑out/tag‑out protocol reinforced, and additional training on valve position verification was scheduled for all field personnel.

on april 12, 2022 at 03:20 am the western interstate gas transmission company (wigtc) initiated a scheduled maintenance shutdown on line 44, a 30‑inch carbon steel pipeline with a maop of 800 psig, located near the oakridge compression station. the work plan required the mainline isolation valve (ml‑iv‑12) to be placed in the automatic position after the pressure test so the emergency shutdown (esd) system could operate normally. however, the field supervisor mistakenly left ml‑iv‑12 in the manual position and failed to reinstall the temporary weep‑hole plugs removed during the pressure test. at 04:05 am the esd system activated due to an upstream pressure surge; because the valve remained manual, it failed to close and gas continued to vent through the 36‑inch downstream relief valve (rv‑d‑7). the vent persisted for approximately 45 minutes, releasing an estimated 4,200 mcf of natural gas, exceeding the 3,000 mcf reporting threshold. after the incident, an investigation identified a breakdown in the pre‑job checklist verification and inadequate communication between the control center and field crew. corrective actions included revising the isolation valve reset procedure, adding a mandatory dual‑sign‑off on valve position, and installing a visual indicator to confirm automatic positioning of critical esd selectors.

on april 14, 2022 at 03:12 am, the atlanta‑memphis mainline, a 12‑inch api 5l steel pipe operated at a design pressure of 850 psi, experienced an unintended vent to the atmosphere. during a scheduled pigging operation, the field operator manually shifted the emergency shutdown valve (esd‑v‑12a) selector to the “manual” position to isolate the pig launcher, but failed to return it to “automatic” after the pig passed. five minutes later, a downstream pressure surge caused by a rapid compressor trip triggered the esd system. because the selector remained in manual, the esd‑v‑12a stayed open, allowing natural gas at 820 psi to escape through the relief valve. the relief valve opened as designed, but the continued flow resulted in an estimated release of 4,200 mcf, exceeding the 3,000 mcf reporting threshold. the incident was reported to the nrc within two hours. investigation revealed that the operator had not been reminded of the selector reset step in the post‑pigging checklist. corrective actions include revising the checklist to require a double‑sign‑off, retraining all station personnel on esd valve positioning, and installing a lock‑out device that automatically returns the selector to automatic after a pigging cycle.

on april 22, 2024, at approximately 06:45 local time, personnel at the midland mainline pump station began a routine restart of the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line after scheduled maintenance on the upstream metering skid. the station supervisor instructed the control room to close bypass valve b‑12 and bring the line up to operating pressure of 850 psi. however, the field crew mistakenly opened relief valve r‑3, which was intended only for emergency depressurization, and left the downstream isolation valve i‑7 partially open. the pump unit 4‑a was then started, rapidly increasing line pressure to 1,150 psi, exceeding the design limit of 1,000 psi for the 30‑inch pipe. the over‑pressure caused a longitudinal seam failure near milepost 42.7, releasing an estimated 4,200 bbl of crude oil and 650 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetland. the automatic shutdown system did not activate because the pressure transducer upstream of the failed section was disabled during the maintenance check. emergency response teams were dispatched within 12 minutes, and the leak was contained after 3.5 hours. investigation later determined that the incorrect valve configuration and failure to follow the standard operating procedure for valve sequencing were the primary contributors to the incident. corrective actions include revising the valve lockout‑tagout protocol and reinstalling the disabled pressure transducer before resuming normal operations.

on august 3, 2022, a routine pressure reduction was scheduled on the 24‑inch mainline transporting sweet natural gas from the north field to the processing plant. at 07:45 the operations crew initiated a manual override of the automatic pressure regulator on the b‑section to lower the setpoint from 850 psi to 600 psi in preparation for a downstream maintenance shutdown. the field supervisor instructed the on‑site technician to open valve‑12 (a 12‑inch gate valve) fully before adjusting the regulator, but the technician mistakenly opened valve‑14, a 6‑inch isolation valve that bypassed the regulator and fed directly into the downstream distribution line. within minutes the downstream line experienced an unexpected pressure surge; the high‑pressure alarm activated at 08:02, and the downstream relief valve lifted, releasing natural gas to the atmosphere at an estimated 350 scfh. the control system showed no change in flow on the primary scada screen because the bypass line was not instrumented. emergency shutdown was initiated at 08:07, isolating the mainline and depressurizing the segment. investigation revealed the valve mis‑identification and the lack of a lockout/tagout on the bypass isolation valve. corrective actions included updating the valve identification signage, revising the standard operating procedure for manual overrides, and retraining all personnel on bypass line isolation.

a maintenance crew was performing a valve replacement on a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the south field station. the line was rated for 850 psig but was being operated at 720 psig at the time of the work. the crew opened the downstream isolation valve without first verifying that the upstream valve was fully closed, assuming the line was depressurized after a recent pigging run. as the valve began to open, residual pressure surged forward, causing a sudden release of high‑velocity natural gas. the escaping gas struck the crew member who was positioned on the valve stem, resulting in a flash fire that ignited a nearby oil‑soaked rag. the employee suffered second‑degree burns to the forearm and was taken to the regional trauma center. the incident also caused a 3‑inch dent in the pipe wall and damaged the adjacent pressure regulator. the investigation found that the standard operating procedure for valve isolation was not followed, the pressure gauge was not cross‑checked with the control system, and the required lockout/tagout steps were omitted. corrective actions included retraining all field personnel on proper isolation verification, updating the lockout/tagout checklist, and installing a secondary pressure monitoring point upstream of critical valve locations.

on september 14, 2022 a maintenance crew at the north ridge compression station was performing a scheduled pigging operation on the 24‑inch, 1200‑psi carbon‑steel transmission line that serves the regional distribution grid. the work order called for the isolation of the line by closing the upstream manual isolation valve (miv‑12) and the downstream automatic shut‑off valve (asov‑7) before inserting the pig. the crew, under pressure to finish before a scheduled night‑time load increase, mistakenly closed the downstream asov‑7 but left the upstream miv‑12 partially open, assuming the valve had been locked out after a previous test. a supervisor, unaware of the incomplete lockout, gave the go‑ahead signal to pressurize the line to normal operating pressure. as the compressor ramped up to 1100 psi, gas began escaping through the partially seated miv‑12 stem, creating a vapor cloud that drifted toward a nearby highway. the leak was not detected by the station’s gas detection system because the sensor was calibrated for downstream locations. by the time the alarm was triggered, approximately 5.4 mmcf of natural gas had vented, prompting an emergency shut‑down and evacuation of the surrounding area. post‑incident review identified a breakdown in lockout/tagout compliance and a lack of verification of valve positions before restart.

on november 3, 2025, at approximately 0715 hours, a kansas gas transmission services crew began routine maintenance on a 12‑inch api 5l seamless steel main (schedule 40) located at the willow ridge pump station, segment b‑12. the task involved removing the hydraulic hand‑pump from the 500‑psi rated valve 27‑b, a 28‑inch dual‑acting gate valve that had been scheduled for replacement due to corrosion at the stem packing. after disconnecting the existing hand‑pump, the technician mistakenly attached a 750‑psi rated pneumatic actuator that had been left in the tool kit from a previous job. without verifying the actuator’s pressure rating or consulting the manufacturer’s operating procedure, the crew engaged the actuator to close the valve. the over‑pressurized actuation caused the valve seat to shear, allowing high‑pressure natural gas (approximately 820 psig) to surge into the downstream isolation line, which was still depressurized for the work. the sudden pressure spike ruptured a 6‑inch tie‑in fitting, resulting in an immediate release of gas and a flash fire that injured two crew members (second‑degree burns) and ignited nearby vegetation. emergency shutdown was initiated at 0723 hours, and the affected segment was isolated and later repaired. the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 1089321) and the cpuc within the required reporting window.

on 04/17/2022 at 14:22 cd t, the riverbend compression station observed an unexpected pressure rise in the 24‑inch mainline feeding the #2 gas turbine. the field operator, responding to a low‑flow alarm, manually opened the downstream isolation valve (isolation valve‑b) to increase flow, unaware that the upstream safety shutdown valve (ssv‑a) had already been tripped due to a high‑pressure condition at 1 250 psig (design limit 1 200 psig). the operator’s action caused the ssv‑a to remain closed while the isolation valve‑b stayed open, resulting in a rapid pressure buildup to 1 380 psig downstream of the turbine inlet. the turbine’s protective shutdown did not engage because the pressure sensor on the turbine inlet was reading the upstream pressure, which was still below its setpoint. after approximately 7 minutes, the over‑pressurization forced the turbine inlet safety valve to lift, venting natural gas to the atmosphere through the flare stack. the incident was reported to the nrc at 15:05 cd t (report no. 2479135). investigation revealed that the operator misinterpreted the low‑flow alarm and failed to verify the status of ssv‑a in the control room display, which incorrectly showed the valve as closed due to a stuck limit‑switch. corrective actions included installing a secondary visual indicator for ssv‑a position, revising the low‑flow alarm procedure to require verification of upstream valve status, and retraining all station personnel on valve interlocks. supplemental report filed 04/20/2022 updated the root cause to operator error during manual valve operation and corrected the initial nrc report date.

on april 12, 2024, a maintenance crew was performing a scheduled valve replacement on the western intertie 30‑inch carbon steel mainline (api 5l grade b) near the silver creek junction in montana. the line was operating at 850 psig, well below its 1200 psig maximum allowable operating pressure. technicians removed the existing block‑down valve and installed a new double‑seal butterfly valve. the installation procedure required the use of a calibrated torque wrench and the application of moly‑based lubricant to all bolt threads prior to final tightening, as specified in the company’s valve‑installation standard (procedure p‑v12). however, due to a rushed shift change, the crew relied on a handheld torque indicator that was not calibrated and omitted the lubricant step. after the valve was hand‑tightened, the line was repressurized to 850 psig without a leak check. within minutes, a low‑frequency vibration was heard, and a faint odor of natural gas was reported by a nearby landowner. the valve seat failed, allowing a release of approximately 2,200 mcf of gas before the automatic shutdown system isolated the segment at 9:18 am. emergency response teams erected a safety perimeter, evacuated two nearby farms, and initiated a controlled blow‑down to zero pressure. investigation later determined that the improper torque application and missing lubricant caused uneven bolt preload, leading to seat deformation and gasket failure. corrective actions included retraining on torque verification, mandatory calibration logs for torque tools, and revision of the valve‑installation procedure to require a documented torque‑recording step and verified lubrication before each installation.

04/15/24 07:12 am: during scheduled restart of the midstream gathering system, the operations crew initiated the mainline isolation valve (isolation valve‑b, 30‑in. carbon steel, rated 1200 psi) at 6:55 am, believing the downstream segment had been depressurized. pressure transducer p‑305 on the upstream side indicated 750 psi, well below the normal operating pressure of 950 psi. at 7:09 am the crew opened the starter pump discharge valve to begin flow. within seconds the downstream pressure rose to 1120 psi, exceeding the design limit of 1100 psi. the high‑pressure alarm triggered, and the automatic shut‑down (asd) system closed the emergency vent valve (ev‑12, 4‑in. steel, rated 1500 psi). however, because the vent line to the flare stack was blocked by a maintenance clamp that had not been removed, the excess gas accumulated in the low‑pressure separator, reaching 18 % le l and activating the secondary eod (eod‑2) at 7:13 am. the station was placed in a safe state, and the flare was manually ignited at 7:22 am. investigation revealed that the isolation valve had been incorrectly assumed to be closed; a lock‑out tag‑out (lot) was never applied after a previous line‑pull. the missing lot and the unremoved clamp caused the over‑pressurization and vent blockage. after corrective actions, the system returned to service at 18:30 hrs.

on 4/12/2026 at 02:17 am mst, the maintenance crew began a scheduled hot‑tap on the 24‑in. carbon steel transmission line (diameter 610 mm, rated 1500 psi, operating at 1120 psi) at the ridgecrest pump station. the tap‑off manifold was isolated using the mainline isolation valve (ilv‑07) and a temporary block valve (tbv‑03) installed upstream. the crew proceeded to open the hot‑tap valve (htv‑02) without first verifying that the tbv‑03 was fully closed and that pressure had been relieved from the tap section. as a result, pressurized gas at 1120 psi entered the tap manifold and forced the htv‑02 open abruptly. the sudden surge caused a 4‑in. vent line to rupture, releasing an estimated 18.4 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding area. the gas migrated down a low spot toward a nearby drainage ditch, where an ignition source from a nearby diesel generator ignited the cloud, producing a flash fire that burned two contractors. an immediate shutdown was initiated using the station’s emergency depressurization system, and the area was secured. post‑incident review identified that the operator had failed to follow the lock‑out/tag‑out procedure for tbv‑03 and had not confirmed zero pressure with the handheld pressure gauge before opening htv‑02. corrective actions now require a dual‑verification step for all hot‑tap operations and additional training on lock‑out/tag‑out compliance.

on 3 march 2025 at 22:17 utc the control room received an alarm indicating a loss of pressure in the mainline serving the northwest region. operators initiated an emergency shutdown and dispatched a crew to the 24‑inch api 5l x70 steel transmission line near ridgefield. arrival at the site occurred at 22:45, when field personnel discovered that the 12‑inch isolation valve at the ridgefield station had been left in the open position after completing a routine pigging operation earlier that day. the open valve allowed downstream pressure to drop from 950 psig to 210 psig, causing a downstream compressor to surge and automatically trigger its safety shutdown. subsequent inspection revealed that the valve handle was not returned to the locked “closed” position due to a miscommunication between the pigging crew and the valve maintenance team. the valve was finally closed at 23:12, restoring line pressure and allowing the compressor to restart after a 45‑minute cooldown. the incident resulted in an unplanned service interruption affecting approximately 3,200 customers for 2.5 hours and incurred a lost‑sale cost estimated at $75 000. an internal review cited incorrect procedural hand‑off and inadequate verification of valve position as the root causes.

on october 3, 2025 at 08:12 the field crew began a routine restart of compressor unit c-12 at the marshallville gathering station after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the unit was a 6000 hp centrifugal compressor feeding a 30‑inch carbon steel mainline operating at a design pressure of 950 psig. the operating procedure called for the high‑pressure control loop to be set to a set‑point of 720 psig before reopening the inlet isolation valve. the technician entered 620 psig – a set‑point intended for the downstream 18‑inch line – into the control system hmi. the inlet valve was opened at 08:18 and the compressor accelerated, but the high‑pressure transmitter reported only 560 psig, well below the actual line pressure. within five minutes the line pressure rose to 845 psig, exceeding the relief valve set‑point of 800 psig. the over‑pressure protection valve on the 30‑inch main opened, venting approximately 5.2 mmscfd of natural gas to the flare network for 12 minutes before the automated shutdown engaged. the flare system experienced a brief flameout, triggering an automatic fire‑department alarm. post‑incident review identified the incorrect set‑point entry as the root cause, and the operator’s qualification for high‑pressure control was placed on hold pending retraining.

on october 13, 2023 at approximately 06:14 am central texas gas transmission reported a sudden increase in line pressure on the 24‑inch carbon steel main feeding the san antonio compression hub. field crews arrived at the 12‑mile marker and observed that the 18‑inch upstream isolation valve, valve‑b‑12, had been left in the partially closed position after a routine maintenance shutdown the previous night. the valve was intended to be fully opened prior to restart, but the lock‑out tag was not removed. as a result, the upstream compressor unit 3‑4 accelerated to its set point of 1150 psig, while the restricted flow caused pressure to spike to 1380 psig downstream of the valve. the high pressure forced the downstream pressure‑relief valve, a 6‑inch spring‑loaded unit, to lift continuously for about 42 minutes, venting an estimated 4.2 mmcf of natural gas before the valve was manually closed. after the incident, the isolation valve was fully opened and the system pressure returned to normal at 1125 psig. a subsequent investigation identified a procedural lapse in the post‑maintenance checklist and recommended revised lock‑out/tag‑out verification steps to prevent premature valve closure.

on april 14, 2026, at approximately 03:47 a.m. central standard time (cst), a high‑pressure gas transmission line experienced an over‑pressure event while personnel were performing a scheduled restart of compressor unit c‑7 on the western interconnect. the line, a 30‑inch api 5l sch 40 carbon steel pipeline (dn 750) operated at a normal service pressure of 850 psig, had been isolated for maintenance using isolation valve iv‑12 and downstream valve dv‑04. after the maintenance crew completed valve replacements, the control system was set to return the line to service. however, the operators inadvertently opened isolation valve iv‑12 to 75 % instead of the required 100 % before initiating the compressor start‑up sequence. this partial opening caused a restriction that increased the upstream pressure to 1 040 psig within two minutes of compressor rotation, triggering the high‑high pressure alarm at 03:50. the automatic shut‑down system engaged, closing the mainline regulator r‑02 and initiating an emergency depressurization. inspection later revealed that the valve position indicator had been miscalibrated, leading to the incorrect opening percentage. the line remained out of service for 6 hours while the valve was fully opened, pressure normalized, and a full functional test of the valve position sensors was performed. corrective actions include recalibration of all valve position indicators on critical isolation valves and a revised start‑up checklist requiring dual‑operator verification of valve positions before compressor energization.

on september 14, 2023 at 03:27 cd t the north ridge compression station (cs 8421) was scheduled for a routine valve inspection. the 24‑inch carbon steel main (api 5l x70) downstream of the station was operating at a max allowable operating pressure (maop) of 720 psig. during the inspection the operator manually opened the upstream isolation valve (isv‑a) to bleed pressure from the line for gauge reading, but mistakenly left the downstream block valve (bv‑12) fully open instead of setting it to the required closed position indicated in the work procedure. as a result, when the compressor kicked back in at 04:02 cd, gas surged through the unisolated segment, causing the pressure in the downstream 30‑inch loop to rise to 845 psig, exceeding its maop of 800 psig by more than 5 %. automatic relief valves at the downstream junction opened, releasing approximately 3.2 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding area. the incident was reported to the operating authority at 04:15 cd. there were no injuries, but the release triggered a temporary shutdown of the affected loop and required a leak detection survey. the post‑incident review identified the operator’s failure to verify the block valve position as the primary cause and led to revised lock‑out/tag‑out procedures and additional training on valve sequence verification.
