on september 5, 2022 at 02:14 am the riverbend gas compression facility experienced an unscheduled shutdown after a field technician performed a routine pressure test on the 24‑inch carbon steel mainline feeding unit 4. during the test the technician mistakenly opened the high‑pressure isolation valve (rated 1500 psi) instead of the low‑pressure bleed valve, causing an abrupt pressure drop from 1150 psi to 300 psi. the rapid depressurization triggered the emergency shutdown (esd) sequence, and the downstream safety valve opened partially, venting approximately 420 msc​f of natural gas into the containment pit. site personnel arrived at 02:46 am, secured the area, and manually closed the isolation valve. a subsequent walk‑down revealed that the valve handle had been left in the “open” position after the test, and the lockout‑tagout tag was not applied. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission and the local emergency services. corrective actions included revising the pressure‑test procedure to require a dual‑verification step for valve selection, installing distinct color‑coded handles on isolation versus bleed valves, and conducting a refresher training on lockout‑tagout compliance for all field staff.

a western interstates gas transmission, l.p. crew was performing routine valve maintenance on the 24‑inch, api 5l carbon steel mainline (operating at 820 psi) near the houston, tx interchange. at 1430 hours the crew removed a 1‑inch pressure‑relief valve to replace a leaking seat. after completing the repair the technician re‑installed the valve but failed to reset the manual lockout‑tagout device and did not verify the valve was fully seated. the control system subsequently initiated an automatic pressure‑up sequence when a downstream compressor start‑up caused a surge. because the pressure‑relief valve remained partially open, the line pressure rose to 980 psi, exceeding the design limit of 900 psi. an alarm triggered an emergency shutdown at 1442 hours, but the upstream isolation valve failed to close due to a mis‑set actuator range. gas escaped through the partially open relief valve, venting an estimated 1,200 mcf to the atmosphere over a 15‑minute period before the line was manually isolated at 1450 hours. no injuries were reported, but the incident caused a temporary service interruption to three customers and required replacement of the damaged valve and recalibration of the actuator settings. corrective actions included revising lockout‑tagout procedures and retraining operators on post‑maintenance verification steps.

on july 14, 2022, a 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) operated by western midstream inc. experienced a sudden rupture near the milepost 112 valve station. the line was being taken off‑line for a scheduled pigging operation. after the pig launcher was activated, the operator manually closed the upstream isolation valve but failed to verify that the downstream block valve was fully seated. the control system indicated a closed status for the downstream valve, however a pressure transducer downstream showed a residual pressure of 1,200 psi, well above the 950‑psi design limit for the pipe segment. the operator proceeded to start the pig pump, increasing line pressure to 1,350 psi to overcome friction losses. the incomplete seal on the downstream valve allowed the pressurized gas to flow past the valve housing, creating a high‑velocity jet that impacted the pipe wall at a stress concentration near a girth weld. the pipe wall fractured in a circumferential mode, releasing approximately 8 mmcf of natural gas. nearby personnel heard a loud “pop” and reported a cloud of vapor. emergency shutdown was initiated after the pressure drop was detected, and the incident was later attributed to the operator’s failure to confirm valve position before pressurizing the line. a root‑cause review recommended additional interlocks and a double‑verification procedure for valve isolation during pigging.

on april 14, 2025, during routine maintenance of the south ridge gas compression station, a shift crew from the operations control center initiated a planned depressurization of the 30‑inch carbon steel mainline to allow valve 12‑b to be removed for gasket replacement. at 07:12 the crew verified that the line pressure was 720 psig and that the upstream 24‑inch interstage valve (isv‑04) was closed. a supervisor instructed the junior operator to open the downstream 30‑inch isolation valve (iv‑07) to bleed the line to atmospheric. the operator, following an outdated procedure sheet, opened iv‑07 to 30% instead of fully closing it, inadvertently creating a vent path while the interstage valve remained closed. at 07:18 the station’s automatic shut‑in system detected a rapid pressure drop and opened isv‑04 to protect the compressors, but the partially opened iv‑07 allowed high‑velocity gas to escape through a 4‑inch vent line that was not rated for the resulting flow. the vent line ruptured, releasing a jet of gas at approximately 650 psig. the incident triggered a high‑high alarm at 07:20, and the emergency shutdown sequence was initiated. after the event, investigations determined that the operator had misinterpreted the valve position indicator and that the procedure had not been updated to reflect the current valve configuration. corrective actions include retraining on valve identification, revising the depressurization work instruction, and installing a position‑feedback sensor on iv‑07.

on april 12, 2024 a subcontractor from an authorized maintenance firm was tasked with performing a pigging operation on the 24‑inch, 900‑psi carbon‑steel transmission line “t‑112” near the midsouth processing hub. the crew arrived at 06:15 and, after a brief safety briefing, began pressurizing the line to the pig launch pressure of 850 psi. at 06:42 the lead technician mistakenly opened the downstream isolation valve (valve‑b‑07) instead of the intended upstream valve (valve‑a‑07), causing a sudden pressure drop to 300 psi. the pig stalled in the 30‑foot straight segment and the line experienced a rapid depressurization event. a hissing sound was heard and a faint gas plume escaped from a joint at milepost 45.5. the crew shut down the pump at 06:45 and notified the pipeline operator’s control center at 06:48. emergency response was initiated, the leak was contained by closing a nearby emergency shut‑off valve, and the affected segment was depressurized to 0 psi by 07:30. repairs required cutting out a 6‑inch section of the pipe and installing a new welded splice, completed by 14:00. no injuries occurred, but service to three downstream customers was interrupted for 8 hours. the post‑incident investigation determined that the technician had not consulted the standard operating procedure for pig launch sequencing and was unfamiliar with the valve identification markings, leading to the incorrect valve operation.

on 04/12/2026 an operations technician in the central division was conducting a line pigging run on the south ridge transmission line, a 30‑inch, api 5l steel pipe rated for a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 1250 psig. the line runs from the oak ridge compression station to the valley terminal, crossing the foothills of the green ridge area. prior to pig insertion, the standard operating procedure required the downstream isolation valve (valve d‑12) to be closed and the upstream isolation valve (valve d‑5) to be opened to allow the pig to be propelled by the line pressure of approximately 1100 psig.

the technician mistakenly opened valve d‑12 while leaving valve d‑5 closed, believing the sequence to be reversed. as a result, the pig was trapped between the two closed valves. when the line was subsequently pressurized for the purge, pressure built up behind the pig and exceeded the pipe’s design limit, reaching an estimated 1350 psig. the excess pressure caused a rupture at a girth weld near milepost 42.7, releasing an estimated 0.9 mmcf of natural gas before the automatic shut‑off activated.

the incident was reported to the regional control center at 09:14, and emergency response was initiated. an investigation determined that the error stemmed from the technician’s failure to verify valve positions on the handheld display, an incorrect interpretation of the electronic lockout tagout status, and inadequate pre‑run verification. the company has since revised the pigging checklist, added a mandatory two‑person verification step for valve sequencing, and retrained all personnel on the updated lockout procedures. additionally, the affected girth weld has been replaced and a pressure test conducted to confirm integrity.

during a scheduled pigging run on the 24‑inch mainline between station delta and station echo, the field crew entered the control room at 06:40 am and initiated the pig launch sequence without verifying that the downstream isolation valves had been fully closed. the valve at point b‑12, a 30‑inch ball valve rated to 800 psig, was inadvertently left in a half‑open position due to a mis‑read of the digital position indicator. as the pig entered the line, a sudden pressure spike occurred, raising the line pressure from the normal operating pressure of 610 psig to 845 psig within seconds, exceeding the maop of 800 psig. the high‑pressure event triggered the upstream safety relief valve (set point 820 psig) on the 24‑inch line, which vented approximately 4,200 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere before reseating at 07:05 am. the downstream pressure relief valve (set point 785 psig) on the 30‑inch branch line also opened, releasing an additional 1,750 mcf. the crew shut the pig launcher at 07:10 am, isolated the line, and manually closed the ball valve, but the incident resulted in a reportable release and a temporary shutdown of service to the surrounding delivery points. an investigation identified the failure to follow the pre‑job checklist and confirm valve positions as the primary operational error.

on august 14, 2023 at approximately 03:27 a.m. cdt the midwest transmission system (mts) was conducting a routine restart of the 24‑inch mainline (segment id: mt-07) after scheduled maintenance at the hillcrest regulator station. the upstream pressure regulator was set to a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 720 psi, but the operator mistakenly entered 820 psi into the control interface while re‑pressurizing the line. the elevated pressure propagated downstream, causing the 18‑inch branch line serving the springfield industrial park (segment id: sp‑12) to exceed its maop of 650 psi, reaching 785 psi (121% of maop). at 04:02 a.m. cdt the automatic shut‑off valves at the springfield delivery point opened, releasing approximately 2.8 mmcf of natural gas into the atmosphere, surpassing the phmsa reporting threshold. the incident triggered an immediate evacuation of the nearby commercial complex, and service to 2,300 customers was interrupted for 6 hours. no fire or explosion occurred, and there were no injuries. post‑incident review determined the incorrect pressure entry was due to a misread of the digital readout and a lack of verification step in the restart procedure. corrective actions include updating the restart checklist, retraining operators on pressure set‑point entry, and installing a secondary confirmation alarm for pressure overrides.

on april 2, 2026, at 08:46 a.m., a maintenance crew from transenergy pipelines was performing routine pigging operations on the 30‑inch, api 5l grade b steel main that transports sweet natural gas at a design pressure of 1 200 psi through the hillcrest corridor. the crew was required to isolate a 6‑inch branch line serving a local distribution hub by closing the isolation valve and installing a temporary blind flange in accordance with the company’s s‑215 lockout/tagout procedure. however, the on‑site supervisor authorized the removal of the blind flange before the isolation valve was fully closed, citing schedule pressure. as a result, residual pressure in the branch line forced the valve seat open, causing a sudden release of approximately 4 000 scfd of gas at 850 psi into an open trench. the escaping gas found an ignition source from a nearby diesel generator, resulting in a flash fire that burned three crew members, two of whom sustained second‑degree burns. emergency services were notified at 08:52 a.m., the fire was extinguished by 09:07 a.m., and the area was evacuated. the internal investigation concluded that the crew failed to follow the lockout/tagout sequence and bypassed the required verification checklist, leading to an unsafe release. corrective actions include a mandatory safety stand‑down, retraining on s‑215 procedures, and implementation of a dual‑approval electronic lockout system for all isolation activities.

on august 14, 2025 at approximately 07:45 utc a natural gas leak was reported on the 30‑inch carbon steel transmission line (spec 5l) near the meadow ridge compression station in north dakota. the line was operating at 950 psi when maintenance personnel initiated a routine pigging operation to remove debris. the pigging crew opened valve v12 to allow the pig to enter the line but failed to verify that the downstream isolation valve v13 was fully closed. as a result the pig entered the high‑pressure segment and became lodged at a 24‑inch reducer, creating a blockage. pressure began to build upstream and exceeded the design limit, causing a rupture at a welded joint near milepost 112.5. a bright orange flame was observed and a 3500 cf/m3 natural gas release was measured before the emergency shutdown system activated. emergency response teams arrived within 12 minutes, evacuated the surrounding area, and extinguished the fire. subsequent investigation determined that the incorrect sequencing of valve operations and the lack of a lock‑out/tag‑out procedure during pigging were the primary factors. the operator implemented revised standard operating procedures, added interlock verification for critical valves, and retrained all field crews on pigging safety protocols.

on september 14, 2022 at approximately 07:42 a.m. the east ridge gathering station experienced a release of natural gas during a routine restart of the 20‑inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the downstream metering skid. the line had been isolated for maintenance and the isolation valves were manually closed with a lockout/tagout procedure. during the restart, the operator incorrectly selected the “manual open” position on the control panel for valve‑03 instead of valve‑02, causing valve‑03 to open while valve‑02 remained closed. this resulted in a sudden pressure differential of 750 psig upstream and 150 psig downstream, forcing gas through a partially removed gasket on a 6‑inch service connection that had not been reseated after previous work. a jet of gas escaped from the gasket, traveled along the low point of the pipe, and ignited when it encountered an open pilot light on the nearby heater bank. the flash burned two maintenance technicians, causing first‑degree burns, and triggered an automatic shutdown of the station. an internal investigation determined the root cause was failure to follow the standard operating procedure for valve sequencing and lockout verification. corrective actions included retraining all operators on valve interlock logic, revising the lockout/tagout checklist, and installing a software interlock that prevents manual opening of valve‑03 unless valve‑02 is confirmed open. the station returned to service on october 3, 2022 after the damaged gasket was replaced and the safety system validated.

on august 3, 2022 at 0845 hrs, a pacific gas and electric field operator was adjusting the high pressure regulator at station rp-12 on the mainline 24‑inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) feeding the desert region. the operator intended to raise the set point from 720 psig to 750 psig to accommodate increased demand, but mistakenly entered the new value into the downstream pressure reduction station (prs‑7) instead of the regulator. within seconds the downstream prs‑7 opened its pilot valve, causing a sudden pressure surge to 820 psig upstream of the 12‑inch distribution line. the surge exceeded the maop of 800 psig, forcing the emergency relief valve to lift at 815 psig. a release of natural gas was observed at the relief valve vent pipe, estimated at 18 mmcf over a 30‑minute period before the valve reseated. the operator immediately initiated the emergency shutdown, isolated the affected segment with remote shut‑off valves, and notified local fire‑rescue and the state pipeline safety office. evacuations were ordered for two residences within 200 ft of the vent. no injuries or ignition occurred. after the incident, the regulator was reset to its original set point, the relief valve was tested and cleared, and a review of the control system software was conducted to add a confirmation step for set‑point changes. the incident was reported to the dot (report # 2022‑08957) and the cpuc.

on 5/14/2025, a field operator at the riverbend gathering station initiated a startup of the 30‑in. x‑80 carbon steel main to increase throughput for a scheduled delivery. the operator entered the manual start sequence in the control system but failed to verify that isolation valve iv‑12, which isolates the downstream 24‑in. line to the south‑west loop, was fully closed. iv‑12 was left partially open, allowing high‑pressure gas at 1150 psig to flow into the 24‑in. line that was still depressurized to 350 psig for maintenance. within minutes, the pressure differential caused a rapid expansion at the junction, exceeding the design rating of the 24‑in. pipe and rupturing a weld at the tee. a pin‑hole fissure developed, releasing approximately 18.5 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding meadow before the emergency shutdown was engaged. emergency response teams were dispatched, the leak was contained, and the area was evacuated. investigation determined that the operator bypassed the required pre‑start checklist and did not confirm valve positions on the handheld verification tablet. corrective actions include mandatory electronic lockout of valve status before startup, retraining of all shift personnel on the revised checklist, and installation of an interlock that prevents pressurization of downstream lines when isolation valves are not fully closed.

on may 14, 2025, a south dakota transmission line operated by prairie sky pipelines experienced an unplanned release of natural gas at the river bend pump station. the incident occurred during a scheduled maintenance shutdown of the 30‑inch mainline that transports gas from the williston field to the minneapolis hub. an operator manually opened the isolation valve on the suction side of compressor unit 4 while the unit was still under load, believing the unit had been fully depressurized. the valve was a 4‑inch carbon steel ball valve rated for 850 psig; the line pressure at the time was approximately 720 psig. because the unit remained energized, gas surged through the valve and escaped through a downstream vent, releasing an estimated 3,200 msc​f of gas over a 12‑minute period before the emergency shutdown (esd) system was activated at 14:23. investigation revealed the operator had not followed the revised lockout‑tagout checklist that required verification of compressor shutdown and pressure isolation before valve actuation. the incident prompted prairie sky pipelines to revise its standard operating procedures, implement a dual‑confirmation electronic lockout system for all isolation valves, and conduct refresher training on lockout‑tagout compliance for field personnel.

on july 22, 2024, the midwest gas transmission company was conducting a routine restart of the 30‑inch, carbon‑steel mainline (api 5l x70) that runs from the duffield hub to the oakridge distribution complex. after a planned maintenance shutdown, the control room initiated the start‑up sequence at 09:15 am cdt. the field crew was instructed to close isolation valve iv‑12 and open the bypass valve bv‑5 to reroute flow during the turbine compressor start. due to a miscommunication, the crew closed iv‑12 but failed to open bv‑5. as the compressor accelerated, pressure built up behind the closed isolation valve, reaching approximately 1150 psig, well above the design limit of 1050 psig for that segment. the upstream pressure safety valve (psv‑3), set at 1100 psig, lifted and discharged an estimated 18.4 mmcf of natural gas into the vent stack before the automated shutdown engaged. the incident caused a brief service interruption and a minor release that was reported to the regulatory agency. an internal investigation identified the incorrect valve operation as the root cause, and the company has implemented a double‑check verification step for all valve configurations during future restart procedures.

on april 22, 2024 at 07:45 a.m. the ridgeview gas processing facility initiated a scheduled pigging run on the 24‑inch mainline that transports raw natural gas from the west field to the east processing unit. the operations crew opened the pig launcher valve and set the launch pressure to 350 psi, which was the standard for a 30‑inch pipe but exceeded the 24‑inch line’s maximum allowable launch pressure of 300 psi. the pig entered the line and began moving toward the downstream pig catcher. however, because the launch pressure was too high, the pig’s speed increased to approximately 12 ft/s, causing it to strike a recently installed 3‑inch bypass valve that was still partially open for maintenance. the impact forced the bypass valve to close abruptly, creating a pressure surge that traveled back toward the launch site. the surge caused the upstream isolation valve to fail to close, and the control system recorded a closed‑valve status even though the valve remained partially open. gas escaped through the isolation valve seat for about 45 minutes, resulting in an estimated loss of 6.2 mmcf. the incident was reported to the nrc at 13:20. investigation revealed that the operator had referenced the wrong line specifications in the pigging procedure checklist. corrective actions included revising the pig launch pressure limits for all pipe sizes, implementing a double‑check verification step in the electronic work order system, and retraining the crew on line‑size specific parameters. the bypass valve was inspected, repaired, and a pressure‑relief bypass was installed to prevent future surges.

on april 15, 2025, operations crew at the 12-mile south interconnect of the clyde transmission corridor performed a routine line pressure increase to validate the new 4kmmcf storage facility's integration. the 8‑inch schedule 80 carbon steel line, rated at 1200 psi maop and operating at a steady 650 psi, was scheduled to be raised to 950 psi for the test. the relief valve, installed at the 15th junction and set to 850 psi, had not been re‑programmed for the test because the shift supervisor assumed the valve was already in the correct position from the last maintenance cycle. the crew opened the high‑pressure test valve, brought the line pressure up to 950 psi over a span of fifteen minutes. within seconds, the relief valve opened and discharged approximately 6 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere. the release went unnoticed until a nearby field crew reported a faint odor at 13:12. because no pressure alarm was linked to the relief valve, the crew did not realize the valve had been activated. the incident was reported to phmsa within 24 hours. root‑cause analysis identified a failure to follow the pressure test procedure, specifically the omission of a relief valve re‑calibration step, and inadequate communication between shift supervisor and field crew. corrective actions included mandatory checklist updates and training on relief valve settings for pressure tests.

on march 12, 2025 at 08:45 (cst), the east coast regional office received a notification of an abnormal pressure spike on the 24‑inch, 560‑psi natural gas transmission line that feeds the metropolitan distribution hub. the line was under routine pressure control by the automated control system, but the alarm was triggered by a sudden drop in the upstream pressure transmitter reading, which indicated a possible valve malfunction. at 08:52 (cst), the shift supervisor dispatched the field crew to the 300‑meter access point to inspect the 2‑inch isolation valve that had been closed for a scheduled maintenance check last week. upon arrival, the crew found that the valve had not fully closed; the valve bonnet had been left partially open because the crew had used the hydraulic jack to maneuver the valve rather than the designated hand‑wheel. the crew attempted to close the valve with the hydraulic jack again, inadvertently opening the valve a few degrees more. this caused a rapid pressure surge that exceeded the pipe burst pressure of the 8‑in, 90‑percent carbon steel segment, leading to a burst at the weld between the 12‑in and 8‑in sections. the rupture released approximately 1.2 million cubic feet of gas over 18 seconds. no injuries were reported, but the burst caused a temporary shutdown of the downstream 16‑inch, 200‑psi service line. the incident was contained by the automatic shut‑off at the downstream compressor station. post‑incident, the field crew reviewed valve operation procedures and a new training session on hand‑wheel versus hydraulic jack use was scheduled.

on 3 april 2024 at 08:45 (est) a maintenance crew performed a routine pressure test on the 24‑inch seamless carbon steel section of the east‑bound crude line that runs from the mid‑stream terminal to the storage facility. the line is rated for 1,200 psi and was operating at 900 psi during normal flow. the crew was instructed to isolate the line by closing the isolation valve at the terminal and venting the test chamber. however, the field technician incorrectly opened the downstream isolation valve instead of the upstream one and opened the test chamber vent line. this mistake caused an uncontrolled pressure surge that pushed the 900‑psi fluid into the downstream section, creating a sudden 1,500‑psi spike. within seconds the weld joint at the 24‑inch flange failed, and the pipe ruptured, releasing approximately 2,300 barrels of crude into the surrounding gravel pit. the fire suppression system automatically activated, and a burst of vapor ignited, resulting in a flash fire that forced the crew to evacuate the area. two employees sustained second‑degree burns and were transported to the local emergency department, while one was taken for observation at the county hospital. the incident was reported to the regional safety office, and an internal investigation confirmed that the operator had misread the valve tag and performed the wrong isolation maneuver. corrective actions include revised valve training and a mandatory double‑check procedure for all pressure‑test operations.

on march 12, 2026 at approximately 1405 hours, a pipeline operations supervisor at the westbrook transmission line misidentified the pressure gauge reading on the 36‑inch diameter x70 steel main, believing the line was under 8,000 psi. the supervisor authorized the opening of the remote control valve 12‑3, which had been set to 0 psi for maintenance. as the valve opened, a sudden surge of natural gas at 8,200 psi flowed through the 36‑inch line and caused the downstream 20‑inch, 304 stainless steel isolation valve to fail. the failure produced a high‑pressure spike that blew the valve flange and released a 3,500‑liter volume of gas into the surrounding airspace. the gas ignited when the valve assembly was struck by a passing crane boom, creating a 12‑meter radius flame. crew members responded within 35 seconds, but the incident resulted in a minor burn injury to the crane operator. a post‑incident review determined that the supervisor had incorrectly interpreted the pressure readout due to a mis‑calibrated gauge and had not followed the standard operating procedure that requires a secondary verification by a senior engineer before valve operation. corrective actions include re‑training and installing a redundant pressure monitoring system.

on march 15, 2024, at 03:45am, the east coast natural gas pipeline company (ecng) received a pressure alarm at compressor station 12 in tennessee. gas control dispatched a technician. the technician inspected valve 12a-3, an emergency isolation valve that was inadvertently left in the manual position during a routine pressure test. the valve selector had been set to 'manual' to allow the valve to open for a scheduled flow test. when the pressure rose to 1,800 psi, the emergency valve failed to close because the selector was not in 'automatic'. this caused a prolonged gas release that continued until the technician manually moved the selector to 'automatic' at 04:30am. the released volume was estimated at 3.2 million scf, exceeding the 3,000 scf reporting threshold. subsequent investigation revealed that the technician had not followed the updated operating procedure that required the valve to be re‑engaged in the automatic position after every test. ecng suspended the technician's operator qualification, installed permanent signage at the valve station, and revised the test checklist to include a mandatory selector check. the incident resulted in a 0.2% reduction of line pressure and no personnel injuries.

on may 3, 2024, at approximately 07:30 a.m. est, the midwest natural gas pipeline system experienced a rapid pressure excursion on the 12‑inch lmr 452 branch at milepost 18.7. the branch was operating at an average pressure of 680 psi and had a wall thickness of 0.310 inches. the incident began when the shift supervisor, attempting to relieve pressure following a reported sensor anomaly, manually opened the pressure‑reducing valve (prv) 1.2 inches above the calibrated set point. the valve was designed to be operated in the closed‑to‑open direction with a 45‑degree torque specification. instead, the operator turned the valve clockwise beyond the limit screw, bypassing the lock‑out tag. the result was a sudden pressure rise to 950 psi within 12 seconds, exceeding the 100 % maximum allowable operating pressure (mao). the pressure surge caused a 0.020‑inch radial crack to propagate in the pipe wall, which grew to a 0.050‑inch breach over the next 15 seconds. gas escaped at a rate of 2,400 scf/min, totaling an estimated 1,200 mscf loss before the system shut off at 07:45 a.m. the root‑cause investigation concluded that the operator performed the valve adjustment incorrectly, violating the standard operating procedure for pressure relief.

on april 12, 2023 at approximately 03:47pm, the midwest natural gas transmission company, llc (mngc) received a pressure alarm at its compressor station 308 located in illinois. a technician assigned to perform a routine pressure relief test was instructed to open valve 308a‑r, a manual isolation valve, and install a pressure relief valve (prv) with a weep hole for the test. the technician, following a misinterpreted procedure manual, left the weep‑hole plug removed and set the valve selector to the manual position. during the test the line was pressurized to 150 psig, causing the prv to open, but because the isolation valve remained open the gas escaped uncontrolled through the main line. the loss was estimated at 2,500 mcf, exceeding the reporting threshold. the incident was discovered when the plant's automatic monitoring system detected a pressure drop and the operator was notified. mngc suspended the operator’s certification for esd testing and updated the test procedure to require reinstallation of the weep‑hole plug and confirmation that all isolation valves are in the automatic position before ending a test. signage was installed at all stations to remind employees of the proper sequence for pressure relief tests.

on 5/19/24 at 07:10 am, the east coast transmission line (line 42) experienced a sudden drop in pressure from 1.6 mpa to 0.4 mpa at the western terminal. the release was traced to a mis‑engaged 8‑inch flare valve at compressor station 18. the valve was manually set to “open” during a routine pressure test, but the operator mistakenly selected the “open” position on the control panel while the valve was physically in the “closed” position. the downstream pressure transducer recorded the anomaly, and the automated safety relief system did not trip because the set point was 1.2 mpa. as a result, approximately 2,200 mscf of natural gas escaped through the flare line into the atmosphere over a 30‑minute period before the field crew shut the station down at 07:45. operations confirmed that the flare line had a 5‑inch stainless steel section rated for 1.8 mpa, and the gas loss was calculated by comparing the pre‑incident and post‑incident meter readings. the incident was reported to the tceq and rrc within 1 hour, and corrective measures included installing a lock‑out tag on the flare valve and updating the operating procedure to require a second operator verification for all manual valve changes.

on april 12, 2025, a crew at the southern terminal performed a routine pigging of the 48‑inch natural gas line. during the operation, the operator mistakenly believed the 20‑inch isolation valve on the main line had been closed and proceeded to open the 30‑inch discharge valve (30‑48) to relieve pressure. the isolation valve had actually remained open because the crew had forgotten to lock it after a prior maintenance task. when the 30‑inch valve opened while the line was still at 3,500 psig, a sudden pressure drop caused a water‑hammer surge that fractured the stainless steel section at flange 12‑b. the fracture released approximately 45 mcf of natural gas, which ignited when it contacted the hot valve seat. the event triggered an automatic station esd and activated the fire suppression system. the operator initially tried to close the valve with a hand‑power tool, which was not authorized for use on a 30‑inch line and caused further damage to the valve seat. after the incident, a root‑cause investigation revealed that the lock‑out tag had been removed during the pigging prep and the operator had not performed a valve‑position verification. all valves were re‑tagged and the crew received additional training on proper valve‑position checks and the use of authorized tools.

on october 12, 2023, a 6-inch x 24-inch pig launcher at the midstream compressor station experienced an unintended release of natural gas during routine maintenance. the vessel was connected to an 8-inch x 26-inch transmission line segment with a max allowable operating pressure (maop) of 1,000 psig, but the line was currently operating at approximately 650 psig. the relief valve on the pig launcher was set at 700 psig to protect the gauge and skid equipment. during the changeout of a faulty pressure transducer, field technicians failed to isolate the vessel from the main supply header via the existing 2-inch shutoff valve. instead, they assumed the valve was blocked in due to a tag on the handle from a previous unrelated ticket. when the gas control room received a request to boost pressure for downstream demand, they increased the line pressure to 850 psig without verifying the isolation status of the maintenance branch. this sudden pressure surge exceeded the 700 psig set point of the relief valve, causing it to lift and vent approximately 2.5 mmcf of gas to the atmosphere over a 45-minute period until the field crew isolated the valve and notified control. no injuries occurred, and the area was deemed safe after toxicity testing. the investigation determined that the root cause was a failure to verify the actual isolation status of equipment prior to energizing the pipeline, compounded by a lack of real-time communication between field operations and the control room regarding the specific maintenance activity and the conservative pressure settings established for the work scope.

on august 14, 2024, a maintenance crew was tasked with removing the existing gate valve on the 24-inch natural gas line at compressor station 402 for replacement. per the job plan, the line was to be isolated by closing the manual block valves on both ends and subsequently blowing down the section to atmospheric pressure. despite radio confirmation that the upstream valve was closed, the downstream valve operator remained partially engaged due to a previous mechanical snag that had not been cleared. when the crew initiated the pig trap vent to depressurize the segment, the pressure gauge dropped to 15 psig but did not reach zero. believing the residual pressure was within safe limits, a technician manually cranked the downstream valve to "check" its seating integrity. the valve, which was designed for automated pneumatic actuation, was not rated for manual override under differential pressure. upon cranking, the stem housing fractured, allowing high-pressure gas from the upstream feed to flash rapidly into the low-pressure segment. the sudden overpressure caused the pig trap bladder to rupture, resulting in an uncontrolled release of natural gas into the enclosure. the alarm system detected the leak, but the e-stop was not tripped automatically because the detection loop was bypassed for calibration work. crew members immediately activated the esd button, fully closing the main line valves. the isolated section was subsequently purged with nitrogen and re-pressurized. no injuries occurred, but approximately 12,000 mcf of gas was vented. an investigation revealed that the manual cranking procedure violated standard operating protocols for non-rated manual operations on active lines.

during routine maintenance on the 12-inch natural gas line at junction j-402, the maintenance crew attempted to isolate the downstream segment for valve packing. the operator engaged the manual override on the 14-inch block valve, but the limit switch calibration was outdated, causing the dcs to display a closed status while the valve was physically only 15% open. the control room confirmed isolation via the hmi and authorized the start of the work. within minutes, a hissing noise was detected near the flange, indicating significant pressure leakage. monitoring showed a rapid drop in upstream pressure from 750 psig to 620 psig. emergency shutdown procedure esd-04 was initiated, tripping the station. upon securing the line, field personnel discovered the block valve seat was not seated due to a debris accumulation on the actuator stem, which the manual force was insufficient to overcome. the limit switch mechanism had also fouled, preventing accurate position feedback. the valve was replaced, and the limit switch was recalibrated to align with the physical mechanical stops. a review of the operating log revealed that the valved was last calibrated two years prior, exceeding the recommended 18-month inspection interval. additionally, the manual override procedure did not require a direct visual confirmation from field personnel before the control room acknowledged isolation. revised procedures now mandate a two-person verification rule for manual overrides, requiring both a local physical check and a pressure decay test of 30 minutes before work authorization is granted. hardware upgrades include installing non-fouling guides on the valve stem and automated limit switch diagnostics to alert operators of divergence between feedback signals and actual valve travel.

during routine maintenance on the 18-inch high-pressure natural gas transmission line, field technicians were tasked with isolating a section for leak detection verification. the operating protocol required closing the respective isolation valves and verifying zero return pressure before opening the downstream block valve for venting. however, the lead technician mistakenly operated the upstream remote operated valve (rov) instead of the local gate valve due to a labeling error on the control panel. this incorrect actuation resulted in a rapid pressure drop across the 24-inch pipe segment, causing a violent cavitation event that damaged the internal packing of the adjacent check valve. the compromised check valve failed to seal, allowing approximately 4,500 mcf of natural gas to escape through the damaged flange gasket into the trench. the gas release was detected by the local area gas monitor, triggering an automatic alarm. personnel immediately evacuated the immediate work area and established a 200-foot perimeter. emergency response teams were dispatched, and the gas flow was halted by remotely closing the next available upstream isolation point. no injuries were reported, but the station was idled for 72 hours to replace the damaged check valve assembly and reseal the flanges. an internal review concluded that the incident stemmed from a failure to independently verify valve identification prior to operation and inadequate visual differentiation between remote and local control mechanisms in the control cabin layout.

on october 14, 2023, at approximately 1430 hours, a field technician was performing routine maintenance on the 48-inch diameter transmission line near mile marker 112 in harrison county, texas. the line, constructed of grade b x52 steel, was operating at 840 psig. the technician was tasked with replacing a failed pig bumper assembly at an existing valve station. according to the work order, the 12-inch inlet valve was to be closed and locked out prior to entering the casing. however, the technician failed to verify the valve position gauge or apply a lockout tag before opening the casing access panel. prematurely, the technician initiated the removal of the retaining bolts while the downstream pressure remained high. as the last bolt was loosened, pressurized natural gas escaped rapidly, causing the internal pig bumper assembly to eject from the casing with significant force. the displaced debris struck the technician in the chest, resulting in a cardiac arrest. emergency services were dispatched immediately, and the technician was transported to the local trauma center. the line was isolated remotely via the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system two minutes after the initial alarm. an internal investigation reviewed the sequence of events via site cameras and found that the technician had skipped the mandatory mechanical verification step in the standard operating procedure. the procedure explicitly required a physical wheel count and pressure decay check before any dismantling. furthermore, the technician was not wearing the required personal protective equipment for high-pressure isolation areas. corrective actions included immediate retraining of all field crews, implementation of dual-person verification for all isolation lockouts, and updated procedural steps to mandate electronic pressure confirmation before casing access.

on november 14, 2022, a field technician at the jasper county station in texas was performing routine maintenance on the 24-inch gas receiving line. during the task, he was instructed to isolate the line by closing the remote operated ball valve, designator rv-204. however, due to a miscommunication in the work permit, the technician failed to verify the position indicator on the actuator before energizing the close sequence. the valve stem, which was in a partially open position due to a previous manual override, jammed during the automated closure attempt. this prevented the internal ball from fully seating against the seat ring. as a result, a high-pressure leak of approximately 900 psig natural gas escaped from the valve body packing area. the release was detected by the local siren within three minutes. emergency response procedures were initiated, and the station was depressurized to safe levels by manually operating the bleed-down valve. no ignition occurred, and there were no personnel injuries. a subsequent investigation revealed that the operator qualification training regarding remote valve verification had been overlooked in the recent revision of the operating manual. the company has since implemented a mandatory double-verification step before actuating any remote isolation valves and updated the post-incident review process to include a specific check for valve position confirmation. the damaged valve was replaced, and new actuators with position feedback sensors were installed to prevent similar occurrences in the future.

during the routine maintenance of the 24-inch transmission line, field technicians were tasked with isolating a section for valve replacement. the procedure required closing the upstream and downstream block valves before bleeding off the residual pressure. however, a new technician misidentified the valve layout schematic and operated the wrong actuator, believing it was the downstream isolation. this error left the upstream 1500 psi supply line open and connected directly to the work area. when the crew attempted to open the section for inspection, the high-pressure gas surged through the partially open bypass, causing significant vibration and noise that masked the initial leak. the ambient temperature sensors eventually triggered a high-pressure alarm, but by then, approximately 5000 scf of natural gas had been released into the confined space. the emergency shutdown system activated, but the delayed isolation resulted in a site evacuation and a minor deflagration hazard assessment. review of the control room logs confirmed that the valves were operated out of sequence due to a lack of verification steps and inadequate supervision during the transition process. subsequent audits revealed that the valve tags were faded and difficult to read, contributing to the human error. corrective actions included a full re-tagging of the manifold and mandatory retraining for all field staff on proper lockout/tagout procedures and valve identification standards.

during routine pigging operations on the 24-inch carbon steel transmission line, the launch station operator failed to verify the isolation status of the downstream check valve before initiating the launch sequence. the pig was propelled through the line at a velocity exceeding the recommended limit, causing excessive pressure fluctuations that triggered the high-pressure alarm on the remote terminal unit. the automated safety system did not engage because the controller logic had been bypassed for maintenance purposes without proper restoration. the resulting overpressure condition caused a gasket failure at the 12-inch connection flange, leading to a visible gas release. field personnel immediately isolated the affected segment using the emergency shutdown valves and confirmed the leak was contained within the right-of-way. no injuries were reported, and the area was secured by local fire authorities. subsequent investigation revealed that the operator had not completed the mandatory pre-launch checklist, specifically the verification of valve positions and controller status. the bypassed controller logic was restored, and the operator was retrained on standard operating procedures for pigging activities. the damaged gasket was replaced, and the line was returned to service after passing a pressure test. the incident was reported due to the potential for a larger release had the isolation failed.

operators at the blue ridge compressor station initiated a routine startup sequence on unit 3 at 14:15 local time. the unit successfully spooled but failed to reach holding speed, prompting the control room to execute a manual reset. during the subsequent troubleshooting process, the field crew mistakenly opened the manual recycle valve while the electronic speed controller was still in automatic mode. this incorrect sequencing bypassed the low flow protection interlocks that were designed to prevent recirculation damage. as a result, the compressor entered a surge condition, causing a rapid pressure spike in the 30-inch x 0.500 inch carbon steel suction header. the pressure exceeded the design limit of 1250 psig, triggering the activation of the central relief valve assembly. approximately 5,000 mcf of natural gas was released to the atmosphere before the emergency shutdown (esd) system fully isolated the unit. initial investigation revealed that the operator relied on outdated pre-startup checklists that did not reflect the recent modification to the control logic. the facility has since updated all operating procedures to mandate a lockout tagout verification for the recycle system and conducted refresher training on proper startup protocols to prevent recurrence of such operational errors.

on march 12, 2022, a contractor crew performing hot-tap operations on a 24-inch, 60-pound x65 pipe segment at milepost 42.5 experienced an uncontrolled gas release. at 14:00 hrs, the crew initiated the cutting process using an electric boom saw. during the procedure, the operator adjusted the feed rate controller incorrectly, causing the saw to apply excessive downward pressure on the pipe wall rather than allowing the rotation to perform the cut. this misoperation resulted in the cut depth exceeding the allowable limit for hot-tapping, penetrating the entire pipe wall and creating a full-bore release. the resulting hole measured approximately 0.5 inches in diameter, and an estimated 850 mcf of natural gas was vented to the atmosphere before the emergency shutdown device (esd) actuated at 14:04 hrs. the crew immediately evacuated the immediate work area to a safe distance and monitored the surrounding area for potential ignition sources. following the event, an internal review determined that the cause was the operator's failure to calibrate the feed rate mechanism prior to commencing the cut, a specific requirement detailed in the in-service repair procedure manual. the operator had not completed the advanced in-service repair training required for diameters exceeding 20 inches. subsequent root cause analysis identified that the work permit was issued without verifying the specific competency of the individual operating the equipment. corrective actions included mandatory retraining for all hot-tap operators and the implementation of a dual-verification step for feed rate settings before tool engagement. the pipeline segment was repair patched and returned to service on march 15, 2022, after passing all required in-line inspection and pressure testing requirements.

on october 14, 2021, at approximately 0930 hours, an incident occurred at the pines cross-country compressor facility during planned maintenance on the discharge station piping. personnel were executing the replacement of a failed 24-inch full-bore ball valve on the main suction line, operating under a type a hot work permit. the line was isolated using remote-operated gate valves and depressurized to atmospheric levels. during the initial break-bolt process, a residual pressure spike was observed on the local gauge, indicating that a downstream check valve had failed to seat properly against the isolation boundary. before the field team could fully locate the true source of the residual flow, a manual bleed valve was opened to equalize pressure, resulting in a rapid release of unaccounted-for natural gas. the sudden release created a sonic jet that struck a maintenance technician standing within the defined exclusion zone. the individual suffered minor thermal burns to the forearms due to the rapid expansion of the gas. emergency services were dispatched immediately, and the employee was transported to the regional medical center for monitoring and treatment. subsequent investigation revealed that the blowdown procedure did not adequately account for the failure mode of the inline check valve, and the operational team proceeded with the line cut without verifying zero energy state via multiple independent indicators. phmsa was notified of the incident per regulatory requirements. corrective actions included mandatory retraining on isolation verification procedures and the implementation of additional mechanical locking devices on critical isolation points.

on february 14, 2022, a 12-inch transmission line operated by gaspy-49 pipeline corporation, llc (company) experienced a partial release at a valve operating station in trinity county, east texas. the incident occurred during the reconfiguration of the segment feedercamp loop to transfer right of way assets from the company to a third-party operator. maintenance crew members were tasked with closing the mainline valve and opening a previously isolated tie-in valve to bypass the section. according to the task order, the tie-in valve was to remain in the manual position during the pressure test phase. however, field personnel mistakenly engaged the pneumatic actuator of the tie-in valve before the mainline pressure had been sufficiently reduced. this action caused the valve to travel rapidly against a significant backpressure differential, approximately 450 psig, resulting in a sudden surge of force transmitted through the 20-inch api 5l x65 pipe welds. the hydraulic shock overwhelmed the gasket seal on an adjacent branch connection, leading to a high-velocity gas release. the event triggered the station's automatic emergency shutdown (esd) system, which isolated the affected segment within 30 seconds. no injuries were reported. post-incident review revealed that the crew had deviated from the standard operating procedure by releasing the pneumatic air supply lockout tag before verifying zero line pressure. the company has since implemented a mandatory two-person verification protocol for actuator engagements and updated their control room software to interlock pneumatic operations with upstream pressure transmitters to prevent similar misoperations.

on july 14, 2024, a maintenance crew was performing routine inspection on a 24-inch nominal diameter type i steel pipeline operating at 625 psig. the workflow involved the hydrostatic testing of a newly installed pig launcher located at mile marker 42. the site supervisor authorized the operation after confirming that the upstream isolation valves were in the closed position and locked out. however, during the filling phase, a shift change occurred, and the incoming technician mistakenly believed the manual gate valve at the bottom of the launcher was fully open when it was actually in a half-open position. the technicians commenced high-pressure water injection using a portable pump rated for 1,500 psig. because the drain line was not properly purged, the restricted flow caused a rapid pressure spike within the confined space of the launcher hull. at approximately 10:45 am, the internal gauge registered a dangerous exceedance of 950 psig. the crew member manning the pump failed to monitor the secondary pressure indicator mounted on the remote manifold, relying solely on the primary gauge which had a broken needle. within two minutes, the 6061-t aluminum flange on the launcher failed, causing a catastrophic rupture. high-velocity water and debris escaped, damaging adjacent low-carbon steel piping and deploying safety netting. no personnel were injured as the crew was positioned outside the designated exclusion zone. the investigation determined that the root cause was the incorrect execution of the pre-operation checklist, specifically the failure to verify valve position and the inadequacy of pressure monitoring procedures during the hydrotest. corrective actions included implementing a dual-verification protocol for valve positions and installing automatic pressure relief alarms on all portable testing units.

on 11/12/2023 at 14:45, operators at the ridgeline station reported a sudden drop in suction pressure on the 24-inch gas line. the primary compressor train was operating at 62% load with a discharge pressure of 980 psig. in an effort to balance the system load following a downstream reduction at the northfield junction, the shift supervisor instructed the operator to open the bypass manual gate valve around the automatic control valve. the operator misidentified the valve configuration due to poor lighting in the battery room and fully opened the maintenance isolation valve instead of the slow-opening bypass. this action created a short circuit, causing approximately 4,500 mcf/hr of gas to bypass the metering skid and flow directly into the storage field. the system pressure rapidly declined to 30 psig below the minimum operating limit, triggering a low-pressure alarm on the central control system. simultaneously, the unregulated flow caused vibration in the downstream 10-inch lateral line, leading to minor seal leakage at the flanged connection near the pigging launcher. field personnel were dispatched to the site at 15:20, where the abnormal flow sound confirmed the bypass had been opened. they immediately closed the offending valve and restored normal operations by 15:45. investigation revealed that the valve tags were faded and the specific bypass procedure required the use of a torque wrench to prevent over-tightening or misalignment. the incident was attributed to the operator selecting the wrong valve assembly during a high-stress manual intervention. corrective actions include replacing all valve tags with high-visibility color coding, installing mechanical locking devices to prevent accidental full-open positions, and implementing mandatory spot-check protocols before executing bypass maneuvers on critical flow control lines.

on 03/14/2022, a natural gas release occurred at the red rock compressor station during routine maintenance activities. at approximately 10:15 am, a maintenance technician was tasked with isolating the 12-inch inlet piping for compressor unit 3 to replace a flange gasket. the technician manually operated the quarter-turn ball valve shut-off, believing the handwheel was tight against the stop due to corrosion buildup on the stem. verification via the local local supervisory control and data acquisition panel showed the valve status indicator reporting "closed," but this signal was delayed due to a known limiter fault that had not been cleared. when the isolation flange was broken, pressurized gas at approximately 850 psig was immediately released from the downstream segment, creating a significant jet of gas that ignited upon contact with a hot surface from a nearby exhaust manifold. operations were notified at 10:17 am and performed an emergency shutdown of the station at 10:19 am, limiting the total release to an estimated 4,200 mscf. post-incident inspection revealed the ball valve seat was only partially seated, allowing flow through the centerline. the facility subsequently updated its operating procedures to require physical position verification via gauging rods for all critical isolation valves before breaking flanges, and installed mechanical limiters on all existing ball valves to prevent over-torquing.

during a scheduled maintenance window on the north field gathering line, field technicians were tasked with isolating a 12-inch carbon steel segment for hydrostatic testing. standard procedure required closing two 6-inch gate valves at the segment ends and verifying low pressure via the local gauges. however, the lead technician observed a slight pressure reading on the downstream gauge and, without consulting the revised piping and instrumentation layout, assumed the downstream valve had failed to seat properly. lacking a direct bleed line access at that location, the technician decided to manually purge the line through a nearby 2-inch sample point to force the downstream gauge to zero. this action was not authorized by the shift supervisor and bypassed the required secondary isolation check. as the sample valve was opened, unknown high-pressure fluid, later identified as 14-inch diesel fuel from an adjacent parallel header, surged into the isolated low-pressure natural gas section. the sudden pressure differential exceeded the design rating of the sample tubing, causing the flexible pipe to rupture. the resulting spray of fuel created an ignitable cloud near an active electrical enclosure on the skid. although the station eir quickly tripped due to gas detection, the initial mechanical failure and safety violation constituted an operational error. the incident resulted in minor scarring to the skid frame and a 45-minute shutdown while the misrouted sample line was replaced and hydrotested.

on 03/14/2023 at 14:45, a technician at the harper field compressor station was performing routine maintenance on the unit lube oil filtration system. while replacing the upstream 2-inch strainer, the technician failed to prioritize the lockout tagout procedure for the 8-inch polyethylene suction line connected to the skid. the line was currently delivering 14.5 mmcf at 600 psig. upon removing the last retaining bolt, the valve handle on the adjacent 6-inch stainless steel isolation valve was inadvertently bumped, rotating it 90 degrees from the open position to closed. this action isolated the lube oil pump and caused a rapid pressure drop in the hydraulic accumulator bank. the resulting loss of hydraulic pressure triggered an unplanned trip of the compressor unit. simultaneously, the sudden closure of the isolation valve created a transient pressure surge in the downstream 4-inch carbon steel discharge header, reaching 650 psig, which activated the high-pressure interlock. the emergency shutdown sequence automatically opened the automatic vent valve, releasing approximately 12,000 scf of hydrocarbon vapor into the flare system. field operations responded to secure the area and verify line integrity. after inspection, no mechanical damage to the piping was observed. the isolated valve was manually reopened to restore normal flow. the incident was attributed to the technician incorrectly positioning the valve stem access panel, which obstructed the operating handle, leading to accidental actuation during the strainer removal process. corrective actions included installing a protective guard over the valve handle and revising the maintenance procedure to mandate visual confirmation of valve position before and after all upstream line operations.

on october 14, 2019, a maintenance crew was performing routine inspection and lubrication of the pneumatic actuator on a 24-inch diameter 600 psi transmission line gate valve at kilometre 45. the operator, following a standard work permit, intended to manually override the actuator to cycle the valve stem for maintenance verification. however, the operator failed to properly secure the manual override loop and engaged the hydraulic power unit while the main supply line remained fully pressurized at 580 psi. upon engagement, the unsecured linkage snapped and the valve stem rotated fully closed in less than two seconds without the required gradual sequencing. this sudden closure caused a severe pressure surge in the upstream section of the pipeline, triggering the high-pressure alarm and automatic shutdown sequence in control room. the abrupt shut-in resulted in a temporary loss of transmission service for approximately 45 minutes, disrupting flow to a major compressor station downstream. no personal injuries or gas releases were reported. the investigation revealed that the operator had not completed the mandatory pre-operation checklist verifying the isolation of the hydraulic power source. additionally, the physical guard designed to prevent manual override engagement while under load was found to be damaged and non-functional. the operator’s qualification for operating critical safety protection systems was suspended pending retraining. the valve and hydraulic system were repaired, tested, and returned to service on october 16, 2019. corrective actions included replacing the damaged guard, revising the procedural lockout/tagout requirements, and implementing a new digital verification step in the work management system to ensure power sources are confirmed de-energized before manual interventions.

at 06:45 hours on november 12, 2023, a line isolation valve (liv) failed to close during a planned maintenance window at the red haw consolidation point. two operators were performing a routine blowdown of pipeline segment 45-78, a 36-inch diameter x 0.375-inch wall, api 5l x65 pipe. the objective was to reduce the line pressure from 850 psig to less than 50 psig to allow safe removal of a leaking gate valve. according to the work order, the upiside liv was to be closed first, followed by the downiside liv, before opening the manual blowdown valve. the field crew initially closed the downiside liv but accidentally left the upiside liv in the open position due to a visual confirmation error caused by heavy fog accumulation on the control valve position indicator. subsequently, the manual blowdown valve was opened, causing uncontrolled depressurization from the upstream segment connected to the main transmission line. this action released approximately 1,200 mmcf of natural gas into the atmosphere through the vent stack at a rate of 4.5 dscfh for nearly three hours before the pressure drop in the upstream segment was detected by the scada system. the upstream liv was manually closed via the remote panel, halting the release. an internal review determined that the confusion between lever positions on the actuator head, combined with the lack of a witness check by the lead operator, resulted in the sequence error. no injuries were reported, but the incident triggered a station-wide alarm. corrective actions included the installation of distinct color-coding on valve handles and mandatory two-person verification steps for all isolation operations during low-visibility conditions.
